The image boots with just PIPELEX_GATEWAY_API_KEY; the secret is only required when you actually use POST /api/v1/pipeline/start with a callback_url. See docs/pipe-run.md → "Async Completion Callbacks".

docs.title: Added
docs.text: • docs/configuration.md — explains the env vars this Docker image accepts, the Pipelex config layering inside the container, and how to mount your own .pipelex/ overrides. The actual Pipelex configuration syntax (storage, tracing, inference, Temporal, …) lives at https://docs.pipelex.com.

docs.title: Fixed
docs.text:
• Move Pipelex.make() from module top-level into a FastAPI lifespan handler in api/main.py. Importing api.main no longer mutates the global Pipelex singleton, which was causing make t to fail under pytest-xdist once enough unit tests existed for workers to share processes with the e2e import-smoke test.
  • Set a placeholder COMPLETION_CALLBACK_SECRET in tests/conftest.py so test collection succeeds in CI environments where .env isn't present. api/routes/pipelex/pipeline.py reads this var at import time, which was breaking make gha-tests collection as soon as any test transitively imported api.routes.

docs.title: Security
docs.text: • /upload now rejects unauthenticated and anonymous callers with 401 Unauthenticated, mirroring /resolve-storage-url. Previously, anonymous uploads were silently accepted and stored under an anonymous/assets/… prefix.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• /upload returns 400 InvalidBase64 (instead of 500) when the request body's data field isn't valid base64. Genuine storage failures still surface as 500.
  • UploadRequest now uses ConfigDict(extra="forbid"), so unknown fields produce 422 instead of being silently ignored.
  • mthds_content → mthds_contents — Updated ApiRunner.start_pipeline, pipeline routes, and build routes to use mthds_contents: list[str] | None instead of singular mthds_content. Aligns with the updated RunnerProtocol in mthds>=0.2.0.
  • bundle_uri → bundle_uris — Renamed to bundle_uris: list[str] | None in ApiRunner to match the updated PipelexRunner interface.

docs.title: Changed

docs.title: Resolve & Codegen
docs.text:
Resolve a library closure into its normalized library crate, and project that crate into typed artifacts (zod schemas, pydantic models, runtime structures) — over HTTP, with the same engine and the same trust chain as the local pipelex resolve / pipelex codegen commands.

Both are Pipelex API extensions, not MTHDS Protocol routes: they are not tagged x-mthds-protocol in the OpenAPI artifact, and an MTHDS runner is not required to serve them. The crate is a different matter — its shape is the standard's Library Crate Format, so the wire fields are brand-neutral and any MTHDS tool can read one. What is ours is the HTTP surface that produces it, and the type projection on top (the standard specifies none).

Both endpoints speak the POST /v1/validate verdict discipline: a produced verdict is always a 200 discriminated on is_valid; the invalid arm carries the structured errors[], one problem item per finding from pipelex's one shared builder — each item optionally carrying a suggested_fix. Non-2xx is reserved for no verdict could be produced: request-shape errors (an unknown projection kind/target, a malformed method selector) are 422 request.invalid RFC 9457 application/problem+json, a method tree that cannot be read is a 422 naming its refusal, custom Python on a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted is a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox (the refusal of Python structure classes a 422), a registry-form method_ref is a 422 request.unsupported whose reason is registry_form_method_ref, an address-form method_ref that fails to resolve maps per the method_ref error table, auth is 401/403, server faults are 5xx.

docs.title: Selecting the method
docs.text:
Both endpoints take the method the way POST /v1/validate and the run routes take it, as a method tree, read by the same machinery, so a tree one route accepts, refuses or resolves, the others accept, refuse or resolve the same way. The request names it with exactly one of:

  • files (object): the method as the MTHDS protocol's map of file entries, each key a tree path and each value the file's text, {"base64": "…"} or {"sha256": "…", "size": n} naming bytes this runner already holds in its blob store. The tree is written whole and loaded as the caller's library directory: every .mthds bundle is named by its tree path, which threads onto diagnostics and the crate's source_map, and every other file is one a step may read, such as a PipeDocGen template beside its bundle.
  • method_ref (string): a reference to a published method. The address form, github.com/<owner>/<repo> plus an optional package selector and @<tag>, is resolved server-side through the same fetch path as a method_ref run: the package's whole tree is read from the commit and loaded as a tree sent in files is, and the packages it ships under its own .mthds/methods/<name>/ are loaded beside it, so a call into one resolves. The registry form (any non-address reference) stays reserved: the server answers a 422 request.unsupported, whose reason is registry_form_method_ref, until method-registry resolution lands.

Providing neither or both is a request-shape 422. Beside files, the request may also carry:

  • dependencies (object): the method packages the method calls by address, each a map of file entries keyed by its address, as on a run. They are loaded beside the method, never merged into it, so a cross-package call resolves without the server fetching or holding a copy. dependencies without files is a request-shape 422.
  • resources (object): Being retired, and refused by a later release: a file the steps read travels inside the method's tree, in files, at its path beside the bundle that names it. Files the method's steps read, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, keyed by the path from the tree's root, each in standard base64, joining the tree with the rules and refusals of /v1/validate. A step that names a template file the tree does not hold cannot be built, so the method is invalid. resources beside a method_ref is a request-shape 422: a published method's files are its package's own.
  • read_scope (string): Pipelex-API extension. The scope the request reads the method under, as on /v1/validate: a hash entry of files resolves in that scope's blob store, else in the caller's own id's, and only a request carrying a read_scope records the tree it read in the blob store; a jwt caller may send only a scope under its own id, else a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is read_scope_under_caller.

The tree's refusals produce no verdict, exactly as on /v1/validate: a key the tree's rule refuses is a 422 method.package_invalid naming the rule as its reason, or security.input_path_refused for a key leaving the tree's root, a malformed entry a 422 request.invalid, a hash the runner does not hold a 422 request.blobs_missing, a tree past its limits a 422 method.package_invalid naming the limit, and a tree holding no .mthds bundle of its own a 422 method.package_invalid whose reason is no_bundle. A files member that is not a map, such as a list, is a 422 request.invalid naming files.

Python follows the run routes' policy. A projection runs nothing, but loading a method's library on a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted imports each of its .py files that declares a structure class (a StructuredContent subclass), which runs that file's module-level code in the server's process. So there a tree, sent or fetched, that holds any .py file is refused with a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox before anything is written. On a sandbox-hosted deployment, a tree whose Python declares a structure class is refused with a 422 problem, pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused, as on a run.

A call by address resolves only from what was shipped. A package the method calls by its address is loaded from the packages the request sends in dependencies, or that a fetched package ships under its .mthds/methods/, and from nowhere else: these routes never read a method installed on the runner and never fetch one. A call into a package nothing shipped is therefore the invalid verdict, one method.dependency_missing item per package, located on the pipe that calls it, naming the package's address as its name with the reason not_found. The method is written out, loaded, projected and released in a worker thread of the bounded method-load pool, so a slow load never holds up the server's other requests.

docs.title: Resolve
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /v1/resolve

Resolution is a first-class language operation alongside validation: the closure is merged, every ref fully qualified, refinement flattened, natives materialized, and the crate's canonical fingerprint computed. Resolution is static — it runs no dry-run sweep (runnability is /validate's vocabulary), and the crate is emitted only from a library that loaded and validated.

Request Body:

{
  "files": {
    "main.mthds": "...bundle one...",
    "steps/extract.mthds": "...bundle two...",
    "templates/invoice.docx": { "sha256": "3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0", "size": 18342 }
  }
}

Response (valid verdict):

{
  "is_valid": true,
  "crate": {
    "mthds_version": "…",
    "concepts": { "…": {} },
    "pipes": { "…": {} },
    "domains": { "…": {} },
    "source_map": { "…": "main.mthds" },
    "fingerprint": "…"
  },
  "message": "MTHDS library resolved successfully"
}

crate is the canonical JSON encoding of the normalized crate — the same bytes pipelex resolve --format json prints, so fingerprints computed from either surface agree.

Response (invalid verdict): 200 with is_valid: false and errors[] (no crate exists).

docs.title: Codegen
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /v1/codegen

Resolves the closure exactly like /resolve, then projects the crate through the two explicit axes:

  • kind (string, required): what to project. Served: types (the crate's concept set as typed models). Membership follows the trust chain — a kind is served here exactly when its artifacts are stamped and locked, which is the promise the valid arm makes by carrying a lock. Input templates are user-editable scaffolds, never stamped or locked, so they cannot make that promise: a client projects one from the input form POST /v1/pipe-io serves, and inputs is deliberately not a kind here.
  • target (string, required): for whom. ts-zod (zod schemas + inferred types), python-pydantic (self-contained pydantic models), or python-structures (runtime StructuredContent classes, for a Pipelex host).
  • pipe_ref (string, optional): pipe selector for future per-pipe kinds — not accepted for types (request-shape 422).

An unknown kind or target is a request-shape 422 problem+json, never a 200 with an error body.

Request Body:

{
  "files": { "main.mthds": "...bundle..." },
  "kind": "types",
  "target": "ts-zod"
}

Response (valid verdict):

{
  "is_valid": true,
  "kind": "types",
  "target": "ts-zod",
  "crate_fingerprint": "…",
  "engine_version": "…",
  "artifacts": [
    { "path": "types.ts", "content": "// >>> pipelex-codegen-stamp >>>\n…" }
  ],
  "lock": "# codegen.lock — generated artifact set (Pipelex codegen). Do not edit by hand.\n…",
  "lock_filename": "codegen.lock",
  "message": "Codegen artifacts generated successfully"
}

docs.title: The trust chain over HTTP
docs.text:
Every artifact ships stamped (source-crate fingerprint, engine version, projection, content hash) and the response carries the matching codegen.lock. A client that writes each artifacts[] entry and the lock verbatim reproduces a local pipelex codegen types run byte-for-byte — so the offline pipelex codegen check passes on the written tree exactly as it would on locally generated files.

There is deliberately no server-side check route: the drift check is pure hashing over local files, offline by design.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
This page covers how to configure the Docker image — the env vars it needs at boot, and how to pass your own Pipelex config files into the container.

For the syntax and meaning of Pipelex config itself (storage backends, tracing, inference routing, model decks, …), see the official Pipelex documentation: https://docs.pipelex.com. This page does not duplicate that.

The official pipelex/pipelex-api image is generic and orchestrator-agnostic. It runs every pipeline in-process (no distributed orchestrator), with no S3, no remote tracing, and openai as the only enabled model provider. Anything environment-specific is meant to be supplied by you, on top of the image, via a mounted .pipelex/ override file. Distributed execution (Temporal, Mistral Workflows, …) is not built in — it is added by installing exactly one orchestrator plugin on top of this base to produce a deployment flavor (see "Execution mode" below).

docs.title: Environment variables
docs.text:
The API reads its settings from environment variables. With Docker, the easiest way is a .env file:

# OpenAI API key — the image enables the openai backend, which serves every
# default language-model and image-generation tier of its model deck.
# Required only if you keep the bundled backends. If you enable other providers
# (Anthropic, Bedrock, OpenRouter, …) in a mounted backends override, you'll
# need those providers' own env vars instead — see https://docs.pipelex.com.
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-api-key

# Authentication for the API itself (optional — defaults to AUTH_MODE=none)
AUTH_MODE=none                 # one of: none | api_key | jwt (any other value refuses to start)
API_KEY=your-api-key           # used when AUTH_MODE=api_key
JWT_SECRET_KEY=your-jwt-secret # used when AUTH_MODE=jwt

# Selects which pipelex_{PIPELEX_ENV}.toml override file is layered on top
# (see "Pipelex configuration files" below). Defaults to "dev" when unset.
PIPELEX_ENV=dev

# ── Webhooks (see webhooks.md) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# The secret the caller's webhooks (`callback_urls` on /v1/execute and /v1/start)
# are signed with, in the Standard Webhooks format: one `whsec_` secret, or
# several separated by spaces during a rotation, the current one first. Unset,
# the server refuses a request carrying `callback_urls` with a 422
# pipelex.webhook.secret_not_configured; requests without them never need it.
# Read when a request needs it. Set it on every process that runs deliveries,
# a Temporal worker included.
# CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_<base64-of-at-least-24-random-bytes>
#
# The deployment's own completion target, which every /v1/start run notifies
# when it ends: an absolute http(s) URL that may name the run's id once with
# `{pipeline_run_id}`, in its path or query only. Unset, there is none. A
# malformed value stops the boot.
# COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL=https://ops.example.com/runs/complete/{pipeline_run_id}
# The HMAC secret of the completion target's X-Completion-Signature, shared with
# its receiver. Required once COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL is set: the server refuses
# to boot with a completion target and without it.
# COMPLETION_CALLBACK_SECRET=<shared-with-your-completion-receiver>

# Maximum request body size, in MiB, before the body-size middleware
# rejects with 413. Defaults to 100 MiB. Raise it for larger documents,
# lower it to harden the server. Read at startup — change requires a restart.
# MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB=100
# A JSON body may also nest its arrays and objects at most 128 levels deep. That bound is
# fixed, not configurable (see error-responses.md).

# The files a request sends beside its bundle in `resources`, such as a PipeDocGen step's
# template file (see pipe-validate.md → "Sending the files the steps read"). Over any of
# them is a 413. Read at startup.
# MAX_RESOURCES_PER_REQUEST=32   # files in one request
# MAX_RESOURCE_FILE_KIB=5120     # decoded bytes per file (default 5 MiB)
# MAX_RESOURCES_TOTAL_KIB=10240  # decoded bytes across the request (default 10 MiB)

# ── Methods sent as trees, and the blob store (`files`, `/v1/blobs/*`) ─────
# See pipe-run.md → "Sending a method as a tree" and "Sending files by hash".
# Each tree of a request is bounded on its own; over any limit is a 422
# method.package_invalid naming the limit. All read at startup.
# MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILES=1000          # files in one tree
# MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILE_KIB=32768      # bytes per file, and per uploaded blob (default 32 MiB)
# MAX_METHOD_TREE_TOTAL_KIB=65536     # bytes across one tree (default 64 MiB)
# A method and the dependency trees it sends beside it are also bounded together:
# MAX_METHOD_DEPENDENCIES=32          # dependency trees in one request
# MAX_METHOD_REQUEST_TOTAL_KIB=131072 # bytes across the method's trees (default 128 MiB)
# BLOB_UPLOAD_URL_TTL_SECONDS=3600    # how long an upload target stays valid
# The address clients reach this API at, which upload targets start with. Set it
# behind a proxy that terminates TLS or serves the API under a path prefix, since
# the URL a request arrives at is then not the one a client can upload to. Unset,
# a target starts with the URL of the request that asked for it.
# PUBLIC_BASE_URL=https://runner.example.com
# The key the upload targets are signed with. Unset, each process draws its own,
# so a deployment serving one API through several instances sets it, the same on
# every instance. Blobs live in the configured storage under <scope>/blobs/.
# BLOB_UPLOAD_SIGNING_KEY=<a-long-random-secret>

# ── Running a method by address (`method_ref`) ────────────────────────────
# See pipe-run.md → "Running a method by address". All read at startup.
#
# The per-instance clone cache (one entry per resolved commit SHA):
# METHOD_CACHE_DIR=/var/cache/pipelex-api-methods  # default: under the OS temp dir
# MAX_METHOD_CACHE_CLONES=64          # cached clones kept before oldest-first eviction
# MAX_METHOD_CACHE_TOTAL_KIB=524288   # total bytes across cached clones (default 512 MiB)
# MAX_METHOD_CACHE_AGE_HOURS=24       # a clone unused this long is evicted
#
# Fetched-package ceilings (enforced by the pipelex runtime on every fetch):
# PIPELEX_MAX_FETCHED_PACKAGE_FILES=256       # files in the selected package
# PIPELEX_MAX_FETCHED_PACKAGE_TOTAL_KIB=8192  # bytes across the selected package (default 8 MiB)
# PIPELEX_MAX_SCANNED_MANIFESTS=100           # METHODS.toml files considered per repository
# PIPELEX_MAX_MANIFEST_FILE_KIB=256           # per METHODS.toml read during package location

Pipelex config TOML files can reference env vars via ${VAR} substitution — that's how secrets like provider API keys flow from the container's environment into Pipelex's runtime config without hard-coding them. Set whichever vars your mounted .pipelex/ files reference.

docs.title: Setting env vars in Docker
docs.text:
You have three idiomatic options. Pick whichever fits your workflow — they all do the same thing.

Option 1 — .env file (recommended). Edit your .env and pass it to the container with --env-file. Best for long-lived deployments and when you want the config in version control next to your docker-compose.yml.

# .env
OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-api-key
MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB=200
AUTH_MODE=api_key
API_KEY=your-strong-secret

docker run --name pipelex-api -p 8081:8081 --env-file .env pipelex/pipelex-api:latest

Option 2 — Inline -e flags on docker run. Best for one-off overrides or quickly testing a single value without editing files.

docker run --name pipelex-api -p 8081:8081 \
  -e OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-api-key \
  -e MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB=200 \
  pipelex/pipelex-api:latest

Option 3 — Compose environment: block. Same as env_file: but inline, useful when you want the values visible in docker-compose.yml itself.

services:
  pipelex-api:
    image: pipelex/pipelex-api:latest
    ports: ["8081:8081"]
    env_file: .env                # for shared values + secrets
    environment:                  # for explicit per-service overrides
      MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB: "200"

You can mix env_file: and environment: — values in environment: win.

After changing any env var, restart the container. All API-side env vars are read once at startup; live changes don't take effect until the process restarts (docker restart pipelex-api or docker compose up -d after editing).

docs.title: Pipelex configuration files
docs.text:
The Pipelex runtime loads .toml config files in a layered, deep-merged order. Later layers override earlier ones:

  1. Package defaults (shipped inside the pipelex Python library)
  2. Global config — ~/.pipelex/pipelex.toml
  3. Project config — {cwd}/.pipelex/pipelex.toml (if present and different from global)
  4. pipelex_local.toml
  5. pipelex_{PIPELEX_ENV}.toml — picked from the PIPELEX_ENV env var (e.g. pipelex_dev.toml, pipelex_prod.toml)
  6. pipelex_{run_mode}.toml
  7. pipelex_override.toml — your final override
  8. pipelex_temporary_override.toml — ephemeral, safe for tools to write/delete

In the official Docker image, the server's .pipelex/ directory (api/.pipelex/ in the pipelex repository) is copied to /root/.pipelex at build time, and the image holds no project-level .pipelex/. That means /root/.pipelex/ is the single config dir the runtime reads from, and any file you mount there participates in the layering above. To override anything, you only need to provide the keys you want to change — the layering does the rest.

The inference tree the image ships is the defaults of the pipelex it runs. The image is released together with pipelex, under the same version, and every file under inference/backends/, the routing profiles and the numbered model deck files are that release's defaults, unchanged, so the models an own-key backend offers are the ones that pipelex lists: read api/.pipelex/inference/backends/<backend>.toml in the pipelex repository at the image's tag to see them. Only two things are this image's own choice: the enabled switches in inference/backends.toml, which leave openai and the software-only internal backend on and every other backend off, and the x_custom_* deck overrides. A copy of inference/backends.toml you mount yourself therefore keeps the backend list of the release you took it from, so take it again when you move to a newer image. The numbered deck points its default language-model and image-generation tiers at models that only openai and azure_openai serve, so a deployment that runs on another provider also repoints those aliases in an x_custom_llm_deck.toml override of its own.

For the schema and meaning of every key in these files, see https://docs.pipelex.com.

docs.title: Orchestration mode
docs.text:
The base is orchestrator-agnostic. WHICH backend a top-level run dispatches to is a deployment choice, read from a separate api.toml config file (not the main pipelex_{env}.toml — the core config rejects unknown sections). It is layered exactly like the Pipelex config above, but with its own base name: api.toml (packaged default) → api_{PIPELEX_ENV}.toml → api_override.toml. Two keys:

Key Meaning Base default orchestration_mode Which backend (orchestrator) a top-level run dispatches to. An open string token: direct (in-process), temporal, and any plugin-provided token are accepted; an unregistered token fails loud at dispatch with the plugin's install hint. direct allow_request_orchestration_mode_override Whether a caller may set orchestration_mode per request on POST /v1/execute, POST /v1/start, and POST /v1/validate. When false, a requested token that differs from the deployment default is refused with a 422 pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden. false

The packaged default (orchestration_mode = "direct", override off) is what the generic image ships.

Boot-coherence guard. A process boots under exactly one orchestrator (the server derives it from orchestration_mode), so enabling allow_request_orchestration_mode_override on a direct default is refused at boot: a request overriding to a non-direct mode would resolve that orchestrator's dispatch arm while the process claimed no async execution hub, failing only at dispatch. The app fails fast at startup instead — set a non-direct orchestration_mode default (which claims the hub, and still serves a per-request direct override in-process) or leave override off.

orchestration_mode is one of two orthogonal axes. It names only the backend. The other axis — delivery, i.e. whether the caller waits — is endpoint-intrinsic, never configured and never requestable:

  • POST /v1/execute and POST /v1/validate are synchronous (BLOCKING delivery): they return the full output / the verdict.
  • POST /v1/start is fire-and-forget (FIRE_AND_FORGET delivery): it returns immediately with a workflow_id. It works only on a backend that is genuinely async-capable. A Temporal deployment (orchestration_mode = "temporal") enqueues on /start and returns a workflow_id. On the orchestrator-agnostic base (orchestration_mode = "direct") the in-process orchestrator is blocking-only, so /start is HONEST: it refuses with a 501 runtime.unsupported — use /execute — rather than silently running blocking and acking.

So a deployment sets one orchestration_mode and each endpoint applies its own delivery — there is no fire-and-forget token to configure or request.

orchestration_mode vs boot_orchestrator — two knobs, two jobs. orchestration_mode (here) selects the backend a top-level entry (/execute, /start, /validate) dispatches to. boot_orchestrator (a core Pipelex setting) selects the execution stack used wherever a pipe actually runs — on a distributed worker, and for the in-process scoping inside the direct orchestrator. On a correctly-configured deployment the two agree (a Temporal flavor sets orchestration_mode = "temporal" and boots under Temporal); keeping them distinct is what lets orchestration_mode be the single source of truth for top-level dispatch without coupling it to how the stack is booted. A temporal orchestration_mode still requires the process to be booted under Temporal — set them together on a Temporal flavor.

A flavor image (e.g. the hosted Temporal flavor) installs one orchestrator plugin and bakes an api_{env}.toml to flip the default, e.g.:

# api_prod.toml  (keys at the file root — no [api] wrapper)
orchestration_mode = "temporal"   # /start is fire-and-forget (async-capable); /execute + /validate stay blocking
allow_request_orchestration_mode_override = false

Mount your own api_{env}.toml / api_override.toml into /root/.pipelex/ exactly like any other override file (see below).

docs.title: Providing your own configuration to Docker
docs.text: Two patterns. Both rely on mounting files into /root/.pipelex/ inside the container.

docs.title: Option 1 — Override individual files
docs.text:
You can mount any single file that lives under /root/.pipelex/ in the image. The bind mount replaces just that one file; everything else stays as shipped. Recommended for most users.

Common targets:

services:
  pipelex-api:
    image: pipelex/pipelex-api:latest
    ports: ["8081:8081"]
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      # Layer your overrides on top of the baseline (one of the override tiers
      # — see "Pipelex configuration files" above for the load order):
      - ./pipelex_override.toml:/root/.pipelex/pipelex_override.toml:ro

      # Or env-specific (selected by PIPELEX_ENV):
      - ./pipelex_dev.toml:/root/.pipelex/pipelex_dev.toml:ro

      # Or replace inference layer files directly:
      - ./backends.toml:/root/.pipelex/inference/backends.toml:ro
      - ./routing_profiles.toml:/root/.pipelex/inference/routing_profiles.toml:ro

      # Or the telemetry config:
      - ./telemetry.toml:/root/.pipelex/telemetry.toml:ro

In other words: any .toml file the runtime reads from /root/.pipelex/ (top-level files OR nested files like inference/backends.toml) is replaceable via a single-file bind mount. The image keeps everything else, so you only ship what differs.

For overrides that fit the layering model (pipelex_override.toml, pipelex_<env>.toml, …), Pipelex deep-merges them on top of the baseline. For files that aren't layered (like inference/backends.toml), the mount fully replaces the file — so include all the keys you need.

docs.title: Option 2 — Replace the entire config directory
docs.text:
Drop a full .pipelex/ next to your docker-compose.yml:

services:
  pipelex-api:
    image: pipelex/pipelex-api:latest
    ports: ["8081:8081"]
    env_file: .env
    volumes:
      - ./.pipelex:/root/.pipelex:ro

Use this when you want full control — for example, to ship your own inference backends, model deck, or routing profiles. You're now responsible for keeping the contents in sync with the version of Pipelex inside the image (the image's bundled inference/, pipelex.toml, etc. are no longer present at runtime).

Your pipelex.toml must re-supply the logging keys

The shipped pipelex.toml is what puts this server on structured logs, and replacing the directory replaces it. Without these three keys Pipelex falls back to its own defaults, which are written for someone at a terminal: the Rich console sink instead of JSON lines, and the "Output of pipe" panel rendered on the thread serving each request. Copy them into your own file:

[runtime.log]
sink = "json"
console_log_target = "stderr"
pretty_print_mode = "silent"

See Logging for what each one does. Option 1 above does not have this problem — a layered override keeps the keys you did not mention.

docs.title: docker run equivalent
docs.text:
docker run --name pipelex-api -p 8081:8081 \
  --env-file .env \
  -v $(pwd)/pipelex_override.toml:/root/.pipelex/pipelex_override.toml:ro \
  pipelex/pipelex-api:latest

docs.title: Local, default everything
docs.text:
.env:

OPENAI_API_KEY=your-openai-api-key

docker-compose.yml:

services:
  pipelex-api:
    image: pipelex/pipelex-api:latest
    ports: ["8081:8081"]
    env_file: .env

docker compose up, then curl http://localhost:8081/health. No override file needed.

docs.title: Local, with API key auth
docs.text:
Same as above but add:

AUTH_MODE=api_key
API_KEY=your-strong-secret

Clients now need Authorization: Bearer your-strong-secret.

docs.title: Documents on an intranet host, or egress through a proxy
docs.text:
When a run fetches a URL that a value carries (a document to extract, a prompt image for a provider that does not take URLs, a generated image a provider returned as a link), the runtime refuses a host that is localhost, a cloud metadata alias, or that resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or metadata address, on the first request and on every redirect hop. The pipe fails with SsrfBlockedError naming the host. The guarded fetch also connects directly, ignoring HTTP_PROXY and HTTPS_PROXY. The image ships with the guard on, which is right for any deployment that runs methods it did not write.

A deployment whose documents live on an intranet host, or whose only way out is an HTTP proxy, turns it off in a pipelex_override.toml:

[runtime.network]
is_fetch_ssrf_guard_enabled = false

Webhook delivery stays guarded whatever this says.

docs.title: Customizing Pipelex (storage, tracing, inference, model decks, …)
docs.text:
Write a pipelex_override.toml (or env-specific pipelex_<env>.toml) with the keys you want to change. Reference any provider credentials from env vars via ${VAR} so they stay out of the file. Mount it into the container as shown above. Refer to https://docs.pipelex.com for the full set of available keys and their semantics.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: Error Responses
docs.text: Every error returned by the API is an RFC 9457 application/problem+json problem document, named by a registry code and seen through the view the request's identity gives it. That holds for a failure the Pipelex runtime raised, which is every domain error, every run failure and the catch-all, and for a refusal the runner authors itself at its own boundary, such as a malformed body, a missing token, a payload over its limit or a path no route serves: there is one shape, and a client branches on its code.

docs.title: Envelope
docs.text:
A failure the runtime raised looks like this, in the caller view:

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/method.invalid",
  "title": "The method does not validate",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "The method does not validate.",
  "code": "method.invalid",
  "domain": "method",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_method",
    "detail": "Fix each fault the problem's errors list, then validate the method again."
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "code": "method.input_undeclared",
      "detail": "Pipe 'summarize' reads names its inputs do not declare: tone.",
      "params": { "pipe": "summarize", "variables": ["tone"] },
      "location": { "pipe": "summarize", "file": "summaries.mthds" }
    }
  ],
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

Content-Type is application/problem+json and X-Request-ID is always echoed in the response headers. No member is ever written as null: a member with no value is absent.

docs.title: Members
docs.text:
The RFC's members — type, title, status and detail are always present:

  • type — the page of the error's code. See The type URI.
  • title — the code's title, the same for every occurrence of the code.
  • status — the HTTP status the code declares, repeated in the body. See Status codes.
  • detail — the sentence stating this occurrence, rendered from the code's template with the problem's parameters. It is written for a person to read: a program branches on code, never on a sentence.

The MTHDS standard's members — code, domain, retry and next_step are always present, and the others appear when they hold a value:

  • code — the registry code naming the fault, such as method.invalid or pipelex.config.variable_missing: a code of the MTHDS standard, or a pipelex. code of the Pipelex error registry, listed on the Error Codes page. The code decides type, title, status, domain, retry and the sentences, so a consumer branches on it rather than on the class that raised the error, which a caller is never told.
  • domain — who must act: input (the caller, by changing the request or its inputs), method (the method's author), account (the account's owner), operator (whoever runs this server) or runtime (nobody beforehand: wait, retry or report).
  • retry — whether repeating the same request can succeed: yes, as for an inference provider's rate limit; no; or outcome_unknown, when the request may have taken effect. A client retries blindly only on yes.
  • retry_after — on a code whose verdict is yes, the delay in seconds the provider asked for before a retry. A 429 also carries it as a Retry-After header, rounded up.
  • next_step — what the reader does next: its kind, such as change_input, change_method, change_model, wait, retry, fix_configuration or report, and its detail, a sentence rendered from the code's template. The step is the reader's own, so the caller view and the operator view of one failure can give different steps.
  • params — the facts the code's sentences name, by the registry's names, such as the failing pipe or the model a method named. Every parameter the code's registry entry requires rides here, so the sentences state this occurrence rather than the code's generic wording, and a list a code requires, such as the suggestions of request.pipe_not_found, is given empty when nothing is near. Those suggestions name only pipes the caller may select: the method's own pipes for a bare or domain-qualified code, and for an alias->… code the pipes that dependency exports, never its private ones; the candidates of method.pipe_unresolved for a reference into a dependency are likewise only that package's exported pipes, its private ones included only for a reference written in the package itself. Beside the server's own library directories, the method's own pipes are those of the bundles the request sent: a pipe of the server's library is never offered, as its files are never named. A parameter only the operator may read never rides here.
  • location — where the fault is: on a run failure the failing pipe and its path from the entry pipe, and elsewhere an input, a field, a batch item, an attempt, or a file with its line and column. See Run failures.
  • errors — one item per fault, for a refusal of several at once: each with its own code, detail, params and location, and on a method that does not validate the suggestions and suggested_fix of its validation item. A refusal of one fault carries no list: the item that would restate the problem's own code gives the problem its parameters and its location instead. When that item carries suggestions or a suggested_fix, which only an item has members for, it gives the problem its parameters and location all the same and stays the list's one item, so the fix is never lost. See Structured validation errors.
  • pipeline_run_id — the run the problem belongs to.

Pipelex's members:

  • request_id — server-correlated identifier for the request. Echoed from inbound X-Request-ID if provided, otherwise generated. Use this when reporting issues.
  • diagnostics — present in the operator view alone. See Views chosen by identity.

docs.title: The runner's own refusals
docs.text:
A refusal the runner authors itself, before the runtime is asked anything, is a problem document like any other, named by its code and seen through the view the request's identity gives it. Its detail and next_step are its code's sentences, and the runner's own account of what it checked rides the operator view's diagnostics.message. The codes it answers are listed under Status codes. A few conventions hold across them:

  • A field the route's rules refuse is request.invalid, whose field parameter, also its location.field, names the field as the request spells it, or a dotted path into the body such as callback_urls.0. When several fields fail at once, errors carries one request.invalid item per refused field, so a client fixes them all in one go, and the problem's own field is the first of them. The items stop at a bound, since a list the caller sent can fail item by item, and the operator view's diagnostics.message, which names each fault with pydantic's account of it, stops at the same bound and says how many more faults there were. A rule of the request model that concerns several fields together names the one to change: sending two of mthds_contents, files and method_ref names the second, sending none names the first, and mthds_sources beside a method_ref, or of another length than mthds_contents, names mthds_sources. Only a body that is not a JSON object names the field body.
  • A body, or an encoded part of one, that cannot be parsed is request.malformed, whose reason says why: not_json, not_utf8, integer_too_long, bad_base64, bad_zip, too_deeply_nested or body_incomplete, and unreadable for a 400 or a 422 the framework raised while reading the request that no check of the runner's own made first, which keeps the status it was raised with. A client's malformed request is never answered as a fault of the server.
  • Any other refusal the framework raises keeps its status and its meaning, under a code whose required parameters the runner can fill: the framework says nothing about a refusal but its status and a header, so a code whose parameters it cannot know gives way to one whose parameters it can. A 401 is auth.missing_credential, keeping the WWW-Authenticate challenge it was raised with; a 403 is auth.invalid_credential, since auth.forbidden names a requirement the framework does not; a 404 is request.not_found, and a 405 request.method_not_allowed, keeping its Allow; a 413 is request.malformed with the reason too_large, since request.too_large states a limit and a size the framework does not; and a 429 is runtime.unavailable, whose verdict invites a retry, keeping its Retry-After, since account.rate_limited states a limit and a window the framework does not. Any other 4xx, such as a 415, is request.malformed with the reason unreadable. Each answers with the status it was raised with, whichever status its code declares. A 5xx the framework raises is its own fault, runtime.unexpected.
  • A request past one of this runner's size limits is request.too_large, a 413 whose limit and size parameters give the limit and what the request carried, always in bytes: an encoded value, a file of resources or a bundle_b64 archive, is measured by the bytes its encoded length carries, read before it is decoded.
  • A method tree the runner refuses to read as a method is method.package_invalid, whose reason names the rule the tree breaks and whose path or limit says where or how far.
  • A dependency the request keys by another address than the one its own METHODS.toml declares, such as its repository's address alone, is pipelex.request.dependency_key_mismatch, a 422 whose key parameter is the key the request used and whose address is the declared address the dependency must be keyed by.

The members the runner's refusals used to carry are gone: no refusal carries an error_type, error_domain, retryable or instance. The request's path is not echoed, since request_id, which the runner takes from an inbound X-Request-ID or mints, is what correlates a response with the server's records.

docs.title: Views chosen by identity
docs.text:
A failure the runtime raised is one problem seen through a view, and the identity the request authenticated picks the view. No deployment setting picks it.

How the request authenticated View AUTH_MODE=api_key: the static API key is the operator's own credential The operator view AUTH_MODE=none with TRUST_FORWARDED_IDENTITY_HEADERS=true: the only party reaching this server is the trusted proxy in front of it, such as the hosted platform, which owes its own callers their caller view The operator view AUTH_MODE=jwt: a caller's token The caller view AUTH_MODE=none without the trusted proxy, or a request refused before any authentication ran The caller view

A refusal the runner authors before any authentication ran, such as a body over the size limit or a path no route serves, is answered in the caller view.

The caller view carries the code's sentences, rendered from the parameters a caller may read, and the step for the caller: for a code of the operator domain, whose actor is whoever runs this server, that is what the caller can do meanwhile, such as choosing another model. It never carries the error's own message, its class, a path on the host, a provider's answer or a foreign exception's text, whatever the failure. A problem this server relays with a code its own registries do not hold, such as one a newer worker built, reaches the caller with the generic step of its kind, and report for a code of the operator domain, since its recorded step was written for the operator.

The operator view adds the operator's step and diagnostics:

  • error_class — the class of the error the problem was built from.
  • message — that error's own message.
  • causes — the errors along its cause chain, each with its class and the code it carries by itself.
  • params — the parameters only an operator may read, such as the variable pipelex.config.variable_missing names, which also render into the operator's step.
  • model — the model handle, when the failure is attributable to one.
  • provider — what the inference provider answered: its name (the backend), status, code, request_id and message.
  • migration — a pending configuration migration that explains the failure.
  • runtime_version — the version of the Pipelex runtime that built the problem.
  • trace_id, span_id — the OpenTelemetry span the failure happened in, when one was recording.

Every text in a problem that the runtime did not write itself, a message, a provider's answer or a parameter, is cut to a bounded length, keeping its head and ending with […].

The catch-all, a failure no more specific handler matched, answers runtime.unexpected with a 500 in both views: the caller reads that code's sentences, and the operator view reads the exception's class in diagnostics, never its text, which can carry anything of a run's data, a pydantic refusal adding its reasons without the values it refused. A traceback never reaches a response in either view, and neither the traceback nor the exception's text reaches a log: the server's error line names the classes of the exception's chain and the frames it was raised through (see Logging).

The server's own record of a failure the runtime raised is built from the operator view, whichever view the response carries, so it names the error's class, its code and what the inference provider answered (see Logging).

docs.title: Structured validation errors
docs.text:
When a bundle fails validation, the runtime builds one structured item per fault — the per-error diagnostics an editor maps to per-line problems — and every surface of this server carries them as the MTHDS standard's problem items. On the diagnostic routes (/validate, /resolve, /codegen, /pipe-io) an invalid bundle is the successful product of the call: a 200 is_valid: false verdict carrying the items as errors (see Pipe Validate). On the run routes (/execute, /start), where an invalid bundle means the run cannot proceed, it is a 422 method.invalid problem carrying the same items as its errors. Built by pipelex's one shared builder, the items name the same faults at the same places wherever they appear, and the same as the agent CLI's. A valid verdict's warnings are problem items too, in the same shape.

Each item is one fault:

Member Meaning code The registry code of the fault: the code its type maps to, such as method.input_undeclared for an input a pipe reads but does not declare, model.unknown for a model the deck does not define, method.syntax for a TOML syntax error or method.dependency_missing for a package the method calls and no one supplied. A dry_run item's code is its failure's own, and an item no stage classified takes method.schema_violation, or the code of the refusal behind it. detail The code's sentence, rendered from the item's parameters, or the code's title when the item lacks a parameter the sentence names. A program branches on code, never on a sentence. params Every parameter the item's code requires, by the registry's names: the facts its locators give, such as the pipe, the variables it reads, the concept or model it names, the model_type and a finding quoting the validation's own account, and those the check that found the fault knows, such as the concept a pipe declares and those that would fit, the name and the kind of conflict of a name declared twice, or the declared concepts nearest one that resolves to nothing. location Where the fault is: the pipe, the field within the bundle, and the file with its 1-based line and column when the parser stopped there. A name two bundles declare is one item per bundle, each located on its own file. For a method sent in files or fetched by method_ref, the file is the bundle's tree path. On the mthds_contents path, which is being retired, the file is the matching mthds_sources[i] (see Sourcing submitted files), so it is absent when the caller sent no sources. Beside a server's own library directories, an item never names one of their files, nor a template file one of their PipeDocGen steps names. suggestions On a model.unknown item, the deck's close matches of the kind the pipe needs. suggested_fix A structured, deterministic fix for this fault — present only when the fix planner derived one. See Suggested fixes.

An item writes no member that has no value: an absent member is not null.

Every invalid verdict carries a non-empty list of items — the structured-info invariant is total. A parse-level failure the runtime cannot attribute to a known pipe, concept or field — an empty blueprint, an elaborator failure — still becomes one residual item carrying the failure as its finding, so the list is never empty on an invalid verdict. A TOML syntax error is a method.syntax item whose location holds the line and column the parser stopped at, and the file when the caller sent one. A failing dry run is one item per failing pipe, located at the innermost pipe that failed. A dry run whose every failure belongs to someone other than the method's author, such as a storage outage, is no verdict about the method: it answers the failure's own code, with every failure riding its errors.

On the run routes, every refusal of the bundle while it loads is this verdict, and the load happens before any pipe runs: a misspelled concept, a wiring mismatch, an unknown model, a TOML fault, a refusal raised while a pipe is built and a line of the method's requirements.txt that the PipeFunc sandbox does not meet or that the standard refuses, which the runner judges before the load opens (Pipe Run), all answer the same 422 method.invalid carrying the same items validating the bundle gives. None of them reaches a run as a 500. An entry pipe the bundle does not declare answers request.pipe_not_found, and a bare code matching pipes in several domains request.pipe_ambiguous.

docs.title: Suggested fixes
docs.text:
A problem item may carry a suggested_fix: a deterministic repair the runtime's fix planner derived from the typed error data — never by parsing a message string. It is the MTHDS standard's fix, the same object on a verdict's item and on a problem's. It is optional and additive. An item the planner has no rule for simply omits the member, and a client that ignores suggested_fix entirely behaves exactly as before.

{
  "code": "method.output_concept_mismatch",
  "detail": "A pipe's output concept does not fit",
  "params": { "pipe": "summarize_and_translate" },
  "location": { "pipe": "summarize_and_translate", "file": "translate.mthds" },
  "suggested_fix": {
    "fix_code": "match-sequence-output",
    "description": "Set output of pipe 'summarize_and_translate' to 'Translation' to match its last step",
    "safety": "safe",
    "file": "translate.mthds",
    "ops": [
      {
        "kind": "set_key",
        "table_path": ["pipe", "summarize_and_translate"],
        "key": "output",
        "value": "Translation"
      }
    ]
  }
}

Fields:

  • fix_code — the kebab-case rule id that produced the fix (match-sequence-output, sync-controller-inputs, strip-native-concept-redecl, strip-namespace, delete-redundant-dotted-input, …). Stable; use it to allow-list or suppress rules.
  • description — human-readable summary of what the fix does.
  • safety — safe or unsafe. Only apply an unsafe fix behind an explicit opt-in: it is a likely correction, such as the one close match for an unknown model, that a person or an agent must confirm, and pipelex fix bundle never applies one on its own.
  • file — the file the ops target, when known. An applier must only apply ops to the file they target — in a multi-file library the ops are meaningless against any other file.
  • ops — the semantic TOML patch operations, in order.

Ops are addressed by table_path (the containing table, e.g. ["pipe", "my_seq"]). Each op's kind names its shape: read kind off the wire and you know exactly which other fields the op carries, because each kind is its own shape in the OpenAPI artifact rather than one open shape with everything optional. An op whose kind is none of those below, which a newer runtime could send, is read as an unknown op that an applier never applies.

kind Effect Carries besides table_path set_key Set (or add) a key in the table key, value ensure_table Create the table when it is absent — delete_key Remove a key from the table key delete_table Remove the table — rename_table_key Rename a key in place, keeping its position key, new_key move_key Relocate a key to another table, creating missing destination parents key, new_table_path, new_key remap_value Rewrite a key's string value through an explicit old-to-new mapping, doing nothing when the current value is not a mapped one key, mapping

For ensure_table and delete_table, table_path addresses the table itself rather than its parent, so it is never empty — the document root always exists and is never a target. move_key is addressed at both ends and the two ends follow different rules: table_path is the table the key currently sits in, per the general convention above, while new_table_path addresses the destination table itself. Neither is constrained to be non-empty: an empty table_path reads a key off the document root, and an empty new_table_path moves it there. move_key moves a table-valued key with its whole subtree.

value is a TOML scalar (string, integer, float, boolean) or a flat scalar mapping, which a fix that must create a whole table at once — a missing inputs mapping, say — writes as an inline table.

The ops are the machine contract; any rendered diff is presentation. Apply them with a style-preserving TOML editor rather than reconstructing the file from a diff: that is what keeps the caller's formatting, comments, and key order intact.

docs.title: Run failures: the root fault, located at the failing pipe
docs.text:
When a run fails, the problem describes the root fault, never the run-level wrapper around it: the first Pipelex error down the cause chain that carries a code of its own, or the innermost one when none does. The wrappers that only locate the failure take their cause's code, so every member is the root fault's — code, type, title, domain, retry, the HTTP status, the sentences and the parameters — and the wrappers add only where it happened, as the location members: pipe, the pipe that failed, and path, the pipe codes from the entry pipe down to it. A code that declares a pipe parameter names the failing pipe in its sentences too. A consumer reads the location from those members, never from a sentence.

So a run the caller's own method or request refuses says what to change: a PipeCondition whose outcome is fail, a PipeParallel branch whose multiplicity does not match its output field, a step started without a required input, or a model named inline that the deck does not define all answer a 422 whose code is the caller's own, in the input or the method domain, with a step saying what to change. A model the deck names but does not serve is model.unavailable, a 501 in the operator domain: the caller's step is to choose another model or ask whoever runs the server to serve it, and the operator's to configure a backend for it.

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/pipe.output_multiplicity",
  "title": "A step produced a list instead of one result, or the reverse",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "Pipe 'analyze_topic' produced an output of the multiplicity 'list', but its output 'ideas' is declared 'single'.",
  "code": "pipe.output_multiplicity",
  "domain": "method",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_method",
    "detail": "Declare the output 'ideas' as 'list', or make pipe 'analyze_topic' produce 'single'."
  },
  "params": {
    "pipe": "analyze_topic",
    "output": "ideas",
    "produced": "list",
    "declared": "single"
  },
  "location": {
    "pipe": "analyze_topic",
    "path": ["review_topic", "analyze_topic"]
  },
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

In the operator view the same failure adds diagnostics, whose message is the combine's own restatement, naming the branch whose result it could not combine and the setting to change. The failure of a run reaches its webhooks as the same problem, in each webhook's view (see Async callbacks).

docs.title: Status codes
docs.text:
The HTTP status of a failure the runtime raised is the one its code declares in the registry, the status member's value, and each code's page on Error Codes states it. A code the registries give none, which only a client's own failure has, answers 500. Two codes of the same domain can answer different statuses, so a client reads code, domain and retry, never the status, to decide what to do. The statuses a run meets most:

  • 422 — the caller's request or method: method.invalid and the method's other codes, input.missing and the input's other codes, request.pipe_not_found, request.pipe_ambiguous, model.unknown, model.content_refused.
  • 429 — provider.rate_limited: an upstream inference provider rate-limited the run, a retry can succeed, and Retry-After is set when the provider gave a delay. Only POST /v1/execute runs inference, so only /execute can produce it.
  • 500 — the operator's configuration, such as pipelex.config.variable_missing or pipelex.config.invalid, and the catch-all runtime.unexpected.
  • 501 — something this deployment does not serve: model.unavailable, a model it serves no backend for; runtime.unsupported, async pipeline execution (POST /v1/start) on a deployment that does not provide it. Nothing is broken, and a caller meets the refusal each time it asks, so its log line is a warning, never an error (see Logging).
  • 502 — an upstream service failed: provider.unavailable, provider.failed, provider.quota_exhausted, provider.credential_refused, method.fetch_failed. A 504 is provider.timeout.

A few runtime refusals worth knowing by their code:

  • 404 — method.not_found: the method_ref repository was fetched, but no package in it matches the requested address by manifest identity, or it holds no such tag. The problem's sentences name the reference.
  • 409 — pipelex.run.already_exists: the submitted pipeline_run_id is already registered for a run that is still in flight on this server. Completed and failed runs free their id, so this only fires for genuinely concurrent duplicates — resubmit after the in-flight run finishes, or pick a fresh id. Only POST /v1/start accepts a client-supplied pipeline_run_id, so only /start can produce it.
  • 422 — the method_ref resolution refusals the caller can fix: request.invalid for a reference that does not parse, method.ambiguous, and method.package_invalid for a package past its limits or carrying a symbolic link. security.integrity_mismatch is a 422 too: a package the method calls by address, which the server fetched, differs from the tree digest the method's methods.lock records for it, and its dependency names the address (see Pipe Run). pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused is a 422 too: a method, fetched by method_ref or sent as a tree, declares in-process Python structure classes (StructuredContent subclasses), which hosted execution always refuses, sandbox or not — express the types as MTHDS concepts with inline structures instead (see Pipe Run).

The runner's own refusals answer these codes:

  • 401 — auth.missing_credential for a request carrying no bearer token, auth.invalid_credential for a token the runner refuses, and auth.credential_expired for an expired one, each with WWW-Authenticate: Bearer set. Only reachable when the deployment enables auth (AUTH_MODE=api_key or AUTH_MODE=jwt), or trusts a proxy, which then answers auth.missing_credential when it forwarded no identity, with no WWW-Authenticate, since that deployment reads no bearer token. A forwarded X-User-Id that is not a single path-safe segment is no credential of the caller's: it is a 422 request.invalid naming the field X-User-Id.
  • 403 — auth.forbidden, whose requirement names what the request lacks: signed_upload_target for a PUT /v1/blobs/{sha256} without a valid upload target, its signature missing, forged, expired, or signed for another hash or scope, so ask POST /v1/blobs/missing for a fresh target; read_scope_under_caller on a jwt deployment, for a request that sent a read_scope not lying under the caller's own user_id, which is the only scope its token may read (see Pipe Run).
  • 404 — request.not_found: no route serves the request's path.
  • 405 — request.method_not_allowed: the route does not accept the request's HTTP method. The response carries the Allow header listing the methods it accepts.
  • 413 — request.too_large: the request body exceeds the configured size limit (MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB, 100 MiB by default), or a part of it exceeds its own: an encoded bundle_b64 archive over MAX_BUNDLE_TOTAL_KIB, a file in resources over MAX_RESOURCE_FILE_KIB, the files in resources over MAX_RESOURCES_TOTAL_KIB, or a blob upload over the per-file tree limit.
  • 422 — request.invalid for a field the route's rules refuse, request.malformed for a body or an encoded part that cannot be parsed, request.unsupported for a registry-form method_ref — not a github.com/... address — which no server-side method registry resolves yet (its reason is registry_form_method_ref; use an address or send the method's tree in files), and pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden, naming the requested_mode, for a request asking for an orchestration_mode this deployment does not allow overriding per request (allow_request_orchestration_mode_override = false).
  • 500 — runtime.misconfigured: the runner's own configuration cannot serve the request, such as a missing API_KEY or JWT_SECRET_KEY, a PUBLIC_BASE_URL that is not an HTTP URL, or missing package metadata. Which setting is at fault is the operator's to read, in diagnostics.params.component, and in the error.params.component of the server's error line whichever view the response took. pipelex.deployment.token_claims_invalid is a 500 too: a token whose signature holds carries a user_id claim that is missing, unsafe or reserved, which its issuer, not its bearer, must fix.
  • 501 — runtime.unsupported naming the capability asynchronous execution: POST /v1/start is fire-and-forget by nature, and this deployment's orchestrator is blocking-only (the in-process direct default), so it refuses honestly rather than blocking and acking — use POST /v1/execute instead. pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox: the method holds custom Python .py files and this deployment is not sandbox-hosted, so running caller-supplied code in-process is refused; its origin says whether the code came in the request's bundle or a fetched package.
  • 500 — pipelex.storage.damaged, naming the kind of storage as scheme (local, s3, gcs, memory, or plugin for a store a storage plugin provides), on the routes that read files a request names by hash (POST /v1/execute, POST /v1/start, POST /v1/validate, POST /v1/resolve, POST /v1/codegen and POST /v1/pipe-io): the bytes the blob store holds under a hash do not hash to it, or are not the size it holds them at, so the object stored there is damaged. PUT /v1/blobs/{sha256} answers it too for an upload whose bytes hash to an object held at another size, since the runner never writes over a blob. Its verdict is not to retry, since a retry reads the same damaged object, and its step is to report it: the operator removes the object the server's line Stored blob bytes do not match their hash names under blob_sha256 (see Logging), after which the blob is uploaded again.

A client that disconnects before its request body was received in full is answered request.malformed with the reason body_incomplete, which only the server's logs show, at warning level, since the client is gone before the answer.

Every route that takes a JSON body refuses one whose arrays and objects nest more than 128 levels deep, the body's own envelope included, with a 422 request.malformed whose reason is too_deeply_nested. The depth is checked before the body is parsed, so the answer does not depend on the Python version or the stack size the server runs with. The bound is fixed rather than configurable, and real inputs stay far below it.

The run routes read their body as plain JSON before anything else, and the routes that declare a typed body parse it before validating it, so the same refusals come from that step, all 422. A body that is not valid UTF-8 or not valid JSON answers request.malformed with the reason not_utf8 or not_json, and one holding an integer longer than Python reads from text (sys.get_int_max_str_digits(), 4,300 digits by default) the reason integer_too_long; and one that is not a JSON object request.invalid naming the field body. A body carrying, in any object at any depth, a key named __class__ or __module__, or a key starting with __kajson, answers pipelex.security.reserved_key, whose keys parameter names the key, cut short when it is long. Those are the keys a kajson decoder reads as an order to import and instantiate a class, so the runner refuses them rather than carry them as data, and logs the refusal's security event. Only keys are checked: a string value that mentions __class__ is accepted.

A pipe selection the server cannot make is an input 422 named for its failure: request.pipe_not_found when the selector names no pipe, and request.pipe_ambiguous when a bare code, or a dependency's alias->code, matches pipes in several domains, naming the pipes it matched as its candidates. The run routes answer an unknown or ambiguous pipe_code that way. POST /v1/pipe-io answers every selection refusal that way, counting a request with no pipe_ref over a method that declares no main_pipe, or whose domains declare several, as request.pipe_unspecified, which names the declared ones as its candidates, and a manifest main_pipe the method lacks or declares in several domains as the method's own method.pipe_unresolved or method.ref_ambiguous (see Pipe I/O).

The run routes' extension fields are validated before any method is fetched or any library loaded, and a failure there is a 422 request.invalid naming the field that failed, callback_urls, storage_scope, read_scope or analytics_groups, or a path into it (see Pipe Run). A storage scope that does not lie under the run's read scope, whether either was sent or defaulted, names read_scope. A body failing on several fields at once carries one item per refused field in errors. A callback URL whose scheme is not http or https, or whose host the SSRF rules refuse, is the security refusal security.input_url_refused, which logs its security event and names the class of destination it refused, never the URL. A request carrying callback_urls to a server whose operator configured no signing secret is a 422 pipelex.webhook.secret_not_configured naming the setting, CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET, in params.setting, located at callback_urls (see Webhooks). POST /v1/validate takes analytics_groups too and refuses it the same way.

A method sent as a tree, in files or bundle_b64, is read under the MTHDS standard's tree rule before anything loads, on the run routes and /validate alike (see Pipe Run). A key or an entry the rule refuses, two shipped packages a reference could not tell apart, or a tree past MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILES, MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILE_KIB or MAX_METHOD_TREE_TOTAL_KIB, or a method past MAX_METHOD_DEPENDENCIES or MAX_METHOD_REQUEST_TOTAL_KIB across its trees, is a 422 method.package_invalid whose reason names the rule: the standard's tree refusal codes, such as invalid_tree_path, duplicate_key, excluded_name or path_collision, with the path it refuses, or the runner's own, one per rule and one per limit: too_many_files, file_too_large and tree_too_large for a tree, too_many_dependencies and method_too_large for a request's trees together, bundle_too_many_files and bundle_too_large for a bundle_b64 archive, manifest_missing, manifest_invalid, package_name_invalid, dependency_address_collision and no_bundle, with the path or the limit it names. A key that is not a tree path without leaving the tree, empty or holding a backslash or a colon, is invalid_tree_path. A path of the tree that would leave its root is the security refusal security.input_path_refused, naming the rule it broke, absolute or parent_segment, never the path. A malformed entry, or dependencies that do not fit the request, is a 422 request.invalid naming the field. The bytes a hash entry names are checked last, only for a map that breaks no other rule, and never under a key the rule refuses, as the MTHDS Protocol orders a map's refusals: a hash entry this runner does not hold is then a 422 request.blobs_missing whose missing_blobs parameter lists the SHA-256 hashes to upload through the blob routes before sending the request again, and one it holds at another size than the entry states a 422 request.invalid: the entry's size is the one to correct, since uploading the bytes again would not change the size they are held at. The blob routes answer in the same vocabulary: a body whose SHA-256 is not the one its path names is a 422 request.invalid naming the field body, one hash listed with two sizes a 422 request.invalid naming blobs, and a blob past the per-file limit a 413 request.too_large. None of them invites a retry, since the same request is refused again. A methods.lock at the tree's root is read only when a package the method calls by address resolves to a copy the runner fetched, for this request or an earlier one: a lock the runner cannot read, such as one written before tree digests that records a hash, then refuses the method with the 422 verdict method.invalid, whose item is method.package_invalid with the reason lock_invalid and the path methods.lock, and a lock recording another tree digest for the fetched package's address is the 422 security.integrity_mismatch.

The files a request sends in resources are checked before the bundle loads and again once it is parsed (see Pipe Validate). A key that would leave the bundle is the security refusal security.input_path_refused, naming the rule it broke; any other key that cannot name a file inside the bundle, two keys naming the same file, more files than MAX_RESOURCES_PER_REQUEST, a file none of the bundle's steps names, and files that cannot make one method tree, such as two keys equal once case-folded, are 422 request.invalid naming the field resources; and a value that is not base64 is a 422 request.malformed with the reason bad_base64. They answer the same on every route, the diagnostic ones included: they are the request's fault, not the bundle's.

The HTTP status is the source of truth for success vs failure — there is no success: true/false field anywhere in the envelope.

Which statuses a given route can actually produce is documented per operation in the committed OpenAPI artifact, each as an application/problem+json ProblemDocument.

What is not an error status: an invalid .mthds bundle. On the diagnostic routes — /validate, /resolve, /codegen, and /pipe-io — a bundle that fails validation is the successful product of the call, so it rides a 200 discriminated on is_valid: false, carrying the same errors[] items described above. Non-2xx on those routes is reserved for no verdict could be produced. See Pipe Validate.

docs.title: The type URI
docs.text:
type is the page of the error's code:

https://mthds.ai/errors/<code>              a code of the MTHDS standard, such as method.invalid
https://docs.pipelex.com/errors/<code>      a pipelex. code, such as pipelex.config.variable_missing

Both families are listed on the Error Codes page, and title is the code's title. A Pipelex code's type URI names no documentation version: the documentation site answers it with the code's page in the latest release (see The pages and the type URI).

The runner's own refusals carry a code like every other error, so their type is their code's page too.

Before every error carried its code, the type of an error was derived from its class or, for a refusal the API authored, from its error_type, and named a page per class. Those pages are retired, and the documentation site redirects each one to the page of its class's code, or to the Error Codes index when the class is gone or raises no single code, so a stored type still leads somewhere useful.

docs.title: Request correlation
docs.text:
Every response carries X-Request-ID. The middleware respects an inbound X-Request-ID header if present and valid, otherwise mints one, a ULID. A valid id is 1 to 128 ASCII letters, digits, _ and -, the rule a run applies to the id it is handed too (pipelex.system.job_metadata.is_valid_request_id): the id is echoed in a header and written into log lines, where a space, a quote or an = could forge a field. It also binds that id onto the Pipelex runtime's log context for the duration of the request, so every record emitted underneath carries it as a request_id field — the server's own error lines and the runtime's lines from inside a run alike. Both run routes, POST /v1/execute and POST /v1/start, also put the id on the run's metadata, so when a run is dispatched to a worker, the lines the worker writes while it runs the run's workflow and activities carry the same id. What those lines look like, which fields they carry and where the id does not reach are in Logging.

When opening an issue, include the request_id from the response (or response headers) and the timestamp.

docs.title: 422 — a method that does not validate
docs.text:
POST /v1/execute
{
  "files": {
    "summaries.mthds": "domain = \"summaries\"\nmain_pipe = \"summarize\"\n\n[pipe.summarize]\ntype = \"PipeLLM\"\ndescription = \"Summarize a text\"\ninputs = { text = \"Text\" }\noutput = \"Text\"\nprompt = \"Summarize $text in the style of $tone.\"\n"
  }
}

HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Request-ID: 9f2c1ab3-…

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/method.invalid",
  "title": "The method does not validate",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "The method does not validate.",
  "code": "method.invalid",
  "domain": "method",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_method",
    "detail": "Fix each fault the problem's errors list, then validate the method again."
  },
  "errors": [
    {
      "code": "method.input_undeclared",
      "detail": "Pipe 'summarize' reads names its inputs do not declare: tone.",
      "params": { "pipe": "summarize", "variables": ["tone"] },
      "location": { "pipe": "summarize", "file": "summaries.mthds" }
    }
  ],
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

The detail is the human summary; errors is the machine-readable list a client maps to per-line diagnostics. Only the run routes answer an invalid bundle with this 422 — on the diagnostic routes the same bundle is a 200 is_valid: false verdict carrying the same items as errors — see Structured validation errors and Sourcing submitted files.

docs.title: 500 — deployment configuration fault
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 500 Internal Server Error
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Request-ID: 9f2c1ab3-…

{
  "type": "https://docs.pipelex.com/errors/pipelex.config.variable_missing",
  "title": "A configuration variable is not set",
  "status": 500,
  "detail": "A variable the runtime's configuration refers to is not set.",
  "code": "pipelex.config.variable_missing",
  "domain": "operator",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "report",
    "detail": "Report this to whoever runs the runtime."
  },
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

pipelex.config.variable_missing is a code in the operator domain: the deployment, not the caller, has to fix it, so the caller's step is to report it. The operator view of the same failure carries the fix_configuration step and diagnostics, whose message names the variable, such as Missing required environment variable: <NAME>, which no caller reads.

docs.title: 401 — missing bearer token
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 401 Unauthorized
Content-Type: application/problem+json
WWW-Authenticate: Bearer
X-Request-ID: 9f2c1ab3-…

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/auth.missing_credential",
  "title": "No credential was sent",
  "status": 401,
  "detail": "This route needs a credential, and the request carried none.",
  "code": "auth.missing_credential",
  "domain": "account",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "check_credentials",
    "detail": "Send the request with a credential this runtime accepts."
  },
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

docs.title: 422 — two fields the route refuses
docs.text:
HTTP/1.1 422 Unprocessable Entity
Content-Type: application/problem+json
X-Request-ID: 9f2c1ab3-…

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/request.invalid",
  "title": "The request does not match the route's schema",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "The request's field 'storage_scope' does not match the route's schema.",
  "code": "request.invalid",
  "domain": "input",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {
    "kind": "change_input",
    "detail": "Correct the field 'storage_scope' as the route's schema requires, then send the request again."
  },
  "params": { "field": "storage_scope" },
  "location": { "field": "storage_scope" },
  "errors": [
    {
      "code": "request.invalid",
      "detail": "The request's field 'storage_scope' does not match the route's schema.",
      "params": { "field": "storage_scope" },
      "location": { "field": "storage_scope" }
    },
    {
      "code": "request.invalid",
      "detail": "The request's field 'analytics_groups' does not match the route's schema.",
      "params": { "field": "analytics_groups" },
      "location": { "field": "analytics_groups" }
    }
  ],
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

The operator view of the same refusal adds diagnostics, whose message holds the rules each field broke, in the request model's own words, which can quote what the caller sent and so never reach a caller.

docs.title: Async callbacks (webhook payload)
docs.text:
A run's webhooks do not use this envelope: a failed run's problem rides inside their bodies, so a non-HTTP receiver such as a queue or a log shipper reads the same code, domain, retry, sentences and location as the synchronous answer, without an HTTP status and without the status member.

  • A caller's webhook, each of a request's callback_urls, receives the run.finished event, whose data.error is the run's problem in the caller view, whoever started the run, so it never carries diagnostics, even when an operator's credential started it.
  • The deployment's completion target, COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL, receives a completion notice carrying pipeline_run_id, the delivery state (also sent under the legacy status key) and, when results were stored, result_url, with the problem under an error key in the operator view, diagnostics included. A host that builds its own webhook targets picks the view with WebhookTarget.problem_view, which is the caller view when it names none.

The problem is built only when the run has a webhook to deliver it to, and building it never changes how the run fails: a problem that cannot be built is logged as an error, and the webhooks receive runtime.unexpected while the run fails with its own error.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: Logging
docs.text: The server writes structured logs: one JSON object per line, on stderr, with every value the line carries sitting as a key of its own. That is the shape a log agent in front of a container ingests without a parser — the CloudWatch agent, the Google Cloud Logging agent, an OTLP collector — so a query filters on a field rather than matching a substring of a message.

docs.title: What a line looks like
docs.text:
An error response produces exactly one line. A caller mistake:

{"time": "2026-10-17T13:53:17.919Z", "severity": "WARNING", "logger": "pipelex_api.exception_handlers", "message": "A request ended in an error response", "request_id": "01M2TCP02W04RZG6DTM8AR508C", "url.path": "/v1/models", "error.code": "request.invalid", "error.type": "RunnerRequestError", "error_domain": "input", "retryable": false, "http.response.status_code": 422, "error.chain": ["RunnerRequestError"]}

A fault the server has to fix looks the same at ERROR, and adds error.frames, where the deepest exception of its chain was raised.

The message is the same sentence on every error line, A request ended in an error response, whichever failure it reports, so it is the key a query or an alert selects this server's error stream by, following the log-call conventions.
