Everything about the failure, the HTTP status, the code and the error type included, rides a field of its own, and nothing a caller supplied ever reaches the message. No error line carries an exception's text or its traceback, whatever the failure: a traceback prints the text of every exception of its chain, and a foreign exception's text, a pydantic ValidationError's or a method function's, can quote a run's inputs or a model's answer. The line names the classes of the chain under error.chain and, on an ERROR line, where the deepest was raised under error.frames, and the operator reads the error's message, cut to a bounded length, in the operator view's diagnostics of the response. Two layers keep the values a caller can shape, such as the url.path, safe to write. Before any sink sees a record, the Pipelex runtime's redaction processor replaces a control character in a field's value with its printable escape, and replaces a credential it recognises, an Authorization header's token or an API key, with [REDACTED]. The sink then escapes what it writes, so a quote or an = stays inside its value. The processor is configured under [runtime.log.redaction] and is on by default.

docs.title: The fields a line carries
docs.text:
These keys come from the sink itself and are on every line written by the process, this server's and the Pipelex runtime's alike:

Key What it is time When the record was created — ISO 8601, UTC, milliseconds, Z severity The level name: WARNING, ERROR, … logger The module that emitted it message The human-readable summary exception The traceback, when the record carries one trace_id, span_id, trace_flags The process's current OpenTelemetry span, in lowercase hex, when one names a trace. This server registers no tracer and instruments nothing, so as shipped no line carries them; they appear only when the deployment runs it under OpenTelemetry instrumentation of its own that makes a span current pipelex.trace_id, pipelex.span_id The Pipelex span a runtime line was logged in, the pipe's or the LLM call's, in lowercase hex. Present on the runtime's lines inside a live run the runtime traces, which it does when AI span tracing is enabled on your own PostHog; never on the server's own lines, an error line included

The two pairs name different traces. Pipelex's spans belong to a trace of their own, which only Pipelex's exporters receive, so if you export them to a backend of your own, such as Langfuse, an OTLP collector or your PostHog, join a line to them on pipelex.trace_id and pipelex.span_id. To gather a run's lines whether or not anything traces, use request_id or pipeline_run_id. How each sink writes both pairs is in the Pipelex documentation's trace context section.

request_id reaches a line in one of two ways, depending on which process writes it. In this server's own process, the request-id middleware binds it on the runtime's log context for the whole request, so every record emitted there while the request is in flight carries it: the server's own lines, like the example above, and the lines the Pipelex runtime emits from inside a run executed in-process (orchestration_mode = "direct"), without any call site passing it along. A run dispatched to a worker, under a distributed orchestration_mode such as temporal, happens in another process, which that binding does not reach, so the id travels with the run instead: both run routes, POST /v1/execute and POST /v1/start, put it on the run's metadata, and the worker binds it from there while it runs the run's workflow and activities, so the lines written inside them carry the same id. A line the worker writes outside those bindings does not, such as the one the orchestration SDK logs after an activity has failed. One path does not carry it at all yet: when POST /v1/validate dispatches its dry run to a worker, the lines that worker writes for it have no request_id. The value is the one echoed in the response's X-Request-ID header and in the problem document's request_id member, so a caller reporting a failure hands you the key to its log lines.

The remaining keys are what the error handlers attach to an error line. The ones OpenTelemetry's semantic conventions define keep their keys verbatim, and the rest are spelled as the runtime's own lines spell them, so a query written for the runtime's lines finds these too:

Key What it is url.path The request's URL path http.response.status_code The HTTP status actually sent, including any API-level override error.code The code of the problem the response carries: the body's code error.type The class of the exception that escaped, which for an exception that is not a Pipelex error is that exception's own class, and for a failure a route received as a value the class its problem names. A refusal the framework raised, FastAPI's RequestValidationError, Starlette's ClientDisconnect or an HTTPException, is answered by one of the runner's refusals standing in for it, RunnerRequestError or RunnerAuthError, which error.type names and which error.chain follows with the framework's class error.chain The classes of the exceptions the failure was raised from or while handling, by name, outermost first, as a traceback would print them, without their text error.frames On an ERROR line alone, a fault the server has to fix, where the deepest exception of the chain was raised, as file:line in function from the outermost frame inward, without the source lines error_domain input, config or runtime — who fixes it. On a failure the runtime raised it is read from the problem's domain, the input and method domains reading input, and the account and operator domains config error_category The inference error category, on a failure the cause chain of which carries one retryable Whether a blind retry can help: the problem's retry is yes error.params.<name> Each parameter of the problem that the registry declares operator-only, one key per parameter, such as error.params.component for the setting a runtime.misconfigured names, or error.params.dependency for the service a runtime.unavailable could not reach. Such a parameter names the runtime's own configuration or one of its components, never a caller's content, and a caller's response leaves it out with the rest of the diagnostics, so the line is where the operator reads it whichever view the response took user.id The authenticated caller, when auth bound one. An identity the server refused, a token's user_id claim or a forwarded X-User-Id that is not a path-safe segment, is never written under it: the warning about the refusal carries the claim's type as claim_type, and no value at all for the header pipe_code The pipe the request named, on a run route whose body parsed pipeline_run_id The run the request named, on a run route whose body parsed backend_name, model_handle The inference backend that served the model and the handle the pipe named it by, on a failure that reached one; the operator view's diagnostics carries them as provider.name and model. backend_name is only ever the backend the error names, which a worker attributes its failure to: a failure no worker attributed carries none, even when the provider's own metadata names who answered, openai or gateway, since that is neither a backend's name nor an SDK's as the backends configuration spells them, and the record leaves it off rather than write it under backend_name or sdk provider_status_code, provider_request_id The inference provider's own status and request id, on a failure that reached one: the operator view's diagnostics.provider.status and diagnostics.provider.request_id

A key whose value is not set for this request is absent from the line rather than written as null, so a query filtering on presence gets an honest answer.

The record took these keys when the server's lines were brought to the log-call conventions, and it dropped two things it carried before: the event key, whose one value, api_error, the fixed message now plays the part of, and the message built from the status and the error type, API error 422: InvalidModelCategory. A query, a dashboard or an alert written for the earlier record moves to the keys of this one:

Earlier record This record event = api_error message = A request ended in an error response message = API error <status>: <error type> message = A request ended in an error response, with http.response.status_code and error.type route url.path user_id user.id error_type error.type status http.response.status_code provider backend_name model model_handle

The other keys, error_domain, error_category, retryable, pipe_code, pipeline_run_id, provider_status_code and provider_request_id, kept their names. error.code came later, with the problem document.

Every error line carries error.code, since every failure, the runner's own refusals included, is answered by a problem with a registry code. The record is built from the problem's operator view, whichever view the response carried, so error.type names the class of the error behind it, and the sentence the response carried is the code's, which error.code already names. Build an operator query on error.code or error.type, with url.path. The error's message, which can quote what the caller sent or a foreign exception's text, never rides the line: it rides the operator view's diagnostics alone, which only a request the operator authenticated reads in its response (AUTH_MODE=api_key, or a trusted proxy's forwarded identity). A request authenticated by a caller's token reads the caller view, so for it the line is the operator's whole account: the code, the classes of the chain, the frames of a fault the server has to fix and the operator-only parameters. Two keys the line carried before the runner's refusals took codes are gone: detail, the explanation an API-authored refusal wrote, which error.code replaces, and the exception key holding a 5xx's traceback, which error.chain and error.frames replace without any exception's text.

Every field in that table is a record attribute, which is a different thing from the message. A structured sink — json here, and the OTLP sink — writes them beside the message as keys. The Rich console sink shows them after the message as a key=value suffix, each value on one line and cut short when long, a handled exception's error.message at a far more generous length, and leaves out the run identifiers (request_id, pipeline_run_id), which a person at a terminal does not need on every line, so A request ended in an error response is followed by the path, the status, the error type and the rest of the fields above. That rendering is for a person reading a terminal; keep sink = "json" wherever the lines are read by anything else.

The level says who has to act, read from the HTTP status and from the domain of the code, the registry's answer to who must act. A 4xx is the caller's to act on, a mistake or a benign conflict, and logs at WARNING. A 5xx logs at ERROR, with error.frames, only when the server has something to fix: its code's domain is runtime or operator. A 501 logs at WARNING without frames whatever its domain, because it states that this deployment does not offer what the request asks for, custom Python without a sandbox, /v1/start on a blocking-only orchestrator, a model it serves no backend for: nothing is broken, and any caller could fill the error-rate alerts by asking again. A 5xx whose code's domain is the caller's, input, method or account, such as a webhook receiver of the caller's own refusing a delivery, logs at WARNING too. A request no route serves, a 404 for its path or a 405 for its method, logs at DEBUG: scanners probe for such paths by the thousand, and nobody has anything to do about them. See Error Responses for the response side of the same failure.

docs.title: Security events
docs.text:
A request a security rule refused writes one more line beside its error line: the security event, so that whoever runs the server learns that someone tried to reach what a rule forbids, a private address, another tenant's stored file, a path on the server's disk, a template reaching for a private name. It is a record of its own kind, which a query or an alert selects without reading any text: its logger is pipelex.errors.security_event, its message is A security rule refused a request, and its event.name is pipelex.security.refusal. It is written at WARNING, with no traceback.

{"time": "2026-10-17T09:12:03.512Z", "severity": "WARNING", "logger": "pipelex.errors.security_event", "message": "A security rule refused a request", "request_id": "01M2TCP02W04RZG6DTM8AR508C", "event.name": "pipelex.security.refusal", "error.code": "security.input_url_refused", "error.domain": "input", "error.type": "UriReadRefusedError", "security.target": "url", "security.target_class": "scheme", "run.extras.org_id": "org_abc"}

Its keys name the refusal and never its content: the refusal's code under error.code, the code's domain under error.domain, the class of the error under error.type, the kind of thing refused under security.target, the class of destination under security.target_class when the rule could tell it, the run and the request under pipeline_run_id and request_id, and each of the labels the body names as analytics_groups, the run's extras, under a key of its own, run.extras.<key>. The labels are read as soon as a JSON body is parsed, before any of its fields is refused, on every route, so a diagnostic route that runs nothing, /validate, /resolve, /codegen or /pipe-io, names whose request it refused as a run route does; labels the runtime's own rules refuse are never written. Never the URL, the path, the template or an input value, which are the caller's content or the method's. The Pipelex documentation's error model lists every value.

The server writes it for the refusals its own boundary decides too, which keep the response they always had: a run body carrying a reserved object key (pipelex.security.reserved_key, security.target object_key), a callback URL whose scheme is not http or https or whose host is a loopback, private, link-local or cloud metadata address (security.input_url_refused, with the class of destination), and a resource path or a key of a method tree, files or a bundle_b64 member, that leaves the method: absolute, naming a drive or a network share, or climbing out with a .. segment, read with either separator, so ..\secrets\key.pem, C:/Windows/win.ini and \\server\share are among them (security.input_path_refused). A refusal of the shape of a field, an empty callback URL, one with no scheme or no host, or a path that is empty or holds an empty segment, a backslash or a colon, is the caller's mistake and writes no event, under resources as under files. The event never carries a pipeline_run_id a body names: before any run exists, that id is the caller's claim.

A refusal is written once, by the process that raised it, whichever part of that process saw it: during a run executed in-process, before the run while its inputs are read or its method loads, while an orchestration plugin prepares a run in this process before it dispatches it, or in the handler answering the request. A run dispatched to a worker under a distributed orchestration_mode is refused in the worker's process, so its event is in the worker's logs, written there by its orchestration plugin, and never in this server's: the failure the server receives back, or never receives for a /start run, is not logged a second time. The Pipelex documentation's error model states the rule an orchestration plugin follows.

docs.title: Authentication lines
docs.text:
The error line above is the record of every refused request, a 401 included, at WARNING. The authentication check before it says why it refused, at a level that depends on who has to act:

  • A caller's own mistake logs at DEBUG: no bearer token, an expired or invalid token, a wrong API key. Each is the line A caller's credentials were refused, its auth_mode naming the mode in force and its auth_refusal_reason one of missing_bearer_token, expired_token, invalid_token and api_key_mismatch, with an invalid token's error.type and error.message beside it. The operator can do nothing about a client holding a stale token, so its refusals add nothing to the warnings beyond the error line of each request.
  • A misconfiguration of the deployment keeps its level: forwarded identity headers trusted while a request arrives without a user id log at WARNING, and an unset JWT_SECRET_KEY or API_KEY at ERROR, each naming the variable in env_var. An unknown AUTH_MODE writes no line here, because the server refuses to start with it (see Authentication). A token that verifies against the server's secret but whose user_id claim is missing, is not a path-safe segment or is the reserved single-tenant id logs at WARNING too: whoever minted it holds the secret, so it is the deployment's token issuer that needs fixing, which the line's user_action says.

docs.title: Configuration
docs.text:
The keys live in [runtime.log] of the server's own api/.pipelex/pipelex.toml, which the image copies to /root/.pipelex/:

[runtime.log]
default_log_level = "INFO"
sink = "json"
console_log_target = "stderr"
pretty_print_mode = "silent"

[runtime.log.package_log_levels]
pipelex = "INFO"
  • sink = "json" selects the one-object-per-line renderer. The alternative, "console", is the Rich renderer meant for a terminal. This server does not ask for Pipelex's cli extra, but that does not put the renderer out of reach: typer and instructor are core Pipelex dependencies that require Rich unconditionally, so Rich is installed in the image and an import pipelex loads it. Selecting "console" here would therefore give you a working console sink, not a refusal. This key is what keeps the renderer unused, and it is the only thing that does.
  • console_log_target = "stderr" keeps logs off the data channel.
  • pretty_print_mode = "silent" suppresses the "Output of pipe" panel an operator pipe would otherwise draw: there is no terminal to draw into, and a server should not spend time rendering on the thread serving a request.
  • [runtime.log.package_log_levels] raises or lowers one package's level independently of default_log_level.

To change any of this for a deployment, mount a pipelex_override.toml into /root/.pipelex/ with just the keys you want different — see Configuration. Note that replacing the whole config directory, which that page documents as Option 2, drops the shipped pipelex.toml along with the three keys above and silently returns the server to Pipelex's terminal-facing defaults; a layered override does not.

docs.title: Blob store lines
docs.text:
A file a request names by its hash is read from the runner's blob store and checked against that hash. Bytes that do not hash to it, or are not the size the store holds the blob at, are a damaged object in the deployment's storage, and the request is answered 500 pipelex.storage.damaged, whose verdict is not to retry, since a retry reads the same object (see Error Responses). Beside the request's error line, the store writes one line at ERROR naming the object, the one place the operator reads which object to remove, after which the blob is uploaded again:

{"time": "2026-10-17T10:41:09.204Z", "severity": "ERROR", "logger": "pipelex_api.blob_store", "message": "Stored blob bytes do not match their hash", "request_id": "01M2TCP02W04RZG6DTM8AR508C", "blob_sha256": "9f86d081884c7d659a2feaa0c55ad015a3bf4f1b2b0b822cd15d6c15b0f00a08", "blob_size_bytes": 14, "read_size_bytes": 14, "storage_scheme": "s3"}

Its keys are the blob's hash under blob_sha256, the size the store holds it at under blob_size_bytes, the size of the bytes read under read_size_bytes, and the kind of storage under storage_scheme, null for a storage plugin whose kind the registry does not list. Never the bytes themselves, which are a caller's file.

docs.title: Uvicorn's own lines
docs.text:
Uvicorn logs through its own handlers, not through the sink above, so its startup banner and its access log are plain text rather than JSON: the banner on stderr, the access log on stdout. Uvicorn also logs, with its traceback, any exception that leaves the app it runs, and Starlette's own catch-all raises the exception it answered again for that purpose; the server stops every exception there (AnsweredErrorBarrier in pipelex_api/exception_handlers.py), so uvicorn never writes an exception's text. The error line above stays the one record of a failure the catch-all answered, even one that ended a response already streaming, since Starlette runs the catch-all then too. A failure no handler recorded, the catch-all's own failure while a response was streaming, or the server's failure to send the answer the barrier built, such as to a client already gone, is written at ERROR before it is dropped, as A request failed after its response had started, with url.path, the status already sent under http.response.status_code, absent when the catch-all failed before any status was sent, and error.type and error.chain naming its classes, never any exception's text. No response answers it: the status and part of the body had already left. Pass --no-access-log to turn the access log off, which is what the hosted deployment does; configure uvicorn's --log-config if you want its lines structured too.

docs.title: Models
docs.text: Two routes tell a client about the models a method may name on this runner: the deck it routes to, and whether one model reference resolves on it. A client asks them rather than keeping its own table of providers, its own parser of model references or its own copy of the deck.

docs.title: List the deck
docs.text:
Endpoint: GET /v1/models

The MTHDS Protocol's models operation, tagged x-mthds-protocol in the OpenAPI artifact. It answers the protocol's model deck: a flat models list of the deck's presets, each a {name, type} entry whose type is one of the protocol's model categories, plus this implementation's routing extensions, aliases and waterfalls, keyed by category because the same alias name exists in several categories.

The optional type query parameter filters the deck to one category: llm, extract, img_gen, search or judgment. It takes a single value, so a repeated type, and an unknown or empty one, is a 422 request.invalid naming the field type.

docs.title: Check a model reference
docs.text:
Endpoint: GET /v1/models/check

Answers whether one model reference resolves on this runner, as what kind of reference, to which model, and, when it does not, what the caller most likely meant. It reads the runner's deck and the models the runner can call, and runs no inference.

It is a Pipelex API extension, not an MTHDS Protocol route: it is not tagged x-mthds-protocol. The answer comes from pipelex's own reference parser and the deck lookups a validation runs, so a reference the check finds resolved in a category is one a pipe of that category may name in its model field, and one it finds not found is one a validation refuses. A client therefore needs no grammar of its own to read a reference.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
Query parameter Required Meaning reference yes, once The reference as a method's model field writes it: $preset, @alias, ~waterfall, a bare model handle, or one of the spelled-out namespaces preset:, alias:, waterfall: and handle:. Leading and trailing whitespace is ignored, and the trimmed reference holds at most 199 characters. type no, at most once The category to check in. When it is absent, the check is made in every category it covers.

The check covers the protocol's model categories, in the protocol's order (llm, extract, img_gen, search, judgment), then doc_gen, the family of PipeDocGen. The protocol defines no category for doc_gen, so GET /v1/models leaves it out, but a method names a doc_gen model like any other, so the check answers in it. Every list the check returns that is ordered by category follows this order.

docs.title: Resolution
docs.text:
The reference is parsed as a method's model field is: a sigil first ($ preset, @ alias, ~ waterfall), then a spelled-out namespace, and otherwise a bare handle. alias:best-gpt and @best-gpt are the same reference. handle: is the bare kind's own namespace: it writes a bare name without reading a sigil, so handle:@best-gpt is the bare name @best-gpt, not the alias best-gpt, and handle:best-gpt is the bare name best-gpt. Like any bare name, it resolves as a model of that name, then an alias, then a waterfall of that name: where the runner serves a model @best-gpt, the check resolves to it and a run calls it, and where the deck holds nothing of that name, a validation refuses it as the check finds it not_found. A suggestion naming a handle spelled like a reference writes it with the namespace, handle:@best-gpt, so it can be written back as it is.

A reference resolves in a category when the runner holds its name there:

  • a preset, an alias or a waterfall, when the deck defines that name in the category;
  • a bare handle, as a run reads it: when the runner can call a model of that name in the category, among every model it can call and not only those the deck names; failing that, when the category defines an alias of that name, or a waterfall of that name while model fallback is on. A model of that name in another category does not make it resolve, so an LLM handle checked as img_gen is not_found, as a validation refuses it in a PipeImgGen.

The reference is resolved when it resolves in at least one category in scope, and not_found otherwise. Both values are definitive: a client that reads a value it does not know treats the reference as unresolved.

Resolution is a matter of names, like a validation. A preset, an alias or a waterfall the deck defines resolves even when its binding reaches no model the runner can call (a target on a backend the runner has not enabled, a waterfall none of whose usable steps it serves, a binding that leads back to itself through aliases and waterfalls), and its match says so with a resolves_to of null. A sigiled reference resolves by its sigil, in the check and in a run alike: ~best-gpt is the waterfall even where an alias or a model is also named best-gpt. A waterfall step that leads back to an alias or a waterfall being resolved is a step no model serves, and so is a step reaching another waterfall none of whose models the runner serves, so the waterfall goes on to its next step. The check reads the deck as a run would and leaves no trace: it logs nothing, and the one-time notice a run logs when a waterfall falls back is left to that run. A run through such a reference fails where a validation passes, so a client shows it as a warning rather than as an unknown name.

docs.title: The verdict
docs.text:
A verdict is a 200, whatever the resolution:

Field Type Meaning reference string The caller's reference, trimmed. kind "preset", "alias", "waterfall" or "handle" What the reference names, from its parsing. name string The reference without its sigil or namespace. category string or null The type asked, or null when none was. resolution "resolved" or "not_found" Whether the reference resolves in a category in scope. matches list One entry per category in scope where the reference resolves, in category order. Empty on not_found. suggestions list of strings On not_found, the nearest names the caller may have meant. other_kinds list of strings On not_found, the same name under another kind, in the categories in scope. other_categories list of strings On not_found with a type, the categories outside it where the same reference resolves.

A matches entry says what the reference is in one category. A field that does not apply to the reference's kind is absent rather than null:

Field Present for Meaning category every kind The category the entry is about. resolves_to every kind The model handle a run through the reference would call now in this category, or null when it would find none: a preset and an alias through their target, a waterfall through the first of its steps the runner serves (its first step alone when model fallback is off), and a handle itself, or, for a bare name that resolves through an alias or a waterfall, what that alias or waterfall resolves to. target preset, alias The model the deck binds the name to, as the deck writes it, which may itself be a reference (@default-premium). description preset The preset's description, or null when the deck gives it none. fallbacks waterfall The waterfall's steps, in order. via handle The presets, aliases and waterfalls of the category whose binding names the handle directly, each written as a reference.

A preset, checked in its category:

{
  "reference": "$writing-factual",
  "kind": "preset",
  "name": "writing-factual",
  "category": "llm",
  "resolution": "resolved",
  "matches": [
    { "category": "llm", "resolves_to": "gpt-5.6-sol", "target": "@default-premium", "description": "Factual writing with high accuracy" }
  ],
  "suggestions": [],
  "other_kinds": [],
  "other_categories": []
}

docs.title: Suggestions
docs.text:
On not_found, suggestions, other_kinds and other_categories say what the caller may have meant. They follow the rule a validation follows when it refuses an unknown model, so the check offers what a failing validation of the same reference offers, applied in each category in scope and joined in category order, a name two categories give appearing once, at its first place:

  • suggestions: up to five names of the reference's own kind, nearest first, then, for each other kind under which the name does not exist exactly, up to three names of that kind, with a stricter threshold of nearness. For a handle, the candidates are every model the runner can call in the category.
  • other_kinds: the same name under each other kind the category defines it as (best-gpt asked as a preset, found as @best-gpt). It is the likeliest fault, so a client shows it first.
  • other_categories: when type was given, each other category where the same reference resolves ($gen-image asked as llm, found in img_gen).

Every name is written as a method would write it, a sigil for a preset, an alias or a waterfall and a bare name for a handle, without the kind labels a validation's report adds.

A preset name asked under the alias sigil:

{
  "reference": "@writing-factual",
  "kind": "alias",
  "name": "writing-factual",
  "category": "llm",
  "resolution": "not_found",
  "matches": [],
  "suggestions": [],
  "other_kinds": ["$writing-factual"],
  "other_categories": []
}

docs.title: Refusals
docs.text:
A request the route cannot produce a verdict for is a 422 application/problem+json with the code request.invalid, carrying no verdict, whose field parameter names the query parameter it refuses:

Cause field reference missing or given more than once, blank once trimmed, a sigil or namespace with nothing after it, or longer than 199 characters reference type given more than once, unknown or empty type

A reference that parses and resolves nowhere is never refused: it is the not_found verdict, which is the successful product of the call. See Error Responses for the problem document's shape.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: MTHDS Tools
docs.text: The MTHDS Tools endpoints expose lightweight editor tooling for a single .mthds file. They are Pipelex API extensions, not MTHDS Protocol routes.

docs.title: Lint
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /v1/lint

/lint checks one .mthds file with pipelex-tools-py. It validates fully offline against the embedded official MTHDS schema; the request path does not fetch schemas or read local catalog files.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
• content (string, required): one .mthds file's contents
  • source (string | null, optional): logical filename reserved for diagnostic locators; accepted for parity with pipelex-tools-py
{
  "content": "domain = \"hello\"\nmain_pipe = \"echo\"\n",
  "source": "hello.mthds"
}

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
/lint is a diagnostic endpoint: malformed .mthds content returns HTTP 200 with diagnostics in the body. Request-shape problems, such as missing content or a file over the configured per-file limit, return RFC 9457 problem responses.

{
  "diagnostics": [
    {
      "kind": "syntax",
      "severity": "error",
      "message": "expected value",
      "location": null,
      "range": {
        "start_offset": 6,
        "end_offset": 6,
        "start_line": 1,
        "start_col": 7,
        "end_line": 1,
        "end_col": 7
      }
    }
  ]
}

An empty diagnostics array means the file is clean.

docs.title: Format
docs.text:
Endpoint: POST /v1/format

/format formats one .mthds file with the canonical formatter from pipelex-tools-py.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
• content (string, required): one .mthds file's contents
  • options (object | null, optional): formatter options passed through to pipelex-tools-py, such as column_width
{
  "content": "a=1",
  "options": { "column_width": 120 }
}

docs.title: Response
docs.text:
Syntax errors return HTTP 200 with the original content unchanged and diagnostics describing the blocking issue. Malformed formatter options, such as a non-numeric column_width, are caller input errors and return RFC 9457 422 responses.

{
  "formatted": "a = 1\n",
  "changed": true,
  "diagnostics": []
}

changed is true when formatted differs from content.

Copy Markdown

docs.title: Pipe Builder (/v1/build/*) — REMOVED
docs.text: The five build routes are gone from this server: POST /v1/build/inputs, POST /v1/build/output, POST /v1/build/runner, POST /v1/build/concept and POST /v1/build/pipe-spec now answer 404. The runtime code that only these routes and their local twins used went after them: the concept and pipe specs, pipelex-agent concept, pipelex-agent pipe and pipelex build runner.

docs.title: What replaces each one
docs.text:
• An inputs template (/v1/build/inputs) is projected by the client from the input form that POST /v1/pipe-io returns, with the mthds packages' projection: renderInputsTemplate from mthds/protocol, which @pipelex/sdk re-exports, or mthds.protocol.inputs_template in Python. mthds-agent inputs does exactly that. pipelex build inputs still writes the engine's own rendering locally, the template the removed route returned, which differs from the client projection where the projection fixture corpus records.
  • A pipe's declared output (/v1/build/output) is described by the output_form and the pipe I/O contract that POST /v1/pipe-io returns. The rendered output example has no HTTP replacement; pipelex build output renders it locally.
  • The typed structures a runner script imported (/v1/build/runner) are the python-structures target of POST /v1/codegen. The runner script itself has no replacement: Build Runner says how to write one.
  • The concept and pipe spec conversions (/v1/build/concept, /v1/build/pipe-spec) have no replacement: a method is written as MTHDS directly and checked with POST /v1/validate.

docs.title: Pipe I/O
docs.text:
Return a method's I/O artifacts — its pipe I/O contracts, its input form and its output form — without validating it.

Endpoint: POST /v1/pipe-io

The route resolves the closure through the same static core as POST /v1/resolve, selects a pipe with the selection chain below, and derives the three artifacts with the builder that POST /v1/validate and every run already call. It runs no dry-run sweep, so a call costs one load and one derivation, where /v1/validate mock-runs every pipe of the method. A caller that shows a method, prepares its inputs or generates types for it reads this route; a caller that needs the dry-run verdict or the dry-run graph stays on /v1/validate, whose views still attach both forms beside the verdict.

It is a Pipelex API extension, not an MTHDS Protocol route: it is not tagged x-mthds-protocol in the OpenAPI artifact. The artifacts it carries are the standard's, under their neutral names — see the MTHDS specification's pages on pipe I/O contracts, the input-form descriptor and the output-form descriptor.

It speaks the /v1/validate verdict discipline: a produced verdict is always a 200 discriminated on is_valid, and a non-2xx is reserved for a request that produced no verdict.

docs.title: Request
docs.text:
The body names the method as the crate routes do, a method tree read exactly as /v1/validate and the run routes read it, plus a pipe selector and two opt-ins:

  • files (object) or method_ref (string), exactly one: the method, as on /v1/resolve. files is the MTHDS protocol's map of file entries, each key a tree path and each value the file's text, {"base64": "…"} or {"sha256": "…", "size": n}; method_ref an address-form reference to a published package, whose whole tree is fetched. Neither or both is a request-shape 422.
  • dependencies (object, optional): the method packages the method calls by address, each a map of file entries keyed by its address, as on a run. It accompanies files only.
  • pipe_ref (string, optional): the qualified ref domain.pipe_code of the pipe to describe. Omitted, the selection chain below decides.
  • all_pipes (boolean, default false): describe every pipe the closure loads instead of the selected one.
  • include_files (boolean, default false): echo the text of the method's own .mthds bundles on the valid arm.
  • resources (object, optional): Being retired, and refused by a later release: a file the steps read travels inside the method's tree, in files, at its path beside the bundle that names it. Files the method's steps read, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, keyed by the path from the tree's root, each in standard base64, joining the tree as on /v1/validate. It accompanies files only. A step whose template file the tree does not hold makes the method invalid.
  • read_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The scope the request reads the method under, as on /v1/validate: a hash entry of files resolves in that scope's blob store, and only a request carrying it records the tree it read there; a jwt caller may send only a scope under its own id, else a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is read_scope_under_caller.

There is no views field, because the valid arm always carries all three artifacts. The hosted API also accepts a catalog method_id, which the platform resolves into the method's files before forwarding, so this server never declares it.

{
  "files": {
    "METHODS.toml": "...manifest...",
    "main.mthds": "...bundle...",
    "templates/invoice.docx": { "base64": "UEsDBBQABgAIAAAAIQ..." }
  },
  "all_pipes": true,
  "include_files": true
}

The tree's refusals produce no verdict, as on /v1/validate: a 422 method.package_invalid naming the rule or the limit as its reason, security.input_path_refused, request.invalid or request.blobs_missing, and the custom-Python policy's refusals (see No verdict).

docs.title: Pipe selection
docs.text:
The selection chain takes the request's pipe_ref; else the main_pipe of the METHODS.toml at the tree's root, whether the tree was fetched by method_ref or sent in files; else the closure's own main_pipe declaration, when exactly one domain declares one. A root METHODS.toml the route cannot read as a manifest, being no UTF-8 text or no valid manifest, is a 422 problem coded method.package_invalid when the request names no pipe. A request naming its pipe in pipe_ref never reads the manifest to select it, so there a manifest the route cannot read refuses nothing and only leaves default_pipe_ref a stated null. The chain stops at the first link that is present, so a manifest main_pipe the closure does not declare, or declares in several domains, is a failed selection rather than a fall-through to the closure's declarations.

The closure is resolved first, so an invalid closure answers its invalid verdict whatever pipe_ref names. For a valid closure these selections are refused with a 422 problem whose code names the failure, never the request.invalid of a malformed request, so a client tells a selection refusal from a request-shape one by that member:

  • request.pipe_not_found for a pipe_ref that names no pipe of the closure, with the selection as its pipe parameter;
  • request.pipe_ambiguous for a bare code that matches pipes in several domains, with the selection as its pipe parameter and the qualified refs to choose from as its candidates;
  • request.pipe_unspecified, without all_pipes, for a request with no pipe_ref whose closure declares no main_pipe, or several, whose qualified refs are then its candidates;
  • method.pipe_unresolved for a manifest main_pipe the closure does not declare, the method's own declaration to fix, with the declared selection as its missing parameter;
  • method.ref_ambiguous for a manifest main_pipe that matches pipes in several domains of the closure, the method's own declaration to fix, with the declared selection as its ref parameter and the qualified refs it matches as its candidates.

The problem's type, title, sentences and step are the code's: a request's selection asks the caller to select a pipe the method declares, and a manifest's asks the method's author to correct the declaration.

An unknown or ambiguous pipe_ref answers the code the run routes answer for the same pipe_code. A closure declaring no main_pipe, or several, has no run-route twin: this route refuses both as the pipe-selector design classifies them, while a run over such a closure today fails with a 500 or runs the first declaration.

A bare pipe_ref that matches one pipe (echo where smoke.echo is meant) is still resolved today, and the valid arm reports the qualified ref.

With all_pipes: true the route never refuses for want of an entry pipe, so a method that declares no entry pipe, or several, is still describable. The valid arm's pipe_ref is then the requested ref (an unknown one is still a 422), else the chain's answer, else null.

docs.title: Response (valid verdict)
docs.text:
{
  "is_valid": true,
  "pipe_ref": "smoke.echo",
  "pipe_io_contracts": { "smoke.echo": { "inputs": { "…": {} }, "output": { "…": {} } } },
  "input_form": { "smoke.echo": { "fields": [ { "kind": "prose", "name": "text", "…": "…" } ] } },
  "output_form": { "smoke.echo": { "field": { "kind": "prose", "name": "output", "…": "…" } } },
  "default_pipe_ref": "smoke.echo",
  "pending_signatures": [],
  "is_runnable": true,
  "files": { "main.mthds": "...bundle..." }
}
  • is_valid (true): the closure parsed, loaded and passed static validation. It does not mean a dry run passed; this route runs none.
  • pipe_ref (string | null): the qualified ref the selection resolved, read off the resolved pipe and never echoed from the request. null only under all_pipes when nothing resolves.
  • pipe_io_contracts, input_form, output_form (objects keyed by qualified pipe_ref): the three artifacts, sharing one key set — the resolved pipe_ref alone by default, every pipe the closure loads under all_pipes.
  • default_pipe_ref (string | null): the method's own entry pipe, the selection chain without the request's pipe_ref. A request that omits pipe_ref therefore always answers pipe_ref == default_pipe_ref. When the request named a pipe, or asked for all_pipes, and the chain finds no entry pipe or several, the field is a stated null, as it is when the request named a pipe and the root METHODS.toml cannot be read.
  • pending_signatures (list of strings) and is_runnable (boolean): exactly what they mean on /v1/validate — the qualified refs of the pipes still declared as signatures, and not pending_signatures. Both come from the loaded library with no dry run, so a method whose dry run would fail is still reported runnable here.
  • files (object, only with include_files: true): the text of each .mthds bundle of the method's own tree, keyed by its tree path. For a tree sent in files, it is the request's bundles, whatever entry form carried them; for a method_ref, the fetched package's bundles, each keyed by its path from the package root. The tree's other files and the bundles of its dependencies are never included. Without include_files the field is absent, not empty.

The artifacts are pinned to /v1/validate. For a closure both routes accept, each artifact map equals the same-named field of /v1/validate's valid arm (requested with views: ["input_form", "output_form"]) restricted to the same keys: both routes derive them with the one builder and dump them the same way, keeping null members such as a contract's item_count: null. Both routes read the same tree, but they do not accept exactly the same methods: this route loads a package the method calls by its address only from what was shipped with it (see Resolve & Codegen), where /v1/validate also looks among the methods installed on the runner and fetches one on a miss; /v1/validate refuses a method whose dry run fails, which this route accepts, and checks the tree's Python by syntax and a method_ref package's requirements.txt, which this route does not; this route refuses a root METHODS.toml it cannot read when the request names no pipe, since its selection chain then reads the manifest, where /v1/validate still answers a verdict.

default_pipe_ref is not /v1/validate's field of the same name. That one is the run default: where several domains declare a main_pipe, it names the first declaring blueprint's, because a run would take it, while this route refuses to choose and states null.

docs.title: Response (invalid verdict)
docs.text: An invalid closure is the 200 crate verdict /v1/resolve gives: is_valid: false, the structured errors[] and a message. A call into a package nothing shipped is one, its method.dependency_missing item naming the package's address as its name. It carries no artifacts, no pipe_ref or default_pipe_ref, no runnability facts and no files, whatever the request asked for.

docs.title: No verdict
docs.text:
Every non-2xx is RFC 9457 application/problem+json (see Error Responses):

  • 422 for a malformed body or neither or both method selectors, request.invalid naming the field; for a tree the runner cannot read, method.package_invalid, security.input_path_refused or request.blobs_missing, as on /v1/resolve; for an unreadable root manifest on a request naming no pipe, method.package_invalid; and for the selection refusals above, by their codes.
  • The method_ref fetch outcomes, exactly as on /v1/resolve: 404 method.not_found when no package in the fetched repository matches the address, 422 for a reference that does not parse (request.invalid) or a package the server cannot accept (method.ambiguous, method.package_invalid), 502 method.fetch_failed when the fetch itself failed, and 422 request.unsupported for a registry-form reference.
  • The custom-Python policy of /v1/validate and the run routes, whose tree the route loads: a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox for a tree holding a .py file on a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted, where loading the library would import each .py declaring a structure class and run its module-level code in the server's process, and a 422 pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused for one whose Python declares a structure class.
  • 401 / 403 for authentication, a 403 auth.forbidden naming read_scope_under_caller among them, and 413 request.too_large for a body over the size limit.
  • 500 when an artifact cannot be derived: a pipe whose input or output JSON Schema cannot be rendered raises PipeIOContractError, which answers 500 as it does on /v1/validate — a fault of the tool, not a verdict about the method.

docs.title: Pipe Run
docs.text:
Execute pipelines with flexible input formats. Choose between synchronous execution (wait for completion) or asynchronous execution (non-blocking). Both routes are part of the MTHDS Protocol — this server is the protocol's reference implementation.

About files and MTHDS. An "MTHDS file" is a Pipelex pipeline definition written in TOML (with the .mthds extension), and a method is the folder holding its .mthds files with the other files its steps read. Both endpoints below take the method in files, a map from each file's path in the method's folder to that file's content, such as {"summarize.mthds": "domain = \"hello\"\n…"} — see Sending a method as a tree. With no pipe_code, the run starts at the method's entry pipe, its main_pipe; pipe_code names another pipe of the method to start at, or, sent alone, a pipe already registered on the server. A published method is run by its address instead, in method_ref.

mthds_contents is being retired. The older field, a JSON array of .mthds texts that must include a file declaring main_pipe when no pipe_code is sent, is still accepted, together with bundle_b64 and resources, but a later release refuses all three. Send the method in files.

docs.title: Execute Pipeline
docs.text:
Execute a Pipelex pipeline with flexible inputs and wait for completion.

Endpoint: POST /v1/execute

Backend selected by orchestration_mode. /execute dispatches through the deployment's orchestration_mode (config default + optional policy-gated per-request orchestration_mode override), symmetric with /start — see Configuration → Orchestration mode. On the orchestrator-agnostic base (direct, the default) it runs in-process; a temporal flavor dispatches the run to a worker and awaits it. /execute is synchronous (it returns the full output) and always uses BLOCKING delivery — wait-semantics is endpoint-set, never requestable, so there is no fire-and-forget option here (use POST /v1/start). A per-request backend override is honored only where the deployment sets allow_request_orchestration_mode_override = true; otherwise a token differing from the default is refused with a 422 pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden.

Request Body:

{
  "pipe_code": null,
  "files": {
    "my_method.mthds": "domain = \"my_domain\"\nmain_pipe = \"my_pipe\"\n…"
  },
  "inputs": {
    "input_name": "simple text or object"
  },
  "output_name": null,
  "output_multiplicity": null,
  "dynamic_output_concept_ref": null
}

Request Fields:

  • files (object, optional): The method as a map of file entries, the MTHDS standard's method tree: each key a tree path, each value the file's text, {"base64": "…"}, or {"sha256": "…", "size": n} naming bytes this runner holds — see Sending a method as a tree. Mutually exclusive with mthds_contents, bundle_b64 and method_ref.
  • pipe_code (string, optional): The code identifying the pipe to execute. Beside a method sent in files, it names the pipe to start at in place of the method's entry pipe; beside method_ref, it overrides the package's main_pipe; sent alone, it must name a pipe already registered on the server.
  • inputs (PipelineInputs, optional): Flexible input format - see Input Format: PipelineInputs below
  • output_name (string, optional): Name for the output slot
  • output_multiplicity (string, optional): Output multiplicity setting ("single", "variable", or a specific number)
  • dynamic_output_concept_ref (string, optional): Override output concept ref
  • dependencies (object, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The method packages the method calls by address that the runner cannot fetch, each a map of file entries keyed by its address — see Sending the method packages the method calls. Accompanies files.
  • method_ref (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. Run a published method by address instead of inline source — see Running a method by address. Mutually exclusive with mthds_contents and with a method sent as a tree; pipe_code may accompany it to override the package's main_pipe.
  • mthds_contents (list[str], optional): Being retired: send the method in files. Inline MTHDS file contents as raw strings (always an array, even for a single file). If provided without pipe_code, the bundle must contain a file with a main_pipe property. Still accepted until a later release refuses it.
  • bundle_b64 (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension, being retired with mthds_contents: send the method in files. Base64-encoded zip of the method's folder, read as a map of its entries, which may carry the method packages it calls under .mthds/methods/<name>/. Mutually exclusive with files.
  • resources (dict[str, str], optional): Pipelex-API extension, being retired with mthds_contents: put the files in the method's tree, in files. The files the bundle's steps read, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, as a map from the path the step names to the file's bytes in standard base64 — see Sending the files the steps read. It accompanies mthds_contents or a method sent as a tree, whose tree each file joins at its path from the root; beside method_ref, or with no bundle at all, it is a 422. The job names the method's tree by its digest and carries none of its files: the step that reads one, on an orchestrator that runs the job remotely such as Temporal included, reads it through the deployment's method file store.
  • storage_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The prefix every object this run writes lands under — see Host-supplied run context.
  • read_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The prefix every stored object this run reads must lie under — see Host-supplied run context.
  • analytics_groups (dict[str, str], optional): Pipelex-API extension. The groups this run's telemetry belongs to, such as {"organization": "org_acme"} — see Host-supplied run context.
  • pipeline_run_id (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension on /execute. The run's id, at most 128 characters, chosen by the caller as on /start: the response and the run's webhooks carry it, and a run still in flight under the same id refuses the request with a 409 pipelex.run.already_exists. When absent, the server generates one.
  • callback_urls (list[str], optional): Pipelex-API extension. The URLs that each receive the run's signed run.finished event once it ends, before the response is sent; their delivery never changes the response, but a receiver that never answers delays it by about 51 seconds at most, the delivery's three attempts of 15 seconds and its waits between them. See Webhooks.

Validation Rules:

  • At least one of files, method_ref, pipe_code or a method sent the older way (mthds_contents or bundle_b64) must be provided
  • If only pipe_code: Must reference a pipe already registered in the library
  • With files and no pipe_code: the run starts at the method's entry pipe, the main_pipe of its root METHODS.toml or else the one main_pipe its bundles declare (see Sending a method as a tree)
  • With mthds_contents and no pipe_code: a file must declare main_pipe
  • With pipe_code beside a method: pipe_code specifies which pipe of that method to execute

Response:

{
  "pipeline_run_id": "abc123...",
  "created_at": "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z",
  "state": "COMPLETED",
  "finished_at": "2026-01-15T12:00:05Z",
  "main_stuff_name": "result",
  "crate_fingerprint": "9f2c41…",
  "pipe_output": {
    "working_memory": {
      "root": { "result": { "content": { "...": "..." } } },
      "aliases": { "main_stuff": "result" }
    }
  }
}

Response Fields:

  • pipeline_run_id (string): Unique identifier for the run.
  • created_at (string): ISO timestamp when the pipeline was created.
  • state (string): One of "RUNNING", "COMPLETED", "FAILED", "CANCELLED", "ERROR", "STARTED".
  • finished_at (string | null): ISO timestamp when the pipeline finished, or null if still running.
  • main_stuff_name (string | null): Key under pipe_output.working_memory.root where the main result lives. Use this to extract the typed output: pipe_output.working_memory.root[main_stuff_name].content.
  • crate_fingerprint (string | null): Pipelex extension. The fingerprint of the library crate the run's method was loaded into, the identity of its concepts and pipes, which changes with their meaning and not with their formatting or comments; a host records it on its run beside the digest of the method tree that ran. null when the run was built from no crate.
  • pipe_output (object): Result of the pipeline execution. Contains working_memory with root (every named stuff produced during the run) and aliases (built-in name mappings such as main_stuff).
  • pipe_output.tokens_usages (array | null): Per-inference-call token usage in the client wire shape (TokensUsageRecord): model_type, model name/id, pipe_code, job-kind fields, nb_tokens_by_category, computed USD cost (null when the model has no rate table), and ISO timestamps. null when usage assembly was off for the run, [] when no inference happened. pipe_output.usage_assembly_error (string | null) is non-null when usage assembly failed. See the pipelex runtime's TokensUsage Wire Records for the full field reference.
  • pipe_output.graph_spec (object | null): Best-effort execution graph of the run — the nodes and edges the run actually traversed. null when graph generation was off for the run, which is the interpreter.pipeline_execution.is_generate_graph setting (true in the packaged config); it does not depend on runtime.tracing, whose is_enabled selects a trace-emission backend rather than gating assembly. pipe_output.graph_assembly_error (string | null) is non-null when assembly ran and failed, which is what distinguishes a failed assembly from generation having been off.
  • pipe_output.pipe_io_artifacts (object | null): The I/O artifacts describing the graph's data, carried beside graph_spec so that wherever the graph travels its description travels with it. It groups the same artifacts /validate produces — pipe_io_contracts, input_form and output_form — each keyed by namespaced pipe_ref, over the run library's own pipes: a dependency package's pipes are keyed by alias in the library but by bare pipe_ref in the artifacts, where they would collide with the host's, so they are left out and a graph node contributed by a dependency has no entry here. Holding it with the graph is what lets a viewer show a data node's value rather than only its shape. It is built only when the run generated a graph and interpreter.pipeline_execution.graph.graphs_inclusion.graphspec_json is on (both default to true), and only when graph_spec itself came out non-null — so a run with graphspec_json = false returns a graph with no artifacts beside it and no error, which is the one case where the two fields disagree. pipe_output.pipe_io_artifacts_error (string | null) is non-null when the build ran and failed. See Pipe Validate for the artifacts' own field reference.
  • method_provenance (object, only on method_ref runs): {address, tag, commit_sha, tree_digest, display_name} — the package's resolved full address, the requested tag (null for a bare address), the commit SHA that was actually fetched, the digest of the method tree the run loaded, and the display_name the package's METHODS.toml declares (null when it declares none). Absent for runs from inline source or a bundle. See Running a method by address.

Errors are returned as RFC 9457 application/problem+json bodies with HTTP 4xx/5xx status codes. The successful response body has no status/error field — the HTTP status code is the source of truth. An invalid bundle is refused before any pipe runs with a 422 method.invalid problem whose errors are the same located items validating it gives (Structured validation errors), and a run that fails reports its root fault at the pipe that failed (Run failures).

docs.title: Start Pipeline
docs.text:
Start a pipeline execution and get its pipeline_run_id back with a 202 ack.

Endpoint: POST /v1/start

Fire-and-forget is a property of this endpoint, honored only by an async-capable backend. orchestration_mode names only the deployment's backend; /start sets FIRE_AND_FORGET delivery and requires an orchestrator that can honor it. A Temporal deployment (orchestration_mode = "temporal") enqueues the run and returns immediately with a workflow_id. On the orchestrator-agnostic base (orchestration_mode = "direct", the default — see Configuration → Orchestration mode) the in-process orchestrator is blocking-only, so /start is HONEST: it refuses with a 501 runtime.unsupported naming the capability asynchronous execution — use POST /v1/execute — rather than silently running blocking and acking. The run's webhooks fire on the async path.

Request Body:

{
  "pipe_code": null,
  "files": {
    "my_method.mthds": "domain = \"my_domain\"\nmain_pipe = \"my_pipe\"\n…"
  },
  "inputs": {
    "input_name": "simple text or object"
  },
  "output_name": null,
  "output_multiplicity": null,
  "dynamic_output_concept_ref": null
}

Request Fields:

  • files (object, optional): The method as a map of file entries, the MTHDS standard's method tree: each key a tree path, each value the file's text, {"base64": "…"}, or {"sha256": "…", "size": n} naming bytes this runner holds — see Sending a method as a tree. Mutually exclusive with mthds_contents, bundle_b64 and method_ref.
  • pipe_code (string, optional): The code identifying the pipe to execute. Beside a method sent in files, it names the pipe to start at in place of the method's entry pipe; beside method_ref, it overrides the package's main_pipe; sent alone, it must name a pipe already registered on the server.
  • inputs (PipelineInputs, optional): Flexible input format - see Input Format: PipelineInputs below
  • output_name (string, optional): Name for the output slot
  • output_multiplicity (string, optional): Output multiplicity setting ("single", "variable", or a specific number)
  • dynamic_output_concept_ref (string, optional): Override output concept ref
  • dependencies (object, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The method packages the method calls by address that the runner cannot fetch, each a map of file entries keyed by its address — see Sending the method packages the method calls. Accompanies files.
  • method_ref (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. Run a published method by address instead of inline source — see Running a method by address. Mutually exclusive with mthds_contents and with a method sent as a tree; pipe_code may accompany it to override the package's main_pipe.
  • mthds_contents (list[str], optional): Being retired: send the method in files. Inline pipeline definitions (always an array, even for a single file). If provided without pipe_code, must have a main_pipe property. Still accepted until a later release refuses it.
  • bundle_b64 (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension, being retired with mthds_contents: send the method in files. Base64-encoded zip of the method's folder, read as a map of its entries, which may carry the method packages it calls under .mthds/methods/<name>/. Mutually exclusive with files.
  • resources (dict[str, str], optional): Pipelex-API extension, being retired with mthds_contents: put the files in the method's tree, in files. The files the bundle's steps read, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, as a map from the path the step names to the file's bytes in standard base64 — see Sending the files the steps read. It accompanies mthds_contents or a method sent as a tree, whose tree each file joins at its path from the root; beside method_ref, or with no bundle at all, it is a 422. The job names the method's tree by its digest and carries none of its files: the step that reads one, on an orchestrator that runs the job remotely such as Temporal included, reads it through the deployment's method file store.
  • storage_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The prefix every object this run writes lands under — see Host-supplied run context.
  • read_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The prefix every stored object this run reads must lie under — see Host-supplied run context.
  • analytics_groups (dict[str, str], optional): Pipelex-API extension. The groups this run's telemetry belongs to, such as {"organization": "org_acme"} — see Host-supplied run context.
  • callback_urls (list[str], optional): Pipelex-API extension. The URLs that each receive the run's signed run.finished event once it ends. See Webhooks.

Validation Rules:

  • At least one of files, method_ref, pipe_code or a method sent the older way (mthds_contents or bundle_b64) must be provided
  • If only pipe_code: Must reference a pipe already registered in the library
  • With files and no pipe_code: the run starts at the method's entry pipe, the main_pipe of its root METHODS.toml or else the one main_pipe its bundles declare (see Sending a method as a tree)
  • With mthds_contents and no pipe_code: a file must declare main_pipe
  • With pipe_code beside a method: pipe_code specifies which pipe of that method to execute

Important Notes:

  • This endpoint answers 202 Accepted immediately with a StartAck carrying the pipeline_run_id
  • The pipeline continues executing in the background
  • pipe_output will be null in the response (pipeline hasn't completed yet)
  • The request body MAY carry a client-supplied pipeline_run_id (max 128 chars): this server honors it, and the StartAck.pipeline_run_id echoes it back. When absent, the server generates one. (StartAck.pipeline_run_id is always authoritative — protocol rule.)

Response (202):

{
  "pipeline_run_id": "abc123...",
  "created_at": "2026-01-15T12:00:00Z",
  "state": "STARTED",
  "finished_at": null,
  "main_stuff_name": null,
  "pipe_output": null,
  "workflow_id": "pipeline-abc123...",
  "crate_fingerprint": "9f2c41…"
}

Response Fields:

  • pipeline_run_id (string): Unique identifier for the run. Use this to correlate the run's webhooks (see Webhooks).
  • created_at (string): ISO timestamp when the pipeline was started.
  • state (string): Always "STARTED" from this endpoint — the pipeline is queued, not finished.
  • finished_at (null): Always null; the pipeline hasn't completed.
  • main_stuff_name (null): Always null; the run's result is read once it ends.
  • pipe_output (null): Always null; the result isn't ready yet.
  • workflow_id (string | null): The async orchestrator's workflow ID. A 202 ack is only ever returned by an async-capable backend (e.g. a Temporal flavor), so this carries that orchestrator's id; the in-process direct base never acks here — it returns a 501 runtime.unsupported instead.
  • method_provenance (object | null): {address, tag, commit_sha, tree_digest, display_name} for a method_ref run — see Running a method by address; null for runs from inline source or a bundle.
  • crate_fingerprint (string | null): Pipelex extension. The fingerprint of the library crate the run's job was built from, as on the /execute result, known as soon as the run is queued, so a host records it from the acknowledgement.

Errors follow the same convention as /execute: HTTP 4xx/5xx with an RFC 9457 application/problem+json body.

docs.title: Webhooks (optional)
docs.text: POST /v1/start, like POST /v1/execute, accepts callback_urls, a pipelex-api extension: a list of HTTP(S) endpoints that each receive the signed run.finished event when the run ends. The server needs a signing secret, CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET, to accept them, and a deployment may also configure a completion target of its own, COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL, which every /start run notifies. See Webhooks for the event, its signature, the delivery and the completion target.

docs.title: Sending a method as a tree
docs.text:
A method is more than its bundles: a custom PipeFunc's Python, a PipeDocGen step's template, a requirements.txt, a METHODS.toml. Both /execute and /start, and /validate, take the whole method as a method tree, the MTHDS standard's unit of a method, in one of two mutually exclusive forms:

  • files: a map of file entries, the standard's form, and the way to send a method. Each key is the file's tree path, its path relative to the method's folder, and each value one of three entries: the file's text as a JSON string, {"base64": "…"} for bytes that are not text, or {"sha256": "…", "size": n} naming bytes this runner already holds in its blob store. One request may mix all three.
  • bundle_b64: a base64-encoded zip of the method's folder, a Pipelex-API extension, read as a map of its entries. It is being retired with mthds_contents.

The older mthds_contents, which carries only .mthds text, and resources, which carries the files its steps read beside it, are being retired too: a later release refuses mthds_contents, bundle_b64 and resources, and a method sent in files needs none of them.

{
  "files": {
    "main.mthds": "domain = \"demo\"\nmain_pipe = \"crunch\"\n\n[pipe.crunch]\ntype = \"PipeFunc\"\ndescription = \"Crunch numbers\"\ninputs = { data = \"Text\" }\noutput = \"Text\"\nfunction_name = \"pipe_func.crunch\"\n",
    "pipe_func.py": "def crunch(working_memory):\n    return \"...\"\n",
    "templates/logo.png": { "base64": "iVBORw0KGgo…" },
    "templates/invoice.docx": { "sha256": "3e9b68b71cc667168399f0bccfb64b2d16314cdc0ed78fac4819aba0dda121a0", "size": 18342 }
  },
  "inputs": { "data": "1,2,3" }
}

One rule for every path. The map is the tree: the runner reads it with the standard's reader and holds every key to the tree's one rule, whatever form the method came in. A key that is not a tree path (absolute, with a . or .. segment, an empty segment, a backslash, a colon), a key the membership rule keeps out of every tree (a dotfile or a file under a dot directory such as .mthds/, .git/ or .env, __pycache__/, node_modules/), one key given twice, two keys naming one file once normalized, or a file that is another entry's directory is a 422 method.package_invalid whose reason is the standard's refusal code, such as invalid_tree_path, excluded_name, duplicate_key or path_collision, and whose path is the first name it refuses; a key that would leave the tree's root, absolute or climbing with .., is the security refusal security.input_path_refused, naming the rule it broke, never the path. A malformed entry, such as a size written 13.0, is a 422 request.invalid naming the field. A zip's member names are judged by the same rule, so a name given twice in an archive is a duplicate key.

The tree is written whole and loaded as the caller's. The runner writes the tree into a temporary directory, exactly as the map holds it, and loads it as one library directory that belongs to the caller: every bundle is a member of the tree and is named by its tree path, every other file is one a step may read where the bundle sits, a PipeDocGen template beside its bundle or a PipeFunc module at the tree's import root, and a refusal of the load is the caller's 422, or an is_valid: false verdict on /validate, naming files by their tree paths and never by the directory on the server. The directory is written in a worker thread of the bounded method-load pool, off the server's event loop, and removed there once the request returns, whether it succeeded, failed or was cancelled. The run's job names the tree by its digest, so an orchestrator that runs the job remotely reads its files from the deployment's method file store.

The entry pipe. With no pipe_code, the run starts at the pipe the MTHDS protocol's rule names: the main_pipe of the METHODS.toml at the tree's root, in the bundle of a domain exporting it, or, in a tree with no manifest, the one main_pipe its bundles declare. A manifest declaring none, or bundles declaring none or several, is a 422 request.pipe_unspecified, which names the bundles' main_pipes as its candidates when they declare several; name the pipe with pipe_code instead.

Limits. A tree is bounded before any of its bytes is read, on the sizes its entries state, and again once read: at most MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILES files (default 1,000), MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILE_KIB per file (default 32 MiB) and MAX_METHOD_TREE_TOTAL_KIB in all (default 64 MiB), each tree of a request counted on its own, and, across the method's tree and the dependency trees beside it, at most MAX_METHOD_DEPENDENCIES dependency trees (default 32) and MAX_METHOD_REQUEST_TOTAL_KIB in all (default 128 MiB), refused with a 422 method.package_invalid whose reason names the limit, too_many_files, file_too_large, tree_too_large, too_many_dependencies or method_too_large, and whose limit gives it. A bundle_b64 archive is also bounded as an archive: a member-count ceiling (MAX_BUNDLE_FILES) and a decompressed-size ceiling (MAX_BUNDLE_TOTAL_KIB), each a 422 method.package_invalid with the reason of its own limit, bundle_too_many_files or bundle_too_large, its decompression bounded so a zip bomb cannot expand past the ceiling, and an oversized bundle_b64 refused on its encoded length before it is decoded, as a 413 request.too_large. Supplying both bundle_b64 and files is a 422 request.invalid, invalid base64 or a corrupt zip a 422 request.malformed with the reason bad_base64 or bad_zip, an archive holding no file a 422 request.invalid naming bundle_b64, and a tree holding no .mthds bundle of its own a 422 method.package_invalid with the reason no_bundle.

Files sent in resources join the tree. Beside a tree, each file of resources is added at its path from the tree's root: a file the tree already holds must have the same bytes, or it is a 422 request.invalid naming the field resources, and a file no step names is kept like any other file of the tree. The tree they make is held to the tree's limits again, so files that take it past one are a 422 method.package_invalid naming the limit.

Sandbox-hosted only for custom Python. A tree that holds any .py file is honored only on a sandbox-hosted deployment, where the load reads the source without importing it and execution happens in an isolated sandbox. On a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted it is refused with a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox, whose origin is bundle, before anything is written: running caller-supplied code in-process is never done implicitly. A tree without Python is accepted on any deployment.

No Python structure classes. A structure class (a StructuredContent subclass) can only be used by importing its module into the runner's own process, which a sandbox-hosted deployment never does, so a tree whose Python declares one is refused with a 422 problem, pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused, before anything is loaded; its operator view's message names each file and class. The rule is the same however the method arrives: sent as a tree, or fetched by method_ref. Declare the types as MTHDS concepts with inline structures instead; a PipeFunc returns them by importing the classes the sandbox generates from those concepts (from structures import <domain>__<Concept>). The structures module that pipelex build structures writes is accepted as long as it is left as generated, and it is not sent to the sandbox, which generates its own.

Requirements are checked against the sandbox. A requirements.txt at the root of the tree declares the packages its Python imports, one PEP 508 requirement per line (see Method Trees). Nothing is installed into a running sandbox: the packages the deployment states its PipeFunc sandbox offers for the method's requirements are the whole offer, a fixed package set or an environment the deployment builds for those requirements, and a method asking for a package the sandbox does not offer, or for a version it does not offer, is refused before the method loads and before anything is dispatched with a 422 method.invalid, the problem an invalid bundle is refused with, whose errors hold one method.dependency_missing item per requirement not met, located at location.file requirements.txt and the requirement's location.line, its params naming the distribution that fails it (name) and why (reason: not_found, or no_matching_version for a version the requirement refuses). A deployment that can build no environment holding the requirements refuses them with the same 422, its one method.dependency_missing item located on the file alone, and its own explanation in the operator's diagnostics. A line the standard refuses, such as -r base.txt, a URL or a comment after a requirement, is the same 422 with a method.package_invalid item on the line, whose reason is requirements_invalid. These are the items /validate gives the same tree, and the ones a local run of the method is refused with. The refusal names the file by its tree path, requirements.txt, and no path on the server:

{
  "type": "https://mthds.ai/errors/method.invalid",
  "title": "The method does not validate",
  "status": 422,
  "detail": "The method does not validate.",
  "code": "method.invalid",
  "domain": "method",
  "retry": "no",
  "next_step": {"kind": "change_method", "detail": "Fix each fault the problem's errors list, then validate the method again."},
  "errors": [
    {
      "code": "method.dependency_missing",
      "detail": "The method depends on the requirement 'pydantic', which is not available here (reason: no_matching_version).",
      "params": {"kind": "requirement", "name": "pydantic", "reason": "no_matching_version"},
      "location": {"file": "requirements.txt", "line": 2}
    }
  ],
  "request_id": "9f2c1ab3-…"
}

A deployment that states no package set for its sandbox refuses every method declaring requirements with a 500 (PipeFuncPackageSetUnstatedError), a fault of its configuration, and so does a method of the server's own library directories whose requirements are not met (HostLibraryRequirementsError), whose message is withheld from the caller. A method_ref package is checked the same way, on a run as on /validate, where the refusal is an is_valid: false verdict located on the requirement's line.

docs.title: Sending files by hash
docs.text:
This runner keeps a blob store, declared by blob_store: true in GET /v1/version, so a sender uploads each file at most once and then sends the method by hash: a second run of an unchanged method uploads nothing, and editing one template uploads one file. These are the MTHDS Protocol's blob routes.

  1. The sender lists its method's tree and computes each file's SHA-256 and the tree's digest.
  2. It asks POST /v1/blobs/missing which blobs the runner lacks, sending {"blobs": [{"sha256": "…", "size": n}, …], "digest": "sha256:…"}, the digest being optional.
  3. It uploads each missing blob as the answer says: the blob's bytes as the whole body of a request with the answer's method to its url, carrying exactly its headers.
  4. It sends the run, or the validation, with a hash entry for each file it chose to send by hash.

The answer is {"missing": [{"sha256": "…", "size": n, "upload": {"method": "PUT", "url": "…", "headers": {"content-type": "application/octet-stream"}}}, …]}, listing only the blobs the runner does not hold; an empty list means there is nothing to upload. Each target is the runner's own PUT /v1/blobs/{sha256}, its query signed for that hash and the caller's scope and valid for BLOB_UPLOAD_URL_TTL_SECONDS (default an hour). The target starts with PUBLIC_BASE_URL when the deployment sets it, the address its clients reach the API at, which a deployment behind a proxy terminating TLS or adding a path prefix sets, and otherwise with the URL the request arrived at. The upload route needs no bearer token, since the signed target is its authorization: a missing, malformed, forged or expired signature is a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is signed_upload_target, a body whose SHA-256 is not the path's a 422 request.invalid naming the field body, and a body past MAX_METHOD_TREE_FILE_KIB a 413 request.too_large. A blob is written whole and never changed, so uploading bytes the runner holds answers 204 and changes nothing. On POST /v1/blobs/missing, one hash listed with two sizes is a 422 request.invalid naming the field blobs, and blobs past the tree limits a 422 method.package_invalid naming the limit, both before anything is uploaded.

Writes are create-only.
