The runner creates a blob, or a tree's listing, only when its key holds nothing, and never replaces an object already there: on S3 the write carries If-None-Match: * and its SHA-256 as x-amz-checksum-sha256, which S3 checks against the body, on GCS it is conditional on generation 0, and on the local filesystem the file is created through a hard link, so the local storage's folder must sit on a filesystem that supports them. A key already holding an object is the object already held, the same bytes since the key is their hash, and the write succeeds without changing it. A deployment's bucket can therefore refuse every unconditional write under blobs/ and trees/ without refusing any of the runner's, as the hosted platform's does.

Sizes. A blob is held at a size, which the runner reads from the storage's metadata without reading the bytes. POST /v1/blobs/missing lists a blob the runner does not hold at the size the sender states, an object held at another size included. Its upload then tells the two cases apart: bytes of the size held are the ones held, and change nothing, while bytes of another size mean the object held is damaged, which only a storage that does not publish a write whole could leave, a 500 pipelex.storage.damaged naming the kind of storage, whose verdict is not to retry, since nothing writes over a blob and the deployment's operator removes the object for it to be uploaded again. On a run or a validation, every hash entry is read in one request, a bounded number at a time, which reads at most one byte more than the size the entry states, so the bytes read stay within the sizes the request states however large the object held is. A hash the runner holds at another size than the entry states, which that read shows, is a 422 request.invalid naming the field the entry is in, since the bytes under a hash have one size and uploading them again would change nothing, so the entry's size is the one to correct; the operator view's diagnostics.message names each such hash with the size it is held at, which the runner looks up from the storage's metadata when the read stopped short of the object's end. Bytes read at the size their entry states are checked against their hash; bytes that do not hash to their key mean the storage holds a damaged object, a 500 pipelex.storage.damaged naming the kind of storage, whose verdict is not to retry, since a retry reads the same object. In both cases the operator repairs it by removing the object the line Stored blob bytes do not match their hash names under blob_sha256, for it to be uploaded again.

The bytes are checked last. A map's keys are judged first, then the entries of the keys the tree's rule admits, and the bytes a hash entry names last, as the MTHDS Protocol orders a map's refusals: a map refused for a key or for a malformed entry is refused for it before any blob is read, so a hash entry under a refused key is never looked up, and request.blobs_missing, a hash held at another size and a damaged object answer only a map that breaks no other rule. A sender therefore never uploads blobs for a map the runner refuses anyway.

The digest shortcut. Once the runner has read a request's tree in full, it records the tree's listing beside its blobs, after every file it names is held, and an upload never records one. A validation records it only when its request carries a read_scope: without one, its scope would be the caller's own id, where a dry run must leave nothing stored. Asking POST /v1/blobs/missing with the digest of a recorded tree then answers an empty list in one lookup, however many files the tree has, when every blob listed is a file of that tree; a blob outside it is looked up as if no digest were sent.

Scopes. Blobs live in the deployment's configured storage, under <scope>/blobs/<sha256>, and recorded listings under <scope>/trees/<digest>. The scope is the request's read_scope, which a multi-tenant host sends for the organization it serves (a query parameter on POST /v1/blobs/missing, a body field on the run and validate routes), else the caller's own id, so a hash entry resolves only in the caller's own blobs and asking whether a hash is held tells a caller nothing of another's files. On a jwt deployment a sent scope must lie under the caller's own id, else a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is read_scope_under_caller (see Host-supplied run context). A hash entry the runner does not hold, at the size it states, is a 422 request.blobs_missing whose missing_blobs parameter lists the hashes to upload before sending the request again.

Signing key. Each process draws its own signing key unless BLOB_UPLOAD_SIGNING_KEY is set. A deployment serving one API through several instances must set it, the same on every instance, since an upload may reach another instance than the one that named its target.

docs.title: Sending the method packages the method calls
docs.text:
A method can call a pipe of another method package by its address, such as github.com/Pipelex/methods/documents->documents.extract_page_contents_and_views. A request can carry that package with the method, so the run needs no copy installed on the server and no fetch:

  • With files, send each package in dependencies, a map from the package's address to the package's own map of file entries, its METHODS.toml at its root declaring that address. A package keyed by another address than its manifest declares is a 422 request.invalid naming the field dependencies, and so is dependencies without files.
  • In a bundle_b64 archive, put each package under .mthds/methods/<name>/, with its METHODS.toml at .mthds/methods/<name>/METHODS.toml, which is the layout of a local method store. The store's .provenance.json sidecar is left out of the package.
bundle.mthds
.mthds/methods/documents/METHODS.toml
.mthds/methods/documents/documents.mthds
  • A reference finds the package by its manifest. The package that answers is the one whose METHODS.toml declares the referenced address and name. A reference pinned with @<tag> is answered by the shipped copy too, and the server logs a warning when the copy's version is not that tag.
  • The shipped copy comes first. The server searches the shipped packages before the copies installed on it and before fetch-on-miss, so a shipped package wins over an installed copy of the same address, and it runs even where fetching is disabled or the address is not one the server can fetch. It serves this request alone: nothing is installed.
  • It is a tree of its own. Each package is written into a methods directory of its own, never into the method's tree, so its domains never merge with the method's, and a method whose only bundles are shipped ones is refused as holding no bundle of its own. Its keys are held to the tree's rule as the method's are.
  • Its Python never runs in the server's process. A .py file in a shipped package counts for the sandbox gate like any other. On a sandbox-hosted deployment, a shipped package whose Python declares a structure class is refused with the same 422 pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused, as a package fetched by address is.
  • A shipped bundle that does not parse refuses the run with the 422 verdict, whose items name the file as <address>/<path inside the package>, never by a path on the server.

Two shipped packages a reference could not tell apart, whose manifests declare the same address and name compared without regard to case, the name being the directory's when the manifest has none, are a 422 method.package_invalid with the reason dependency_address_collision, whose path is the second package's directory, since nothing but their order would decide which one answers. In an archive, a package directory without a valid METHODS.toml is a 422 method.package_invalid with the reason manifest_missing or manifest_invalid, naming the manifest's path, and any other entry under .mthds/, such as a file directly under .mthds/methods/, one under a directory whose name no package's directory can take, such as a dot directory, or a package's own .mthds/ store, is refused by the tree's rule; a package fetched by method_ref holds its .mthds/methods/ to the same rule, its other entries left out of its tree. A package whose manifest declares no name takes the last segment of its address, which must then be a name a directory can take: a dependency keyed by an address ending in . or .. with a nameless manifest is a 422 method.package_invalid with the reason package_name_invalid.

The validation of a method sent as a tree, or fetched by method_ref, resolves the packages it calls as the run does, its shipped packages first, then the methods installed on the server and a fetch on a miss, so /validate resolves a dependency the run would resolve (see Validating a method tree). Both write the method to disk and load it in worker threads of the bounded method-load pool, off the server's event loop, so a large tree or a slow load never holds up the server's other requests.

A package the server fetches is checked against the method's methods.lock. When the method, sent as files or in a bundle_b64 archive or fetched by method_ref, carries a methods.lock at the root of its tree, a package it calls by address that the server fetches on a miss, or finds installed by an earlier fetch of its own, must have the tree digest the lock records for that address. A different digest refuses the run with a 422 security.integrity_mismatch, whose dependency names the address, and the operator's diagnostics name the digest and version the lock records and the version and digest that were fetched; /validate answers the same 422, as a security refusal is never a verdict, and the deployment logs the refusal's security event. A lock naming another version than the one fetched refuses the run as well, since the version is part of the package's tree, and the server never fetches the locked version in place of the reference. A lock that does not name the address, or no lock, checks nothing, and a package shipped with the request is not checked, as it travels with the lock. The lock is read only when a dependency the method calls resolves to a copy the server fetched, for this request or an earlier one. A lock the server then cannot read, such as one written before tree digests that records a hash, refuses the run with a 422 verdict whose item is method.package_invalid with the reason lock_invalid and the path methods.lock. See Include by Address: Fetch-on-Miss.

docs.title: Running a method by address (method_ref)
docs.text:
Both /execute and /start accept method_ref — a globally resolvable address of a published method package, resolved by this server (a Pipelex-API extension; the hosted-only catalog selector method_id is a different, platform-resolved field that never reaches this runner):

{
  "method_ref": "github.com/Pipelex/methods/documents@v0.1.0",
  "inputs": { "document": "https://example.com/report.pdf" }
}

The reference grammar is <address>[@<tag>]. The address is github.com/<owner>/<repo> optionally followed by a package selector within the repository (github.com only for now). A bare address means the repository's default branch at HEAD; @<tag> pins the repository at that git tag (recommended form vX.Y.Z) — branch names are refused, so a reference can never silently track a moving branch. Full browser URLs (https://github.com/..., including /tree/<branch>/... deep links) are accepted and normalized.

Resolution. The server fetches the repository (shallow clone, at the tag when one is named), records the commit SHA of what was fetched, and locates the requested package by manifest identity: it scans the clone for METHODS.toml manifests and selects the one whose declared address (plus name, for a package in a library repo) equals the requested address — never by directory path. It then reads the package's directory from the commit's git objects, never from the clone's working tree, and lists it as a method tree under the standard's rule: the package is a tree like one sent as files, written whole and loaded as the caller's, its templates and Python beside its bundles, and the packages it ships under its own .mthds/methods/<name>/ become dependency trees (Sending the method packages the method calls), under the same refusals.

Entry pipe. The pipe to run is the tree's entry pipe by the protocol's rule, the package manifest's main_pipe; an explicit pipe_code in the request overrides it (to run another pipe from the fetched package).

Provenance. The response carries method_provenance = {address, tag, commit_sha, tree_digest, display_name} — on /execute only for method_ref runs, on the /start ack as a nullable field. Tags can move; the recorded SHA is what keeps a run explainable after the fact, and tree_digest names the exact tree the run loaded. display_name is the human-readable name the package's METHODS.toml declares at that commit, such as Slide Designer, which a host can name the run's method by, and null when the manifest declares none.

Custom Python follows the tree rules, plus one more. What decides is where the code would execute: .mthds content is data, always acceptable. On a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted, a fetched package carrying any .py is refused with a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox, whose origin is package. On a sandbox-hosted deployment, PipeFunc .py is accepted (the runner never imports it: validation reads its text, and each PipeFunc call runs in the isolated sandbox, which receives the files of the step's tree) — but a package declaring Python structure classes (StructuredContent subclasses) is refused with a 422 (pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused), exactly as a tree sent with the request is: see No Python structure classes.

Errors. Every resolution failure is an RFC 9457 problem+json named by its code (see Error responses):

Failure Status code Reference does not match the grammar 422 request.invalid Repository could not be fetched 502 method.fetch_failed @<tag> is not a tag of the repository, or no package matches the address 404 method.not_found More than one package matches 422 method.ambiguous Package exceeds the fetched-package ceilings, or contains a symlink (file or directory) 422 method.package_invalid Package declares Python structure classes 422 pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused A package it calls, fetched by the server, differs from the tree digest its methods.lock records 422 security.integrity_mismatch Package ships .py on a non-sandbox deployment 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox

The clone cache. Fetched repositories are cached on local disk keyed by resolved commit SHA — never by tag. Each request first resolves the reference to its current SHA with a cheap git ls-remote (no clone); a cached SHA is reused, a new one (a moved tag, an advanced HEAD) triggers a fresh clone. The cache is per server instance and bounded by count, total bytes, and age, oldest first; a clone a request is still reading is never evicted, though it counts toward the bounds. That protection holds within one process, so a deployment running several worker processes gives each its own METHOD_CACHE_DIR.

Environment knobs. The cache: MAX_METHOD_CACHE_CLONES (default 64), MAX_METHOD_CACHE_TOTAL_KIB (default 512 MiB), MAX_METHOD_CACHE_AGE_HOURS (default 24), METHOD_CACHE_DIR (default: a fixed directory under the system temp dir). The fetch itself is bounded by the pipelex runtime's fetched-package ceilings: PIPELEX_MAX_FETCHED_PACKAGE_FILES (default 256), PIPELEX_MAX_FETCHED_PACKAGE_TOTAL_KIB (default 8 MiB), and the manifest-scan bounds PIPELEX_MAX_SCANNED_MANIFESTS (default 100 manifests considered per fetched repository) and PIPELEX_MAX_MANIFEST_FILE_KIB (default 256 KiB per METHODS.toml read during package location). All are read once at process start.

method_ref also selects the method on the tooling routes: on POST /v1/validate, /resolve and /codegen and /pipe-io, which read the fetched package's tree as a run does (address form resolved; on the crate routes the registry form is a 422 request.unsupported).

docs.title: Host-supplied run context: storage_scope and analytics_groups
docs.text:
Both /execute and /start accept optional fields that describe the run's tenancy rather than its method: storage_scope, read_scope and analytics_groups. All are Pipelex-API extensions, and all are data the host computes, which is why they ride in the body: the caller's identity arrives separately, on the trusted X-User-Id header or the bearer token (see Authentication), because it is something a proxy vouches for rather than something the caller chooses. The runtime carries them opaquely and never reads a value by name, so it has no notion of what an organization or a tenant is.

{
  "pipe_code": "your_pipeline_code",
  "inputs": { "input_name": "..." },
  "storage_scope": "org_acme/method_42/run_7",
  "read_scope": "org_acme",
  "analytics_groups": { "organization": "org_acme" }
}

storage_scope is the prefix every object the run writes lands under: one to three path-safe segments, onto which the runtime composes its own leaves (assets/, generated/, results/, payloads/). Omit it and the run is scoped to the caller's own id, which is right for a single-tenant deployment and wrong for a multi-tenant one: a host serving many tenants must send it. Each segment is one or more characters from A-Za-z0-9_-, so an empty segment, a leading or trailing slash, a . or .., or a fourth segment is refused with a 422 request.invalid naming the field storage_scope.

read_scope bounds what the run may read: every pipelex-storage:// key the run reads, whether an input, a URL a pipe builds or an image it shows a model, must lie under it, and a scoped run reads no local path at all. It follows the same segment rule as storage_scope, and the storage scope must be the read scope or lie under it, since a run reads back what it writes: org_acme covers org_acme/method_42/run_7, while org_other does not. Omit it and the run is scoped to the caller's own id when the deployment identifies its callers, which is also where their writes land by default, and unscoped when the deployment is single-tenant. A host serving many tenants must send it: a host that sends its own storage_scope but no read_scope is refused, since that storage scope lies under no caller's id. A malformed read scope, a storage scope outside it, or the local storage scope local beside one is a 422 request.invalid naming the field read_scope, answered before any method is fetched or library loaded. On a jwt deployment the read scope is bound to the caller: the caller reaches the runner with its own token rather than through a trusted host, so a read scope it sends must be its token's user_id or lie under it, else the request is a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is read_scope_under_caller, answered before anything is read. Every route taking a read_scope applies the same rule (/v1/validate, /v1/resolve, /v1/codegen, /v1/pipe-io and POST /v1/blobs/missing too), and since the storage scope must lie under the read scope, a jwt caller writes only under its own id as well. With AUTH_MODE=none and the shared api_key, the caller is a trusted host or a single tenant, and the scope it sends is taken as it is. A read the scope does not allow is refused when the run makes it, as the security refusal security.input_url_refused, which says where the URL sat without quoting it. On /execute it is a 422. On /start it is a synchronous 422 when an input breaks the rule, and a run that ends FAILED with that error in its webhooks when a pipe reaches for the URL during the run.

analytics_groups names the entities the run's telemetry belongs to, as a mapping of group type to group key. The runtime carries it on the run as its opaque extras and stamps it on every span of the run as the attribute pipelex.run.extras, so every OpenTelemetry exporter receives it, and the deployment's own PostHog stream, when telemetry.toml sets mode = "identified", attaches it to each capture as PostHog groups. That is what lets a generation made for one of your customers appear inside that customer's organization instead of under one identity for the whole deployment. The rules are the runtime's own, imported rather than restated here:

  • A group type (a key of the mapping) is lowercase snake_case starting with a letter, at most 32 characters, such as organization.
  • A group key (a value) is 1 to 128 characters from A-Za-z0-9_-. Whitespace, control characters and separators are refused, because the key is quoted into log lines and capture payloads.
  • The mapping holds at most five entries, since a telemetry backend registers only a small fixed number of group types per project.
  • It is optional. Omitting it, sending null or sending {} all mean the run belongs to no group, which misattributes nothing.

A mapping outside these rules is refused with a 422 request.invalid naming the field analytics_groups, or a path into it, before any method is fetched or any library loaded. A body that fails on more than one of the extension fields at once carries one request.invalid item per refused field in its errors.

The caller's id is the run's person on that same stream, with one exception: a deployment with no user model attributes every run to the literal single-tenant, which the runtime declines as a person and replaces with the user_id configured in telemetry.toml. The groups do not depend on it, so a single-tenant deployment that sends analytics_groups still has them on every capture.

docs.title: Input Format: PipelineInputs
docs.text:
The inputs field accepts several shapes. Pipelex picks how to interpret each value from its structure — pass a string to a Text input and you get TextContent, pass a dict with concept and content keys and you get explicit concept resolution, etc. The cases below enumerate every supported form.

The request body is plain JSON. The Python objects in Cases 1.3 to 1.5, and the DictStuff instances further down, are what a Python caller writes; a Python client of this API serializes each one to plain JSON before sending it, and the server never rebuilds a Python class from the request. The class name does not travel, so each value is read against the entry pipe's declared input. A structured object (Case 1.3) arrives as its fields and a list of them (Case 1.4) as a list of those, and both are read as intended; a DictStuff arrives as the Case 2 envelope. A ListContent wrapper (Case 1.5) arrives as {"items": [...]}, which the server reads as one item rather than a list, and a native TextContent arrives as {"text": ...}, which a Text input refuses: over HTTP, send the bare list of items or strings instead, or the {"concept": ..., "content": [...]} envelope of Cases 2.2, 2.4 and 2.6. A body carrying a __class__ or __module__ key, or a key starting with __kajson, in any object at any depth is refused with a 422 pipelex.security.reserved_key (see Error Responses).

docs.title: How Input Formatting Works
docs.text:
Case 1: Direct Content - Provide the value directly (simplest)

  • 1.1: String → "my text"
  • 1.2: List of strings → ["text1", "text2"]
  • 1.3: StructuredContent object → MyClass(arg1="value")
  • 1.4: List of StuffContent objects → [MyClass(...), MyClass(...)]
  • 1.5: ListContent of StuffContent objects → ListContent(items=[MyClass(...), MyClass(...)])

Note: Cases 1.3 and 1.5 are at the same level - both handle content types that inherit from StuffContent, but for different purposes (custom classes vs. list wrappers).

Case 2: Explicit Format - Use {"concept": "...", "content": "..."} for control (plain dict or DictStuff instance)

  • 2.1: String with concept → {"concept": "Text", "content": "my text"}
  • 2.2: List of strings with concept → {"concept": "Text", "content": ["text1", "text2"]}
  • 2.3: StructuredContent object with concept → {"concept": "Invoice", "content": InvoiceObject}
  • 2.4: List of StructuredContent objects with concept → {"concept": "Invoice", "content": [...]}
  • 2.5: Dictionary (structured data) → {"concept": "Invoice", "content": {"field": "value"}}
  • 2.6: List of dictionaries → {"concept": "Invoice", "content": [{...}, {...}]}
  • 2.7: File / document URL → {"concept": "Document", "content": {"url": "https://…/file.pdf"}}

Pro Tip: For text inputs specifically, skip the verbose format. Just provide the string directly: "text": "Hello" instead of "text": {"concept": "Text", "content": "Hello"}

docs.title: Case 1: Direct Content Format
docs.text: When you provide content directly (without the concept key), Pipelex intelligently infers the type.

docs.title: 1.1: Simple String (Text)
docs.text:
The simplest case - just provide a string directly:

{
  "inputs": {
    "my_text": "my text"
  }
}

Result: At a Text input, automatically becomes TextContent with concept native.Text

The input's declaration decides the reading for two native concepts. At an Anything input, the string becomes a native.Anything value holding the text, and a number, a boolean or an object is taken the same way, as a value of its own kind; a date sent as a string is read as text. An Anything input refuses null and a list, both with a 422: a list is taken only by an Anything[] input, whose items are such values and can be neither null nor a list themselves. At a JSON input, a string is refused: a JSON input reads a JSON object literally, and a JSON[] input a list of objects. NaN and the infinities are refused at Number, JSON and Anything inputs, since JSON cannot carry them.

docs.title: 1.2: List of Strings (Text List)
docs.text:
Provide multiple text items as a list:

{
  "inputs": {
    "my_texts": ["my text1", "my text2", "my text3"]
  }
}

Result: Becomes a ListContent containing multiple TextContent items

Note: The concept must be compatible with native.Text or an error will be raised. The one exception is an Anything[] input, where the list keeps the native.Anything concept and holds each string as text.

docs.title: 1.3: StructuredContent Object
docs.text:
Provide a structured object directly (for Python clients):

# Python client example
from my_project.domain.domain_struct import MyConcept, MySubClass

inputs = {
    "invoice_data": MyConcept(arg1="arg1", arg2=1, arg3=MySubClass(arg4="arg4")),
}

What is StructuredContent?

  • StructuredContent is the base class for user-defined data structures in Pipelex
  • You create your own classes by inheriting from StructuredContent
  • These classes are defined in your project's Python files
  • Learn more: Python StructuredContent Classes

Concept Resolution (in-process calls only, where the object itself reaches the runtime; over HTTP the class name does not travel, and the declared input decides):

  • The system searches all available domains for a concept matching the class name
  • If multiple concepts with the same name exist in different domains → Error: Must specify domain
  • If no concept is found → Error

docs.title: 1.4: List of StuffContent Objects
docs.text:
Provide multiple content objects in a plain Python list:

# Python client example
inputs = {
    "invoice_list": [
        MyConcept(arg1="arg1", arg2=1, arg3=MySubClass(arg4="arg4")),
        MyConcept(arg1="arg1_2", arg2=2, arg3=MySubClass(arg4="arg4_2")),
    ],
}

What it accepts:

  • Lists of StructuredContent objects (user-defined classes)
  • Lists of native content objects (TextContent, ImageContent, etc.), in in-process calls only (over HTTP, see the plain-JSON note above)

Requirements:

  • All items must be of the same type
  • Concept resolution follows the same rules as 1.3
  • Creates a new ListContent wrapper internally

docs.title: 1.5: ListContent of StuffContent Objects
docs.text:
Provide an existing ListContent wrapper object (in-process Python calls only; over HTTP, send the bare list of items, as the plain-JSON note above explains):

# Python client example
from pipelex.core.stuffs.list_content import ListContent

inputs = {
    "invoice_list": ListContent(
        items=[
            MyConcept(arg1="arg1", arg2=1, arg3=MySubClass(arg4="arg4")),
            MyConcept(arg1="arg1_2", arg2=2, arg3=MySubClass(arg4="arg4_2")),
        ]
    ),
}

Key Difference from Case 1.4:

  • Case 1.4: Plain Python list [item1, item2] → Creates a new ListContent wrapper
  • Case 1.5: Already wrapped ListContent(items=[item1, item2]) → Uses the wrapper directly

Why Case 1.5 is Separate from Case 1.3:

  • StructuredContent and ListContent are sibling classes (both inherit from StuffContent)
  • Case 1.3 handles user-defined structured data classes
  • Case 1.5 handles list container wrappers
  • They're at the same inheritance level, not parent-child

Requirements:

  • All items within the ListContent must be StuffContent objects (this includes both StructuredContent and native content like TextContent, ImageContent)
  • All items must be of the same type
  • The ListContent cannot be empty
  • Concept is inferred from the first item's class name (not from "ListContent")

Use Case: This format is useful when you already have data wrapped in a ListContent object from a previous pipeline execution or when working with Pipelex's internal data structures.

docs.title: Case 2: Explicit Format (Concept and Content)
docs.text: Use the explicit format {"concept": "...", "content": "..."} when you need precise control over concept selection or when working with domain-specific concepts.

docs.title: 2.1: Explicit String Input
docs.text:
{
  "inputs": {
    "text": {
      "concept": "Text",
      "content": "my text"
    }
  }
}

Concept Options:

  • "Text" or "native.Text" for native text
  • Any custom concept that is strictly compatible with native.Text

docs.title: 2.2: Explicit List of Strings
docs.text:
{
  "inputs": {
    "documents": {
      "concept": "Text",
      "content": ["text1", "text2", "text3"]
    }
  }
}

Result: ListContent with multiple TextContent items

docs.title: 2.3: Structured Object with Concept
docs.text:
{
  "inputs": {
    "invoice_data": {
      "concept": "Invoice",
      "content": {
        "invoice_number": "INV-001",
        "amount": 1250.00,
        "date": "2025-10-20"
      }
    }
  }
}

Concept Resolution with Search Domains:

When you specify a concept name without a domain prefix:

  • ✅ If the concept exists in only one domain → Automatically found
  • ❌ If the concept exists in multiple domains → Error: "Multiple concepts found. Please specify domain as 'domain.Concept'"
  • ❌ If the concept doesn't exist → Error: "Concept not found"

Using Domain Prefix: 

{
  "concept": "accounting.Invoice"
}

This explicitly tells Pipelex to use the Invoice concept from the accounting domain.

docs.title: 2.4: List of Structured Objects
docs.text:
{
  "inputs": {
    "invoices": {
      "concept": "Invoice",
      "content": [
        {
          "invoice_number": "INV-001",
          "amount": 1250.00
        },
        {
          "invoice_number": "INV-002",
          "amount": 890.00
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

Result: ListContent with multiple structured content items

docs.title: 2.5: Dictionary Content
docs.text:
Provide structured data as a dictionary:

{
  "inputs": {
    "person": {
      "concept": "PersonInfo",
      "content": {
        "arg1": "something",
        "arg2": 1,
        "arg3": {
          "arg4": "something else"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}

The system will: 1. Find the concept structure (with domain resolution as explained above) 2. Validate the dictionary against the concept's structure 3. Create the appropriate content object

docs.title: 2.6: List of Dictionaries
docs.text:
{
  "inputs": {
    "people": {
      "concept": "PersonInfo",
      "content": [
        {
          "arg1": "something",
          "arg2": 1,
          "arg3": {"arg4": "something else"}
        },
        {
          "arg1": "something else",
          "arg2": 2,
          "arg3": {"arg4": "something else else"}
        }
      ]
    }
  }
}

docs.title: 2.7: File / Document Input
docs.text:
For pipes whose inputs declare Document, Image, or PDF (any URL-bearing native concept), provide a url inside content. The URL can be public HTTP(S), a pipelex-storage:// URI, or a base64 data URL.

{
  "inputs": {
    "cv": {
      "concept": "Document",
      "content": { "url": "https://example.com/resume.pdf" }
    },
    "headshot": {
      "concept": "Image",
      "content": { "url": "https://example.com/photo.jpg" }
    }
  }
}

Optional fields on Document content:

  • mime_type (string) — e.g. "application/pdf". Inferred from the URL when omitted.
  • filename (string) — the original filename. Auto-extracted from local-file URLs.
  • title (string) — display title for the document.
  • snippet (string) — text excerpt or description.
  • public_url (string) — public HTTPS URL when url is a private/storage URI.

If you pass Document content as a list ([{"url": "…"}, {"url": "…"}]), Pipelex wraps it in a ListContent automatically — same rules as Case 2.4.

docs.title: Using DictStuff Instances (Python Clients Only)
docs.text:
For Python clients, you can also pass DictStuff instances instead of plain dicts. DictStuff is a Pydantic model with the same structure as the explicit format.

from pipelex.client import PipelexClient
from pipelex.core.stuffs.stuff import DictStuff

client = PipelexClient(api_token="YOUR_API_KEY")

# Using DictStuff instance with dict content
response = await client.execute_pipeline(
    pipe_code="process_invoice",
    inputs={
        "invoice": DictStuff(
            concept="accounting.Invoice",
            content={
                "invoice_number": "INV-001",
                "amount": 1250.00,
                "date": "2025-10-20",
            },
        ),
    },
)

# Using DictStuff instance with list of dicts content
response = await client.execute_pipeline(
    pipe_code="process_invoices",
    inputs={
        "invoices": DictStuff(
            concept="accounting.Invoice",
            content=[
                {"invoice_number": "INV-001", "amount": 1250.00},
                {"invoice_number": "INV-002", "amount": 890.00},
            ],
        ),
    },
)

# Using DictStuff instance with list of strings (for Text concept)
response = await client.execute_pipeline(
    pipe_code="analyze_texts",
    inputs={
        "documents": DictStuff(
            concept="Text",
            content=["document 1", "document 2", "document 3"],
        ),
    },
)

DictStuff Structure:

  • concept (str): The concept code (with optional domain prefix)
  • content (dict[str, Any] | list[Any]): The actual data content

Content Types:

  • Dictionary: Single structured object → Creates a single Stuff
  • List of dicts: Multiple structured objects → Creates ListContent with validated items
  • List of strings (for Text-compatible concepts): Creates ListContent of TextContent

Note: DictStuff instances are automatically converted to plain dicts and processed through the standard Case 2 logic.

docs.title: Search Domains Explained
docs.text: When you reference a concept by name (like "Invoice" or "PersonInfo"), Pipelex needs to find it in your loaded domains.

docs.title: Automatic Search
docs.text:
{
  "concept": "Invoice"
}

What happens: 1. Pipelex searches all available domains for a concept named "Invoice" 2. If found in exactly one domain → ✅ Uses that concept 3. If found in multiple domains → ❌ Error: "Ambiguous concept: Found 'Invoice' in domains: accounting, billing. Use 'domain.Invoice' format." 4. If not found → ❌ Error: "Concept 'Invoice' not found in any domain"

docs.title: Explicit Domain Specification
docs.text:
To avoid ambiguity, specify the domain explicitly:

{
  "concept": "accounting.Invoice"
}

Format: "domain_name.ConceptName"

This tells Pipelex exactly which concept to use, bypassing the search.

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
• Use simple names ("Invoice") when you have unique concept names across domains
  • Use domain-prefixed names ("accounting.Invoice") when:
  • You have concepts with the same name in different domains
  • You want to be explicit about which concept to use
  • You're building APIs that need to be unambiguous

docs.title: Multiple Input Combinations
docs.text:
Combine different input types in a single request:

{
  "inputs": {
    "text": "Analyze this contract for risks.",
    "category": {
      "concept": "Category",
      "content": {"name": "legal", "priority": "high"}
    },
    "options": ["option1", "option2", "option3"],
    "invoice": {
      "concept": "accounting.Invoice",
      "content": {
        "invoice_number": "INV-001",
        "amount": 1250.00
      }
    }
  }
}

In this example:

  • text uses direct string format (Case 1.1)
  • category uses explicit format with structured content (Case 2.5)
  • options uses direct list format (Case 1.2)
  • invoice uses explicit format with domain prefix and structured content (Case 2.5)
Copy Markdown

docs.title: Pipe Validate
docs.text:
Validate a method by parsing, loading, and dry-running its pipes without executing them.

Endpoint: POST /v1/validate

/validate is a diagnostic endpoint: any verdict the validator can produce — valid, invalid, or valid-but-not-runnable — rides an HTTP 200, discriminated in the body on is_valid. "Invalid, here are the problems" is the successful product of the call, not a transport failure. Non-2xx is reserved for the cases where no verdict could be produced (a malformed request body, an mthds_sources length mismatch, a method tree that cannot be read, a method_ref that could not be resolved, auth, or a server fault).

Request Body:

{
  "files": {
    "my_domain.mthds": "domain = \"my_domain\"\ndescription = \"My domain\"\nmain_pipe = \"my_pipe\"\n\n[concept.MyResult]\ndescription = \"A result\"\n\n[pipe.my_pipe]\ntype = \"PipeLLM\"\ndescription = \"Process input\"\ninputs = { text = \"native.Text\" }\noutput = \"MyResult\""
  }
}

The method to validate is sent in files, a map from each file's path in the method's folder to that file's content, exactly as a run sends it, or named by its address in method_ref. The older mthds_contents, an array of .mthds texts, is still accepted, but it is being retired together with mthds_sources and resources, which serve it, and a later release refuses them.

Request Fields:

  • files (object, optional): The method as a map of file entries, the MTHDS standard's method tree, each value the file's text, {"base64": "…"} or {"sha256": "…", "size": n}, read as on a run — see Validating a method tree. Exactly one of files / method_ref / mthds_contents must be provided
  • dependencies (object, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The method packages the method calls by address that the runner cannot fetch, each a map of file entries keyed by its address, as on a run. Accompanies files
  • method_ref (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. Validate a published method by address — github.com/<owner>/<repo> plus an optional package selector and @<tag> — resolved by this server through the same fetch path as a method_ref run: the repository is fetched at the tag, the package located by manifest identity, and its tree read from the commit's git objects and validated as a tree sent in files is — see Validating a method tree. Exactly one of files / method_ref / mthds_contents; mthds_sources cannot accompany it. A package holding Python and a requirements.txt has its requirements checked on this server against the packages the deployment's PipeFunc sandbox offers for them before anything is validated, and a requirement the sandbox does not meet, or a line the standard refuses, makes the verdict is_valid: false with one item per line, whose source is requirements.txt and whose line is the line's number; a deployment refusing the requirements with its own explanation, no environment it can build holding them, makes it is_valid: false with one item on requirements.txt and no line
  • mthds_contents (list[str], optional): Being retired: send the method in files. MTHDS contents to validate (always an array, even for a single file). Exactly one of files / method_ref / mthds_contents must be provided. Still accepted until a later release refuses it
  • read_scope (string, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The scope the validation reads the method under, as a run's read_scope, which a multi-tenant host sends for the organization it serves; a jwt caller may send only a scope under its own id, else a 403 auth.forbidden whose requirement is read_scope_under_caller. A hash entry of files resolves in that scope's blob store — see Sending files by hash — and the runner hands the scope to its validator, so a validation dispatched to a worker can hand it the method through that store — see Where validation runs. Omitted, a hash entry resolves in the caller's own id's store, but only a validation carrying it records the tree it read in the blob store, and the validator is handed no scope, so a dry run without one leaves nothing stored
  • allow_signatures (boolean, optional, default false): controls only the sweep mechanics for PipeSignature placeholders — whether signature pipes are mock-run during the dry-run sweep and therefore listed in validated_pipes. It does not change the verdict: an unimplemented signature is never a rejection, it is a runnability fact reported via pending_signatures + is_runnable in both modes
  • mthds_sources (list[str] | null, optional): Being retired with mthds_contents: the files of a method sent in files are named by their tree paths. Per-file sources, parallel to mthds_contents — see Sourcing submitted files. When present it must match mthds_contents in length (a mismatch is a 422 request error), and it accompanies mthds_contents alone, since a tree's files are named by their tree paths
  • resources (object | null, optional): Pipelex-API extension, being retired with mthds_contents: put the files in the method's tree, in files. The files the bundle's steps read, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, as a map from the path the step names to the file's bytes in standard base64 — see Sending the files the steps read. It accompanies mthds_contents or files, whose tree each file joins; beside method_ref it is a 422
  • render (list[str], optional, default []): opt-in rendered text to attach to the verdict — see Opt-in extras
  • views (list[str], optional, default []): opt-in structured views to attach to the verdict — see Opt-in extras
  • orchestration_mode (string | null, optional): per-request backend override for the validation dispatch — see Where validation runs. Honored only when the deployment allows it; a forbidden override is a 422 pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden
  • analytics_groups (object | null, optional): Pipelex-API extension. The groups the caller belongs to, as a mapping of group type to group key, with the same rules as on a run — see Who the validation is done for. A mapping outside those rules is a 422 request.invalid naming the field analytics_groups

Response (the verdict union):

The 200 body is one of two arms, discriminated on the mandatory is_valid field. A consumer pattern-matches is_valid to learn the verdict — it never inspects a status code or catches an exception body.

Valid arm (is_valid: true) — the canonical Pipelex validation report (the exact same artifact shapes PipelexMTHDSProtocol.validate returns when the runtime is used locally) plus this server's wire-only extras (mthds_contents echo, message, default_pipe_ref):

{
  "is_valid": true,
  "bundle_blueprint": {
    "domain": "my_domain",
    "description": "My domain",
    "main_pipe": "my_pipe",
    "concept": { "...": "..." },
    "pipe": { "...": "..." }
  },
  "pipe_io_contracts": {
    "my_domain.my_pipe": {
      "inputs": { "text": { "concept_ref": "native.Text", "presence": "plain", "multiplicity": "single", "item_count": null, "json_schema": { "...": "..." } } },
      "output": { "concept_ref": "my_domain.MyResult", "multiplicity": "single", "item_count": null, "optional": false, "json_schema": { "...": "..." } }
    }
  },
  "graph_spec": { "...": "..." },
  "validated_pipes": [
    { "pipe_ref": "my_domain.my_pipe", "status": "SUCCESS" }
  ],
  "pending_signatures": [],
  "is_runnable": true,
  "tree_files_read": {
    "my_domain.my_pipe": []
  },
  "tree_file_readers": {},
  "mthds_contents": ["..."],
  "message": "MTHDS content validated successfully",
  "default_pipe_ref": "my_domain.my_pipe"
}

Response Fields (canonical report — valid arm):

  • is_valid (true): the discriminant of the valid arm — always true on this report
  • bundle_blueprint (object): the batch's primary blueprint — the first file declaring main_pipe, else the first file
  • pipe_io_contracts (object): per-pipe input/output contracts, keyed by the namespaced pipe_ref (domain.code). Each input carries its concept_ref, presence, multiplicity (single | variable | fixed), item_count and the JSON Schema of its content; the output carries its fully qualified concept_ref, multiplicity, item_count, optional and the JSON Schema of its payload. item_count is the exact count on fixed, always greater than one since Concept[1] reads as single, and null otherwise, so an output declared Text[3] reports "multiplicity": "fixed", "item_count": 3
  • graph_spec (object, optional): best-effort execution graph of the pipe a selector-less run of this request would execute — the pipe default_pipe_ref names — dry-run against the validated library; absent when no entry pipe is determined or the graph dry-run degrades
  • validated_pipes (list): per-pipe sweep outcomes — {pipe_ref, status} entries with status SUCCESS | FAILURE | SKIPPED
  • warnings (list): advisory findings that never flip is_valid, each a problem item with the same shape as an item of the invalid arm's errors, so one parser reads both. Four families, always in this order: the useless-! lint (method.optional_force_redundant), the entry-pipe vacuous-presence lint (method.input_presence_vacuous), the intent-hint lints (method.hint_invalid, whose reason is unknown_key, unknown_intent or inapplicable_intent, whose hint names the hint, and whose location names the declaration the hint is on: field concept.<Concept> for a concept, concept.<Concept>.structure.<field> for a field of its structure, pipe and input for a pipe's input), and the warnings a PipeDocGen step's template check found in its office template file during the dry run (pipelex.docgen.template_warning, whose template names the file and finding says what the check found, located at the step by its pipe). A member an item does not have is absent, never null. Empty when there is nothing to report
  • pending_signatures (list[str]): namespaced refs of pipes still declared as signatures (contract-only pipes — inputs/output with no type and no implementation) in the assembled library — what remains to implement
  • is_runnable (boolean): pending_signatures is empty — whether the validated library is complete enough to run
  • tree_files_read (object): per step, the files of the method's tree it reads, keyed by the same namespaced pipe_ref as pipe_io_contracts. Each entry is a list of {tree_path, use} items, tree_path being the file's path from the root of the method's tree with forward slashes, never a path on the server, and use one of template (a PipeDocGen step's template_file), template_asset (a file an HTML template names by a literal relative URL, such as an image, a stylesheet or a font, or a file a stylesheet it names refers to) and python_module (the module holding a PipeFunc step's function, module.py or a package's __init__.py). A step that reads no file, a controller or a step whose template is written inline with no asset, has an empty list, and so does a PipeFunc whose function is found on the runtime's import path rather than in the tree. See Validating a method tree
  • tree_file_readers (object): the same facts read the other way, keyed by tree path in sorted order, each listing the pipe_refs of the steps that read that file. A file of the tree that no step reads, the bundles themselves, a README or a package's __init__.py beside its modules, has no entry

Response Fields (wire extras, valid arm only, this server only):

  • mthds_contents (list[str]): the text of the validated bundles: the .mthds files of a method sent in files or fetched by method_ref, in tree path order, or the request's own mthds_contents
  • message (string): status message
  • default_pipe_ref (string, optional): the qualified domain.pipe_code a caller gets by omitting the pipe selector — the pipe a selector-less run of this same request would execute; absent when no entry pipe is determined. See The effective entry pipe below

A top-level member the verdict has no value for is absent from the body, never written as null.

Response Fields (opt-in, present only when requested):

  • input_form (object, valid arm only, requires views: ["input_form"]): per-pipe input-form descriptors, keyed by the same namespaced pipe_ref as pipe_io_contracts. Each entry carries an ordered fields list describing what a caller must collect to run that pipe — a field's kind (drawn from a closed vocabulary), its name, whether it is required, whether an empty value should gate the run, and the per-kind detail (choices, item_count, default_value, nested concept_ref, …). It is a projection of facts the verdict already states, derived from what the bundle authored rather than from the emitted JSON Schema, so a client can render a run form from the verdict alone
  • output_form (object, valid arm only, requires views: ["output_form"]): per-pipe output-form descriptors, keyed by the same namespaced pipe_ref as pipe_io_contracts. Each entry carries a single field, drawn from the same closed field vocabulary input_form uses, describing what that pipe produces — so a caller rendering a result, or registering a tool signature with a return type, reads the output's shape without inferring it from a value. Its JSON Schema is not here: that rides pipe_io_contracts[…].output.json_schema, and the pairing is the point — the descriptor states what the output IS, the schema names the property its payload arrives under
  • rendered_markdown (string, both arms, requires render: ["markdown"]): a server-rendered Markdown view of the verdict. The valid arm's is produced by the renderer the local CLI uses; the invalid arm's presents the very items errors holds, in the same view, each numbered under its code's title with its code, where it is, its sentence, its suggestions and its suggested fix, so it never says what that view of the items leaves out

Invalid arm (is_valid: false) — the per-error diagnostics plus the runnability facts; the structural artifacts (bundle_blueprint, pipe_io_contracts, graph_spec, validated_pipes) and mthds_contents are absent, because they do not exist when load/parse/wiring failed:

{
  "is_valid": false,
  "errors": [
    {
      "code": "method.identifier_invalid",
      "detail": "A name is not a valid identifier",
      "location": { "file": "broken.mthds" }
    }
  ],
  "pending_signatures": [],
  "is_runnable": false,
  "message": "The method does not validate."
}

Response Fields (invalid arm):

  • is_valid (false): the discriminant of the invalid arm
  • errors (list): the structured per-error diagnostics a client maps to per-line problems, each a problem item — built by pipelex's one shared builder, so they are the same findings the agent CLI reports. Each item carries the registry code a program branches on, the detail its code renders from the item's params, and the location the runtime can attribute (pipe, concept, field, file, line, column). A member an item does not have is absent, never null. An item may also carry a suggested_fix — a structured, deterministic repair (fix_code, description, safety: safe|unsafe, the file to apply it to, and the ops[] of semantic TOML patch operations to apply). It is present only when the fix planner derived one from the typed error data; a client that ignores it behaves exactly as before. See Error Responses → Structured validation errors and → Suggested fixes for every field. The array is never empty on an invalid verdict (the structured-info invariant is total): a failing dry run becomes one item per failing pipe, under the failure's own code, located at the innermost pipe that failed (its pipe and, when known, its file), a TOML syntax error is a method.syntax item carrying the line and column the parser stopped at, and a parse-level failure with no attributable locator (an empty blueprint, an elaborator failure) becomes one residual item under the code of the refusal. Every refusal of the bundle while it loads is an item of the verdict, never a no-verdict 5xx: an unknown model is a model.unknown item on the pipe's model field, naming the model and its model_type (a reference the deck does not define, or a bare handle it serves only as another model type, such as an LLM named in a PipeImgGen; GET /v1/models/check answers the same question for one reference), a model setting the model it resolves to refuses (a reasoning setting on a model that does not reason, for instance) is a model.capability_unsupported item on the field naming the setting, a PipeFunc step whose function its method's files do not hold, or do not define as a top-level function marked @pipe_func(), is a method.function_invalid item on its function_name field, and a call into a method package this runtime cannot resolve (not installed and not fetchable, or a fetch that failed) is a method.dependency_missing item on the first pipe naming the package, whose name is the package as the reference names it
  • pending_signatures (list[str]): best-effort outstanding signatures (empty on the invalid arm, since no library was assembled)
  • is_runnable (false): an invalid bundle is never runnable
  • message (string): the human-readable verdict summary, the sentence the refusal's code renders

docs.title: What This Endpoint Does
docs.text: The route wraps the runtime's protocol validate: parse → load → dry-run-sweep every pipe → build the per-pipe IO contracts → best-effort graph of the entry pipe → assemble the canonical report. The runner returns the verdict as a value — the canonical report on the valid arm, or a BundleValidationFailure (the refusal's problem with its validation items, a bundle the caller can fix) on the invalid arm — and the route maps the invalid verdict to the 200 invalid arm by matching the returned value, never by catching a transport error. A bundle that declares no main_pipe, when no manifest names one either, validates normally and simply carries no graph_spec — there is no main-pipe precondition.

docs.title: The effective entry pipe
docs.text:
default_pipe_ref states which pipe this request's closure would run if the caller named none. It applies the run routes' own precedence, minus the request selector /validate does not have:

  1. a method_ref's fetched package manifest (METHODS.toml) main_pipe — the package author's declared entry pipe, qualified against the closure;
  2. otherwise, and when the manifest declares none, the closure's primary blueprint's main_pipe (the first file declaring one), qualified by its domain.

It is absent when no entry pipe is determined — no blueprint declares main_pipe, or a manifest names a pipe the closure does not declare, or declares in several domains. In those last two cases a selector-less run by that address would fail to resolve the manifest's pipe too, so the field says nothing rather than naming the closure's pipe, which no such run would execute.

The field exists because the canonical report is manifest-blind: bundle_blueprint is the batch's primary blueprint, so for a package whose METHODS.toml entry differs from — or exists without — a bundle-level main_pipe, a consumer deriving the entry pipe from bundle_blueprint.main_pipe alone gets the wrong pipe, or none. Reading default_pipe_ref is how a client projects an entry signature that matches what POST /v1/execute and POST /v1/start actually default to.

The graph follows the same precedence: on a method_ref request whose manifest names a main_pipe, the route hands that pipe to the runtime as the graph target, so graph_spec draws the pipe default_pipe_ref names — including for a package whose bundles declare no main_pipe at all, whose entry pipe only the manifest states. A manifest main_pipe the closure does not resolve leaves both fields absent rather than graphing the closure's own main_pipe, which no run by that address executes. The target travels with the dispatch, so a validation sent to a worker is graphed the same way.

It states the run default, which is looser than the /pipe-io selection chain on one point: a closure whose domains each declare a main_pipe cannot be defaulted on /pipe-io (a 422), but /execute and /start run its first declaring blueprint happily — so this field names that pipe rather than being absent.

The field rides the valid arm only. The invalid arm assembles no library, so there is no entry pipe to name and the field is absent, like the other structural artifacts.

docs.title: Opt-in extras (render and views)
docs.text:
A caller that wants the artifacts without the verdict — to show a method, prepare its inputs or generate types for it — reads POST /v1/pipe-io instead: it returns pipe_io_contracts, input_form and output_form for one pipe or every pipe, equal to this route's for a closure both accept, with no dry-run sweep.

The verdict body is lean by default: a request that sends neither list gets exactly the structured contract described above, byte-identical to a request that omits both fields. This matters because the highest-frequency callers of /validate — editor hooks, CI gates, agent loops — read a handful of fields and discard the rest, and should never pay for bytes they throw away.

Two independent opt-in axes attach more:

  • render produces rendered text, attached under a mechanical rendered_<format> key. The supported token is markdown, which attaches rendered_markdown on both 200 arms — failure text is exactly what a human-facing surface wants.
  • views attaches a structured artifact under a same-named top-level field. The supported tokens are input_form and output_form, each attaching a field of its own name on the valid arm only: the descriptors derive from a library that was never assembled when load/parse/wiring failed, so they follow bundle_blueprint, pipe_io_contracts and graph_spec into absence on the invalid arm.

Both lists share the same mechanics, and both are deliberately typed as plain list[str] rather than closed enums at the request boundary:

  • Each token is resolved independently against the server's supported set. A known token is honored; an unknown or unsupported one is silently dropped — never a 422. A stale token from an older client must not fail the call, and one bad token in a list does not poison the good ones.
  • The lists are treated as sets: order-insensitive and deduped.
  • They are independent of each other. A request may carry both, and each resolves its own tokens against its own supported set. A token is unknown to the other list — sending render: ["input_form"] attaches nothing at all.
  • Neither ever appears on a no-verdict response. No verdict, no view.

Neither axis is part of the verdict contract: a machine consumer branches on the structured fields, and an extra is a presentation or a projection layered on top. That is what keeps adding a token, or changing what one renders, a non-breaking change.

docs.title: Sourcing submitted files
docs.text:
A method sent in files needs no sources: each of its bundles is named by its tree path, which is the location.file of every item it owns. This section concerns mthds_contents, which is being retired, and mthds_sources goes with it.

The mthds_contents path carries bundle text, not file paths, so by default the runtime cannot tell the client which file an error belongs to — an item's location carries no file. Send mthds_sources parallel to mthds_contents to fix this: each source is the logical identity of that content (e.g. the file's path relative to the submitted directory), and the runtime threads it onto the corresponding blueprint.source. The source then rides back on both arms — bundle_blueprint.source on the valid arm, and errors[].location.file on the invalid arm — so a multi-file editor client can map a cross-file diagnostic to the file that owns it. Omit mthds_sources (or send null) and behavior is exactly as before. The list, when present, must be the same length as mthds_contents; a mismatch is a request-shape 422 (it is the caller's wiring bug, caught before the validation sweep runs). A source is a label for diagnostics and nothing more: even one naming a real file on the server is never a directory the server reads from, so a step's template file comes from resources alone, and an address-based reference is not searched for above it.

docs.title: Validating a method tree
docs.text:
A method sent in files, or fetched by method_ref, is validated whole, as it would run: the runner reads the tree under the standard's rule, writes it into a temporary directory, and validates it as one library directory of the caller's, with the packages it ships in dependencies (or, for a method_ref package, under its own .mthds/methods/<name>/) loaded beside it, so a call into one resolves as on a run. Every bundle is named by its tree path, so errors[].location.file names the owning file, and no item names a path on the server.

  • Python is checked by syntax. Every .py file of the tree is read and compiled, never imported or run, whether or not a step names it: a file that does not parse, or is not UTF-8, makes the verdict is_valid: false with an item whose location.file is the file's tree path and whose location.line is the line of the error. A PipeFunc step's function is then located in the tree and its form checked statically. As on a run, a tree holding Python is refused with a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox on a deployment that is not sandbox-hosted.
  • A call by address resolves as on a run. A package the method calls by its address is searched for in the packages the request ships, then among the methods installed on the runner, and is fetched when it is in neither and the runner fetches on a miss, as a run of the same method finds it, so the verdict says what that run would do. This is deliberate, and unlike the crate routes, /resolve and /codegen and /pipe-io, which resolve only from what was shipped: their artifacts describe the method as sent, while a verdict answers whether it runs here. A package found nowhere, or whose fetch fails, makes the verdict is_valid: false, with a method.dependency_missing item naming the package's address as its name.
  • The tree is written and loaded off the event loop. Writing the tree to disk, removing it afterwards, finding its entry pipe for the graph and every load of the validation run in worker threads of the bounded method-load pool, so a slow step, such as a large tree, a fetch on a miss or a sandbox's judgment of the method's requirements.txt, never holds up the server's other requests.
  • The default pipe and the graph follow the tree's entry pipe. default_pipe_ref is the pipe the protocol's rule names, the main_pipe of the root METHODS.toml or the one main_pipe its bundles declare, and the graph is drawn from it. A tree with no entry pipe validates with neither default_pipe_ref nor graph_spec.
  • Refusals of the tree itself produce no verdict: a key the tree's rule refuses is a 422 method.package_invalid naming the rule as its reason, or security.input_path_refused for a key leaving the tree's root, a malformed entry a 422 request.invalid, a hash the runner does not hold a 422 request.blobs_missing, and a tree past its limits a 422 method.package_invalid naming the limit, as on a run.
  • The mthds_contents echo holds the text of the tree's own bundles.
  • The report names the files each step reads. tree_files_read lists, for each step, the files of the tree it reads, each by its tree path and its use, and tree_file_readers lists, for each such file, the steps that read it, so an editor can show which step uses which file and warn before a file a step reads is renamed or removed. The paths are derived from what each step already names, a PipeDocGen step's template_file and the literal relative URLs of its HTML template, and a PipeFunc step's function_name located in the tree, with no reference syntax of their own. A file sent in resources is named by its key, collapsed as the key is.

docs.title: Sending the files the steps read (resources)
docs.text:
A method sent in files carries the files its steps read in its own tree, each at its path beside the bundle whose step names it, so it needs no resources:

{
  "files": {
    "invoicing.mthds": "domain = "invoicing"
...
[pipe.print_invoice]
type = "PipeDocGen"
...
format = "docx"
template_file = "templates/invoice.docx"",
    "templates/invoice.docx": {"base64": "UEsDBBQABgAIAAAAIQ..."}
  }
}

resources is being retired on every route that takes it, and a later release refuses it: here and on the run routes it goes with mthds_contents, and on the routes that take a method only as a tree, a file the steps read travels inside the tree. Until then, a bundle sent as content has no directory, so a file one of its steps reads from beside the bundle, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, can be sent with it in resources. The same field, with the same rules, is accepted by /v1/execute and /v1/start, /v1/pipe-io, and /v1/resolve and /v1/codegen.

{
  "mthds_contents": ["domain = "invoicing"
...
[pipe.print_invoice]
type = "PipeDocGen"
...
format = "docx"
template_file = "templates/invoice.docx""],
  "resources": {"templates/invoice.docx": "UEsDBBQABgAIAAAAIQ..."}
}
  • Each key is the path a step names, relative to the bundle and written with forward slashes, exactly as in its template_file. . segments and repeated slashes collapse, so ./templates/invoice.docx names the same file; every bundle of the request is read as sitting in one directory. An empty or absolute path, a drive or a network share, or a .. segment is a 422 security.input_path_refused, whose rule is absolute or parent_segment, and a backslash, a colon, or two keys naming the same file is a 422 request.invalid naming the field resources, each refused before any value is decoded. A method sent as a tree may hold the file instead, beside the bundle whose step names it; beside a tree, each key of resources joins it at that path from the tree's root, and a file the tree already holds must have the same bytes (see Pipe Run).
  • Each value is the file's bytes in standard base64 (RFC 4648, with padding). A value that does not decode is a 422 request.malformed whose reason is bad_base64.
  • Beside inline contents, every file must be one a step names. A file no step of the bundle reads is a 422 problem with the code request.invalid, whose operator view's message lists the unnamed paths: a misspelled key fails loudly rather than leaving its step without its file. This is a request error, never an is_valid: false verdict. Beside a tree, a file no step names is kept like any other file of the tree.
  • The sizes are bounded: at most MAX_RESOURCES_PER_REQUEST files (32 by default), each at most MAX_RESOURCE_FILE_KIB once decoded (5 MiB by default), and at most MAX_RESOURCES_TOTAL_KIB across the request (10 MiB by default). Too many files is a 422 request.invalid naming the field resources, and a file or a request over its size limit a 413 request.too_large giving the limit and the size in bytes, an oversized file refused on the size its encoded length carries before it is decoded. The whole body stays under MAX_REQUEST_BODY_MIB as well.
  • The files make one method tree, with the request's bundles at its root. A run names that tree by its digest, as it names the tree of a method loaded from a directory, and carries none of the files in its payloads, a remote orchestrator's included: the step that reads one reads it from the tree, through the deployment's method file store. Two files colliding in one tree, such as two keys equal once case-folded, are a 422 request.invalid naming the field resources.

The files are checked as files on disk are. An .html template file is checked against the step's inputs when the bundle loads, and the document engine's template check runs on an office template file in the validation's dry run, where its errors are validation errors on the step. A step whose template_file could not be a key, being empty or absolute, or holding a .. segment, a backslash, a colon or a NUL character, is refused when its bundle is parsed, whatever the request sends: the verdict's one item is located at the step by its pipe and by the field pipe.<code>, and its sentence names the field without repeating the path. A step whose template_file could be a key but was not sent is refused at load, and the verdict's errors[] holds a method.resource_missing item, located at the step, whose file parameter is the key the file is expected under.

docs.title: Where validation runs
docs.text:
Validation is orchestration_mode-aware, the same way /start is: the runner resolves the effective backend (the deployment default plus the optional per-request orchestration_mode override) and dispatches through the bundle-validator registry. Validation is inherently blocking, so there is no delivery axis here — only the backend varies. On the orchestrator-agnostic base — and for orchestration_mode: direct — the whole job runs in-process in one library load on the API side. On an orchestrator flavor whose mode is selected (e.g. temporal), the whole job is dispatched to a worker instead, and the API side assembles the same canonical report from the worker's result without loading a library. Either way the verdict is byte-identical: the backend changes, the contract does not. A per-request override the deployment forbids is refused with a 422 pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden.

The validator is handed the request's read_scope, the scope a run of the same request reads under, so a validator that dispatches to a worker can hand it the method's trees through that scope's blob store and the worker read them by digest, as a run's worker reads its method's files under the run's read scope. A tree sent in files is already recorded there when the validator is called. A request without a read_scope hands the validator none, never the caller's own id, so a dispatched validation stores nothing under a prefix no host lists or erases.

Resource note for deployment. When validation runs in-process (the agnostic base, or direct mode), the API server loads the method library to validate, so a deployment that receives large or frequent in-process /validate traffic should be sized for that load (memory + CPU for library assembly and the graph dry-run). On a distributed-execution flavor that dispatches validation to a worker, the library work happens worker-side; size the workers accordingly.

The graph is best-effort: a bundle that validates but whose graph dry-run fails still returns 200 on the valid arm, with no graph_spec.

docs.title: Who the validation is done for
docs.text: A validation is not a run, but it still emits telemetry: the sweep's pipe_dry_run event and every dry run it performs. The route hands the runtime the caller it is working for — the authenticated user, exactly as a run states it (the single-tenant placeholder when the deployment has no user model), and the request's analytics_groups, or none — and the runtime attributes that telemetry to them rather than to the deployment's configured identity. The caller travels with the dispatch, so a validation sent to a worker is attributed the same way. How each telemetry stream then treats the caller is the runtime's decision, described with analytics_groups on a run.

docs.title: No-verdict (non-2xx) responses
docs.text:
Only conditions where the endpoint could not produce a verdict are non-2xx, rendered as RFC 9457 problem documents:

  • 422 — a malformed request body (request.malformed), an mthds_sources / mthds_contents length mismatch, more or fewer than one of files / method_ref / mthds_contents, or a malformed analytics_groups (request.invalid, naming the field), or a per-request orchestration_mode override the deployment does not allow (pipelex.deployment.orchestration_override_forbidden) — request-shape errors caught before the runtime.
  • 422 on a method tree — a key the tree's rule refuses (method.package_invalid, or security.input_path_refused), a malformed entry (request.invalid), a hash entry the runner does not hold (request.blobs_missing), or a tree past its limits (method.package_invalid) — see Validating a method tree.
  • 422 and 413 on resources — a path that cannot name a file inside the bundle (security.input_path_refused, or request.invalid), a file no step names (request.invalid), files that cannot make one tree (request.invalid), too many files (request.invalid), a file or a request over its size limit (request.too_large), or a value that is not base64 (request.malformed) — see Sending the files the steps read.
  • 401 — unauthenticated (auth.missing_credential, auth.invalid_credential, auth.credential_expired).
  • method_ref resolution failures — a selector that could not be resolved produced no verdict, so it is never rendered as is_valid: false: a malformed reference is a 422 request.invalid, a failed fetch a 502 method.fetch_failed, no matching package in the repository a 404 method.not_found, the sandbox gate on custom Python a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox, and the refusal of Python structure classes a 422 pipelex.deployment.python_structures_refused — the same statuses and codes as on the run routes (see the error table).
  • 5xx — a server fault (including a host-wiring programmer error, surfaced as runtime.unexpected).

Read it as one rule: a non-2xx on /validate always means "the endpoint could not produce a verdict," never "your bundle is bad."

Copy Markdown

docs.title: Storage transport (/upload, /resolve-storage-url) — REMOVED
docs.text: Both routes are gone from this server. They were never part of the published Pipelex API contract — neither the MTHDS Protocol nor the build extensions — and their docstrings said so. The "Future ownership" section this page used to carry predicted the move; it has happened, and the removal decision it left open was taken with it.

docs.title: Where they went
docs.text: To the hosted Pipelex platform, still at POST /v1/upload and POST /v1/resolve-storage-url on api.pipelex.com, with byte-identical request and response shapes. Released SDK versions keep working: @pipelex/sdk's uploadFile / prepareInputs and pipelex-sdk's upload_file / prepare_inputs are unchanged, and the pipelex-storage:// scheme is unchanged.

docs.title: Why they could not stay here
docs.text:
Both keyed S3 objects under the caller's own id — {user_id}/assets/{uuid}.{ext} — and authorized a read by comparing that first path segment against the requester. That is an ownership model with no notion of a team, and on the hosted side those URIs get saved onto organization-scoped rows, so the second member of a team to open a shared method got a 403 on their own team's file.

Fixing it means putting the organization at segment 0, and this server has no organization concept to put there. It is a generic execution engine: a single opaque caller id is its entire trusted identity surface, by design. So the routes belong where membership is already resolved before the request arrives.

docs.title: What a self-hoster does now
docs.text:
Nothing in the runtime changed — only the two HTTP routes are gone. The storage provider is untouched: get_storage_provider(), pipelex-storage:// URIs, and everything the runtime does with them work exactly as before, and a pipeline still reads and writes assets through the configured backend.

What a self-hosted deployment no longer gets is an HTTP surface for putting bytes in and getting them back out. If you need one, it is yours to build, and its authorization model is yours to choose — which is the honest outcome, since the one removed here only ever fit a single-user deployment.

You can also skip storage entirely for most inputs: pass a public HTTP(S) URL or a base64 data URL directly as a Document / Image url.

docs.title: Webhooks
docs.text:
When a run ends, the API server can tell two different receivers about it, and the two never mix:

  • The caller's webhooks: the callback_urls a request to POST /v1/execute or POST /v1/start registers. Each receives the signed run.finished event described below, under a secret the server's operator configures.
  • The deployment's completion target: one URL the operator configures with COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL, which a /start run notifies with a completion notice carrying its own signature. It is how a deployment that hosts the server learns a run ended, and it never receives a caller's event.

callback_urls is a pipelex-api extension, not part of the MTHDS Protocol, which defines no completion channel. SDK clients pass it through the generic extra mapping, e.g. client.start(..., extra={"callback_urls": [...]}).

docs.title: Registering callback URLs
docs.text:
{
  "pipe_code": "your_pipeline_code",
  "inputs": { "input_name": "..." },
  "pipeline_run_id": "order-4242-run-1",
  "callback_urls": ["https://my-app.example.com/pipelex-finished"]
}

Both run routes take the field. A blocking /execute sends its events before it answers, since its caller may have lost the connection by then, so a receiver that never answers delays the response by about 51 seconds at most, three attempts of 15 seconds and the waits of 1 and 5 seconds between them, and a /start run sends them when the run ends. On /execute as on /start, a request may choose the run's pipeline_run_id, which the events then carry: a run still in flight under the same id refuses the request with a 409 pipelex.run.already_exists. A URL listed twice is delivered once.

A callback URL is refused before anything runs with a 422 security.input_url_refused when its scheme is not http or https, or when its host is one the runtime's SSRF rule refuses: localhost, a cloud metadata name such as metadata.google.internal in any case and with or without a trailing dot, or a literal address that is not publicly routable, a loopback, private, link-local, carrier-grade NAT or cloud metadata address among them. A scheme-relative URL, such as //169.254.169.254/latest/meta-data, is refused the same way when its host is one the rule refuses. It is the rule the delivery applies again when the webhook fires, resolving the name, and such a refusal also writes a security event. A callback URL that is not a URL at all, empty, longer than the limit, with no scheme, naming no host, or opening no authority with //, such as example.com:8080/hook or localhost:3000/cb, is a 422 request.invalid naming the field callback_urls and writes none.

A signing secret is required. The server signs every call it makes to a caller's webhook, so a server whose operator set no CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET refuses a request carrying callback_urls with a 422 pipelex.webhook.secret_not_configured, whose params.setting names the variable, before the method is fetched, written or run. A request without callback_urls never needs the secret. A value that is not a whsec_ secret is the server's misconfiguration, a 500 runtime.misconfigured whose component, the variable's name, only an operator reads.

docs.title: The run.finished event
docs.text:
