Each URL receives one POST per attempt, whose body is the run.finished event, compact JSON in UTF-8:

{"type":"run.finished","timestamp":"2026-10-22T11:59:58.250Z","attempt":1,"data":{"pipeline_run_id":"order-4242-run-1","status":"failed","error":{"type":"https://mthds.ai/errors/run.timed_out","title":"The run passed its time limit","detail":"…","code":"run.timed_out","domain":"method","retry":"no","next_step":{"kind":"change_method","detail":"…"},"params":{"timeout":3600},"pipeline_run_id":"order-4242-run-1"}}}
Member Value type run.finished, for every ending: the outcome is data.status. timestamp When the run ended, an RFC 3339 date-time in UTC written with Z. attempt Which attempt of the delivery this call is, counted from 1. data The run as the MTHDS protocol's status read serves it: its pipeline_run_id, its status, completed or failed, and a failed run's problem as error.

A run that was cancelled before it ended, such as when its server stopped mid-run, ended failed: its event reads failed, with the problem run.cancelled, and so does the completion notice of the deployment's completion target. A failed run's error is its problem document in the caller's view, whoever started the run: it carries the code, detail, retry and next_step the caller reads, and never diagnostics. It carries no status member, which is the HTTP envelope's. A member with no value is left out rather than written as null. The event never carries the run's results: the caller reads a /execute run's output from the response, and a /start run's results from storage.

A receiver ignores a member it does not know, and acknowledges an event whose type it does not know with a 2xx.

docs.title: Verifying the signature
docs.text:
Every call carries the three Standard Webhooks headers, so any Standard Webhooks library verifies it:

Header Value webhook-id The delivery's id, whd_ followed by letters, digits and underscores: the same on every attempt of the delivery, and different for every other delivery. webhook-timestamp The attempt's send time, in whole Unix seconds. webhook-signature One v1, signature per secret the server holds, separated by single spaces.

Each signature is the standard base64 of the HMAC-SHA256 of {webhook-id}.{webhook-timestamp}.{body}, the two header values exactly as sent and the body's bytes exactly as sent, under the key the secret carries: the standard base64 after its whsec_ prefix, decoded. A receiver holding the secret recomputes it over the raw body, before parsing it:

import base64, hashlib, hmac, time


def verify(*, secret: str, headers: dict[str, str], body: bytes) -> bool:
    key = base64.b64decode(secret.removeprefix("whsec_"))
    if abs(time.time() - int(headers["webhook-timestamp"])) > 300:
        return False
    signed_content = f"{headers['webhook-id']}.{headers['webhook-timestamp']}.".encode() + body
    expected = "v1," + base64.b64encode(hmac.new(key, signed_content, hashlib.sha256).digest()).decode()
    return any(hmac.compare_digest(expected, signature) for signature in headers["webhook-signature"].split(" "))

The receiver rejects a call whose timestamp is more than five minutes from its own clock, and deduplicates on webhook-id, never on the body: the body changes with each attempt, since attempt is part of it.

Rotating the secret. CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET holds one secret, or several separated by spaces, the current one first. Every call is signed under each of them, so to rotate, set the new secret first and the old one after it, move the receivers to the new secret, then drop the old one.

Trust model. One secret, the operator's, signs every caller webhook the server sends, so any receiver that holds it can sign an event for any run, whoever started it. That suits a server with a single tenant, or with receivers that trust each other. A host that serves several tenants does not hand the secret to them: it receives the events itself and relays them to its tenants under credentials of its own.

docs.title: Delivery
docs.text:
Each URL is delivered on its own and at the same time as the others: one receiver's slowness or failure never delays or fails another's delivery.

  • When it is sent: last, once the run's results are stored and the deployment's completion target notified, and once per URL. A run that completed but whose results cannot be stored, or whose completion target cannot be notified, ends failed, and its event says so, failed with that failure's problem, never completed.
  • What counts as delivered: a 2xx answered within 15 seconds of the call being sent. Anything else fails the attempt: another status, a redirect, which the server never follows, a time-out, a connection or TLS failure, and a host whose name resolves to a private, loopback, link-local or metadata address, which the server refuses to connect to and logs as a security event.
  • Retries: a delivery makes three attempts, the second one second after the first failed and the third five seconds after the second, each keeping the delivery's webhook-id. A refused address is not tried again. The three attempts are those of one delivery step: when the step itself runs again, as a durable orchestrator may run a step that did not finish, the event is sent again under the same webhook-id, with its attempt counted from 1 again, so a receiver may see the same delivery more than once, more than three times in all, and deduplicates on webhook-id.
  • A delivery failure stays a delivery failure. It is logged, as a warning naming the receiver's host, the attempts and the reason, and it never fails a run that succeeded nor replaces a run's own failure: the /execute response and the run's status are the run's.
  • No log, no replay. The server keeps no delivery log and offers no way to send a delivery again. The receiver acknowledges at once and does its work afterwards, rather than spend its 15 seconds processing the run.

The server signs its calls with the secret of the process that runs the delivery. With an orchestrator that runs a /start run in another process, such as a Temporal worker, that process needs CALLER_WEBHOOK_SECRET too.

docs.title: The deployment's completion target
docs.text:
COMPLETION_CALLBACK_URL names the operator's own receiver, an absolute http or https URL which may name the run's id with one {pipeline_run_id} placeholder, in its path or its query only, since a run's id may be the caller's choice and never decides the host the notice goes to, such as https://ops.example.com/runs/complete/{pipeline_run_id}. A malformed value stops the server at boot, and leaving it unset gives the deployment no completion target. When set, every /start run notifies it, once, when the run ends; an /execute run, which answers with its result, does not.

The target receives a completion notice, not the caller's event:

  • A JSON body with the run's pipeline_run_id, the delivery state ("COMPLETED" or "FAILED", also sent under the legacy status key), result_url (when results were stored: the storage key prefix under which the result files sit, not a fetchable URL) and, for a failed run, error, its problem document in the operator's view, diagnostics included (see Error Responses).
  • An X-Completion-Signature header, HMAC-SHA256(COMPLETION_CALLBACK_SECRET, pipeline_run_id) rendered as a hex digest, which the receiver recomputes with its own copy of the secret:
import hmac, hashlib

expected = hmac.new(SHARED_SECRET.encode("utf-8"), pipeline_run_id.encode("utf-8"), hashlib.sha256).hexdigest()
if not hmac.compare_digest(expected, request.headers["X-Completion-Signature"]):
    return Response(status=401)

COMPLETION_CALLBACK_SECRET is required once a completion target is set: the server refuses to boot with a target and without the secret, and a /start that meets that configuration anyway is refused with a 500 runtime.misconfigured before its method is fetched or its run set up. Unlike the caller's event, a failure to notify the completion target fails the delivery step, which a durable orchestrator repeats.

A host that forwards its completion URL among a /start request's callback_urls, as it did before the completion target had a setting of its own, is understood: a callback_urls entry equal to the run's completion URL, compared as URLs, with the scheme and host in any case and the run's id written as it is or percent-encoded, is the deployment's hop, notified once with its completion notice, and never treated as a caller's webhook nor signed as one. An /execute run notifies no completion target, so there the same URL is a caller's webhook like any other, sent the signed event.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Pipelex provides a flexible way to configure and manage your LLM (Large Language Model) integrations through the inference backend configuration system.

The system provides three main concepts for LLM configuration:

  • LLM Handles (Aliases)
  • LLM Presets
  • Model Deck

For complete details about the inference backend configuration system, see the Inference Backend Configuration documentation.

docs.title: LLM Handles (Aliases)
docs.text:
An LLM handle can be either:

  1. A direct model name (like "gpt-4o-mini", "claude-3-sonnet") - automatically available for all models loaded by the inference backend system
  2. An alias - user-defined shortcuts that map to model names, defined in the [llm.aliases] section:

docs.title: Example Alias Configurations
docs.text:
[llm.aliases]
best-gpt = "gpt-5.6-sol"
default-general = "gpt-5.6-terra"
default-small = "gpt-5.6-luna"

A bare name in a pipe's model field is first looked up among the models the enabled backends serve as the pipe's model type, then among the aliases of that type, then among its waterfalls while model fallback is on. A model served as another type does not count: an LLM named in a PipeImgGen is refused when the bundle is validated or loaded, with an unknown_model item naming the pipe, the handle and the type the pipe needs. The deck's own presets and LLM overrides are held to the same rule when the runner boots. A sigiled name is looked up by its sigil alone, so ~name is the waterfall even where a model or an alias shares its name. The system handles model routing through backends automatically.

Alias Naming Convention

Defining an alias is always meant to describe what model it is. Never define an alias to describe what it is for or what it's good at. LLM Presets are for that.

docs.title: LLM Settings & LLM Presets
docs.text:
LLM Settings combine an LLM handle with specific parameters optimized for particular tasks. They help maintain consistency across similar operations and make it easier to switch between different configurations.

An LLM Preset is simply a name for a LLM Settings that you have predefined in order to use it in various places.

docs.title: Example LLM Preset definitions
docs.text:
[llm.presets]

engineering-structured = {
    model = "@default-premium-structured",
    temperature = 1
}

retrieval = {
    model = "@default-large-context-text",
    temperature = 1
}

docs.title: Reasoning Presets
docs.text:
LLM Settings support reasoning_effort and reasoning_budget parameters for enabling extended reasoning (chain-of-thought / thinking). Here are the built-in reasoning presets:

[llm.presets]
deep-analysis = { model = "@default-premium", temperature = 1, reasoning_effort = "high", description = "Deep reasoning and analysis" }
quick-reasoning = { model = "@default-premium", temperature = 1, reasoning_effort = "low", description = "Quick reasoning for simple tasks" }

Both declare temperature = 1 because every model the shipped deck resolves to fixes its temperature at that value. The deck states the temperature the model will actually use, rather than one the runtime would override on every call. A method that needs a temperature of its own writes an inline LLM settings table, shown below: a bare model name is paired with [llm.choice_defaults].default_temperature, which this deck sets to 1, so naming a handle on its own does not give the author control of the temperature.

reasoning_effort accepts values from "none" to "max". For an explicit token budget, use reasoning_budget instead (mutually exclusive with reasoning_effort). For provider-specific behavior and model examples, see Reasoning Controls.

docs.title: Using LLM Settings in Pipelines
docs.text:
Here's how to use these configurations in your pipelines:

[pipe.generate_response]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Generate a creative response"
inputs = { question = "Question" }
output = "Response"
model = {
    model = "gpt-5.4",  # Using inline LLM settings
    temperature = 0.8,
}
prompt = """
Generate a creative response to this question:

@question
"""

[pipe.extract_weather_data]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Extract structured weather data from text"
inputs = { text = "Text" }
output = "WeatherData"
model = "$retrieval"  # Using a preset with $ prefix
prompt = """
Extract the weather data from this text:

@text
"""

docs.title: Model Deck
docs.text:
The Model Deck is your central configuration hub for all LLM-related settings. It's stored in the .pipelex/inference/deck/ directory and consists of numbered deck files loaded in order:

  • 1_llm_deck.toml: LLM aliases and presets
  • 2_img_gen_deck.toml: Image generation configuration
  • 3_extract_deck.toml: Document extraction configuration
  • 4_search_deck.toml: Search configuration
  • 5_doc_gen_deck.toml: The document engines PipeDocGen prints with, by format and source
  • 6_judgment_deck.toml: Judgment configuration
  • x_custom_extract_deck.toml: Custom extraction waterfalls/overrides (loaded last)
  • x_custom_llm_deck.toml: Custom LLM waterfalls/overrides (loaded last)

docs.title: Directory Structure
docs.text:
.pipelex/
└── inference/
    ├── backends.toml              # Backend configurations
    ├── routing_profiles.toml      # Model routing rules
    ├── backends/                  # Individual backend model specs
    │   ├── openai.toml
    │   ├── anthropic.toml
    │   └── ...
    └── deck/                      # Model deck configurations
        ├── 1_llm_deck.toml            # LLM aliases & presets
        ├── 2_img_gen_deck.toml        # Image generation config
        ├── 3_extract_deck.toml        # Document extraction config
        ├── 4_search_deck.toml         # Search config
        ├── 5_doc_gen_deck.toml        # Document engines, by format and source
        ├── 6_judgment_deck.toml       # Judgment config
        ├── x_custom_extract_deck.toml # Custom extraction waterfalls/overrides
        └── x_custom_llm_deck.toml     # Custom LLM waterfalls/overrides

docs.title: Best Practices
docs.text:
1. Consistent Naming: Use clear, descriptive names for handles and presets
  2. Task-Specific Presets: Create presets optimized for specific skills and tasks
  3. Cost Management: Consider using different models based on task complexity and cost requirements

docs.title: Understanding Domains
docs.text:
MTHDS Standard Reference

Domains are part of the MTHDS open standard. For the authoritative language specification, see Domains on mthds.ai. This page documents Pipelex-specific behavior and usage.

A domain in Pipelex is a semantic namespace that organizes related concepts and pipes. It's declared at the top of every .mthds file and serves as an identifier for grouping related functionality.

docs.title: What is a Domain?
docs.text:
A domain is defined by three properties:

  • code (required) - The unique identifier for the domain (must be snake_case)
  • description (optional) - A human-readable description of the domain's purpose
  • system_prompt (optional) - A default system prompt for all PipeLLM operators in bundles using this domain

docs.title: Declaring a Domain
docs.text:
Every .mthds file must declare its domain at the beginning:

domain = "invoice_processing"
description = "Tools for extracting, validating, and processing invoice documents"
system_prompt = "You are an expert in financial document analysis and invoice processing."

Domain Code Naming Convention

Domain codes MUST be in snake_case (lowercase with underscores). Use descriptive names that clearly indicate the domain's purpose.

Valid domain codes: 

✅ domain = "finance"
✅ domain = "invoice_processing"
✅ domain = "medical_records"
✅ domain = "customer_service"

Invalid domain codes: 

❌ domain = "Finance"           # No uppercase
❌ domain = "invoice-processing" # No hyphens
❌ domain = "INVOICE_PROCESSING" # No all caps
❌ domain = "invoiceProcessing"  # camelCase not allowed

docs.title: Hierarchical Domains
docs.text:
Domains support dotted paths to express a hierarchy:

domain = "legal"
domain = "legal.contracts"
domain = "legal.contracts.shareholder"

Each segment must be snake_case. The hierarchy is organizational — there is no scope inheritance between parent and child domains. legal.contracts and legal are independent namespaces; defining concepts in one does not affect the other.

Valid hierarchical domains:

✅ domain = "legal.contracts"
✅ domain = "legal.contracts.shareholder"
✅ domain = "finance.reporting"

Invalid hierarchical domains:

❌ domain = ".legal"              # Cannot start with a dot
❌ domain = "legal."              # Cannot end with a dot
❌ domain = "legal..contracts"    # No consecutive dots
❌ domain = "Legal.Contracts"     # Segments must be snake_case

Hierarchical domains are used in the [exports] section of METHODS.toml to control pipe visibility across domains. See Packages for details.

docs.title: Concept Namespacing
docs.text:
Every concept defined in a bundle belongs to the domain declared in that bundle. The full identifier for a concept is:

domain_code.ConceptName

Example:

domain = "finance"

[concept]
Invoice = "A commercial document for a sale"
Payment = "A financial transaction"

This creates two concepts: - finance.Invoice - finance.Payment

docs.title: Domain as Namespace
docs.text:
The domain code prevents naming conflicts. Multiple bundles can define concepts with the same name if they're in different domains:

# finance.mthds
domain = "finance"
[concept]
Report = "A financial report"

# marketing.mthds
domain = "marketing"
[concept]
Report = "A marketing campaign report"

Result: Two different concepts (finance.Report and marketing.Report) with no conflict.

docs.title: Multiple Bundles, Same Domain
docs.text:
Multiple .mthds files can declare the same domain. They all contribute to that domain's namespace:

# finance_invoices.mthds
domain = "finance"
[concept]
Invoice = "..."

# finance_payments.mthds
domain = "finance"
[concept]
Payment = "..."

Both files contribute to the finance domain, creating: - finance.Invoice - finance.Payment

docs.title: In Bundle Files
docs.text:
Same-domain references (no prefix needed):

domain = "finance"

[concept]
Invoice = "A commercial document"

[pipe.process_invoice]
type = "PipeLLM"
inputs = { invoice = "Invoice" }    # Same domain, no prefix
output = "Text"
prompt = "Process this invoice: $invoice"

Cross-domain references (prefix required):

domain = "accounting"

[pipe.reconcile]
type = "PipeLLM"
inputs = { invoice = "finance.Invoice" }    # Different domain, needs prefix
output = "Report"
prompt = "Reconcile this invoice: $invoice"

docs.title: In Python Code
docs.text:
Always use the full identifier when referencing concepts in code:

from pipelex.core.stuffs.stuff_factory import StuffFactory

invoice_stuff = StuffFactory.make_from_concept_ref(
    concept_ref="finance.Invoice",  # domain_code.ConceptName
    name="invoice_123",
    content=invoice_data,
)

docs.title: System Prompt Inheritance
docs.text:
When you set a system_prompt at the domain level, it applies to all PipeLLM operators in bundles that declare that domain:

domain = "medical_records"
system_prompt = "You are a medical records specialist with expertise in HIPAA compliance."

[pipe.extract_diagnosis]
type = "PipeLLM"
# Automatically inherits the domain's system_prompt
inputs = { record = "MedicalRecord" }
output = "Diagnosis"
prompt = "Extract the primary diagnosis: $record"

Individual pipes can override the domain system prompt by defining their own system_prompt field.

docs.title: Kicking off a Pipelex Method Project
Creating Your First Pipeline
docs.text:
A pipeline in Pipelex is a collection of related concepts and pipes. Start by creating a MTHDS file in your project:

tutorial.mthds 

domain = "tutorial"
description = "My first Pipelex library"
system_prompt = "You are a helpful assistant."

[concept]
Question = "A question that needs to be answered"
Answer = "A response to a question"

[pipe]
[pipe.answer_question]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Answer a question"
inputs = { question = "tutorial.Question" }
output = "tutorial.Answer"
prompt = """
Please answer the following question:

@question

Provide a clear and concise answer.
"""

This creates a simple Q&A pipeline with:

  • A domain called "tutorial"
  • Two concepts: Question and Answer
  • One pipe that transforms a Question into an Answer

The domain property is the most important part of your pipeline file. It groups all your concepts and pipes into a single, easy to read bundle.

Learn More About Domains

Domains are a core concept in Pipelex that organize your pipelines, concepts, and pipes into semantic namespaces. For a comprehensive guide on domains, see Understanding Domains.

See more about designing pipes in Designing Pipelines. See more about concepts in Define Your Concepts See more about domains in Understanding Domains

docs.title: File Naming Conventions
docs.text: Consistent naming makes your pipeline code discoverable and maintainable:

docs.title: MTHDS Files
docs.text:
• Use lowercase with underscores: legal_contracts.mthds, customer_service.mthds
  • Match the domain name when possible: domain "legal" → legal.mthds
  • For multi-word domains, use underscores: domain "customer_service" → customer_service.mthds

See more about pipelex bundle specification in Pipelex Bundle Specification

docs.title: Python Model Files
docs.text:
• It is recommended to name structure files with a _struct.py suffix: legal.mthds → legal_struct.py
  • Pipelex will automatically discover and load structure classes from all Python files in your project (excluding common directories like .venv, .git, etc.)

docs.title: Project Structure
docs.text: Key principle: Put .mthds files where they belong in YOUR codebase. Pipelex automatically finds them.

docs.title: Recommended Patterns
docs.text:
Topic-Based (Best for organized codebases): 

your-project/
├── my_project/                # Your Python package
│   ├── finance/
│   │   ├── models.py
│   │   ├── services.py
│   │   ├── invoices.mthds          # Pipeline with finance code
│   │   └── invoices_struct.py    # Structure classes
│   └── legal/
│       ├── models.py
│       ├── contracts.mthds         # Pipeline with legal code
│       └── contracts_struct.py
├── .pipelex/                     # Config at repo root
│   ├── pipelex.toml
│   └── inference/
└── requirements.txt

Centralized (If you prefer grouping pipelines): 

your-project/
├── my_project/
│   ├── pipelines/              # All pipelines together
│   │   ├── finance.mthds
│   │   ├── finance_struct.py
│   │   ├── legal.mthds
│   │   └── legal_struct.py
│   └── core/
│       └── (your code)
└── .pipelex/

Flat (Small projects): 

your-project/
├── my_project/
│   ├── invoice_pipeline.mthds
│   ├── invoice_struct.py
│   └── main.py
└── .pipelex/

docs.title: Key Points
docs.text:
• Flexible placement: .mthds files work anywhere in your project
  • Automatic discovery: Pipelex scans and finds them automatically
  • Configuration location: .pipelex/ stays at repository root
  • Naming convention: Use _struct.py suffix for structure files
  • Excluded directories: .venv, .git, __pycache__, node_modules are skipped
  • Best practice: Keep related pipelines with their related code

docs.title: Libraries
docs.text: A Library in Pipelex is a complete collection of domains, concepts, and pipes that can be loaded and used together. It represents the full set of Pipelex definitions available for execution within a specific context, typically for a single pipeline run.

docs.title: Library Structure
docs.text:
A Library is composed of three core components:

  • DomainLibrary: Manages all domain definitions
  • ConceptLibrary: Manages all concept definitions across domains
  • PipeLibrary: Manages all pipe definitions

These three components together form what we call a Pipelex Bundle (the content you define in .mthds files). Learn more about bundle structure and syntax in the Pipelex Bundle Specification.

docs.title: Understanding Library Scope
docs.text:
When you execute pipelines using execute or start, a library is created to hold all the necessary definitions. This library:

  • Contains the pipes and concepts available for execution
  • Provides isolation between different pipeline runs when using different library IDs
  • Can be loaded from local directories or from MTHDS content strings

docs.title: Uniqueness Rules
docs.text:
Libraries enforce specific uniqueness constraints to maintain consistency:

Component Uniqueness Scope Example Domains Unique per library Each library can have one marketing domain Pipes Unique per domain Each domain can have one generate_tagline pipe Concepts Unique per domain Each domain can have one ProductDescription concept Domain.Concept Unique per library marketing.ProductDescription is unique within a library

Pipes are identified by their domain-qualified reference (e.g. marketing.generate_tagline), so different domains within the same library can have pipes with the same code.

docs.title: How a pipe reference resolves
docs.text:
A reference written inside a pipe — a sequence step, a parallel branch, a condition outcome, a batch_over target — resolves within its own domain:

  • generate_tagline written inside a marketing pipe means marketing.generate_tagline.
  • To reference a pipe in another domain, write that domain out: sales.generate_tagline.

A bare reference never reaches another domain. This is what makes a domain a real boundary: adding a pipe to one domain cannot change what a pipe in another domain means, and [exports] — which deliberately exempts bare references from its check, because they were never supposed to leave home — is enforceable through every reference form.

If a bare reference names nothing in its own domain, validation says so, names the reference it actually tried, and points at the domain that does declare that code:

Pipe 'marketing.run_campaign' references 'marketing.render_html', which does not exist. A pipe
reference resolves inside its own domain, so 'render_html' is looked for in domain 'marketing'.
Referencing a pipe in another domain requires writing that domain out. 'render_html' is declared
elsewhere in this library — did you mean 'presentation.render_html'?

Pipe codes you type yourself are a different matter. pipelex run generate_tagline, pipelex show generate_tagline, pipelex which generate_tagline, and the pipe code in an API request all accept a bare code and find it in whichever domain declares it — you are pointing at a pipe, not writing a reference. If two domains declare the same code, these commands ask you to say which one rather than picking for you.

Concept codes you supply in inputs follow the same entry rule. A bare code in an input envelope ({"concept": "Memo", "content": ...}) is resolved against the entry pipe's own domain first; if that domain does not declare it, a code unique across the library is found wherever it lives, and a code two domains declare raises an error asking you to qualify it (marketing.Memo). Concept references written inside a bundle never search at all — they are qualified to their own domain when the library is built, exactly like pipe references.

docs.title: Local Libraries (Current)
docs.text:
Currently, all libraries are local, meaning they are loaded from:

  • Directories on your filesystem (using the library_dirs constructor parameter)
  • MTHDS content strings (using the mthds_contents parameter)
  • The current working directory (default behavior)
# Loading from local directories
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_dirs=["./pipelines", "./shared_pipes"])
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="generate_tagline",
    inputs={...},
)
pipe_output = response.pipe_output

docs.title: Remote Libraries (Coming Soon)
docs.text:
In the future, you'll be able to import and use remote libraries, enabling:

  • Sharing pipe definitions across teams and projects
  • Versioned library dependencies
  • Centralized library management

docs.title: 1. Library Creation
docs.text:
When the runner executes a method, a library is created with a unique library_id. Pipelex-specific configuration (library id, directories) is provided on the PipelexMTHDSProtocol constructor:

# Explicit library ID
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_id="my_custom_library")
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
    inputs={...},
)

# Automatic library ID (defaults to pipeline_run_id)
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol()
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
    inputs={...},
)

docs.title: 2. Library Loading
docs.text:
The library is populated based on the parameters you provide:

Option A: Loading from directories

# Loads all .mthds files from specified directories
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_dirs=["./pipelines"])
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
    inputs={...},
)

Option B: Loading from MTHDS content

# Loads only the provided MTHDS content
mthds_content = """
domain = "marketing"

[concept]
ProductDescription = "A product description"
Tagline = "A catchy tagline for a product"

[pipe.my_pipe]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Generate a tagline for a product"
inputs = { desc = "ProductDescription" }
output = "Tagline"
prompt = "Generate a tagline for: $desc"
"""

runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol()
response = await runner.execute(
    mthds_contents=[mthds_content],
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
    inputs={...},
)

docs.title: 3. Library Validation
docs.text:
After loading, the library validates:

  • All pipe input/output concepts exist in the concept library
  • All pipe dependencies (for pipe controllers) exist in the pipe library
  • Domain and concept definitions are consistent

docs.title: Working with Multiple Libraries
docs.text:
You can manage multiple libraries simultaneously by using different library_id values:

# Library for marketing pipelines
marketing_runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_id="marketing_lib", library_dirs=["./marketing_pipes"])
marketing_response = await marketing_runner.execute(
    pipe_code="generate_tagline",
    inputs={...},
)

# Library for analytics pipelines
analytics_runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_id="analytics_lib", library_dirs=["./analytics_pipes"])
analytics_response = await analytics_runner.execute(
    pipe_code="analyze_data",
    inputs={...},
)

docs.title: 1. Use Explicit Library IDs for Long-Running Applications
docs.text:
# Good: Explicit ID for maintaining state
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_id="app_library")
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
    inputs={...},
)

docs.title: 2. Use MTHDS Content for Dynamic Pipelines
docs.text:
When generating or modifying pipelines dynamically, use mthds_contents:

# Generate MTHDS content dynamically
mthds_content = generate_custom_pipeline(user_requirements)

runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol()
response = await runner.execute(
    mthds_contents=[mthds_content],
    inputs={...},
)

A temporary library will be created holding the Pipelex bundle, and the library_id will be pipeline_run_id. Since no pipe_code is passed, the generated content must declare main_pipe at the top of the bundle (e.g. main_pipe = "my_pipe") so the runner knows which pipe to execute — otherwise pass pipe_code= explicitly.

docs.title: 3. Reuse Library IDs for Related Executions
docs.text:
If multiple pipeline runs should share the same library context:

runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(library_id="shared_context", library_dirs=["./pipes"])

# First execution
response1 = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="pipe1",
    inputs={...},
)

# Second execution with same library
response2 = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="pipe2",
    inputs={...},
)

docs.title: Method Trees
docs.text: A method is not one .mthds file but a folder of files: its bundles, the template files its steps print with, its Python modules, its METHODS.toml. The MTHDS standard calls the set of files a method is made of its method tree, and Pipelex reads a method from your disk only through that tree, locally as on the hosted API. A file the tree does not hold is invisible to the method's steps, however close to the bundle it lies.

docs.title: Where a tree is rooted
docs.text:
What you hand Pipelex decides the tree it reads:

  • A folder, as in pipelex run bundle invoicing/ or -L invoicing/, is the method rooted at the nearest METHODS.toml at or above it, or at the folder itself when there is none.
  • A .mthds file named alone, as in pipelex run bundle invoicing/invoice.mthds or pipelex validate bundle invoicing/invoice.mthds, is the member of the tree rooted at the nearest METHODS.toml at or above its folder. With no METHODS.toml there, its method is that one file: a step of the bundle naming any other file, such as a template_file, is refused with a message saying to run the method's folder instead, or to add a METHODS.toml to it. Sending a folder is always your explicit act, so a stray .mthds file never carries its neighbours anywhere.
  • A dependency package is the tree rooted at the package's own directory.

docs.title: What a tree holds
docs.text:
A tree holds the regular files under its root, except those its membership rule keeps out:

  • every file or folder whose name starts with a dot, such as .git/, .venv/ or .env;
  • __pycache__/ and node_modules/ folders, and any folder holding a Python virtual environment;
  • a nested repository (a folder holding .git) and a nested package (a folder holding its own METHODS.toml), each a tree of its own;
  • every file a .gitignore of the tree ignores, matched as git matches it, and every file the manifest's [package] exclude patterns name.

A symbolic link anywhere in the tree refuses the whole tree: a tree holds regular files only, so replace the link with the file it names, or keep it out with a .gitignore pattern.

The tree's .gitignore files are what keeps a run's outputs out of the method: every folder pipelex run creates for its outputs holds a .gitignore ignoring everything in it, and so does the folder pipelex-agent validate bundle --graph writes its flowchart into, so a run or a validation started from the method's own folder leaves its tree, and its digest, as they were.

docs.title: File references
docs.text: A file a bundle names, such as a PipeDocGen step's template_file, is a path relative to the bundle's file, written with forward slashes, and it is resolved in the bundle's tree: joined to the bundle's own place in the tree, a .. may climb out of the bundle's folder to a file elsewhere in the tree, and the result must be a file of the tree. So a bundle in bundles/ can name ../templates/invoice.docx, while a path climbing above the tree's root, an absolute path, a file a .gitignore keeps out and a file of a nested package are all refused, each refusal naming the files by their paths in the tree. Pipelex looks the path up among the tree's files and never opens a path a bundle wrote.

docs.title: Python modules
docs.text: A PipeFunc step names its function by its import path from the root of the tree, such as funcs.totals.compute_totals for the function compute_totals of funcs/totals.py, and its module is found among the tree's files. A run imports the tree's modules with the root first on the import path, refuses the import of a file the membership rule keeps out, such as a .gitignored module, and writes no __pycache__ into the tree. On a sandbox-hosted deployment, each call of the step receives every file of the tree except its .mthds files, read by the tree's digest where the call is made (see Inside a run).

docs.title: Library directories
docs.text: A library directory, such as a -L directory or one of PIPELEXPATH, is a place methods are found rather than one method. Pipelex loads its tree, then the tree of each nested package and nested repository under it, each as a method of its own whose steps read only its own files, so every method in the directory loads. A .mthds file kept out by the membership rule, a hidden one, a gitignored one or one inside a virtual environment, is not loaded.

docs.title: Python packages: requirements.txt
docs.text:
A method whose own Python, such as the module of a PipeFunc step, imports a package declares it in a requirements.txt at the root of its tree. Only the root's file declares anything: a requirements.txt in a subfolder is an ordinary file of the tree. Each line of the file is blank, a comment whose first character other than a space or a tab is #, or exactly one PEP 508 requirement, markers and extras included:

# Reading and writing spreadsheets
pandas>=2.2,<3
openpyxl==3.1.5
tzdata; python_version >= "3.12"

Pipelex refuses, naming each such line, a requirement naming a URL (name @ https://…), an option of any kind (a line starting with -, such as -r, -e, -c or --index-url), a comment after a requirement on the same line, and a line continued with a backslash. A comment after a requirement is refused as a comment whatever it says, a URL in it included. The file must be UTF-8 text.

When a tree holding Python and a root requirements.txt loads, Pipelex checks every requirement against the Python environment its PipeFunc steps run in, before importing any of the tree's Python and before building any of its pipes, and refuses the method when one is not met, naming each requirement and why. A requirement whose marker is false in that environment is not needed there and is not checked. A tree with no Python is not checked, since nothing in it could import a package. A package your method calls by its address is checked the same way when it loads, its refusal naming the package by its address. Pipelex never installs anything.

  • Locally, a PipeFunc runs in the interpreter Pipelex runs in, so the requirements are checked against the packages installed there, extras included. The refusal names the method's folder and gives the command that installs what is missing into that interpreter, such as uv pip install --python /path/to/python 'pandas>=2.2,<3'. When Pipelex was installed as a uv tool, add the packages to the tool instead, which keeps them across upgrades: uv tool install pipelex --with 'pandas>=2.2,<3'.
  • On a sandbox-hosted deployment, such as the hosted API, a PipeFunc runs in the deployment's sandbox, whose packages are the whole offer: nothing is installed into a running sandbox. The requirements are checked against the packages the deployment states its sandbox offers for them, a fixed package set, or an environment the deployment builds for your method's requirements, and a method asking for a package it does not offer, or for a version it does not offer, is refused when it loads and when it is validated, naming each requirement. A deployment that can build no environment holding your requirements, such as one whose packages would conflict with a version its sandbox pins, refuses them with its own explanation. A requirement with extras cannot be checked there and is refused, so list the packages the extra brings directly.

Python declaring a structure class is refused on a sandbox-hosted deployment whatever its requirements: see Python classes.

docs.title: Where a folder's run starts
docs.text:
pipelex run bundle <folder> with no --pipe starts where the MTHDS protocol says a run naming no pipe starts, since the bundles of a folder have no order:

  1. With a METHODS.toml at the tree's root, the run starts at its main_pipe, in the bundle of a domain exporting it that defines it. A manifest declaring no main_pipe is refused.
  2. With no METHODS.toml, the run starts at the one main_pipe the tree's bundles declare. None, or several, is refused, the message naming each bundle by its path in the tree.

--pipe names the pipe to start at, as pipe_code or domain.pipe_code, and needs neither. A .mthds file named alone starts at its own main_pipe.

docs.title: Limits and the tree digest
docs.text:
Listing a tree reads and hashes every file in it. A local load lists each tree under this machine's own limits, set under [interpreter.method_tree_limits]: max_files (10,000 by default) and max_total_bytes (1 GiB by default), with max_file_bytes, the size of one file, unchecked unless you set it. The lister counts before it hashes anything, so a folder handed over by mistake, such as a home directory, is refused in moments, and the refusal says to run the method's own folder or to raise the limits in your project's .pipelex/pipelex.toml:

[interpreter.method_tree_limits]
max_files = 50000
max_total_bytes = 4294967296

These limits are not the hosted API's. A deployment sets its own, which a local run cannot know, and applying them locally would refuse a method rooted in a cluttered folder that loads today; a sender warned of the hosted limits before it sends is the hosted run's concern, not a local load's.

Every listing computes the tree's digest, the SHA-256 of its canonical listing of paths, hashes and sizes, which names the exact files of a method: two folders with the same files have the same digest. A local run records the digest of the tree it ran, and lists that tree once: the command lists the folder or the file it was handed to find the pipe to start at, and the run loads the tree that listing returned rather than listing it again, so the digest recorded is the digest of the tree loaded. validate bundle and fix bundle likewise load the tree they listed to resolve their target, and so does the API server, which lists a request's method once to check its requirements and to load it. pipelex run bundle prints the digest with the run's recap and writes method_tree.json into the run's output folder, holding the digest, the tree's root on this machine, its entry and each file's path, hash and size. pipelex-agent run bundle adds method_tree_digest to the run's output file and, with --with-memory, to its output. A run lists each tree once whichever way it is named: a folder and a symbolic link naming it are one listing, as the lister follows such a link, and a bundle file named alone inside a library directory shares the listing of the tree the directory roots, while a symbolic link to a bundle file, named alone, is refused as the lister refuses it, even after the run listed the file it points to.

The files of a tree may change after it is listed, so a run never trusts them blindly. The load reads each bundle it parses, the requirements.txt it judges and the Python it scans against the hash the listing recorded, and reads every file of a tree listed before the load again, once per run, as the load takes the tree, such as the folder the command resolved: a bundle, a template or any other file of the tree edited, replaced or removed since the listing is refused before anything of the method is parsed or run, with a MethodTreeChangedError (method.package_invalid, reason tree_changed) naming the file by its path in the tree, which run, validate and fix report as an invalid method whose item names that file. Run again once the files stop changing. A file a step reads during the run, such as a template, is read against its hash as well (see Inside a run).

docs.title: Inside a run
docs.text:
A run carries no file of its method. The library a run hands from step to step, its crate, names the tree each bundle belongs to by the tree's digest and the bundle by its path in the tree, and a step names a file it reads, such as a PipeDocGen step's template file, the same way. The files a request submits with bundles sent as text make a tree too, with those bundles at its root, named by its digest like a folder's.

Every method file is read where reading is allowed, at the moment a step uses it: a PipeDocGen step's template file at its print, and the files of a PipeFunc call where the call is made. Each read goes through the method file store, by the tree's digest and under the run's read scope, and is checked against the digest: the listing read must have that digest, and each file the hash the listing gives it. Locally, the store serves the trees the process's libraries hold, from the folder they were listed from or from the files submitted with them. A distributed orchestrator, such as Temporal, runs a step's leaves apart from the process that loaded the method, and its deployment provides the store that serves them there: the orchestrator copies every tree the run names into it while it dispatches the run, before the runner drops the files the trees were listed from.

A run records two identities of its method: the digest of its tree, which changes with any byte of any file, and the fingerprint of its crate, which changes only with the meaning of its concepts and pipes. A method whose bundles were all sent as text, with no file beside them, belongs to no tree, so its run records the fingerprint alone.

docs.title: Packages
docs.text:
A package is a collection of .mthds bundles with a METHODS.toml manifest at the project root. The manifest gives the package an identity and defines which pipes are exported to the outside world.

Opt-in packaging

If your project has no METHODS.toml, Pipelex still loads your local bundles. Packaging is optional.

docs.title: What the Manifest Does
docs.text:
METHODS.toml currently serves two main purposes:

  • Identity: give the package an address, version, and description
  • Visibility: declare which pipes are exported through [exports]

docs.title: The Package Manifest: METHODS.toml
docs.text:
Here is a representative manifest:

[package]
address = "github.com/acme/legal-tools"
version = "1.0.0"
description = "Legal document analysis and contract review methods."
authors = ["Acme Corp"]
license = "MIT"
mthds_version = ">=0.8.0"

[exports.legal.contracts]
pipes = ["extract_clause", "analyze_contract"]

[exports.scoring]
pipes = ["compute_weighted_score"]

docs.title: Field Reference
docs.text: Field Required Description address Yes Package address following a hostname/path pattern such as github.com/org/repo version Yes Semantic version such as 1.0.0 or 2.1.3-beta.1 description Yes Human-readable package description name No Optional short method name display_name No Optional human-readable name, such as Slide Designer; a run of the package fetched by its address records it in its provenance authors No List of author names license No License string such as MIT main_pipe No Optional main pipe code mthds_version No Required MTHDS version constraint

docs.title: Exports and Visibility
docs.text: The [exports] section controls which pipes are visible outside the package.

docs.title: Default Behavior
docs.text:
• Without METHODS.toml, or with one that declares no [exports]: every pipe of the package is visible from outside
  • With an [exports] section: pipes are private by default — only the pipes listed in [exports] (and each bundle's main_pipe) are visible from outside

docs.title: Declaring Exports
docs.text:
Exports are grouped by domain path:

[exports.legal.contracts]
pipes = ["extract_clause", "analyze_contract"]

[exports.scoring]
pipes = ["compute_weighted_score"]

This manifest exports two pipes from legal.contracts and one pipe from scoring. Exports are read by domain: exporting compute_weighted_score from scoring does not export a pipe of the same name declared in another domain of the package.

docs.title: Pipes Call Their Own Package
docs.text:
Inside a package, a pipe calls the package's own pipes, private ones included. A sequence exported by the package can call a helper the manifest does not export, and that helper is loaded with it. A private pipe that no exported pipe calls is not loaded at all, so a problem in it never stops a consumer from loading the package.

A reference written inside a package always reaches that package's pipe. If the consumer declares a pipe with the same domain and code, or another loaded package does, the package's own call is never redirected to it.

docs.title: What a Consumer Is Refused
docs.text:
When a consumer references a loaded package, two mistakes are refused when the consumer loads, rather than surfacing later as an unrelated error:

  • A pipe the package does not have is refused as an unresolved pipe dependency (unresolved_pipe_dependency), naming the reference and the package. The same refusal names the error when the package declares the pipe but it failed to build.
  • A pipe the package does not export is refused as an unexported pipe dependency (unexported_pipe_dependency). The pipe exists, so the remedy is to call one of the package's exported pipes, or to export this one in the package's manifest.

These checks apply to the consumer's references and to a package's references to its own pipes. A package's reference to one of its own dependencies is not checked when the consumer loads, because a package's dependencies are not loaded with it.

A reference by bare code, alias->code, ignores the package's private pipes when it also matches an exported one, so a private helper sharing an exported pipe's code in another domain does not make the reference ambiguous.

Naming a private pipe by hand, as the pipe to run at the command line or in an API request, is not a reference from inside a method, so [exports] does not apply to it: a loaded private pipe can be run that way by its alias->domain.code.

docs.title: Cross-Package References
docs.text:
Pipelex can resolve cross-package references when the required packages are available to the runtime. The reference form is:

alias->domain.code

Example:

[pipe.analyze_item]
type = "PipeSequence"
description = "Analyze an item using another package"
steps = [
    { pipe = "scoring_lib->scoring.compute_weighted_score" },
]

This runtime-level capability exists separately from the current public mthds package CLI workflow documented on this page. If you rely on cross-package references, validate them against the specific runtime setup you are using.

docs.title: Include by Address: Fetch-on-Miss
docs.text:
The alias can also be a full package address, so a bundle can reference a method from a public GitHub repository directly — the same reference grammar as running a method by address:

[pipe.summarize_report]
type = "PipeSequence"
description = "Extract a document then summarize it"
inputs = { doc = "PDF" }
output = "Summary"
steps = [
    { pipe = "github.com/Pipelex/methods/documents->documents.extract_page_contents_and_views", result = "pages" },
    { pipe = "summarize_pages" },
]

An address-based reference resolves against the installed methods — ~/.mthds/methods/ (global), .mthds/methods/ in the working directory (project-local), and a .mthds/methods/ directory beside the bundle being loaded or in a directory above it — matched by the manifest's address + name, case-insensitively. When no installed method matches, Pipelex fetches on miss: it fetches the package by address — honoring an @<tag> pin, through the same grammar, bounds, and tags-only rules as a direct fetch — installs it into ~/.mthds/methods/, records the fetch provenance (address, tag, the commit SHA of what was actually cloned, and the manifest's display_name) in a .provenance.json sidecar beside the manifest, and loads it so resolution proceeds. The next load finds the installed copy and never touches the network again.

A few behaviors worth knowing:

  • Installed wins over a fetch. Once a method is installed, it is used as-is — including when a reference pins a different @<tag> than what is installed (a warning tells you so). Remove the installed directory to re-fetch.
  • A fetched package is checked against the calling method's methods.lock. When the method calling a package by address carries a methods.lock at the root of its tree, beside its METHODS.toml, and Pipelex resolves that package from a copy it fetched itself, whether for this load or by an earlier fetch whose copy carries a .provenance.json sidecar, the tree digest of that copy is compared with the digest the lock records for the package's address (matched without regard to case, any @<tag> stripped). A different digest refuses the load with security.integrity_mismatch, whose message names the address, the digest and version the lock records, and the version and digest that were fetched. The digest is compared whatever version the lock names: the version is part of the tree, in METHODS.toml, so a lock recording another version than the one fetched refuses the load too, and the message says to pin the reference to the locked version or to lock the method again. When the reference pins a @<tag> but an installed copy fetched at another tag or at the default branch answered it (installed wins, above), the message says so instead, naming both, and says to remove that installed copy so the pinned tag is fetched. A bundle loaded in a later batch of the same library, such as the contents a run submits beside its library directories, is checked against the tree an earlier batch fetched and loaded for the same reference, since it runs that tree. Pipelex never fetches the locked version in place of the reference, since a lock verifies what was fetched and never chooses it. A lock that does not name the address, or no lock at all, checks nothing. A package shipped with the method (under .mthds/methods/<name>/ or in a request's dependencies) is not checked, as it travels with the lock from the same author, and neither is a copy another installer wrote without a provenance sidecar, such as mthds install, which checks the lock itself. The lock is read only when a dependency the method calls resolves to a copy Pipelex fetched, for this load or an earlier one; a load whose dependencies are all shipped, or installed otherwise, never reads it. A lock Pipelex then cannot read, including one written before tree digests that records a hash, one whose bytes cannot be read, and one that changed since the method's tree was listed, refuses the load with method.package_invalid, reason lock_invalid, path methods.lock.
  • A package can travel with the method. A method sent over HTTP to a Pipelex API server as files can carry the packages it calls in dependencies, each a map of file entries keyed by its address, and one sent as a bundle_b64 archive under .mthds/methods/<name>/ at its root, each with its METHODS.toml. The server searches them before its installed copies and before fetch-on-miss, for that request alone, so a shipped package wins over an installed copy and runs where fetching is disabled; see Sending the method packages the method calls. On disk, the .mthds/methods/<name>/ layout beside the bundle is one of the local stores above.
  • A package bundle that does not parse refuses the load. When a bundle of a referenced package does not parse, the bundle calling it is refused with the parser's items, each naming the file as <address>/<path inside the package>, never by its path on the machine, whether the package was shipped with the bundle, installed or fetched.
  • A miss that cannot be bridged refuses the bundle, never a silent pass. Fetch disabled, an address this runtime cannot fetch, or a failed fetch (a repository that does not exist, a @tag that is not a tag, a repository holding no package at that address) refuses the load with one unresolved_package_dependency item per package, located on the first pipe that calls it, with the reference as written in missing_pipe_code and the reason and the remedy in its message. It is the same invalid verdict as any other mistake in the bundle: pipelex validate reports it, POST /v1/validate answers 200 with is_valid: false, and a run is refused with a 422 before any pipe runs. Every package of the bundle is tried before the refusal, so two bad references give two items.
  • Hosted parity warning. A fetched method declaring Python structure classes runs locally but triggers the same warning as a direct CLI fetch: hosted execution accepts MTHDS concepts and sandboxed PipeFuncs, not in-process Python. On a sandbox-hosted deployment the fetch refuses such a package outright, with the same rule-naming error. The refusal is not specific to fetching: a sandbox-hosted deployment refuses every method whose Python declares structure classes, however it arrived (see Python classes).

To disable network fetches at load time, set the switch in your pipelex.toml (or use the environment variable, which takes precedence):

[interpreter.methods]
fetch_on_miss = false

export PIPELEX_METHODS_FETCH_ON_MISS=0

With fetching disabled, a miss refuses the bundle with that item, whose message names the address and says to ship the package with the bundle under .mthds/methods/<name>/ or to install it where the runtime runs (for example with mthds install <address>). See Methods Configuration.

docs.title: Example Layout
docs.text:
your-project/
├── METHODS.toml
├── my_project/
│   ├── finance/
│   │   ├── invoices.mthds
│   │   └── invoices_struct.py
│   └── legal/
│       ├── contracts.mthds
│       └── contracts_struct.py
├── .pipelex/
│   └── pipelex.toml
└── requirements.txt

The METHODS.toml file sits at the project root. Pipelex discovers it by walking up from bundle locations until it finds the manifest, stopping at a repository's root, and the folder holding it roots the package's method tree: the files of the package its steps can read.

docs.title: Current Public CLI Workflow
docs.text:
The public package-management commands documented in this repo are provided by the lowercase mthds CLI:

mthds package init
mthds package list
mthds package validate

docs.title: Initialize a Manifest
docs.text:
mthds package init

This command creates METHODS.toml interactively. It asks for package metadata and writes a manifest with an empty [exports] section.

docs.title: Inspect a Manifest
docs.text:
mthds package list

This command reads the manifest from the target package directory and prints the parsed package metadata and exports.

docs.title: Validate a Manifest
docs.text:
mthds package validate

This command validates the manifest syntax and package fields.

docs.title: Target a Different Directory
docs.text:
All three commands accept -C, --package-dir <path>:

mthds package init -C ./my-package
mthds package list -C ./my-package
mthds package validate -C ./my-package

docs.title: Important Compatibility Note
docs.text:
The current public mthds package validate command focuses on package identity and exports. It does not document a public dependency-management workflow here, and it rejects a [dependencies] section in the current JS CLI validation path.

For this reason, this documentation only describes the stable public package-manifest workflow exposed by the current mthds CLI.

docs.title: Pipelex Bundle Specification
docs.text:
MTHDS Standard Reference

The .mthds bundle format is defined by the MTHDS open standard. For the authoritative language specification, see Bundles on mthds.ai. This page documents Pipelex-specific behavior and usage.

A Pipelex bundle is the fundamental unit of organization in Pipelex. It's a single .mthds file that defines a cohesive set of concepts and pipes for a specific domain of work.

docs.title: What is a Pipelex Bundle?
docs.text:
A Pipelex bundle (.mthds file) brings together:

  • Domain declaration - The semantic namespace for all concepts and pipes in this bundle
  • Concepts - The knowledge structures that flow through your pipes (optional)
  • Pipes - The processing units that transform and manipulate your concepts (optional)

Think of a bundle as a self-contained module that solves a specific problem domain. For example, you might have:

  • invoice_processing.mthds - Bundle for invoice extraction and validation
  • marketing.mthds - Bundle for generating marketing content
  • document_analysis.mthds - Bundle for analyzing documents

docs.title: Bundle Structure
docs.text:
Every Pipelex bundle follows this structure:

# 1. Domain Declaration (MANDATORY)
domain = "domain_code"
description = "Description of what this domain handles"

# 2. Optional: Main Pipe Declaration
main_pipe = "pipe_code"

# 3. Concept Definitions (OPTIONAL)
[concept]
ConceptName1 = "Description"
ConceptName2 = "Description"

# 4. Pipe Definitions (OPTIONAL)
[pipe]
[pipe.pipe_code]
type = "PipeLLM"
# ... pipe configuration

[pipe.pipe_code_2]
...

docs.title: 1. Domain Declaration (MANDATORY)
docs.text:
Every bundle must declare a domain. Only the domain field is mandatory; all other fields are optional:

domain = "invoice_processing"
description = "Tools for extracting and validating invoice data"
system_prompt = "You are an expert in financial document processing."
main_pipe = "extract_and_validate_invoice"

Bundle Header Fields:

  • domain (required) - The unique identifier for this bundle's namespace
  • description (Optional) - A human-readable description of what this bundle does
  • system_prompt (Optional) - A system prompt that applies to all PipeLLM operators in this bundle
  • main_pipe (Optional) - The default pipe to execute when no specific pipe is requested when running the bundle (see "About main_pipe" below)

Why domains matter:

  • Domains create unique namespaces for your concepts and pipes
  • They prevent naming conflicts when multiple bundles define concepts with the same name
  • They enable organized, modular pipeline architecture

Learn more about domains in Understanding Domains.

About system_prompt:

When you define a system_prompt at the bundle level, it automatically applies to every PipeLLM operator in the bundle. This is useful for setting domain-specific context:

domain = "medical_records"
system_prompt = "You are a medical records specialist with expertise in HIPAA compliance and clinical documentation."

[concept]
MedicalRecord = "A patient's medical record"
Diagnosis = "A medical diagnosis extracted from a record"

[pipe.extract_diagnosis]
type = "PipeLLM"
# This pipe will automatically use the bundle's system_prompt
description = "Extract the primary diagnosis from a medical record"
inputs = { record = "MedicalRecord" }
output = "Diagnosis"
prompt = """
Extract the primary diagnosis from this medical record:

@record
"""

Individual pipes can override the bundle's system prompt by defining their own system_prompt field.

About main_pipe:

You can specify a default pipe to execute when no specific pipe is requested:

domain = "invoice_processing"
main_pipe = "extract_and_validate_invoice"

How main_pipe works:

  • When executing a bundle without specifying a pipe_code, Pipelex runs the main_pipe
  • If no main_pipe is specified, you must explicitly provide the pipe_code when executing
  • The main_pipe value must reference a pipe defined in the same bundle

See more about executing pipes in Executing Pipelines.

docs.title: 3. Concept Definitions (OPTIONAL)
docs.text:
Concepts define the knowledge structures in your domain. While optional, most bundles define at least a few concepts (See more about concepts in Define Your Concepts):

[concept]
Invoice = "A commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer"
Vendor = "A company or individual that provides goods or services"
LineItem = "An individual item or service listed in an invoice"

Concept Naming:

Within a bundle, you reference concepts by their simple name (Invoice). However, their full identifier includes the domain code:

domain_code.ConceptName

For example, if your domain_code is invoice_processing, the concept Invoice has the full identifier:

invoice_processing.Invoice

This full identifier is how other bundles reference your concepts.

docs.title: 4. Pipe Definitions (OPTIONAL)
docs.text:
Pipes are the processing units that transform data. Like concepts, they're optional:

[pipe.extract_invoice]
type = "PipeExtract"
description = "Extract text and images from an invoice PDF"
inputs = { document = "Document" }
output = "Page[]"
See more about designing pipes in Designing Pipelines.

docs.title: Referencing Concepts: When to Use Domain code prefixes
docs.text: Understanding when to use domain code prefixes is crucial for writing clean, maintainable bundles.

docs.title: Same-Bundle References (No Prefix Needed)
docs.text:
When a pipe in a bundle references a concept defined in the same bundle, you don't need the domain code prefix:

domain = "invoice_processing"

[concept]
Invoice = "A commercial document issued by a seller to a buyer"
ValidationResult = "Result of validating an invoice"

[pipe.validate_invoice]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Validate invoice data"
inputs = { invoice = "Invoice" }          # ✅ No prefix needed
output = "ValidationResult"               # ✅ No prefix needed
prompt = "Validate this invoice: $invoice"

This is the most common case and keeps your code clean.

docs.title: Cross-Bundle References (Prefix Required)
docs.text:
When a pipe references a concept from another bundle/domain, you must use the full domain code prefix:

domain = "accounting"

[concept]
Payment = "A financial transaction recording money transfer"
ReconciliationReport = "Report of payment reconciliation"

[pipe.reconcile_payment]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Reconcile a payment with an invoice"
inputs = { 
    invoice = "invoice_processing.Invoice",      # ✅ Different domain, needs prefix
    payment = "Payment"                          # ✅ Same domain, no prefix
}
output = "ReconciliationReport"
prompt = """
Reconcile this payment with the invoice:

@invoice

@payment
"""

docs.title: Bundles Working Together
docs.text:
One of Pipelex's strengths is how bundles can reference and build upon each other, creating modular, reusable pipeline architectures.

When you execute pipelines, multiple bundles are loaded together into a Library - a runtime collection that provides access to all domains, concepts, and pipes from the loaded bundles. This library system enables bundle composition and ensures proper isolation between different pipeline runs. Learn more about how libraries work in Libraries.

docs.title: Calling Pipes from Other Bundles
docs.text:
A pipe in one bundle can call a pipe from another bundle using the full pipe identifier:

domain = "accounts_payable"

[pipe.process_vendor_invoice]
type = "PipeSequence"
description = "Process a vendor invoice end-to-end"
inputs = { pdf_document = "Document" }
output = "PaymentSchedule"
steps = [
    # Call pipe from invoice_processing domain
    { pipe = "invoice_processing.extract_invoice", result = "extracted_data" },

    # Call pipe from validation domain
    { pipe = "validation.validate_data", result = "validation_report" },

    # Call pipe from this domain (no prefix needed)
    { pipe = "schedule_payment", result = "payment_schedule" }
]

[pipe.schedule_payment]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Schedule payment based on invoice data"
inputs = { 
    extracted_data = "invoice_processing.Invoice",   # Concept from another domain
    validation_report = "validation.Report"           # Concept from another domain
}
output = "PaymentSchedule"
prompt = "..."

docs.title: Templating Style
docs.text:
When you write @article in a prompt, Pipelex inserts the content of the article input — wrapped in a tag so the model can tell where your data starts and stops. Templating style is what decides the shape of that wrapper.

It is an authoring decision, not a property of the model you happen to run on. You declare it on the pipe; the model never changes it.

[pipe.summarize_article]
type = "PipeLLM"
description = "Summarize an article"
inputs = { article = "Text" }
output = "Text"
templating_style = "xml"
prompt = """
Summarize the article below.

@article

Keep it to one sentence.
"""

renders as:

Summarize the article below.

<article>
Bees pollinate a third of the food we eat.
</article>

Keep it to one sentence.

docs.title: Two levels, and that's all
docs.text:
A prompt renders under exactly one style, resolved in two steps:

  1. What the pipe declares — the templating_style field on the pipe.
  2. The runtime default — when the pipe declares nothing.

There is no third level. The style is never derived from the model, the provider, or the backend: a method that renders XML on one model renders XML on all of them.

The shipped default is xml with plain text, set in pipelex.toml:

[inference.templating]
default_templating_style = { tag_style = "xml" }

Override it in your project's .pipelex/pipelex.toml to change the house style for every pipe that doesn't declare one.

docs.title: Two ways to write it
docs.text:
Bare string — the common case. The string is the tag style; the text format stays plain.

templating_style = "square_brackets"

Inline table — when you also want to set the text format.

templating_style = { tag_style = "xml", text_format = "markdown" }
Field Type Description Required tag_style string How @variable insertions are wrapped: xml, ticks, square_brackets, no_tag Yes text_format string How values are rendered inside the prompt: plain (default), markdown, html, json No

docs.title: The tag styles
docs.text: Each style below shows what @article produces for an input named article.

docs.title: xml
docs.text:
The default, and the best-supported shape across current models.

<article>
Bees pollinate a third of the food we eat.
</article>

docs.title: ticks
docs.text:
A fenced code block, prefixed with the variable name.

article: ```
Bees pollinate a third of the food we eat.
```

docs.title: square_brackets
docs.text:
BBCode-flavored delimiters.

[article]
Bees pollinate a third of the food we eat.
[/article]

docs.title: no_tag
docs.text:
The value, bare. Nothing is added — use it when your prompt already provides its own framing, or when a wrapper would confuse the task.

Bees pollinate a third of the food we eat.

Tag names come from the variable

@article tags with article. A value with no name of its own — anything piped through with_images, for instance — falls back to data under xml and square_brackets. Under ticks it renders as a bare fence with no prefix, and no_tag adds nothing either way.

docs.title: What the two sigils do
docs.text:
The two insertion sigils are governed by different halves of the style:

  • @variable on its own line inserts the whole input, wrapped per tag_style.
  • $variable inline inserts the value formatted per text_format, with no wrapper.

So a pipe with templating_style = "no_tag" and one with $article instead of @article produce similar-looking output for different reasons — the first chose not to wrap, the second never asked for a wrapper.

docs.title: Beyond PipeLLM
docs.text:
• PipeCompose takes templating_style on its [pipe.name.template] section, for templates that use the tag or format filters directly. A compose pipe that declares nothing renders under the same runtime default.
  • PipeImgGen, PipeSearch and PipeJudge have no authored style of their own — their prompts and questions render under the runtime default. Image and search prompts rarely benefit from tagging, but they do render under a real style rather than an invisible fallback. A PipeJudge's evidence prompt is where tagging earns its keep: @message sets the input out under its name, which is how the judging model learns what each block of evidence is.
  • Construct-mode template fields and the built-in structuring prompts likewise resolve a real style, so a template of yours that uses | tag behaves the same everywhere.

A style is always required, and never invented

The Jinja2 tag and format filters have no fallback of their own. Every prompt-rendering entry point resolves a real style before rendering, so a template using | tag always renders in a shape somebody chose. If you build prompts through the kernel API directly and omit the style, you get a loud error rather than a silent default.

docs.title: Choosing a style
docs.text:
• Stay on xml unless you have a reason. It is unambiguous, it nests, and every major model family handles it well.
  • Reach for no_tag when the input is the prompt — a single block of text that your instructions already introduce.
  • Set text_format = "markdown" when the model's output quality depends on seeing structured values (tables, nested objects) rather than flattened text.
  • Declare the style on the pipe when a specific pipe needs a shape the rest of your method doesn't; change the config default when your whole project wants a different house style.
