docs.title: Telemetry
docs.text:
The telemetry you configure in telemetry.toml never reports to Pipelex. It is yours: it is off until you turn it on, and it goes to analytics and monitoring systems you operate.

Usage statistics are separate

Pipelex does collect anonymous usage statistics, counts of commands, runs, pipe types, models and tokens, through a client of their own that telemetry.toml neither configures nor reaches. They never carry your methods, prompts, inputs, outputs, file names or pipe names, and you turn them off with pipelex usage-stats disable or DO_NOT_TRACK=1. See Usage Statistics.

docs.title: Your Telemetry Streams
docs.text:
telemetry.toml sends observability data to your own analytics and monitoring systems:

  • PostHog: Event tracking and AI span tracing with privacy controls
  • Langfuse: Full LLM observability (receives full span data)
  • OTLP: Send spans to any OpenTelemetry-compatible backend (receives full span data)

Each integration mode allows these streams or not: by default the cli, docker, fastapi, mcp and n8n modes allow them, and pytest, ci and python do not, so a test suite sends nothing unless you allow its mode under [telemetry_allowed_modes] in telemetry.toml. Telemetry Configuration describes each destination's settings.

docs.title: Pipelex's spans in your process
docs.text:
Pipelex traces a run when your PostHog stream is on (mode is anonymous or identified) and its AI span tracing is enabled ([custom_posthog.tracing]); the same tracer feeds your Langfuse and OTLP destinations. Pipelex's tracer stays its own and never becomes the global one, so your own spans never reach Pipelex's exporters, and Pipelex never makes its spans current in your process's OpenTelemetry context:

  • Your own instrumentation, an HTTP client's or a provider SDK's, keeps opening its spans under your own current span, in your own trace, while a Pipelex run goes. It is never re-parented under a pipe or an LLM call, nor kept by a sampler that follows its parent because a Pipelex span was sampled.
  • An error tracker that reads OpenTelemetry's current span sees yours, not Pipelex's.
  • The standard trace fields of a log line, trace_id and span_id in the json sink, the record's trace context in the otlp sink and the entry's trace in the gcp sink, name your current span, inside a Pipelex run as outside one, so your log backend files a line under your own trace. The Pipelex span a line was logged in, the pipe's or the LLM call's, which Pipelex keeps in a context variable of its own, rides beside them as pipelex.trace_id and pipelex.span_id, as Logging describes.
  • If you export Pipelex's spans to your own backend, through your PostHog or an OTLP destination, they arrive in a trace of their own, not yours, so a line inside a run joins them on pipelex.trace_id and pipelex.span_id rather than on the standard fields, which a backend's trace view follows by itself.

docs.title: Quick Setup
docs.text:
When you run pipelex init, a default telemetry.toml configuration file is created:

pipelex init telemetry

The behavior depends on the target:

  • Global init (default — writes to ~/.pipelex/telemetry.toml): an active template is created with all options disabled. Edit it to enable your preferred telemetry destinations machine-wide.
  • Project init (pipelex init telemetry --local — writes to {project_root}/.pipelex/telemetry.toml): a fully commented-out template is created. The project file is layered on top of your global config, so leaving it commented means the project inherits your global telemetry settings as-is. Uncomment a key only when this project should diverge.

Global vs project config

Pipelex looks for telemetry config in both ~/.pipelex/ (machine-wide) and {project_root}/.pipelex/ (per-project). Both are deep-merged, with the project file winning on key collisions — your global Langfuse keys keep applying across every project unless a project explicitly overrides them. See Telemetry Configuration → Global vs project config for the full load order.

docs.title: Example: Enable PostHog Tracing
docs.text:
[custom_posthog]
mode = "anonymous"  # or "identified" with user_id
endpoint = "${POSTHOG_ENDPOINT}"
api_key = "${POSTHOG_API_KEY}"

[custom_posthog.tracing]
enabled = true

[custom_posthog.tracing.capture]
content = false        # Don't capture prompts/completions
pipe_codes = true      # Include pipe codes in span names

docs.title: Example: Enable Langfuse
docs.text:
[langfuse]
enabled = true
public_key = "${LANGFUSE_PUBLIC_KEY}"
secret_key = "${LANGFUSE_SECRET_KEY}"

docs.title: DO_NOT_TRACK Global Override
docs.text:
The DO_NOT_TRACK environment variable provides a universal way to disable all telemetry:

export DO_NOT_TRACK=1

When set, it disables every telemetry destination, whatever telemetry.toml says, and the request logging and tracing of your own Portkey backend too, [custom_portkey]'s force flags included.

docs.title: Attaching your own labels to a run
docs.text:
A host that runs Pipelex for more than one customer usually wants a run's telemetry to belong to the entities it cares about — an organization, a workspace, a tenant. Pipelex carries those labels for you without ever learning what they mean.

The run-level metadata every run carries (RunMetadata) has an extras field: an opaque mapping of string keys to string values that you supply when you start the run, beside user_id and storage_scope. Pipelex never reads a key by name; the telemetry layer forwards the whole mapping as the groups of each capture, each key being a group type and its value a group key. Keys are lowercase snake_case starting with a letter (at most 32 characters), values use only letters, digits, _ and - (1 to 128 characters), and a run carries at most five entries; anything else is refused before the run starts.

extras = {"organization": "org_acme"}

On your own PostHog stream, every span and every event the run produces is then captured under that run's user_id, with its extras attached through PostHog's own groups facet — so a generation made for one of your customers appears on that customer's timeline and inside their organization, instead of under one identity per deployment. The same values reach every OpenTelemetry exporter as the span attributes pipelex.run.user_id and pipelex.run.extras, and Langfuse receives the user id in the field it reserves for it.

Anything that names no caller of its own keeps reporting under the user_id you configured in telemetry.toml, which is what that setting now means: the identity of everything that is not one caller's run. That covers an event outside any run — a CLI command listing your pipes — and a run whose caller is not a distinguishable person either: a run on your own machine is attributed to the literal local, the same string on every machine, so Pipelex declines it as an identity and uses your configured id instead. The same goes for single-tenant, which pipelex-api states for every run when it is deployed with no users. Per-run attribution is for a host that passes a real user_id per run.

The extras do not depend on that. A run that leaves user_id at its default still carries its extras onto every capture, under your configured id — knowing which entities a run belongs to and naming its caller are two separate decisions, and you may take one without the other.

The extras are also available to the inference workers, on the job metadata of every call. None of the backends Pipelex ships sends them anywhere: a provider you reach directly with your own key gets none of your labels. An inference backend plugin of your own may forward them to a service you operate, for instance so that it can attribute each call's spend, and if it does, the run's own ids should win over an extras key of the same name, since the extras are caller data and must not be able to restate whose run it is.

docs.title: Work that is not a run, and crashes
docs.text:
A run is not the only thing a host does on a caller's behalf. Validating a bundle dry-runs its pipes without being a run, and an unhandled exception reaches PostHog through the interpreter's exception hook, which is handed nothing but the error. Both are still attributed to the caller when one is known, so your configured user_id stands only for work that truly belongs to nobody:

  • Validation. The validate entry points take a caller_identity — the user_id and extras you would state on a run, as a CallerIdentity. PipelexMTHDSProtocol.validate passes the caller the protocol was built for, validate_bundles_in_process, validate_bundle and BundleValidator accept one directly, and the BundleValidatorProtocol seam requires one (None meaning "nobody"). The pipe_dry_run event and every dry run the validation performs are then attributed to that caller. A CLI validation on your own machine names nobody and keeps reporting under your configured id.
  • Crashes inside a run. Every pipe runs with its run's caller in scope, and an exception that escapes the pipe carries that caller with it — through any error a host raises from it — so an $exception captured once the error reaches the interpreter lands on the person whose run failed, with their groups. An exception raised outside every run reports under your configured id.
  • Anything else with no run in hand. An event emitted without a run but while a caller is in scope reads that caller. A host can open such a scope around its own work with scoped_caller_identity(caller_identity=...) from pipelex.system.caller_identity.

The same rules apply to all of these as to a run: a placeholder such as local names nobody, mode = "anonymous" identifies nobody, and the caller never becomes an event property.

Anonymous mode covers your users too

With mode = "anonymous", the runtime identifies nobody on your stream: no run's user_id is applied, no groups are sent, and the user_id you configured is not sent either — a mode that identifies nobody would not be one that still named you. Leaving a user_id in telemetry.toml while switching to anonymous therefore changes nothing. Per-run attribution needs mode = "identified".

The rules it follows:

  • Nothing is privileged. organization is a word a host chose, not one Pipelex knows. A deployment that sends {"tenant": "t-1", "plan_tier": "enterprise"} is served identically, because the runtime never reads a key by name — the same boundary that keeps storage_scope opaque.
  • It is validated where it enters. A group type is lowercase snake_case starting with a letter (up to 32 characters); a group key is 1 to 128 characters from A-Za-z0-9_-; a run carries at most five group types. A mapping outside those bounds is refused before the run registers itself or emits anything, and again when a bridge payload is decoded — not later, inside a telemetry capture. The group key is quoted into log lines and capture payloads, so whitespace and control characters are refused outright.
  • It is optional. Omitting it leaves the group facet empty, which misattributes nothing. Unlike user_id and storage_scope, which have no default because a missing one used to be invented, a missing group invents nothing.
  • It travels with the run. The mapping rides the job through every nested pipe, and the bridge payload that crosses a process boundary carries it, so a distributed worker is handed the same groups the entry point was given.

These are labels for grouping, not content: they land in the reserved identity fields of whichever backend understands groups, never in an event property or a span name.

docs.title: Privacy
docs.text:
We take your privacy seriously:

  • Nothing in telemetry.toml reports to Pipelex: every stream is one you configure, sent to a system you operate; the anonymous usage statistics are separate and have switches of their own
  • Your telemetry.toml gives you full control over what data is captured
  • PostHog tracing includes privacy controls to redact sensitive content
  • All telemetry can be completely disabled

For detailed configuration options, see Telemetry Configuration.

For more information about our data practices, see our Privacy Policy.

docs.title: Usage Statistics
docs.text:
Pipelex collects anonymous usage statistics: counts of commands, runs, pipe types, models and tokens, and the country your IP address maps to. The address itself is never stored. Pipelex never collects your methods, prompts, inputs, outputs, file names or pipe names. The statistics tell us which features, pipe types and models people use, so we know where to put our work.

They are on by default, and you can turn them off at any time, for one command, one project or the whole machine, as Turning them off explains.

The first time a Pipelex tool runs with statistics on, it prints this notice on stderr, once per machine. A command whose stderr a program reads rather than a person, pipelex-agent with JSON errors (the command's --error-format json, the program's --error-format json given before the command, or --format json with no --error-format), neither prints nor records it, and still sends its statistics; the next command whose stderr a person reads prints it:

Pipelex collects anonymous usage statistics: counts of commands, runs, pipe types, models and tokens, and the country your IP address maps to; the address itself is never stored. It never collects your methods, prompts, inputs, outputs, file names or pipe names. To turn it off, run pipelex usage-stats disable or set DO_NOT_TRACK=1. Details: https://docs.pipelex.com/latest/setup/usage-statistics/

pipelex init carries the same text: whenever statistics are on, it shows this notice on stderr ahead of its own output, even after the first run printed it. A first run that is itself pipelex init shows it once, not twice. Showing it there records nothing, and with statistics off it shows nothing.

Not your telemetry

The usage statistics are separate from the telemetry you configure in telemetry.toml, which goes only to analytics and monitoring systems you operate and never to Pipelex. See Telemetry.

docs.title: What is collected
docs.text:
Every event is a count, a yes-or-no, or a value from a closed list. No property can hold text you wrote. Each event carries:

  • the tool and its version (pipelex, and the release), and the surface it ran from: the pipelex CLI, the pipelex-agent CLI, the API server or a Python program;
  • the operating system and processor family, the Python minor version, and whether the process ran in CI or in a container;
  • an anonymous installation identifier, a random UUID drawn once per machine and shared by every Pipelex tool on it, never derived from anything about the machine or you.
  • the version of the event contract it follows, schema, which is 2 from the release whose events name a failure by its error's code and that code's domain, so that a receiver tells them from an earlier release's events.

The events themselves are:

Event Sent What it counts command_completed once per command of the pipelex and pipelex-agent CLIs the command's path in the command tree (run bundle, validate pipe, init and so on, a shorthand such as pipelex validate my_pipe counting as the command it runs; never its arguments or option values), its outcome, its duration, for a failure the code of its error from the error registry (client.argument_invalid, method.invalid and so on) and that code's domain, who must act on it (input, method, account, operator or runtime), and whether it ran on the hosted API; for init, also where it set runs to execute and, when it set up backends on this machine, which backend kinds it enabled run_completed once per run, whatever started it the outcome, for a failed run the code of its error and that code's domain, live or dry, the kind of source the method came from (a local bundle, an installed method, a published address), the duration, the bundle's size and nesting depth, which language features it used (batching, parallel branches, conditions, structured outputs, image and document inputs), how many pipes of each type ran, and its inference totals: calls, failures, tokens, images, pages and cost model_used once per model a run used the backend kind (openai, anthropic, mistral, and so on, custom for a backend Pipelex does not ship), the model's name in the backend tables Pipelex ships (other for any other), and that run's calls, its failed calls by the domain of their error's code, tokens, images, pages and cost for it method_validated once per validation of a method the verdict, the duration, the number of errors and warnings, and the bundle's size and depth code_generated once per code generation what was generated (types, input templates or structure classes), the target language, the outcome, the duration and the bundle's size

A refusal a server answered, the hosted API's among them, is counted by the code and the domain its answer sent, never by what Pipelex reads from its HTTP status: a command's event then carries none, and a run's, which must name one, the catch-all runtime.unexpected.

A run's token totals come from the run's own usage events: when you turn tracing or cost reporting off, the run reports that its usage is unknown and no model_used is sent. The statistics never turn tracing on.

docs.title: What is never collected
docs.text:
No event carries a method or its MTHDS source; a pipe code, concept name, domain name, class name or any other identifier you wrote; a prompt, input, output or generated content; a file name, path, URL or repository address; a method name, catalog id or run id; an error message, stack trace or exception; a command argument or option value; an environment variable's value; a hostname, user name or e-mail address; an IP address or any location finer than the country; the order in which a run's pipes executed.

A test in Pipelex runs, validates and generates code from a method whose every name, prompt, input and error message holds a unique marker, and fails if the marker appears anywhere in what would be sent.

docs.title: Turning them off
docs.text:
Statistics are on unless any of these says off, and nothing can turn them back on over another switch that says off:

Switch How to set it Scope DO_NOT_TRACK set to anything but empty, 0 or false, the Console Do Not Track convention the process, and every process it starts PIPELEX_USAGE_STATS set to 0, false, no or off; an unrecognised value also turns statistics off the process, without silencing the rest of your tools the way DO_NOT_TRACK does The machine's choice pipelex usage-stats disable every Pipelex tool on the machine: pipelex, plxt, the VS Code extension and the mthds CLI The mthds CLI's former opt-out DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 in ~/.mthds/config, which mthds telemetry disable wrote before these statistics existed every Pipelex tool on the machine: the first tool that runs turns it into the machine's choice The project setting [usage_stats] enabled = false in the project's .pipelex/pipelex.toml everyone working in the project, once the file is committed The packaged default [usage_stats] enabled = false in the pipelex.toml Pipelex is packaged with, for a distribution or a corporate image every user of that installation The pytest integration mode Pipelex booted with IntegrationMode.PYTEST, as test suites do the test process: no test suite reports

The project setting can only turn statistics off: enabled = true has no effect. It fails closed: a .pipelex/pipelex.toml that cannot be read, is not valid TOML, or holds an enabled that is not a boolean turns them off. Pipelex reads it from the project's own file, found from the working directory the way Pipelex finds its project configuration, and never from your home configuration in ~/.pipelex/.

# .pipelex/pipelex.toml
[usage_stats]
enabled = false

Turning statistics off creates nothing and sends nothing: a process with statistics off writes nothing to the shared state, except when it turns the mthds CLI's former opt-out into the machine's choice.

docs.title: The usage-stats commands
docs.text:
pipelex usage-stats shows and changes the statistics of every Pipelex tool on the machine, pipelex-agent included, which has no group of its own. These commands never send anything, never print the notice, and exit with 0 unless they could not do what they say.

Command What it does pipelex usage-stats status Prints whether statistics are on, every switch that turns them off, the installation identifier and the notice version seen. It changes nothing pipelex usage-stats status --format json The same as one JSON object on stdout, the form other tools read pipelex usage-stats disable Turns statistics off for every Pipelex tool on the machine and deletes every event still waiting to be sent pipelex usage-stats enable Turns the machine's choice back on, and names any other switch that still keeps statistics off pipelex usage-stats reset-id Deletes every event waiting to be sent and the installation identifier, draws a new one and prints it 
{
  "tool": "pipelex",
  "enabled": false,
  "off_by": ["machine_choice"],
  "installation_id": "0f8fad5b-d9cb-469f-a165-70867728950e",
  "notice_version": 1,
  "internal": false,
  "ci": false,
  "container": false,
  "state_dir": "/home/alice/.mthds/usage-stats"
}

off_by names the switches that say off, in the order of the table above: do_not_track, tool_variable, machine_choice, legacy_mthds_choice, project_setting, packaged_default, integration_mode, and invalid_endpoint_override for the test-only endpoint variable below.

docs.title: Where it is kept and where it goes
docs.text:
Every Pipelex tool on a machine shares one directory, ~/.mthds/usage-stats/ (%USERPROFILE%\.mthds\usage-stats\ on Windows), created with owner-only permissions. It holds the installation identifier, the machine's choice, a marker per notice version shown, and each tool's queue of events waiting to be sent, under spool/. A file there is created or deleted whole, so two tools running at once never undo each other's choice. When Pipelex cannot look into that directory, statistics stay off rather than risk ignoring a choice stored there, and your command runs as usual.

Events go straight to PostHog's EU region, to a project that holds nothing but these statistics. PostHog discards the IP address after deriving the country from it, and keeps no finer location. No person profile is ever created. PostHog keeps the events for its retention period, and we delete the events of an installation on request, as our Privacy Policy explains: send us the identifier pipelex usage-stats status prints, after turning statistics off or running pipelex usage-stats reset-id.

How an event leaves depends on the process:

  • A CLI command writes its events to its queue when it ends and starts a small detached sender process, then exits at once; the sender posts the queue within ten seconds. The sender is a single file that needs nothing but Python itself, so it delivers whichever way Pipelex was installed and never loads Pipelex. An event that cannot be sent, because you are offline for instance, stays queued for the next command's sender. In CI or in a container, where a detached process would be killed, the command posts its events itself within one second before exiting and, once PostHog has accepted them, what earlier commands left queued, within that same second.
  • A Python program, or a long-running process such as the API server, posts from a background thread within seconds of each event, and flushes what is left when Pipelex is torn down or the program exits, within a short time budget. Each time its events get through, what earlier processes left queued goes too, within the same budget.

A send never delays you by more than these budgets, and a failure to send never changes what your command or your run does.

docs.title: For developers
docs.text:
• PIPELEX_USAGE_STATS_DEBUG, set to anything but empty, 0 or false, prints each event to stderr as one JSON line, {"usage_stats_debug": {...}}, instead of sending it. The switches still decide, so nothing is printed while statistics are off.
  • PIPELEX_USAGE_STATS_ENDPOINT, for tests, sends the events to a loopback http origin such as http://127.0.0.1:8123 instead of PostHog. Any other value turns statistics off. Each queued file names the endpoint its events were queued for, and a sender posts only the files naming the origin it posts to, plus any file naming none, as earlier builds wrote them. So an event queued while the variable is set is only ever sent to that origin, and one queued for PostHog never goes there.
  • PIPELEX_USAGE_STATS_HOST names the tool that embeds Pipelex, from a closed list (cocode, mthds-agent, other), so its runs can be told apart.
  • Pipelex's own continuous integration sets DO_NOT_TRACK=1, and its test suites turn statistics off and keep the shared state in a temporary directory.
