docs.title: Document Engine Plugins
docs.text:
A PipeDocGen step turns its inputs into a document file in two stages. The compose stage is Pipelex's own and is pure: it lays the inputs out, or renders the step's HTML template, or gathers the inputs as plain data for a template file, and it renders the file's name. The print stage hands the result to a document engine, which returns the file's bytes, and Pipelex stores them.

A document engine is a model of the doc_gen family, chosen the way a step chooses any model: by the step's model, or by the model deck's default. Its worker is contributed by a plugin, through the same add_inference_backend seam the inference backends use. Open Pipelex ships one engine, reportlab-pdf, which prints a pdf from the auto-layout of a step's inputs, and declares it in the kit's internal.toml. The Pipelex document generation plugin, pipelex-doc-gen, ships the engines for a pdf from an HTML template and for the office formats from outside this repository, and declares their models and their deck defaults itself when it loads.

docs.title: Sources, and the engines that print them
docs.text:
A step asks for a format (pdf, xlsx, docx, pptx), and its template decides the source the compose stage hands an engine:

The step has Source What the engine receives No template (a pdf, xlsx or docx; a pptx needs a template file) layout The layout tree of the inputs An HTML template or .html template_file (a pdf only) html The template rendered against the inputs An office template_file template_file The file's bytes and the inputs as plain data

Each engine is a model of the internal backend, declared with the sources it prints from as its inputs and its format as its outputs. The built-in engine is declared in the kit's internal.toml, which pipelex update refreshes, so an existing install receives it:

[reportlab-pdf]
model_type = "doc_gen"
sdk = "reportlab"
model_id = "print-pdf"
inputs = ["layout"]
outputs = ["pdf"]
costs = {}
Engine Prints From Declared by reportlab-pdf pdf layout Pipelex, in the kit's internal.toml pipelex-pdf pdf html, layout pipelex-doc-gen, when it loads pipelex-xlsx xlsx layout, template_file pipelex-doc-gen, when it loads pipelex-docx docx layout, template_file pipelex-doc-gen, when it loads pipelex-pptx pptx template_file pipelex-doc-gen, when it loads

The model deck names the default engine for each format and source, keyed <format>.<source>, and a key naming a format and source no step can ask for fails when the deck loads. The kit's 5_doc_gen_deck.toml sets the one default open Pipelex prints:

[doc_gen.choice_defaults]
"pdf.layout" = "@default-pdf"

[doc_gen.aliases]
default-pdf = "reportlab-pdf"

The plugin declares the defaults for the formats it prints, beneath the deck files: a deck file that sets the same format and source overrides it, and a user sets any default of their own in an x_custom_*.toml deck file, which overrides both. A step that names no engine prints on the deck's default, so it follows the install's deck, as an LLM step does. A step that names one, such as model = "pipelex-pdf" on a pdf without a template, prints on that engine wherever it runs.

docs.title: Registering an engine
docs.text:
A plugin registers a worker factory for its engine's sdk in the doc_gen family, declares the engine's model in the internal backend with add_internal_model, and declares the deck default for each format and source it prints with add_doc_gen_default:

from pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.doc_gen_format import DocGenFormat, DocGenSource
from pipelex.plugins.contract import PLUGIN_API_VERSION
from pipelex.plugins.inference_backend_registry import InferenceFamily
from pipelex.plugins.registrar import PluginRegistrar


class MyDocGenPlugin:
    name = "my_doc_gen"
    targets_api = PLUGIN_API_VERSION

    def register(self, registrar: PluginRegistrar) -> None:
        registrar.add_inference_backend(family=InferenceFamily.DOC_GEN, sdk="openpyxl", make_worker=make_xlsx_worker)
        registrar.add_internal_model(
            name="pipelex-xlsx",
            spec={
                "model_type": "doc_gen",
                "sdk": "openpyxl",
                "model_id": "write-xlsx",
                "inputs": ["layout", "template_file"],
                "outputs": ["xlsx"],
                "costs": {},
            },
        )
        registrar.add_doc_gen_default(doc_gen_format=DocGenFormat.XLSX, source=DocGenSource.LAYOUT, model="pipelex-xlsx")
        registrar.add_doc_gen_default(doc_gen_format=DocGenFormat.XLSX, source=DocGenSource.TEMPLATE_FILE, model="pipelex-xlsx")

The model's spec is exactly the table a backend file would hold for it (model_type, sdk, model_id, inputs, outputs, costs, and any other model-spec field), and it is complete on its own: the [defaults] table of internal.toml is not applied to it. A default names a model, directly or through any reference the deck resolves.

register stores these declarations and validates nothing. The model manager merges them at boot, before it builds the deck, and refuses what it cannot merge with PluginModelDeclarationError, naming the plugin: a model whose name and model type the install's internal.toml already declares (the message names the file too), a table that is not a valid model spec, or a default for a format and source no step composes. A handle names one model per model type, so a plugin may declare another kind of a name the file declares. Model names are not global across backends, so a name another backend declares is left to the routing profile, as it is for a model a file declares. When the install disables the internal backend, or declares none, the plugin's models are not merged, as a disabled backend's own models are not loaded, and its defaults are left out with them, so a plugin never makes a boot fail that would succeed without it. A second plugin declaring the same model, the same name with the same model type, fails at registration with DuplicateInternalModelError, and the same format and source with DuplicateDocGenDefaultError, each naming both plugins. pipelex plugins list shows each declaration on the plugin's row.

A document engine is a kernel-layer capability, and so are its model and its defaults, so an out-of-tree engine publishes under the pipelex.plugins.kernel entry-point group (see Inference Backend Plugins for the groups). make_worker is called for each print, with the model's spec, and imports the engine's library inside it, so register stays import-light and a process that never prints never imports the library. An engine loads its library, fonts and styles once per process, in the module that holds its worker, rather than per worker. A second registration of the same sdk fails loud at boot with DuplicateInferenceBackendError, naming both plugins.

docs.title: Refused at load, not at run
docs.text:
When a method loads, each PipeDocGen step resolves its engine: the model it names, or the deck's default for its format and source. The step is refused right there, before a run spends anything on inference, when:

  • the deck names no engine for its format and source, and it names none (DocGenEngineMissingError, which names pipelex-doc-gen for every format and source but a pdf from the auto-layout, and says to run pipelex update for that one);
  • the engine is reportlab-pdf, named by the step or through a default, and the install's internal.toml predates it (DocGenEngineMissingError, which says to run pipelex update);
  • the engine it names is one of the plugin's, pipelex-pdf, pipelex-xlsx, pipelex-docx or pipelex-pptx, and the plugin is not installed (DocGenEngineMissingError, naming pipelex-doc-gen);
  • the engine it names is any other model the deck does not define (an unknown model, located on the step's model field);
  • the engine does not print its format from its source, by the inputs and outputs it declares (DocGenModelCapabilityError);
  • no installed plugin registers the engine's sdk (DocGenEngineMissingError, naming the engine and pipelex-doc-gen, or saying the built-in engine is disabled).

The other model families find a missing worker only when they build it, at run time; a document engine is checked when the method loads as well. A runtime therefore needs no rule of its own about what it prints: a host that must not print documents disables the built-in plugin with runtime.plugins.disabled = ["reportlab"] and installs no other engine, and every PipeDocGen step is refused at load.

docs.title: The contract: a render job in, bytes out
docs.text:
An engine's worker subclasses DocGenWorkerAbstract from pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.doc_gen_worker_abstract:

def render(self, *, job: RenderJob, resources: RenderResources) -> RenderedDocument: ...
  • RenderJob is plain data, which Pipelex builds in the print stage from the step's composition and hands to the worker in the same process. It has a JSON round trip for an engine that prints in another process, in which the template's bytes are URL-safe base64 and a date or a time is its ISO text. It holds the format and source, the file's name with its suffix, the document's title, and exactly the payload its source names, layout (a LayoutDocument from layout_tree.py), html, or template with data, the inputs as plain data by input name. An HTML job whose template belongs to a method tree also carries base_url, described below. It carries no Pipelex object, so an ordinary Pipelex release does not break an engine; a change to it, or to the worker, is a change of the plugin contract.
  • RenderResources.load(uri=…, position=…) is how an engine reads a file its document names, such as an image or a stylesheet. It resolves pipelex-storage:// keys through the run's storage provider, decodes data: URLs, fetches https:// through the SSRF guard, and refuses what the run's read scope does not allow, a local path included, with UriReadRefusedError. It reads a file of the document's method tree, named by a relative URL, as the next section describes. An engine reads nothing any other way. It returns a LoadedResource: the file's bytes as data, and as mime_type the media type the file's source gives it, described below.
  • RenderedDocument holds the bytes. Their MIME type and suffix are the format's.

render is synchronous and runs on a thread of a print pool of its own, never on the event loop's default executor, which the engine's reads need, while RenderResources.load hands each read back to the event loop the print started from. The print stage that calls it ends the print with the event every inference call ends with, Inference call ends, carrying no tokens and no cost since an engine reports none (see Summary events), logged on the coroutine that awaits the thread, so a print cancelled from outside ends cancelled while the thread finishes its render; an engine overrides render alone and logs nothing for the print itself. An engine keeps no state from one print into the next. It signals a document it cannot print by raising DocGenRenderError, which passes through; anything else it raises, beyond a Pipelex error, is reported as a DocGenRenderError naming the engine and the file. The engine chooses the error's public code where it raises it, with .with_error_code(...): pipelex.docgen.content_unprintable for the run's data it cannot lay out, an element taller than a page or an image that is not one, pipelex.docgen.resource_refused for a file the printed document may not name, pipelex.docgen.template_invalid for a template file it cannot read, and runtime.unexpected, the default, for its own failure. It declares those codes when it registers, as every plugin declares the codes its errors carry (see Declaring the error codes a plugin raises). A Pipelex error raised by RenderResources.load, such as UriReadRefusedError or TemplateUrlRefusedError, is let through as it came, so the caller reads why the file was refused.

The contract is what an engine uses in pipelex.cogt.doc_gen: the worker; the render job, its resources, the LoadedResource they return and the rendered document (render_job.py); the formats and sources (doc_gen_format.py); DocGenRenderError, the one error of exceptions.py an engine raises, MarkdownFormattingBudgetError, the one the contract raises to an engine that formats Markdown outside a template render, and TemplateUrlRefusedError, the one RenderResources.load raises for a relative URL naming no file of the method tree; the layout tree (layout_tree.py); the template check request and the findings a checker returns (template_check.py), with the input shapes the request carries (InputShape and InputShapeKind in input_shape.py); and the modules of the next section. The rest of the package is Pipelex's own side of the print. An engine reaches Pipelex only through the contract and the registration seam every plugin uses, which also hands a worker its model spec, its backend, its SDK clients and its reporting delegate: anything else in Pipelex may move or change in an ordinary release, while a breaking change to the contract moves PLUGIN_API_VERSION. A piece an engine is missing is added to the contract, rather than imported from elsewhere in Pipelex.

docs.title: Relative URLs: the files of the template's method tree
docs.text:
A relative URL in an HTML document, such as the src of the logo beside its template, a stylesheet's href, or a font a stylesheet names with url(), names a file of the template's method tree, by the MTHDS standard's rules for a file reference in a URL (the Method Tree specification, "File References"). An engine resolves it as HTML and CSS resolve one, by joining it to the URL of the file that holds it: RenderJob.base_url for the document's own URLs, and a stylesheet's URL for the URLs the stylesheet holds. The base URL stands for the template's place in its tree: METHOD_FILE_URL_PREFIX (https://method-files.pipelex.invalid/, a host in the .invalid domain, which never resolves), the tree's digest, then the template file's tree path, or the bundle's for an inline template. An engine hands a URL it joined under the prefix to RenderResources.load, like any other, and never fetches one itself: Pipelex resolves it in the tree's listing and reads the file through the method file store, under the run's read scope, never from a disk. A WeasyPrint engine passes base_url to HTML(string=…, base_url=…) and routes a URL under the prefix to load in its URL fetcher.

A URL that climbs above the tree's root, a root-relative one such as /logo.png once joined, a file the tree does not hold, a directory, and a file the tree's membership rule keeps out, such as a hidden or a gitignored one, are refused with TemplateUrlRefusedError, an input error naming the URL's position, what it resolved to and the template. So is a file of the tree that is not an image, a stylesheet or a font, told by its suffix, since a URL may come from a run's input and a printer embeds what a rel="attachment" link names. A job with no base_url has a template that belongs to no method tree, such as an inline template of a bundle loaded from a string with no file sent beside it: a relative URL of its HTML names no file, and load refuses it the same way. A URL under the prefix in a document with no HTML is refused too. An engine that never reads base_url keeps refusing a relative URL, as it did before the field existed. A URL with a scheme, such as https://, data: or pipelex-storage://, is read as it names, as before, and so is a root-absolute local path an engine hands as written, such as /tmp/photo.png, which only an unscoped run reads. A literal relative URL of a template is checked when the method loads, so a refusal at print comes from a URL built from the run's inputs.

docs.title: The media type of a file an engine reads
docs.text:
LoadedResource.mime_type is the type the file's source gives it, lowercased and without its parameters, such as text/css. Pipelex never guesses it, so it is None when the source gives none:

Source mime_type https:// The final response's Content-Type, after redirects; None when the response sends none. data: The type the URL declares. pipelex-storage:// on S3 or GCS The content type recorded when the file was stored. pipelex-storage:// on the local or in-memory provider The type identified from the bytes, which covers binary formats only: a stylesheet or an SVG has none. A local path, read only by an unscoped run None: a file system records no type. A file of the method tree, named by a relative URL None: a method tree records no type.

A declared type is returned as declared, even a generic one such as application/octet-stream, and is not checked against the bytes. An engine that needs a type keeps its own guess, from the URI's extension or from the bytes, for a file whose source gives none or gives one that says nothing. An HTML engine is the case in point, since a print library such as WeasyPrint keeps a linked stylesheet only when its type is text/css, and a stylesheet served from a URL with no extension, as a web font service serves one, can be typed only by what its server declared. The built-in PDF engine reads images only and never looks at the type, because Pillow identifies an image from its bytes.

docs.title: What an engine shares with the built-in one
docs.text:
A document should read the same whichever engine printed it, and a template should be held to the same rules whichever engine fills it, so an engine takes these from the contract rather than writing its own. None of them imports ReportLab, so an engine can use them without loading the built-in engine's library.

pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.layout_display holds the rules by which every engine shows a layout tree's values, the built-in engine included:

  • display_scalar(value=…) writes a scalar as text: blank for nothing, Yes or No for a boolean, a whole float without its decimals, a date as 2026-09-29, a datetime as 2026-09-29 14:05, and a time of day as 09:07, each followed by the UTC offset it states (UTC, +02:00), if any.
  • is_numeric_column(values=…) says whether a table's column holds numbers only, blanks aside, and at least one, a boolean not counting as a number: such a column is aligned right.
  • markdown_as_html(markdown=…) converts a MarkdownBlock to an HTML fragment for an engine that writes HTML, with the one parser Pipelex reads Markdown with, as the markdown filter and the Markdown concept's HTML view do: CommonMark with tables and strikethrough, raw HTML shown as text, and a bare URL turned into a link only when it has a scheme, so a bare README.md stays text. An explicit link follows markdown-it's own rule, keeping any target but a javascript:, vbscript:, file: or non-image data: one, so [x](README.md) is a link, and an image becomes an <img>, where format_markdown below keeps only http, https and mailto links and prints an image's alt text. Called from an engine's own code, outside a template render, it is charged to no render budget, unlike format_markdown, so an engine bounds what it converts itself.

pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.formatted_markdown holds what an engine prints a Markdown text from when it formats it in its own format, as a Word or an Excel template fill does, rather than through HTML. The structure and the conversion live in pipelex/tools/markdown/markdown_formatting.py, where the plain-data templates' markdown filter reads them too, and the contract module names them in its __all__, so an engine imports them from the contract and never from pipelex.tools, which may move in an ordinary release:

  • format_markdown(markdown=…) reads a Markdown text with the one parser Pipelex reads Markdown with, by the rules the built-in PDF engine prints it by, which both take from pipelex/tools/markdown/markdown_rules.py: CommonMark with tables and strikethrough; raw HTML shown as text; a soft line break read as a space and a hard one, two trailing spaces or a backslash, as a line break; bullets alternating • and – by depth and an ordered list numbered from its own start; only an http, https or mailto target kept as a link, any other printing its text alone; an image never fetched, printed as [image: alt] in italics; a table cell aligned as its column's delimiter row sets; inline markup nested past fifty levels, which markdown-it does not cap, dropped and its text kept, as the built-in engine drops it, so a text cannot overflow the stack; and a node the converter does not know printed as its text rather than failing the document.
  • FormattedMarkdown, what it returns, is plain data, as the layout tree is: its blocks, in order, each a FormattedParagraph, a FormattedHeading with its level, a FormattedListItem with its marker as printed, such as • or 3., and the paragraph or heading it opens with, its heading_level set for a heading, a FormattedCodeBlock with its lines, a FormattedRule, or a FormattedTable of rows of cells, each row marked is_header or not and each cell carrying its column's alignment, left, center, right or None; and in the blocks that print text, their spans, each a TextSpan with its bold, italic, strikethrough and code flags and the link it opens, if any, or a LineBreakSpan. Every block has a list_depth and a quote_depth, the list items and the quotations it sits in, 0 outside any: a quotation is its blocks one quote deeper, so > # Title is a heading at quote depth 1, and the rest of a list item, a later paragraph, a nested list, a code block or a table, follows it at the item's list depth. str() of it is its plain text, each block on lines of its own, indented under the list item it sits in with list markers kept, table cells separated by tabs, and every other piece of markup gone, for a place that cannot show formatting; and it is false when it holds no block, as for an empty or a blank text.
  • Its budget. Inside a template render, as the markdown filter below converts, the conversion is charged to the render's budget the way the HTML conversion is, for every character of its source and every cell of its tables before it parses and for its result, bounded from the parsed tokens, before it builds it, a link's address counted with every span that carries it, since writing the structure out, as JSON or as its repr, writes the address once per span, and an overdraft is the render's own RenderBudgetExceededError, a Jinja TemplateError, which a template fill catches with every other error a tag raises. Called from an engine's own code, outside any render, it spends from a budget of its own, as large as one render's, and an overdraft raises MarkdownFormattingBudgetError (from exceptions.py), which the engine reports as its own fill error, naming where the value goes.

pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.template_environment holds make_plain_data_template_environment(), the Jinja environment an engine fills a template file's tags in when it fills them itself, as a Word template's tags are filled through docxtpl. It is synchronous; sandboxed as every Pipelex template is, each render spending from a budget of its own (see Template Sandbox); strict, so a missing value fails the render instead of printing as empty text; and it registers Jinja's built-in filters and one of Pipelex's, markdown, since the plain data it reads holds no stuff for Pipelex's other filters to work on.

{{ invoice.notes | markdown }} reads a text as Markdown into a FormattedMarkdown, as the HTML templates' markdown filter reads it into HTML: None gives an empty one, any other value is read as its string form, and an undefined value fails the render, as it would anywhere in a strict template. An empty one is false, so a template leaves out a section whose notes are None, empty or blank by converting them once into a variable and testing it, {% set notes = invoice.notes | markdown %}{% if notes %}…{{ notes }}…{% endif %}: every conversion is charged to the render's budget, so testing invoice.notes | markdown and then printing invoice.notes | markdown converts the text twice and halves the length a render affords. How a FormattedMarkdown prints is the engine's business, so make_plain_data_template_environment(finalize=…) takes a function applied to every value a tag prints, before the environment converts it to text: an engine turns a FormattedMarkdown into its own form there and hands every other value back as it is. The environment wraps it to charge what is printed, which is why it is passed at construction rather than assigned afterwards. A filter block prints through it too, so {% filter markdown %}…{% endfilter %} formats the text of its body as {{ … | markdown }} formats a text. The block reads its body as printed text, though, so a None value printed in it reaches the filter as the text None: an optional value is converted with the tag form, which turns None into an empty one. Without one, a FormattedMarkdown prints its plain text, so a place that cannot format, such as a document's properties, prints clean text rather than asterisks.

docs.title: The template checker
docs.text:
An office template names the fields it is filled with in its own way, which Pipelex cannot read: an Excel workbook through its defined names and Tables, a Word document through its tags. So an engine that fills a template file overrides its worker's check_template (the request and findings are in pipelex.cogt.doc_gen.template_check):

def check_template(self, *, request: TemplateCheckRequest) -> list[TemplateFinding]: ...

The request carries the template file's bytes and name, the shape of each input as an InputShape tree (which fields exist, which are lists, and what their items hold), and the dry run's mock inputs as plain data, so the checker can also fill the template in memory. The dry run, and so pipelex validate, calls it for every step with an office template file: a finding of severity error fails the step with PipeDocGenTemplateCheckError, listing the findings, and a warning leaves the step valid and joins the verdict's advisory warnings as a template_check_warning item, its message and location becoming the item's message and its template_location. A dry run that returns no verdict logs it instead: pipelex run --dry-run, and a validation run for something other than a verdict, such as pipelex fix bundle's or pipelex build inputs'. Write a finding's message and location for the template's author: the item is returned to whoever validates the method, through the CLI or the API. The default finds nothing. An HTML template, inline or in a .html template file, never reaches an engine's checker: Pipelex checks it itself, against the inputs' concepts, when the method loads. The built-in engine takes no template.

docs.title: Where the print stage runs
docs.text: The print stage is a content-generation leaf, like image generation or extraction: ContentGenerator.make_rendered_document hands a RenderDocumentAssignment, which carries the composition and the resolved engine, to render_document_and_store. The leaf authorizes the images the document names against the run's read scope, takes the dry-run branch, builds the engine's worker, prints and stores the file, and returns only the DocumentContent pointing at it, so the file's bytes never cross a workflow boundary. The dry run composes for real, which checks the templates against mock inputs, runs the template checker, and prints and stores nothing. See Content Generation Across Boundaries for the leaves.

docs.title: Dry Run Mock Generation
docs.text: Dry runs validate pipeline structure without executing inference. This requires generating mock StuffContent objects that satisfy Pydantic field constraints. The DryRunFactory system produces format-compliant mock values for fields with validation rules (e.g., snake_case identifiers, PascalCase concept codes).

docs.title: Why Mock Generation Matters
docs.text:
The structures a method declares can enforce format constraints via field_validator or model_validator:

class ComponentRecord(StructuredContent):
    component_code: str  # A validator requires snake_case
    concept_code: str  # A validator requires PascalCase

Standard mock generators (like Polyfactory) produce random strings like "uygNjiAuDMOtZEyibgHw" which fail validation. The dry run system addresses this at two levels:

  1. Field-level: Generate values matching expected formats (snake_case, PascalCase, concept refs, etc.)
  2. Model-level: Bypass validators using factoVry_use_construct=True

docs.title: When Dry Run Mock Generation Is Used
docs.text:
flowchart TD
    A[pipelex validate --all] --> B[BundleValidator.validate_pipes]
    B --> C[WorkingMemoryFactory.make_mock_inputs]
    C --> D[DryRunFactory.make_dry_run_factory]
    D --> E[Polyfactory with custom providers]

    F[PipeLLM dry run] --> G[cogt leaf: dry_llm_gen_object in dry_mock.py]
    G --> H[DryRunFactory.make_dry_run_factory]
    H --> E

    I[PipeCompose dry run] --> J[StructuredContentComposer.compose]
    J --> K[model_validate with resolved values]

A dry run does not swap in a special content generator: run_mode=DRY rides CogtRunParams on every cogt assignment, and each inference leaf (llm_generate, the *_and_store image/extract leaves, search, judgment, templating) branches to its dry_* mock helper in dry_mock.py — identically whether the leaf runs inline or inside a Temporal activity.

Trigger Entry Point Mock Generation pipelex validate BundleValidator.validate_pipes() WorkingMemoryFactory.make_mock_inputs() PipeLLM output in dry mode dry_llm_gen_object() / dry_llm_gen_object_list() (cogt leaf, dry_mock.py) DryRunFactory via the caller's class in-process, via the schema-reconstructed class on a worker PipeSearch structured output in dry mode dry_search_gen_structured_object() in-process / dry_search_gen_structured() on a worker (cogt leaf, dry_mock.py) Same split as PipeLLM; the worker arm dumps its mock to a dict, because the leaf's result crosses the boundary as data PipeFunc output in dry mode WorkingMemoryFactory.make_mock_content() DryRunFactory (with explicit field constraints) PipeCompose in dry mode StructuredContentComposer.compose() Uses resolved values from working memory; falls back to a DryRunFactory mock of the output class only when a value error hits under mock inputs

docs.title: MockFormat Enum
docs.text:
Located at pipelex/cogt/content_generation/dry_run_factory.py, the MockFormat enum defines all supported mock value formats:

class MockFormat(StrEnum):
    SNAKE_CASE = "snake_case"
    PASCAL_CASE = "pascal_case"
    CONCEPT_REF = "concept_ref"
    IGNORE = "ignore"
    DICT_SNAKE_KEY_PASCAL_VALUE = "dict_snake_key_pascal_value"
    DICT_SINGLE_EXTRACT_INPUT = "dict_single_extract_input"

docs.title: DryRunFactory
docs.text:
The factory dynamically creates a Polyfactory ModelFactory subclass with field-specific providers:

class DryRunFactory:
    @classmethod
    def generate_snake_case_code(cls) -> str:
        suffix = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=4))
        return f"mock_{suffix}"  # e.g., "mock_abcd"

    @classmethod
    def generate_pascal_case_code(cls) -> str:
        suffix = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=4))
        return f"Mock{suffix.capitalize()}"  # e.g., "MockAbcd"

    @classmethod
    def generate_concept_ref(cls) -> str:
        return f"{cls.generate_snake_case_code()}.{cls.generate_pascal_case_code()}"
        # e.g., "mock_abcd.MockCdef"

    @classmethod
    def make_dry_run_factory(
        cls,
        object_class: type[BaseModelTypeVar],
        *,
        snake_case_field_names: set[str] | None = None,
        pascal_case_field_names: set[str] | None = None,
    ) -> type[ModelFactory[BaseModelTypeVar]]: ...

docs.title: Generated Mock Value Formats
docs.text:
Format Generator Example Output Used For SNAKE_CASE generate_snake_case_code() mock_abcd domain_code, pipe_code, the_field_name PASCAL_CASE generate_pascal_case_code() MockAbcd concept_code CONCEPT_REF generate_concept_ref() mock_abcd.MockCdef concept_ref field (domain.ConceptCode format) IGNORE Sets field to Ignore() None/default default_value, structure fields DICT_SNAKE_KEY_PASCAL_VALUE generate_dict_snake_key_pascal_value() {mock_abcd: MockCdef} a dict of input names to concept codes DICT_SINGLE_EXTRACT_INPUT generate_dict_single_extract_input() {mock_abcd: "Image"} a single-entry dict of an input name to an image or document concept Image URL generate_mock_image_url() one of inference.dry_run.image_urls url of an ImageContent, at any depth Document URL generate_mock_document_url() data:application/pdf;base64,… (a blank one-page PDF) url of a DocumentContent, at any depth Random string Polyfactory default uygNjiAuDMOtZEyibgHw All other string fields

A mocked image or document never carries a random string as its url, because resolve_uri takes a random string for a local path. A run with a read scope refuses to read a local path, and it checks before the dry-run branch, so a dry run on such a run would otherwise refuse its own mocks: a mocked input, or an image inside a structure a dry model call returned. An https:// URL and a data: URL are read on nobody's leave, so they are what a mock carries. The providers are keyed on the class (ImageContent, DocumentContent and their subclasses), not on a field annotation, so they apply wherever such a class is nested. They also recognise a copy of either class rebuilt from a JSON schema, by its name and its url field: a worker running a dry model call out of process gets only the output's schema, and the nested file classes it rebuilds are no subclasses of the real ones.

docs.title: Declaring MockFormat on Fields
docs.text:
The DryRunFactory auto-detects format constraints from Pydantic Field definitions using the mock_format key in json_schema_extra:

from pydantic import Field
from pipelex.cogt.content_generation.dry_run_factory import MockFormat


class FieldDefinition(StructuredContent):
    # Snake case field
    the_field_name: str = Field(description="Field name. Must be snake_case.", json_schema_extra={"mock_format": MockFormat.SNAKE_CASE})

    # Concept reference field (domain.ConceptCode format)
    concept_ref: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="For type='concept', the concept reference.",
        json_schema_extra={"mock_format": MockFormat.CONCEPT_REF},
    )

    # Field to ignore during mock generation (use default/None)
    default_value: Any | None = Field(default=None, json_schema_extra={"mock_format": MockFormat.IGNORE})

docs.title: Using Field Examples for Enum-like Values
docs.text:
For fields that should pick from a set of valid values (like enum members or known strings), use the examples parameter. The factory's __use_examples__: True configuration makes Polyfactory randomly select from provided examples:

class Ticket(StructuredContent):
    # Refines should be one of the native concepts
    refines: str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        examples=["Text", "Image", "Document", "TextAndImages", "Number", "Page"],
    )

    # Status should be a valid TicketStatus value
    status: TicketStatus | str | None = Field(
        default=None,
        description="Where the ticket stands",
        examples=list(TicketStatus),  # Polyfactory picks randomly from these
    )

docs.title: Cross-Field Dependencies with PostGenerated
docs.text:
For fields that depend on values generated for other fields, use Polyfactory's PostGenerated directive. The factory automatically handles the main_pipe field which must reference a key from the generated pipe dict:

# Inside DryRunFactory.make_dry_run_factory():
if "main_pipe" in object_class.model_fields and "pipe" in object_class.model_fields:
    class_attrs["main_pipe"] = PostGenerated(cls._main_pipe_from_pipe_dict)

The callback receives all previously generated values and can compute the dependent field:

@staticmethod
def _main_pipe_from_pipe_dict(_field_name: str, values: dict[str, Any]) -> str:
    pipe_dict: dict[str, Any] | None = values.get("pipe")
    if pipe_dict and len(pipe_dict) > 0:
        pipe_keys: list[str] = list(pipe_dict.keys())
        return random.choice(pipe_keys)
    # Fallback to a mock value if pipe dict is empty/not available
    return "mock_" + "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=4))

docs.title: Mock Input Generation
docs.text:
When WorkingMemoryFactory.make_mock_inputs() creates mock working memory:

@classmethod
def make_mock_content(cls, typed_named_stuff_spec: TypedNamedStuffSpec) -> StuffContent:
    mock_factory = DryRunFactory.make_dry_run_factory(
        object_class=typed_named_stuff_spec.structure_class,
        snake_case_field_names=SNAKE_CASE_FIELD_NAMES,
        pascal_case_field_names=PASCAL_CASE_FIELD_NAMES,
    )
    return mock_factory.build(factory_use_construct=True)

The factory_use_construct=True flag bypasses field_validator and model_validator during object creation, preventing validation errors from random nested values.

docs.title: LLM Output Generation
docs.text:
When the dry LLM leaf (dry_llm_gen_object in dry_mock.py) generates mock outputs, it resolves the output class exactly the way the live leaf does — via resolve_object_class — then builds via build_mock_object():

item_class = resolve_object_class(object_assignment=..., object_class=...)
return build_mock_object(item_class)

object_class is the caller's live class when there is one (the in-process case), and None when only the serialized assignment is in hand (the distributed-worker case), in which case the class is rebuilt from the assignment's JSON schema. Keeping the two run modes on one resolution matters: if only the live leaf used the real class, the mock would be built against a weaker class than the one the provider is constrained by — the mock would be less faithful than the thing it mocks.

No explicit field constraints are passed — the factory auto-detects MockFormat from field definitions. On the rebuilt-class path, json_schema_extra hints and custom validators are dropped by the schema round-trip: classes with exotic format constraints should declare examples / mock_format, otherwise re-validation against the original class raises a typed DryRunObjectFidelityError. On the live-class path those invariants are present at build time instead, so an unsatisfiable one surfaces as a typed DryRunMockBuildError naming the same remedy.

docs.title: PipeCompose Resolution
docs.text:
StructuredContentComposer.compose() does not generate mocks. Instead, it resolves field values from working memory and validates the result:

async def compose(self) -> StuffContent:
    field_values = await self._resolve_all_fields()
    try:
        return self.output_class.model_validate(field_values)
    except ValidationError as exc:
        formatted_error = format_pydantic_validation_error(exc)
        msg = f"Cannot validate {self.output_class.__name__}: {formatted_error}"
        raise StructuredContentComposerValidationError(msg) from exc

In dry run mode, the working memory already contains properly formatted mock values (generated by WorkingMemoryFactory), so validation typically succeeds.

There is one fallback: when composition fails with a StructuredContentComposerValueError (e.g. a dotted path that mock data cannot resolve, such as a field on a description-only concept) and the run uses mock inputs, PipeCompose builds a DryRunFactory mock of the output class instead of failing. Type-incompatibility and validation errors still raise, and with real inputs (e.g. pipelex validate) unresolvable paths raise too — those are genuine bugs, not mock artifacts.

docs.title: Behavior Matrix
docs.text: Scenario Format Constraints Validators Bypassed WorkingMemoryFactory.make_mock_content() Yes (from json_schema_extra + explicit params) Yes (factory_use_construct) dry_llm_gen_object() (cogt leaf) Yes (from json_schema_extra surviving the schema round-trip) No (validators run; failures raise typed DryRunMockBuildError) StructuredContentComposer.compose() N/A (uses resolved values) No (validates)

docs.title: Adding a New MockFormat Value
docs.text:
1. Add to the MockFormat enum in dry_run_factory.py:

    class MockFormat(StrEnum):
    ...
    KEBAB_CASE = "kebab_case"

  2. Add a generator method:

    @classmethod
def generate_kebab_case_code(cls) -> str:
    suffix = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase, k=4))
    return f"mock-{suffix}"

  3. Handle the format in make_dry_run_factory():

    for field_name in detected_formats[MockFormat.KEBAB_CASE]:
    if field_name in object_class.model_fields:
        class_attrs[field_name] = Use(cls.generate_kebab_case_code)

docs.title: Using the New Format on Fields
docs.text:
class MyStructure(StructuredContent):
    my_kebab_field: str = Field(description="A kebab-case identifier", json_schema_extra={"mock_format": MockFormat.KEBAB_CASE})

Field name matching is exact

The field name must exactly match a key in object_class.model_fields. No glob patterns or inheritance traversal.

docs.title: File Reference

docs.title: Error Model
docs.text:
In Pipelex, an error is data, not a control-flow accident. Every failure is classified once — at the layer that knows the most about it — and that classification travels intact to every consumer: the human reading a Rich panel, the agent parsing JSON, a distributed worker's retry engine, and the HTTP adapter picking a status code.

This page covers the contract that makes that possible: the problem document every error becomes and the views its readers see it through, the registry code that decides what the problem says, the classification enums, how inference workers classify SDK exceptions, how classification survives every wrapping layer, and how a problem survives serialization across a distributed worker boundary.

docs.title: Design Principle
docs.text:
Three rules hold across the codebase, and everything else builds on them.

Single-rooted hierarchy. Every custom exception inherits from PipelexError (pipelex/base_exceptions.py). There is one root, so one to_problem() contract covers the whole tree.

Classify at the source, never lose it. The layer that catches a third-party exception knows the most about it. It classifies there. Every layer above is a wrapper — it adds context (pipe code, stack) but inherits the classification rather than re-deriving or discarding it.

No broad catches in business logic. except Exception is allowed only at CLI entry points and async task roots. Ruff rule BLE001 enforces this — an unexpected exception crashes loudly instead of being silently swallowed.

Why classify, instead of just propagating the exception?

A raw openai.RateLimitError tells a Python except clause what to catch, but it does not tell a distributed worker's retry engine whether to retry, the HTTP adapter which status to emit, or an agent whether the failure is the user's fault. Classification turns an exception into a decision input that every consumer can act on uniformly.

docs.title: The Layer Model
docs.text:
An error rises through a series of layers. Each layer has exactly one job.

Layer Role What it does with errors 5 — CLI entry points pipelex / pipelex-agent commands Catch, format for human (Rich) / agent (JSON·MD) / HTTP 4 — CLI factories cli_factory.py, agent_cli_factory.py Catch setup errors, route to handlers 3 — Pipeline runner PipelexMTHDSProtocol.execute() Catch + wrap as PipelineExecutionError, which reports the located root fault 2 — Pipe router / operators PipeRouter, pipe operators Catch + locate every failure as a PipeRouterError (pipe_code, pipe_stack); a foreign exception first becomes a PipelexUnexpectedError 1 — Workers / SDK calls pipelex/providers/*/ Catch the SDK exception → classify → raise CogtError 0 — Third-party SDKs OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, … Raise raw, untyped provider exceptions

Classification happens once, at Layer 1. Layers 2–5 are wrappers: they attach context as they catch and re-raise, but the registry code chosen at Layer 1, and the error_category, model and provider beside it, reach Layer 5 unchanged (see Cause-Chain Facts). The worker's classification picks the code, and the code decides the domain, the retry verdict, the next step, the sentences a reader is told and the HTTP status, so a single Layer-1 decision settles them all.

docs.title: The Problem Document
docs.text:
Every error becomes a problem document, PipelexProblem (pipelex/errors/problem.py): the MTHDS standard's problem, an RFC 9457 problem with the members the standard adds, extended with Pipelex's own. It is a frozen Pydantic model, and it is the single source of truth for what a failure says on every surface: the API's error responses, a failed run's completion webhook, a failed node of the execution graph, a distributed worker's packed failure and the agent CLI's error envelope.

Member Meaning type The code's documentation page: https://mthds.ai/errors/<code> for a core code, https://docs.pipelex.com/errors/<code> for a Pipelex code title The code's title, the same for every occurrence of the code status The HTTP status the code declares, which only the HTTP response carrying the problem sets detail The sentence stating this occurrence, rendered from the code's template with the problem's parameters code The registry code the error resolved to, a core code of the MTHDS standard or a Pipelex code: see Error codes domain Who must act, the code's registry domain: input, method, account, operator or runtime retry The code's retry verdict: yes, no or outcome_unknown retry_after The delay in seconds a provider asked for before a retry, kept only on a code whose verdict is yes and only when it is finite and not negative next_step What the reader of this view does next: its kind and its detail, the step's sentence rendered from the code's template params The parameters the code declares that a caller may read, by the registry's names location Where the fault is: the failing pipe and its path from the entry pipe, an input, a field, a batch item, an attempt, or a file with its line and column errors One item per fault, for a refusal of several at once such as a method that does not validate: each with its own code, detail, params and location, and the suggestions and suggested_fix its validation item carries pipeline_run_id The run the problem belongs to request_id The request that carried the failure run_error On a read of a failed run's results, the run's own problem diagnostics What only an operator reads, present in the operator view alone: see Diagnostics

No declared member is ever written as null. The model's serializer drops every member a model declares that holds no value, at every depth and whoever dumps the problem, alone or nested in a model that holds one (a graph node, a trace event, a webhook's payload), so a reader validating against the standard's schema never refuses it. The protocol refuses null on a declared member and nowhere else, so a null an extension member holds, or one inside a free-form object, is a value: every write keeps it as it was read, the caller view included, so {"extension": {"clear": null, "keep": 1}} comes back whole. to_wire() gives the problem in JSON types, and so does as_wire(): both walk the model by hand, as the standard's own Problem.as_wire() does, rather than through Pydantic's serializer, which refuses a value nested a few hundred levels deep, so every problem a reader accepts, up to the standard's MAX_BODY_NESTING, can be written back, a recovered one with a deeply nested extension member included, and its caller view projected (caller_view_of()). A problem dumped inside another model goes through Pydantic's serializer and keeps its limit.

PipelexError.to_problem(view=...) is the entry point. make_problem() builds a problem from a code and make_problem_item() one item of a problem with several faults, both taking everything the code decides from the registries' generated tables.

A problem carries every parameter its code requires. The registry marks each parameter required unless it is optional or read by the operator alone (ErrorCodeSpec.required_params), and both builders log A problem lacks a parameter its code requires, with the code, the parameters missing and whether a problem or an item lacked them, when a raise site gave fewer: the sentence that names a missing parameter falls back on the code's generic wording, so the log is a raise site to fix, never a state to accept. A raise site gives the facts it holds with with_params(), or its class through problem_params(); a refusal of a pipe gives its own through PipeValidationError, whose parameters reach the validation item (PipesAndConceptValidationErrorData.params, ValidationErrorItem.params) beside those the item's locators give, and a code whose required parameter is a list, such as suggestions or candidates, gets it empty when nothing is near. The library's unit tests and the API server's sweep this: an autouse fixture of each (tests/unit/conftest.py, api/tests/unit/conftest.py) spies on the problem builders' warnings before every test and asserts after it (pipelex.test_extras.required_params_sweep), which fails a test during which any problem or item was built lacking a required parameter, unless the test says why with the builds_problems_without_required_params marker. The marker is for a test that builds an error by hand with a message alone, or that stops below the layer giving the fact: a pipe's failure location fills pipe, and a worker's public call fills model and provider, so a test of a provider's private call or of a render outside any pipe lacks them by design. One parameter is withheld on purpose: a template refusal (security.template_refused) of a name the run's data chose, such as {{ topic[topic.text] }}, carries no name, since that name is the run's input, and its sentences come from a wording keyed by the code and the parameter it lacks (_WITHHELD_PARAM_SENTENCES in pipelex/errors/problem.py), saying the template looked a name up from the run's data and the sandbox refused it, rather than from the generic fallback. No raise site is at fault for a parameter withheld by rule, so the builders do not log that the problem lacks it (missing_required_params() leaves it out), and the sweep below does not need the marker for it; any other parameter such a problem lacks is still logged.

A refusal of one fault carries no errors list. When the only item of a problem restates the problem's own code, make_problem() folds it into the problem: the item's parameters and location become the problem's, and the list is dropped. An item carrying suggestions or a suggested_fix gives the problem its parameters and location too, but stays the list's one item, since a problem has no member for either. A problem whose single item has another code, such as method.invalid over one method.concept_unresolved, keeps its list, since the item says what the umbrella does not.

docs.title: Views: who reads the problem
docs.text:
A problem is one document seen through a view, and who reads it picks the view, never a deployment setting. ProblemView has two members:

  • The caller view (ProblemView.CALLER) is for whoever sent the request or wrote the method. It carries no diagnostics, and its step is the one the code gives the actor of its domain, except on a code of the operator domain: that actor is whoever runs the runtime, so the caller reads the code's other step instead, what it can do meanwhile, such as choosing another model.
  • The operator view (ProblemView.OPERATOR) is for whoever runs the runtime. It adds the diagnostics, its step is always the actor's, and it renders into that step the parameters only an operator may read.

The operator view holds everything the caller view does, so a reader holding the operator's record serves its caller from it: caller_view_of() drops the diagnostics, renders the caller's step again from the problem's params, and projects a nested run_error the same way. It fails closed on a code neither registry of this process holds, such as one a newer worker or a stored record carries: that step cannot be rendered again and the operator's may name an operator-only parameter, so the caller reads the generic sentence of the step's kind, and the report step for a code of the operator domain. An item of such a code fails closed the same way: its parameters cannot be told apart, so the caller reads it with no params and with UNKNOWN_CODE_ITEM_DETAIL as its sentence, while the operator reads it as it came.

A third, narrower projection, problem_metadata(), gives a ProblemMetadata: what may leave a perimeter, such as a telemetry event. It holds the codes, the domain, the verdict, the step's kind, the shape of the location (the failing pipe's depth, the attempt and the batch index, naming nothing), the items' codes, the ids and the runtime version, and never a sentence, a parameter or a name a user wrote.

Reader View An API response The view of the identity the request authenticated: the operator view for the operator's own credential and for the trusted proxy in front of the server, the caller view for anyone else (see the API server's Error Responses) A failed run's event to a caller's webhook The caller view, whoever started the run, as the caller-webhook contract specifies (pipelex/pipe_run/caller_webhook_delivery.py) A failed run's notice to a host's own webhook, such as a deployment's completion target The view WebhookTarget.problem_view carries, which the host picks for whoever reads its receiver, the caller view when it names none A failed node of the execution graph The caller view, since whoever reads the run reads its graph The human and agent CLIs, and the API's log record The operator view, since their reader runs the runtime A distributed worker's packed failure The operator view, which the submitter projects to the view of its own reader

docs.title: Sentences come from the code, never from the message
docs.text: What a caller reads is written in the registry, not at the raise site. detail and the step's detail are rendered from the code's templates with the problem's parameters, and an error's own message, which its raise site writes for whoever debugs the runtime, rides only the operator view's diagnostics.message. A raise site can therefore put in its message what helps an operator, such as a path on the host, a configuration value or a foreign exception's text, and no caller reads it; what a caller needs in order to act is given as parameters.

docs.title: What a message may carry
docs.text:
A message reaches the operator's diagnostics, the error tracker and every log line about the failure, so it carries no run's data: never an input's value, a stuff's content, a value a pipe built or a model's answer. A raise site refusing a run's data names it by identifiers, the input, the field, the index of a list item, the concept and the kind and size of the value (a string of 24 character(s), an object of 3 key(s)), and gives the facts its code declares as parameters; a fact its code declares no parameter for is left out. It never names the caller's own text either, a method's template source or a function's own exception text, which only a parameter its code declares as caller_text may carry, capped.

  • A pydantic refusal of a run's data is written by format_validation_error_without_input() (pipelex/tools/typing/pydantic_utils.py): each error's location and reason, the reason being pydantic's own message when nothing in it came from the input, or else the error's type, such as count: int_parsing, each located reason written once, in the order it first comes. A ValidationError's own text quotes every value it refused, and so does the readable analysis format_pydantic_validation_error() gives, which is kept for the documents whose author reads them, a method or a configuration. describe_exception_without_input() writes any exception's text the same way, a ValidationError's by its locations and reasons; a caller describing a foreign exception, whose text can carry anything, names it by its class instead.
  • A location quotes the keys the value holds where it is a dict, and a key the model does not declare, which are the run's data. Every formatter reads it from located_validation_errors(), which reads the error's errors once and walks the schema of the type the error came from, writing only what that schema names, a field, an alias, a position in a list, a union's choice or a tagged union's tag; any other component is written <key>, so a refused value under a dict's key reads entries.<key>.score and a key a nested model forbids reads owner.<key>. The label of a union's choice is read once per validated type and kept with it. A raise site that knows the type it validated passes it as validated_type, a model or a TypeAdapter over a type that is not one, such as the trace event logs' union of events; without it, or when the error came from another type, an error is written by its reason alone, since nothing then tells a field's name from a key of the value's own. So every site that validates an input into a class it knows refuses it there, located: an explicit envelope {"concept": …, "content": …} that its concept's class refuses is refused by the stuff factory as input.invalid naming the input and the first refused field, and a transported stuff by its hydration, while the runner's own catch of a ValidationError and the stand-in for a foreign one, which know no model, give the reasons alone. Instructor validates a structured generation's answer with a subclass of the requested class that keeps its name, so the generated class's refusal is located by the requested class, a list of objects' wrapper (make_object_list_schema()) carrying its name as its title for the same reason. A document no run's data is in, a method author's own or a value Pipelex built for itself such as a dry run's mock, is located as pydantic gives it, by is_authored_input.
  • A validator's own sentence is kept only when it raises InputFreeValueError (pipelex/tools/typing/validation_exceptions.py), the ValueError by which a validator declares that its message names what it expected and never the value. The native contents' validators raise it, a date's, a time's, a number's, an image's and a JSON object's; any other validator's message may quote the value it rejected, so it is written as its type, value_error.
  • A URL is the input's value, and possibly a signed link: a refusal names the input, never the URL, and the scheme only when it is one Pipelex reads, http, https, s3, gs or pipelex-storage, since any other is the caller's own text too, and a URL that does not parse is refused without the part httpx quotes. The host of a URL that could not be fetched, and the input it belongs to, are facts RemoteFileFetchError holds, not parameters its raise site gives: input.url_unreachable takes both, and a catch site that codes the failure otherwise, as a provider's file does with provider.response_invalid, is given neither, rather than a parameter its code would drop with a warning. The fetch knows the URL alone, so a catch site that knows the input names it with with_input(), or wraps the fetch in fetching_for_input() (pipelex/tools/misc/file_fetch_utils.py): an extract worker does, a prompt's image or document carries the input it came from as its input_name, photos[2], which its preparation names, and a document rendered as page views carries it on its assignment.
  • A table an input gives is the caller's file: a CSV refusal names the file by the input it was given as, the CSV file given for input 'people', with the row, the field and the column's position, never the file's path, a cell, or a column the concept does not declare, and gives the input as the problem's input parameter and its location.input, which the site that knows the input names with CsvError.with_input(), the codec not knowing it: the four sites of StuffFactory.try_make_csv_list_content, the three refusals before the table is read and the codec's own refusals it re-raises.
  • A function a PipeFunc calls is named by the class of what it raised, The function raised KeyError: its text is the function's own, and pipe.function_raised declares no parameter for it. Any other failure of the executor is named by its class, and a Pipelex error by the code it reports too, PipeFuncExecutionError (runtime.unexpected), since an out-of-process executor's error, or a transport's, can carry the function's text in its own. A host plugin's carrier of a problem recovered across a transport boundary is named by that problem's code, pipe.function_raised for a function that raised in a sandbox, never by the catch-all runtime.unexpected its class declares (reported_failure_code() in pipelex/pipe_run/located_failure.py, which the run's own failure line reads as well).
  • A template that fails to render is described by a fixed sentence naming the class Jinja2 or Python raised and the template's line, the template reads a value that is not defined (UndefinedError, at line 2 of the template), never by that exception's text, which quotes what the template reached for, a key of the run's data included, nor by the template source. A name is kept only when the parsed template spells it as a variable or an attribute (template_spelled_names() in pipelex/tools/jinja2/jinja2_rendering.py), never because the same word appears in the template's text: the variable an undefined names, the attribute the sandbox refused to read, the name it refused to store a callable under in a namespace, the method it refused to call, the method whose call overran the render budget. The sandbox words each refusal with those names and without them (SandboxRefusalError), as the render budget words its refusal of a call (RenderBudgetExceededError), and a refusal whose names the template does not all spell is written without them, A template may not read an unsafe name on a 'object' value., calling a method of a 'str' value needs about 1,000,000,000,000. A name a replacement field reads in a format string counts as spelled too, but only where the literal is the string a .format or .format_map call formats, such as the _x that '{0._x}'.format(v) reads, since the template's own literal wrote the access being refused; a word any other string literal holds, as mode == 'debug _token' does, and the plain text outside the expressions never count, so the sandbox and the budget read one rule (_spells_every_name()). A template that cannot render as written is described by the kind of fault and its line, syntax error at line 3., never by the token Jinja2 quotes, and a filter or a test its environment lacks is named when the template applies it by that name, No filter named 'frob' at line 1.. Parsing a template to find its variables is refused the same way, by the kind of fault and its line. Pipelex's own filters refuse what they were handed without quoting it: an unknown text format by the formats they know, an undefined value given a tag without the tag's name.
  • A structured generation instructor gave up on is classified from what ended its loop. When its re-asks end on a refused answer, the recovered ValidationError is written by its reasons, located by the requested class (extract_openai_metadata() and its siblings take it as validated_type), and any other failure to parse the answer by its class alone, such as the AssertionError instructor's OpenAI parser raises with a model's refusal in its text: each worker passes its SDK's own error classes as sdk_error_types, and only those keep the text, which is the provider's; when nothing can be recovered, the failure is named by the class of the wrapper's cause, or of the wrapper itself (describe_instructor_failure()), never by a text or a representation, since a retry error's is a Future's, a memory address included. instructor's own text, which is the last validation error's and quotes the model's answer, is never used, and no sink writes instructor's log records (see Logging).
  • A foreign exception a pipe raised stands as a PipelexUnexpectedError whose message is its class, KeyError, never its text, which can be a key of the run's data or a value a function was handed; a ValidationError adds its reasons. A failure that follows the pipe's own, a delivery's or the graph tracer's, is logged by its class and its code, never its text, which names the caller's webhook URL or the trace's file, and a webhook's transport failure is named by its class. A trace event log's refusal, and the tracing assembly's errors on the run's output, are written by their reasons, located by the event models' schema.

Rendering never fails. A template naming a parameter the problem does not hold makes detail fall back to the code's title, and the step to the generic sentence of its kind, such as Correct the method as the problem describes, then validate it again. The fallback is logged as a warning, A problem's sentence could not be rendered from its template, with the code and the reason as fields, so a raise site that forgot a parameter is found in the logs while the reader still reads a sentence.

docs.title: Parameters
docs.text:
A code declares its parameters in the registry, each typed, and its generated parameters model validates them. A problem's parameters come from the error whose code it reports:

  • The class's facts. A subclass holding facts its codes declare overrides problem_params() and returns them by the registry's names. An input-shaping error (InputShapingError), for one, gives the input and what its factory found wrong with it, such as the counts of input.wrong_multiplicity or the concepts of input.wrong_concept, and locates itself at the input. A fact the resolved code does not declare is left out silently, since a class's codes declare different parameters.
  • The raise site. with_params(**params) gives the parameters only the raise site knows, and overrides a fact of the same name: raise PipeRunError(...).with_error_code(CoreCode.PIPE_CONDITION_UNMATCHED).with_params(pipe=self.code).
  • What the run found. A declared parameter neither of them gave is filled from the run: a failure located at a pipe gives a pipe parameter the failing pipe, and the model and the provider found along the cause chain give the model and provider parameters.

A parameter the code does not declare, or one of the wrong type, is dropped when the problem is built and logged as a warning naming the code and the parameter, and a number JSON cannot write, an infinity or NaN, counts as one of the wrong type whatever the code's model says: it is a fault of the raise site, which must never turn the error it reports into another. So does a value that is neither a JSON scalar nor a built-in list, tuple or set of them, such as a collection of collections, a cyclic one, or a sequence of a class of its own whose items raise when read: it is never walked, so reading it cannot raise in place of the error. The parameters kept validate against the code's model and the problem's own params model whatever the raise site gave, so a refusal that names no parameter, such as a model-level one, drops them all rather than fail the problem's construction. A parameter the registry marks operator_only, such as the file and the setting of pipelex.config.invalid or the variable pipelex.config.variable_missing names, never rides params: it renders into the operator's step and rides diagnostics.params, so a caller is never told where the operator keeps a file. Nor does it ride an item's params: make_problem() and caller_view_of() take such a parameter out of every item a problem carries, in every view and whoever built the item, and render the item's sentence again without it (item_in_view()).

docs.title: Diagnostics
docs.text:
ProblemDiagnostics is what the operator view adds:

Member Meaning error_class The class of the error the problem was built from message That error's own message causes The errors along its cause chain, each with its class and the code it carries by itself params The parameters only an operator may read model The model handle, when the failure is attributable to one provider What the provider answered: its name, the backend's, its status, its code, its request_id and its message migration A pending configuration migration that explains the failure runtime_version The version of the Pipelex runtime that built the problem trace_id, span_id The OpenTelemetry span the failure happened in, when one was recording

Every text a raise site, a provider or a caller wrote is bounded in a problem: diagnostics.message, the provider's message, every text parameter and every text of the diagnostics a sandboxed PipeFunc call's report carries (see A PipeFunc Call in a Sandbox) are cut to MAX_PROBLEM_TEXT_LENGTH characters by cap_problem_text(), which keeps the head of the text and appends […]. The full text is left to the logs, so a provider's answer quoting a whole prompt cannot inflate a webhook, a stored run or a graph.

docs.title: The identity, and why renaming an error class or changing its code is a wire break
docs.text:
code is the identity a problem carries, and a consumer branches on it. title and type follow from the code, so no class declares them. The class an error was raised as is no member of the caller's problem: it rides the operator view's diagnostics.error_class, which both CLIs print, and the log records as error.type.

Changing the code a class declares changes what every reader is told to do, and breaks a consumer branching on the old code silently: its build stays green and its branch simply stops matching, falling through to a generic error path. Renaming an error class breaks whoever reads its name the same way: an agent switching on the CLI problem's diagnostics.error_class, or an operator's log query or alert on error.type.

The guard against both is a committed snapshot of every class's name and code declaration at tests/data/errors/error_identity.txt, regenerated with make generate-error-identity (alias make gei) and gated by tests/unit/pipelex/errors/test_error_identity_snapshot.py. A rename or a change of code cannot land without producing a reviewable diff on that file at the moment it is made — which is also the moment to plan the matching consumer updates. The same command rewrites the static redirects of the retired per-class error pages, described below.

docs.title: Error codes and the Pipelex error registry
docs.text:
The MTHDS standard names every error a runner or a client can meet with a code, input.missing or model.unavailable, and publishes them as its core error registry: one entry per code, declaring its title, the domain whose actor must act, its retry verdict, its steps, the templates of its sentences, its typed parameters and its HTTP status. A problem's type is the code's page, https://mthds.ai/errors/<code> for a core code. What the standard leaves to implementations, billing, organizations, the hosted catalog, Pipelex's storage, its configuration and plugins and the components it ships, Pipelex names with codes of its own under the pipelex extension prefix, which the core registry registers to Pipelex: pipelex.billing.credit_exhausted, pipelex.config.variable_missing.

The Pipelex codes are authored in one public file, pipelex/errors/registry/pipelex-error-registry.yaml, in the standard's registry format. Everything else is generated from it with make generate-error-registry (alias make ger): the JSON snapshot pipelex-error-registry.json beside it, which the package ships, every release publishes as an asset, and load_pipelex_error_registry() (pipelex/errors/registry/registry_document.py) reads; the typed Python of the codes, pipelex/errors/registry/pipelex_codes.py, with a PipelexErrorCode member and a closed parameters model per code; and one page per code under docs/errors/, which is where a Pipelex code's type URI, https://docs.pipelex.com/errors/<code>, leads. The Error Registry describes the format's checks and the workflow.

docs.title: Every error declares its code
docs.text:
Every PipelexError subclass declares, in its own class body, the code it raises (pipelex/errors/error_code_declaration.py):

  • A code, a CoreCode from the mthds package or a PipelexErrorCode: every instance raises it.
  • A set, ErrorCodeSet(default=..., others=(...)): the raise site that knows which applies chooses it with with_error_code(code), and an instance whose raise site chose none carries the default. Two cases that need different verdicts are two codes, so a class whose raise sites need different readings declares a set, never a domain or a verdict of its own.
  • Its cause's code, InheritsCause(fallback=..., others=(...)): a wrapper that adds no fact deciding the code takes its cause's, and carries its fallback when no error below it carries one. A raise site that knows the code itself may still choose the fallback or one of the others.
  • An abstract base, ABSTRACT_ERROR: a class never raised directly.
class PipeRunInputsError(PipeRunError):
    error_code = ErrorCodeSet(default=CoreCode.PIPE_INPUT_UNRESOLVED, others=(CoreCode.INPUT_MISSING,))


raise PipeRunInputsError(msg).with_error_code(CoreCode.INPUT_MISSING)

PipelexError.resolve_error_code() walks the __cause__ chain: it stops at the first error that carries a code by itself, the code its raise site chose or its class's, descends through every error that takes its cause's code, and stops at a cause that is not a Pipelex error. When no error on the way carries one, the error reports the code the deepest error implies (implied_error_code, which an inference error built with a category alone names, see below), else the fallback of the deepest wrapper, and runtime.unexpected, whose step is report, when none names one. It is one walk, guarded against a cyclic chain, and no error's code starts a walk of its own. So a wrapper that adds the fact deciding the code keeps its own over a coded cause, as pipe.function_raised does over any coded error raised inside the method's function (the in-process executor raises what the function raised as PipeFuncRaisedError, so a failure of the executor itself keeps its own code; an out-of-process executor must mark the function's failure the same way, with a Pipelex error carrying pipe.function_raised, which the sandbox reports in its result file (see A PipeFunc Call in a Sandbox), since an exception that is not a Pipelex error, such as a transport failure, proves nothing about the function and reads runtime.unexpected), and a wrapper that adds nothing passes its cause's code through.

make_problem() builds every problem from its code: the title, the documentation page, the domain, the retry verdict, the steps, the sentences' templates, the parameters model and the HTTP status are the code's, read from the registries' generated tables (error_code_spec() in pipelex/errors/error_codes.py), so building a problem is a pure lookup with no file read, safe inside a Temporal workflow's sandbox.

Four checks keep the declarations honest, in tests/unit/pipelex/errors/test_error_code_gate.py: every subclass declares a code in its own body, every declared code is registered, no subclass declares what its code decides (error_domain, retryable, a title or a type URI), and no raise constructs an abstract base. A fifth reads every SomeError(...).with_error_code(Enum.MEMBER) chain in the package and the runner, and fails on a code the class does not declare. A closed plugin declares at boot the public codes its errors raise, and a code neither registry holds refuses the boot.

docs.title: Raises outside the root
docs.text: An exception class outside the root carries no code, so a reader that meets one gets nothing better than the catch-all. Our own code therefore raises coded classes wherever a reader can see the raise, and tests/unit/pipelex/errors/test_foreign_raises.py catches a new foreign raise: pipelex/errors/foreign_raises.py reads every module of the package and the runner and allows by their shape the raises that are right (a builtin inside a pydantic validator, NotImplementedError in an abstract method, the data-model dunders Python and Jinja read, the framework carriers a library expects by type, and developer tooling), and every other foreign raise must be listed with its disposition in tests/data/errors/foreign_raises.txt: an invariant raised only on a bug of ours, which a boundary reports as runtime.unexpected, a builtin in a helper only validators call, a private class caught where it is defined, a carrier the scan cannot tell by its name (the import system's ImportError, the standard's method tree refusal its callers translate), developer tooling outside the exempt directories, or a builtin of a module that must import nothing of Pipelex and that its every caller catches. The check fails on an unlisted foreign raise and on a listed one that is gone.

docs.title: The retired per-class pages
docs.text: Before every error carried a code, each class had a page at errors/<kebab-class-name>/, which its class-derived type URI named. Those pages are retired. mkdocs.yml's redirect_maps holds a static redirect for each, generated by make generate-error-identity (pipelex/errors/retired_error_pages.py), so a client following an old type URI, a non-browser one included, lands on the page of the class's code: the default of a set, the fallback of a class that takes its cause's code, or the error codes' index for a class that is abstract or gone. The site's 404.html still sends any other single-segment error path to the index.

docs.title: validation_errors — structured bundle-validation diagnostics
docs.text:
A bundle-validation failure (ValidateBundleError) aggregates per-error data across stages and projects it onto a list of typed ValidationErrorItems, which a validation verdict carries as validation_errors and the failure's problem as its errors items, so every surface carries machine-mappable diagnostics, not just a single detail string. Each item's category is one of the closed ValidationErrorCategory set:

  • blueprint_validation — interpreter / blueprint-validation faults. A blueprint-stage PipeValidationError raised inside a pydantic model validator (e.g. the PipeBatch input_item_name == input_list_name collision, or the SubPipe batch_over == batch_as collision — both batch_item_name_collision) is wrapped by pydantic as a value_error; the blueprint categorizer unwraps it (ctx["error"]) so the item keeps its structured error_type and pipe_code / domain_code locators. The item stays in blueprint_validation (not pipe_validation) because the fault genuinely surfaced at the parse boundary, before any pipe was instantiated — only the error_type is recovered, not the stage. This category also serves as the last-resort residual: a parse-level failure (an empty blueprint, a bundle-elaborator failure) is raised with only a message and no categorized data, so when nothing else produced an item the builder projects that message as one blueprint_validation item (no error_type, no source — the bundle could not become a blueprint at all). A TOML syntax error is its own item of this category, with no error_type, carrying the source and the 1-based line and column the parser stopped at.
  • pipe_factory — pipe-factory failures (e.g. a missing concept).
  • pipe_validation — pipe/concept validation (missing input variable, type mismatch).
  • dry_run — one item per pipe whose dry run failed, with the error_type DryRunError, the pipe's bare pipe_code, its domain_code and, when the library knows it, its source.

Every error is an item, and none hides another.
