docs.title: Class Hierarchy
docs.text:
PipelexError is the single root, and every subclass declares its code (see Every error declares its code). CogtError is the inference branch: an abstract base whose subclasses declare the codes the classification picks from, which overrides problem_facts() to give the model, the backend, the provider's answer and the delay the provider asked for, and implied_error_code to name its category's code for an error built with a category alone.

Exception
└── PipelexError                  base_exceptions.py — error_code, with_error_code(), with_params(), resolve_error_code(), to_problem()
    ├── PipelexUnexpectedError     → runtime.unexpected
    ├── PipelexConfigError         → one of pipelex.config.invalid, .syntax, .file_missing; gives its migration as a fact
    ├── PipelexSetupError          → inherits its cause's code, else runtime.misconfigured
    ├── SecurityError              base_exceptions.py — abstract; the policy refusals never absorbed into a domain answer
    │   ├── UriReadRefusedError / SsrfBlockedError   ← security.input_url_refused, or .method_url_refused (and .provider_url_refused) where the site that knows the URL's author chooses it
    │   ├── UnsafeSchemaError                        → security.schema_refused
    │   └── Jinja2TemplateSecurityError              ← the template sandbox's refusal at render time: security.template_refused, else runtime.unexpected on Pipelex's own template
    ├── CogtError                  cogt/exceptions.py — abstract; error_category, provider_metadata, problem_facts()
    │   ├── LLMCompletionError      ← a set the worker's classification picks from
    │   ├── ImgGenGenerationError   ← a set the worker's classification picks from
    │   └── ... (see worker classification) ...
    ├── PipelineExecutionError      pipeline/exceptions.py — answers its located root fault's problem
    └── ... (one exceptions.py per package) ...

SecurityError is the abstract base class of the policy refusals that are never absorbed into a domain answer: UriReadRefusedError (a read outside the run's scope), SsrfBlockedError (an outbound request the SSRF guard blocks), UnsafeSchemaError (a schema carrying Python code-generation extensions) and Jinja2TemplateSecurityError (a template the sandbox refuses at render time). The handlers that turn a refusal of the caller's input into a verdict, the bundle-validation cascade and the library load, let a SecurityError through as it is, and the cascade also lets through any refusal coded in a security family, whatever its class and whichever arm meets it, a wrapper inheriting its cause's code and a dry run's failures included (security_target_kind in pipelex/errors/security_event.py), and a host that treats this family alike, a durable-execution plugin marking it non-retryable for instance, names that base class. Not every refusal belongs to it: the template sandbox's render-budget refusal, Jinja2TemplateBudgetError, is a ToolError coded pipe.template_budget_exceeded, and TemplateUrlRefusedError, coded security.method_path_refused, derives from PipelexError directly, so each is handled by its code like any other refusal.

docs.title: Factory-time vs Runtime
docs.text:
When What carries metadata How Class definition error_code (a code, a set, its cause's, or abstract), error_category defaults, user_action defaults Class-level attributes — one source of truth per exception type Raise time The code chosen from the class's set, the parameters only the raise site knows, per-instance error_category, user_action, provider_metadata with_error_code(), with_params() and constructor args — set by the raise site or the worker that classified the failure Problem time The resolved code and everything it decides; the parameters, location, items and facts along the chain; the view resolve_error_code(), code_carrier() and the problem hooks; fill_model_and_provider() at the worker chokepoint; make_problem()

The "outcome" exceptions (LLMCompletionError, ImgGenGenerationError, ExtractJobFailureError, SearchJobFailureError) intentionally carry no class-level error_category — their category and their code are genuinely per-instance, decided by the worker.

docs.title: Quick-Ref
docs.text:
# Build the problem of any PipelexError, in its reader's view
problem = exc.to_problem(view=ProblemView.CALLER)  # code, sentences, step, params, location
operator_problem = exc.to_problem(view=ProblemView.OPERATOR, request_id=request_id)  # adds the diagnostics
payload = problem.to_wire()  # JSON types, no declared member written as null


# Declare a class's code; choose one of its set and give its parameters where it is raised
class SomeError(PipelexError):
    error_code = ErrorCodeSet(default=CoreCode.INPUT_INVALID, others=(CoreCode.INPUT_MISSING,))


raise SomeError(msg).with_error_code(CoreCode.INPUT_MISSING).with_params(input="topic")

# Consume a problem
problem.code  # "input.missing" — the code decides everything below
problem.next_step.kind  # "change_input"
problem.location  # the failing pipe and its path, on a run failure
error_code_spec(exc.resolve_error_code()).status  # 422 — the HTTP status

# Project a problem built in the operator's view
caller_view_of(problem=operator_problem)  # what a caller reads
problem_metadata(problem=operator_problem)  # codes, verdicts and shapes, with no sentence or name

# Round-trip across a boundary
PipelexProblem.model_validate(payload)

# Retry decision within a run
InferenceErrorCategory.TRANSIENT.is_retryable  # True — only TRANSIENT

docs.title: Behavior Summary
docs.text: Scenario Behavior Rate limit hit TRANSIENT → repeated within the run; provider.rate_limited, whose verdict invites a retry and which answers 429, with a Retry-After header when the provider gave a delay; transport retry honors Retry-After. ProviderErrorMetadata.limit_verdict reads it, once per classification, as RATE_LIMITED: the throttles a provider documents on another status first, OpenRouter's 402 whose error.metadata.limit_source, in any section of the body, is openrouter_in_flight_budget, its Retry-After the wait when it came and is readable but never the verdict, Groq's own 498 for its flex tier at capacity, and Bedrock's 400 ServiceQuotaExceededException, which Claude on Bedrock carries too, through the Anthropic SDK, in the x-amzn-errortype header the Extract step reads as its provider code when the body names none, the same code the Bedrock worker reads, so the header feeds the service error vocabulary and the content-policy check nothing Bedrock's own SDK does not; then every 429 that is not a spent quota. The OpenAI, Anthropic, Azure and gateway Extract steps read the delay from retry-after-ms before Retry-After, as the OpenAI and Anthropic SDKs do, since Azure OpenAI sends both and the milliseconds are the more precise, and only when it is above zero: for a retry-after-ms of 0, Pipelex deliberately falls back to Retry-After, where the SDKs' header parsers return the zero and only their retry-timeout step discards it. Gemini's delay arrives in the error's google.rpc.RetryInfo detail rather than in a header, and the Extract step reads its retryDelay as the retry-after when no header gave one Quota / billing exhausted CAPACITY → not repeated; UserAction(CHECK_BILLING); provider.quota_exhausted, the operator's → HTTP 502. It is decided by ProviderErrorMetadata.limit_verdict, from the status and the codes and details each provider documents, never the message. Through a gateway and on OpenAI's dialect, which every backend on the OpenAI SDK speaks, one rule, _is_quota_exhaustion_by_code, reads the same codes: the provider_error_code the Extract step kept, the type on the OpenAI dialect and the code through a gateway, and every code and type _error_codes_in_body collects from the body, its nested error section and its top level alike. A 402 is a spent quota whatever its code; a 429 is one only when one of those codes is in _QUOTA_ERROR_CODES (OpenAI's broad insufficient_quota and the billing codes its error-code guide names in error.code, credit_balance_exhausted, organization_spend_limit_exceeded, project_spend_limit_exceeded and organization_usage_limit_exceeded, which Azure OpenAI and the OpenAI-compatible providers relay), and every other 429, one with no code included, is a rate limit, whatever its message says. That code read is all a gateway shares with the direct path: the provider-specific rules, the throttles on another status and the Anthropic and Google rules below, apply only to a provider called directly. On the OpenAI dialect, OpenRouter's in-flight-budget 402 above is a rate limit; Anthropic takes a 402 or a billing_error, a 429 whose error.details.error_code is enforced_spend_limit_reached, and a 400 invalid_request_error whose body message begins with one of _ANTHROPIC_QUOTA_MESSAGE_PREFIXES, the one place a message is read, because Anthropic sends a low credit balance and a self-set usage limit with no code of their own; Google takes a 402, an error whose google.rpc.ErrorInfo reason is BILLING_DISABLED on any status, a 403 in practice, and a 429 whose details say the quota it hit has a limit of zero, an ErrorInfo quota_limit_value or a google.rpc.QuotaFailure violation's quotaValue of "0", which no wait cures, so its every other 429, a per-day cap included, is a rate limit; Mistral takes a 402 alone, so its every 429 is a rate limit; and Bedrock, Azure and the other direct providers report no spent quota at all Bad API key CONFIGURATION → not repeated; provider.credential_refused, the operator's → HTTP 502 Model or deployment not found (provider HTTP 404) Raises a dedicated *ModelNotFoundError sibling (LLMModelNotFoundError, ImgGenModelNotFoundError, ExtractModelNotFoundError, SearchModelNotFoundError) carrying model.unavailable, since a method cannot name a provider's raw model id; operator re-raises PipeOperatorModelAvailabilityError Model reference unknown to the deck (a method naming gpt-5.1, a mistyped @alias or $preset) ModelChoiceNotFoundError → CONFIGURATION category, but the code model.unknown, the method's → HTTP 422, whose sentence names the reference and whose suggestions parameter carries the close matches of every catalog the deck knows, an empty list when none is near, which are all a caller needs to fix the method. A handle the deck serves only as another type of model is model.capability_unsupported The deck's own default or override names a model it does not define ModelDeckChoiceUnresolvedError, naming the deck setting in its message for the operator, never the caller's model.unknown: model.unavailable → HTTP 501, with the reason not_served, for a bare handle no backend serves as the type the step needs, whose caller step offers another model, and pipelex.config.invalid → HTTP 500 for a preset, an alias or a waterfall the deck does not define; docs.title: Execution Graph Tracing
docs.text: Pipelex captures pipeline executions as directed graphs for visualization and debugging. The pipelex/graph/ module provides tracing infrastructure, a canonical data model (GraphSpec), and multiple rendering backends (Mermaid, ReactFlow).

docs.title: Design Principle
docs.text:
Pipeline executions form implicit graphs: pipes call other pipes, data flows between them. The graph module makes this structure explicit:

  1. Trace at runtime: Instrument pipe execution to capture nodes (pipes) and edges (relationships)
  2. Store canonically: GraphSpec is a versioned, renderer-agnostic JSON model
  3. Render as needed: Transform GraphSpec into Mermaid diagrams or ReactFlow visualizations
Pipe Execution → GraphTracer → GraphSpec → Renderers → HTML/Mermaid

Non-Intrusive Design

Graph tracing is opt-in. When disabled, a no-op tracer is used with zero overhead. The tracer is injected via TraceContext in JobMetadata, not global state.

docs.title: Usage Variants
docs.text:
Scenario CLI API Result Generate execution graph pipelex run pipe my_pipe --graph PipelexMTHDSProtocol(execution_config=...).execute(...) GraphSpec JSON + HTML viewers Force include full data --graph --graph-full-data data_inclusion.stuff_json_content=True Data embedded in IOSpec Force exclude data --graph --graph-no-data The stuff and error data_inclusion flags → False (pipe_and_concept_registry unaffected) Previews only Dry run with graph --dry-run --graph PipelexMTHDSProtocol(pipe_run_mode=PipeRunMode.DRY, execution_config=...) Graph of mock execution

JSON Data Included by Default

The default configuration includes the serialized data in graphs: stuff_json_content, error_stack_traces and pipe_and_concept_registry are true. A traced input or output carries that JSON content and nothing else — the text and HTML renderings a run used to build for every one of them are gone, because they cost a render on the execution path, growing with text volume times nesting depth, and only the Mermaid viewer read them. --graph-full-data turns the data flags on and --graph-no-data turns them off, overriding project-specific settings; pipe_and_concept_registry is set only via config.

docs.title: CLI Commands
docs.text:
# Run pipeline and generate graph
pipelex run pipe my_pipe --graph

# Include full serialized data
pipelex run pipe my_pipe --graph --graph-full-data

# Exclude data (previews only)
pipelex run pipe my_pipe --graph --graph-no-data

# Dry run with graph tracing
pipelex run pipe my_pipe --dry-run --graph --mock-inputs

docs.title: API
docs.text:
from pipelex.pipeline.runner import PipelexMTHDSProtocol
from pipelex.system.pipe_run_mode import PipeRunMode

# Execute with graph tracing via config
runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(
    execution_config=config.with_execution_overrides(generate_graph=True),
)
response = await runner.execute(
    pipe_code="my_pipe",
)
pipe_output = response.pipe_output

# Dry run with graph: the same runner in DRY mode with mock inputs — no separate code path.
dry_runner = PipelexMTHDSProtocol(
    pipe_run_mode=PipeRunMode.DRY,
    execution_config=config.with_execution_overrides(generate_graph=True, mock_inputs=True),
)
response = await dry_runner.execute(pipe_code="my_pipe")
graph_spec = response.pipe_output.graph_spec

Dry run from MTHDS content

To dry-run an entire bundle straight from MTHDS content and get back a GraphSpec, use dry_run_pipeline(mthds_contents=...) (pipelex/pipeline/dry_run_pipeline.py) — the shared entrypoint behind the CLI graph commands, which wires the same DRY-mode runner for you. It owns its graph transport (a scoped in-memory event log), so it produces the graph regardless of the host's tracing_config and never writes trace files as a side effect.

docs.title: Outputs
docs.text:
Output File Purpose graphspec_json graphspec.json Canonical graph representation graphspec_json pipe_io_contracts.json The graphspec's companion: each pipe's I/O contract, keyed by pipe_ref graphspec_json input_form.json The graphspec's companion: each pipe's input-form descriptor graphspec_json output_form.json The graphspec's companion: each pipe's output-form descriptor mermaidflow_mmd mermaidflow.mmd Mermaid flowchart code mermaidflow_html mermaidflow.html Standalone Mermaid viewer reactflow_html reactflow.html Interactive ReactFlow viewer

The three companions are the validation report's pipe_io_contracts, input_form and output_form under the standard's names: a graph carries every payload the run produced and nothing that says what those payloads are, and a graph viewer (@pipelex/mthds-ui's GraphViewer) shows a data node's value only when it holds both the contracts and the output form for the producing pipe_ref. They are built once, at the end of PipeRun.run inside the run's own library window (the builders need the loaded library, which PipelineRunner.execute tears down before the CLI writes anything), over the run library's own pipes (the validated bundle and whatever library_dirs loaded beside it; a dependency package's pipes are keyed by alias in the library and described by no blueprint the host holds, so they are left out, as a validation of the bundle leaves them out), and carried on pipe_output.pipe_io_artifacts beside graph_spec; a failure of the builders, whatever its kind, is reported on pipe_output.pipe_io_artifacts_error, mirroring graph_assembly_error, and never fails the run: the build sits in the run's finally ahead of the delivery, so an exception escaping it would replace the run's outcome and skip the delivery of a run that completed. The build is gated by describe_pipe_io on the trace context, which the run setup derives from graphspec_json, and which validate's own graph dry run turns off since validate already built the artifacts for its report. Every writer that serializes the graphspec writes them beside it: save_graph_outputs_to_dir for the CLIs, the delivery executor for a hosted results prefix. They follow the graphspec_json inclusion flag, so a run that asks for no graphspec builds nothing that describes one, and a written graphspec owns the three names beside it: when the run carries no artifacts, a companion left by an earlier run in the same directory is removed, with a warning naming it, rather than paired with the new graph. The agent CLI, which always writes a graphspec with --graph, applies that inclusion before the run so the companions are built in the window rather than lost to a render-time override. Their bytes are those of the projection fixture corpus for the same bundle, since both go through render_pipe_io_artifact_files (pipelex/core/pipes/pipe_io_artifacts.py). The pipe_io_artifacts field crosses the SPI payload as pipe_io_artifacts_dump; the synchronous /execute response carries the description once the API relays that field, and a hosted run's results prefix once our Temporal plugin builds the artifacts in the crate's window.

docs.title: GraphSpec
docs.text:
The canonical, versioned data model for execution graphs. Designed for JSON serialization and renderer-agnostic storage.

class GraphSpec(BaseModel):
    graph_id: str
    created_at: datetime
    pipeline_ref: PipelineRef
    nodes: list[NodeSpec]
    edges: list[EdgeSpec]
    usage: GraphUsageSpec | None
    meta: dict[str, Any]

    def to_json(self) -> str:
        return self.model_dump_json(by_alias=True, indent=2)

usage (and its per-node counterpart NodeSpec.usage) carries the run's inference usage attributed to graph position — see Per-node Usage Attribution for the three usage states and the invariants a consumer must branch on.

meta.format is always "mthds" on newly emitted Pipelex graphs. meta.mode records provenance for renderers and shared tooling: Pipelex execution graphs emit "dry" for dry-run/mock execution and "live" for real execution. The shared renderer also accepts "static" for graphs produced by a static MTHDS graph builder.

Each builder takes the mode from the run itself, never from a default. The in-process tracer takes the run_mode its opener states. The assembler takes the mode its events state: it is given no mode of its own, and it refuses, with TraceEventModeError, a set of events that states more than one mode, which holds more than one run, and an empty set, which states none. assemble_tracing records that refusal as the run's graph_assembly_error and keeps the run's usage.

docs.title: Node Types
docs.text: NodeKind Description PIPE_CALL Generic pipe invocation CONTROLLER PipeController (Sequence, Parallel, etc.) OPERATOR PipeOperator (LLM, Extract, etc.) INPUT Pipeline input node OUTPUT Pipeline output node ARTIFACT Generated artifact ERROR Error node BINDING A PipeSequence binding step, { from = "invoice.total", result = "total_amount" }: its pipe_code is the from path and its pipe_type is BindingStep; its input is the root's stuff and its output the stuff it binds, so DATA edges run from the root's producer to the binding and from the binding to every step reading the result

docs.title: Edge Types
docs.text:
EdgeKind Description CONTROL Execution flow between pipes DATA Data flow (stuff passed between pipes) CONTAINS Parent-child containment (controller → children) SELECTED_OUTCOME From a live PipeCondition to the pipe of the outcome it chose, labelled with the outcome-map key the value matched, unlabelled when the default outcome was taken. Both builders derive it from the condition's condition_resolved event and the start of the chosen pipe (see Decisions at Decision Time) BATCH_ITEM Batch fan-out: input list → item extracted for each batch iteration BATCH_AGGREGATE Batch fan-in: item outputs → aggregated output list PARALLEL_COMBINE Branch outputs → combined output in PipeParallel

Every EdgeSpec also carries an optional boolean (default false). On a DATA edge it marks that the producer's output is declared optional (? presence marker) — the value flowed on this run but may be absent on others. Renderers can use it to draw the edge distinctly (e.g. dashed).

docs.title: Node Status
docs.text:
NodeStatus Description SCHEDULED Not yet started RUNNING Currently executing SUCCEEDED Completed successfully FAILED Execution failed SKIPPED Lifted (skipped) because a plain input resolved absent — a successful outcome, not an error CANCELED Canceled before completion

A SKIPPED node also carries skip_reason (a human-readable sentence naming the absent input, e.g. skipped because input 'source' is absent). A lifted pipe with a plural output still writes a real empty-list value, so its node registers that output and downstream DATA edges resolve normally; a lifted singular output is a recorded absence with no output spec.

A failed node's error is the problem document of the error that ended it, in the caller view, since the graph is read by whoever reads the run: the code, its sentences rendered from the parameters a caller may read, and never the error's own message. Its location names the node's own pipe and that pipe's path from the entry pipe, whatever pipe below it the failure happened in, so each failed node of a nested failure is located at itself while all of them carry the root fault's code. The problem is the error's own, whose code is the one its cause chain resolves to, the code the run fails with: an error that takes its cause's code, such as the PipeRunError a step wraps its failure in, carries its root fault's code, and an error that implies its code, such as an inference error built with a category, keeps the code it implies. When the fault deciding that code is a carrier, below the error, of a problem recovered across a transport boundary, a step run on a far worker or in a sandbox, the node reports that recovered problem as the pipe router does (located_problem() in pipelex/pipe_run/located_failure.py), so it records pipe.function_raised for a function that raised in a sandbox, never its carrier's runtime.unexpected: the node reads the code the run fails with. An exception that is not a Pipelex error records runtime.unexpected. Beside it, error_stack holds the stack trace of the error when the graph's data inclusion asks for it, capped at MAX_STACK_LENGTH (cap_error_stack()) both on the node and on the PipeEndErrorEvent that every trace subscriber reads before any node is built. Tracing never changes how a run fails: the problem is built while the pipe's error is on its way to the caller (pipelex/graph/node_problem.py), so when building it raises, the fault is logged as an error under the message The problem of a failed pipe could not be built for its trace, the node records runtime.unexpected, and the run fails with the pipe's own error.

docs.title: Node Paths
docs.text:
Every node that runs a pipe carries its path, the invocation path of that run of the pipe, which names it the same way in every run of the method, live or dry, on every engine. A binding step's node runs no pipe and has no path. The node_id stays the graph's own key, unique within one graph and different from one run to the next; the path is the name a reader joins the views of a run on.

A node_id, like an edge_id, names the attempt that minted it (make_trace_id_prefix, pipelex/system/trace_context.py). Each attempt of an execution numbers its nodes and edges from 0, so the id carries the whole chain: <graph_id>:<workflow_id>:attempt_<n>:node_<k> for the run's own workflow, followed after the attempt by :lineage_<16 hex digits>, the start of the SHA-256 digest of its lineage's key, for a workflow another one dispatched. Two attempts of one workflow, and a workflow that two attempts of its dispatcher dispatched under the same name, therefore mint different ids, and a reader keyed on node_id never merges a lost attempt's failed node with the one its retry ran. The direct mode's one execution, in its first attempt, mints <graph_id>:node_<k>.

docs.title: Tracing Flow
docs.text:
# 1. Manager opens tracer for pipeline run
manager = GraphTracerManager.get_or_create_instance()
trace_context = manager.open_tracer(
    graph_id=pipeline_run_id,
    data_inclusion=config.data_inclusion,
    pipeline_ref_domain="my_domain",
    pipeline_ref_main_pipe="my_pipe",
    run_mode=PipeRunMode.LIVE,  # required: whoever opens the trace states the run's mode
)

# 2. Context flows through JobMetadata to each pipe
job_metadata = JobMetadata(
    pipeline_run_id=pipeline_run_id,
    trace_context=trace_context,
)

# 3. Each pipe reports start/end to tracer
node_id, child_context = manager.on_pipe_start(
    trace_context=trace_context,
    pipe_code="extract_text",
    pipe_ref="my_domain.extract_text",  # names the entry pipe in every path; None for a binding step
    pipe_type="PipeExtract",
    node_kind=NodeKind.OPERATOR,
    started_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    input_specs=[...],
)

# 4. On completion, report success with output
manager.on_pipe_end_success(
    lookup_key=trace_context.lookup_key,
    node_id=node_id,
    ended_at=datetime.now(timezone.utc),
    output_spec=IOSpec(...),
)

# 5. Manager closes tracer and returns GraphSpec
graph_spec = manager.close_tracer(pipeline_run_id)

docs.title: Event-Log Transport and the Scoped Override
docs.text:
Trace events travel through an EventLogProtocol backend (pipelex/tracing/): the tracer emits events into it during the run (write side, wired in pipeline_run_setup), and assemble_tracing reads them back after the run to build the GraphSpec and usage aggregates (read side, triggered from PipeRun.run). Both sides normally build their backend instance independently from tracing_config via make_event_log — NDJSON files or DynamoDB bridge the two instances through external storage.

The DynamoDB backend (pipelex/tracing/dynamodb_event_log.py) writes each event as one item keyed by the run (PK = PIPELINE_RUN#{pipeline_run_id}, SK = EVENT#{chain_digest}#{writer_id}#{sequence}, see Executions and Their Attempts), and every item carries a ttl in epoch seconds, set to the time of the write plus runtime.tracing.dynamodb.retention_days (30 days by default). DynamoDB deletes an item once its ttl has passed, provided the table names ttl as its TTL attribute, so a run's events, which by default hold its full output data, are not kept forever. The retention counts from the write rather than from the event's own timestamp, and a Temporal replay that re-emits an event overwrites the same item, pushing its expiry back by no more than the time between the two writes. A reader that needs a run's events, such as the graph and usage assembly, must therefore read them within the retention. Only the items written by a version that sets ttl expire: an item an earlier version wrote has no ttl, so it stays in the table until it is deleted or given one.

The assembled usage rides back on pipe_output.tokens_usages (with any assembly failure on usage_assembly_error), which the sync /execute response returns directly. For delivery-enabled runs (a storage target set), the delivery executor (pipelex/pipe_run/delivery_executor.py) also persists it as a tokens_usages.json result artifact — {"tokens_usages": [...], "usage_assembly_error": null} — next to working_memory.json, the main_stuff.* renders, and the graph outputs (graphspec.json with its three companions pipe_io_contracts.json, input_form.json and output_form.json, see Outputs), so a durable client polling result files gets the same usage records a sync caller does. The artifact is written unconditionally on every successful result delivery: explicit nulls mean usage assembly was off for that run. A failed run stores no result files at all, so an absent tokens_usages.json means either the run failed or it was delivered before the artifact existed — tell those apart from the delivery status, not from the file's presence.

For fully in-process runs, pipelex.runtime_hub.scoped_event_log pins one shared instance for both sides instead:

from pipelex.runtime_hub import scoped_event_log
from pipelex.tracing.in_memory_event_log import InMemoryEventLog

with scoped_event_log(InMemoryEventLog()):
    response = await runner.execute(...)  # graph assembles in memory

Semantics:

  • The override is ContextVar-scoped (mirrors scoped_pipe_router), so concurrent runs with separate scopes never cross-contaminate, and the prior value is restored on exit.
  • A set override implies tracing-enabled: it is honored even when runtime.tracing.is_enabled is False, on both the write side and the read side's early-return.
  • Usage events honor it too, ahead of every other route. ReportingManager writes a usage event emitted in the scope into the scoped instance and nowhere else: not into an event log registered with set_event_log, and not into the per-process runner fallback, even inside an isolated sub-execution (an activity, as the isolated-execution probe reports it), where an emission otherwise always takes the fallback. The event names the run of the job's own metadata, as on the fallback, and the gate on the trace context's emit_usage_events still applies. This is what lets code running a leaf inside an activity capture that leaf's usage: it scopes a fresh InMemoryEventLog around the leaf, reads the usage events back and returns them with the activity's result. Each leaf's log needs a writer_id of its own, such as the activity's id: the leaves of one workflow attempt share its chain and each fresh log numbers its events from zero, so two leaves writing as primary would collide on the store key once their events meet in one log, which keeps only the first. It is how a backend with no shared tracing store, such as Mistral Workflows, can collect a run's usage: the run adds each leaf's returned events to its own in-memory log, so the run's usage is a function of the results its history records, and a replay rebuilds it. With no override set, a usage event goes to the event log registered for its run outside an isolated sub-execution, and to the runner fallback inside one or when none is registered.
  • Lifecycle: the read side does not close() the scoped instance and the machinery never calls cleanup() on it — but the write-side tracer DOES call close() on its event log at teardown, before the read side assembles. A scoped event log's close() must therefore be idempotent or a no-op (as InMemoryEventLog's is); scoping a backend whose close() releases a real resource would break its own assembly read.

This is what lets a graph-producing dry-run trace entirely in memory (no NDJSON file, no DynamoDB round-trip). Both dry-run entrypoints rely on it: dry_run_pipe_in_process (pipelex/pipe_run/dry_run_in_process.py — the graph arm of protocol validate and of the single Temporal validation activity) and dry_run_pipeline (pipelex/pipeline/dry_run_pipeline.py) itself — these functions exist to produce a graph, so they install their own scoped InMemoryEventLog rather than depending on the host having tracing configured (a host with runtime.tracing.is_enabled = false, like pipelex-api's /validate in direct mode, still gets its graph). A run that nonetheless finishes without a graph raises the typed DryRunGraphNotProducedError.

docs.title: Trace Events
docs.text:
The tracer writes one event for each thing that happens in the run, in the order it happens (pipelex/tracing/trace_events.py). Every backend carries the events whole: the NDJSON and DynamoDB logs store each one as its JSON and read it back through the discriminated union AnyTraceEvent, and the in-memory and buffering logs hold the objects themselves. Every event carries these fields:

  • pipeline_run_id, workflow_id and writer_id, which name the run, the execution that wrote it, never empty and direct in direct mode, and the process that wrote it;
  • attempt, the attempt of that execution, counting from 1, and lineage, the attempts it was dispatched under (see Executions and Their Attempts);
  • path, the invocation path of the invocation the event is about, null for a binding step, which runs no pipe;
  • timestamp, and sequence, which rises with each event one writer writes;
  • event_kind, which tells the event's kind;
  • mode, live or dry, the mode of the run that wrote it.

An event is frozen, since it records what happened, and it computes its chain, its chain key and its store key once, the first time they are read, since every read and every assembly of a run reads them for each of its events; a copy made with model_copy(update=...) computes them again from its own fields. An event whose workflow_id is empty is refused when it is read, like any event in a shape this version does not accept, with EventLogSchemaMismatchError.

Each event kind that the hosted progress contract, which defines the run progress the hosted API reports, maps to a progress event carries that progress event's fields: the contract's execution is workflow_id, its at is timestamp, and its kind is read off event_kind.

The run's TraceContext carries the mode as run_mode, so a usage event that an activity writes from the context alone states it too. mode is required: an event stored by a version that did not write it is refused with EventLogSchemaMismatchError rather than read as live, and running the pipeline again writes a log in the current shape. run_mode is required too, with no default, on TraceContext, on GraphTracerManager.open_tracer and on the tracer's setup, since a default would stamp a dry run's events as live: whoever opens a trace states the mode, and a workflow that opens a tracer of its own for part of a run passes the run_mode of the context it received.

The mode a trace states is the one the run's pipes run in, which is not always the one requested: a keyless boot (needs_inference=False) runs a requested live run dry. pipeline_run_setup therefore resolves the run's mode once, before it opens the tracer, through resolve_effective_run_mode (pipelex/runtime_hub.py), which first refuses is_mock_usage on a live request and then applies the keyless coercion. The tracer, the trace context, the OpenTelemetry context and the pipe job all take that one value, so a forced dry run states dry on every event and on its graph, and opens no OpenTelemetry trace, as no dry run does. The kernel tier holds to the same rule from the other side: its caller opens the trace, so PipelexKernel.make refuses, with TraceContextRunModeError, a trace context stating another mode than the one resolve_effective_run_mode gives the run (see The Pipelex Kernel).

event_kind Written when What it carries pipe_start A pipe starts The node, its parent, the pipe's code, its pipe_ref, its domain-qualified reference (null for a binding step), its type, description and domain, its node kind and its inputs; a PipeSequence also states step_count, the number of steps its author wrote, and a PipeParallel states branch_count, the number of its branches, both null on every other pipe pipe_end_success A pipe ends with an output The node, the pipe's pipe_code, pipe_ref and pipe_type, as its start states them, its end time, its output and its metrics pipe_end_error A pipe fails The node, the pipe's code, reference and type, its end time, the error's problem in the caller view located at the pipe, and its stack trace when the data inclusion asks for it pipe_end_skipped A pipe is lifted because a plain input is absent The node, the pipe's code, reference and type, its end time, the reason, and the empty list a plural output still writes edge The tracer draws an edge Its source, target, kind, label and stuff digests controller_output A controller registers an output it produced The node and the output batch_item A PipeBatch extracts an item from its input list The list and item digests, the item index and the batch's node batch_aggregate A PipeBatch adds an item's result to its output list The output list and item digests, the item index and the batch's node parallel_combine A PipeParallel combines its branch outputs The combined digest, the branch digests and their producers condition_output_merge A dry-run PipeCondition merges its outcomes' outputs (see A Dry-Run Condition's Output) The merge record condition_resolved A live PipeCondition's choice is final, before anything runs under it The condition's node, rendered_value, the value its expression rendered, and selected_outcome, the outcome-map key the value matched, or null when the default outcome was taken batch_fanned_out A PipeBatch knows how many items it runs, before any item starts The batch's node, item_count, and the pipe each item runs: branch_pipe_code, its bare code, branch_pipe_ref, its domain-qualified reference, and branch_pipe_type execution_data A pipe records details of its execution The node, and the entries merged into its execution_data usage_report An inference job reports what it used The node it is attributed to and its usage

docs.title: Decisions at Decision Time
docs.text:
A controller records each decision the moment it is final, so a reader following the trace while the run goes on knows a condition's outcome and a batch's width before the work under them runs. A live PipeCondition writes condition_resolved once its choice is final: at once for an outcome mapped to continue or fail, which runs nothing, and, for an outcome that runs a pipe, once it has found that pipe's inputs in working memory. A chosen pipe whose inputs are missing fails the condition before it runs, so the trace records no outcome taken, neither the event nor the execution data. A PipeBatch writes batch_fanned_out before its first item starts. A dry run runs every outcome of a condition and chooses none, so it writes no condition_resolved and no SELECTED_OUTCOME edge; a dry batch still writes batch_fanned_out for the items it runs. Both are graph events about a node of the tracer's graph: a run that emits no graph events, in costs-only mode, writes neither, and a tracer records a decision only on a node it started itself, as it records execution data, so a decision looked up on a tracer that does not hold the controller's node is dropped rather than written for a node that tracer's graph lacks.

The controllers register their execution data at the same moments:

  • A PipeSequence registers step_count as it starts. It records no step number as each step starts: the number of a step is in the path of the pipe the step runs, <sequence path>/step_<n>.
  • A PipeParallel registers branch_count, add_each_output and combined_output_concept before any branch runs.
  • A PipeBatch registers item_count and branch_pipe_code with its fan-out. The two spellings of branch_pipe_code differ: the execution data carries the blueprint's field as its author wrote it, which may be domain-qualified, such as my_domain.summarize, while the batch_fanned_out event's branch_pipe_code is always the bare code, summarize, with branch_pipe_ref the qualified reference, my_domain.summarize.
  • A live PipeCondition registers evaluated_expression and selected_outcome with its resolution. Here selected_outcome is the outcome itself, the code of the pipe it runs or continue or fail, where the condition_resolved event names the outcome-map key.

Both graph builders derive the SELECTED_OUTCOME edge from two facts of the run, by the one rule in pipelex/graph/selected_outcome.py: a condition's condition_resolved, and the start of a pipe whose parent is that condition's node, which can only be the pipe of the outcome it chose. The in-process tracer applies the rule at teardown to the resolutions it recorded and the nodes it holds; the assembler applies it after reading every event, whichever tracer wrote them. The edge is never drawn when the chosen pipe starts, because in a distributed run that pipe can start in another workflow, under a tracer of its own that never saw the resolution, so the edge would be missing from one graph of the run and present in the other. An outcome mapped to continue or fail starts no pipe under the condition, so it has no edge, and a resolution whose condition node is not in the graph draws none either, since the edge would have no source. The tracer still writes the edge as an edge event at teardown, as it does every derived edge, and the assembler regenerates it rather than reading that event, so it is never doubled. Neither builder reads batch_fanned_out, because a batch's items are already its children. Both builders therefore build the same graph from the same events.

docs.title: TraceContext Propagation
docs.text:
TraceContext is a serializable context that flows through pipe execution:

class TraceContext(BaseModel):
    graph_id: str  # Unique graph identifier
    parent_node_id: str | None  # Parent pipe's node ID
    node_sequence: int  # Counter for generating node IDs
    data_inclusion: DataInclusionConfig  # What data to capture
    run_mode: PipeRunMode  # Live or dry, stated on every trace event
    parent_path: str | None  # Invocation path of the pipe whose children run under this context
    child_segment: str | None  # Segment a controller gives the next pipe it runs
    chain: list[ExecutionAttempt]  # The lineage of the writing execution, then its own {execution, attempt}; required

    def copy_for_child(self, child_node_id: str, *, next_sequence: int, invocation_path: str | None) -> TraceContext:
        """Create context for nested pipe execution, under the child's own invocation path."""
        return TraceContext(
            graph_id=self.graph_id,
            parent_node_id=child_node_id,
            node_sequence=next_sequence,
            data_inclusion=self.data_inclusion,
            run_mode=self.run_mode,
            parent_path=invocation_path,
            child_segment=None,
            chain=list(self.chain),
        )

A controller names the place of each pipe it runs before it runs it: it hands the pipe job_metadata.for_child_at(segment=...), a copy whose trace context carries the segment, and the pipe's start derives its path from the context's parent_path and that segment (TraceContext.invocation_path). A pipe started under a parent path without a segment, or with a segment and no parent path, cannot be placed: TraceContext.invocation_path raises InvocationPathError, a fault of the runtime, never of the method. Tracing never fails a run, so the tracer catches it, traces the pipe with a null path, which leaves every pipe under it unplaceable too, and logs the fault as an error, A pipe was traced without its invocation path, with the pipe's pipe_ref and node_id in its fields. An inactive tracer and the no-op tracer record nothing and derive no path at all. The invariant that every invocation has a path is enforced by the test suite instead: an autouse fixture in tests/conftest.py fails any test during which a tracer logged that fault.

docs.title: Invocation Paths
docs.text:
The hosted progress contract names every invocation of a run by its path (pipelex/system/invocation_path.py): the run's entry pipe's pipe_ref, then one segment per controller level, such as filings.review_filings/step_3/item_2/step_1. A path holds no counter, no run-scoped id and no engine's name, so the same invocation has the same path in every run of the same method, live or dry, on every engine.

Segment Added by Names step_<n> PipeSequence The pipe its step n runs, numbered from 1 as the author wrote the steps, binding steps included. The binding written for a dotted batch_over is no step of the author's, takes no number and has no path branch_<n> PipeParallel The pipe of its branch n, numbered from 1 in declaration order item_<n> PipeBatch Its branch pipe, run for item n of the list: the item at index 0 is item_1 outcome_<key> PipeCondition The pipe of one outcome group: the outcomes that run one pipe, the default included, form one group, named by the first key of the outcome map that runs it, percent-encoded (high risk gives outcome_high%20risk). Outcomes are grouped by the pipe the library resolves each to, however they spell it, so a dependency's pipe written alias->domain.code by one outcome and alias->code by another is one group default PipeCondition The pipe of its default outcome, when no key runs that pipe

A step or a branch that batches runs as the PipeBatch the runtime makes for it, at the step's or the branch's segment, with its items under it. A live condition, which takes one group, and a dry one, which runs the pipe of every group once (PipeCondition.outcome_group_pipes), name each pipe by the same path.

A path is absolute whichever execution emits it. A batch item that runs as an execution of its own receives its item's place with its input: the item's JobMetadata carries the trace context whose parent_path is the batch's path and whose child_segment is item_<n>, so the execution's tracer, opened with received_context, stamps every path under the item's.

docs.title: Executions and Their Attempts
docs.text:
An execution is a part of a run that emits events and that its engine runs, and may run again, as a whole: the run's own workflow, and each batch item a distributed engine runs as a child workflow. In direct mode the whole run is one execution, direct. Each run of an execution is an attempt, numbered from 1.

GraphTracerManager.open_tracer takes the execution as workflow_id, which must be the id the engine keeps across attempts, the attempt as attempt, and, for an execution another one dispatched, the trace context it received as received_context. A received context naming a place hands the new execution the dispatcher's chain as its lineage; the run's own workflow receives a context naming no place, and its lineage is empty. Every event the tracer writes stamps workflow_id, attempt and lineage, and so does every usage event, which takes them from the chain of the trace context it is reported under: ReportingManager.set_event_log takes no workflow id.

TraceContext.chain is therefore required, with no default, as run_mode is: a context that defaulted to the direct mode's chain would write the usage of a durable workflow's second attempt under direct@1, a chain no attempt of that workflow has: no later attempt would supersede it, and the store keys would no longer tell the two attempts' usage apart. A tracer's setup states the chain on the context it returns; a host that builds a context of its own, as one driving the kernel does, states it too, make_direct_chain() in a single process.

A higher attempt of an execution, dispatched under the same attempts, supersedes the earlier one and everything it dispatched, at any depth (pipelex/system/execution_chain.py, current_chain_keys). The assembler builds the graph from current events only, so a retried invocation appears once, at its path, and a lost attempt leaves no failed node behind; the graph's created_at is the timestamp of its earliest current event, so an attempt lost long before its retry does not date it either. A superseded attempt's inference was spent all the same, so its usage still counts in the run's total, as unattributed usage.

The event logs keep every attempt's events: their dedup key is the event's chain, its writer, its kind and its sequence (TraceEvent.store_key), since attempts of one execution number their events from the same start. The chain key reads <execution>@<attempt> for each entry of the chain, percent-encoded and joined by /. The DynamoDB log's sort key is EVENT#<chain digest>#<writer_id>#<sequence>, the chain digest being the SHA-256 hex digest of the chain key and the sequence zero-padded to ten digits: the chain key grows with the lineage and with the length of its workflow ids, while DynamoDB refuses a sort key over 1,024 bytes, so the digest keeps the key one length at any depth, and, being the same for the same chain, lets a replayed write overwrite its own row. The row's chain is read back from its payload, which holds the whole event. A row an earlier version wrote, whose event carries no attempt, lineage or path, is refused with EventLogSchemaMismatchError when it is read, as in every event log, rather than deduplicated against a current row; the schema is the backend's own, and no other writer's is promised to match it. Every event log returns a run's events by one rule, deduplicate_and_order_events (pipelex/tracing/event_log_protocol.py): one event per store key, ordered by chain, then sequence, then writer, whatever order its store holds them in, which for DynamoDB is the order of the digests. The deduplication drops the second write of an event that a replay wrote again, which a log that appends holds twice; the DynamoDB log's key already keeps one row per event.

The NDJSON log writes one file per attempt of each execution and per writer, <pipeline_run_id>/wf_<workflow_id>__c_<chain digest>.ndjson, with __w_<writer_id> before the extension for a writer other than primary, the chain digest being the one the DynamoDB sort key carries. Two attempts of one workflow, or a workflow that a new attempt dispatched again under the same name while its predecessor still drains, may write at once through handles of their own; naming the file by the chain keeps them from appending to one file, where their partial lines could interleave and leave the whole run's log unreadable. The reader reads every .ndjson file of the run's directory.

docs.title: Producer/Consumer Paradigm
docs.text:
Data flow in the graph follows a producer/consumer model:

  • Producers: Nodes that create or output data (stuff). When a pipe outputs a value, it becomes the producer of that data item.
  • Consumers: Nodes that receive or use data as input. When a pipe takes a value as input, it becomes a consumer of that data item.

Each piece of data is identified by a digest (a unique hash). This allows the tracer to track where data originates and where it flows, even when the same value passes through multiple pipes.

Producer Node ──(outputs)──► Stuff (digest: abc123) ──(inputs)──► Consumer Node

This paradigm enables:

  • Automatic DATA edge generation without explicit wiring
  • Visualization of data lineage across the execution graph
  • Debugging by tracing which pipe produced unexpected output

docs.title: A Dry-Run Condition's Output
docs.text:
A stuff usually has one producer. The exception is the output of a PipeCondition in a dry run, which runs every outcome because it cannot know which one a live run would take. Every outcome writes the condition's one slot, so the graph draws that slot as one stuff with a producer per outcome, which is also the shape the static graph builder in mthds-ui draws for the same method.

The condition runs every outcome but the last on a copy of the working memory and run params it received, as PipeParallel runs its branches, so no outcome reads what a sibling wrote. The last outcome is the default outcome's pipe when the default is a pipe, the others running before it in sorted order. It runs on the condition's own memory, so the steps after the condition read its stuff, which is the condition's output digest.

Once every outcome has run, the condition registers a ConditionOutputMerge (pipelex/graph/condition_output_merge.py) through the tracer's register_condition_output_merge, which the event log carries as a ConditionOutputMergeEvent. It names the condition's node, its output digest and the digests the other outcomes minted for the slot. Only a stuff minted inside the condition is merged: an outcome that hands back a stuff it was given keeps its digest, and nothing is merged when the last outcome resolves its slot absent. Both graph builders apply every merge to the finished graph through apply_condition_output_merges, which moves each merged digest onto the condition's, transitively for a condition run as another condition's outcome, across every io item and every edge's stuff digests. The last step of an outcome sequence and the output list of an outcome batch therefore move with their outcome.

Each outcome's io item keeps its own concept and multiplicity, so its node still says what that outcome writes. When the merged outcomes write different concepts or multiplicities, or declare different ones, the merge also carries the condition's declared output concept, a list when the declaration or the invocation's nb_output or multiple_output makes it one. The declarations count because an outcome's stuff can stand for several: an outcome that is itself a condition hands back only its last outcome's stuff, while its declaration covers every one of them. A list is recorded as True, never as an item count, as on every other io item. A condition run as a PipeBatch's branch is given the branch's stuff code, which every outcome mints under, so there is no digest to merge; when its outcomes still write or declare different outputs, the condition records a merge with no merged digest and the typing alone.

The rewrite gives that typing to every io item on the shared stuff whose node is not inside the condition's outcomes, read off the finished graph's CONTAINS edges: the condition's own item, every controller whose output is the condition's, such as a sequence ending on the condition or a batch branch's sequence, and every step reading the stuff. A consumer typing a stuff from the first item naming its digest, which is an enclosing controller's, therefore reads the declaration rather than the concept of whichever outcome ran last. When several typed conditions are merged onto one stuff, an item takes the typing of the outermost one whose outcomes it is not inside, and a node inside another condition's outcomes takes a typing only when it is that typed condition or encloses it: an outer outcome sequence ending on an inner condition carries the inner typing, while the inner condition's sibling outcome keeps its own concept.

An outcome that is a PipeParallel or a PipeBatch writes the shared stuff as a controller, combining its branches or aggregating its items into it, so it is no producer of the stuff. GraphAnalysis still counts it as one of the stuff's writers, so the stuff belongs to the condition all the same.

docs.title: Data Flow Edge Generation
docs.text:
DATA edges are generated at teardown by correlating input/output digests:

def _generate_data_edges(self) -> None:
    for consumer_node_id, node_data in self._nodes.items():
        for input_spec in node_data.input_specs:
            if input_spec.digest is None:
                continue
            producer_node_id = self._stuff_producer_map.get(input_spec.digest)
            if producer_node_id and producer_node_id != consumer_node_id:
                self.add_edge(
                    source_node_id=producer_node_id,
                    target_node_id=consumer_node_id,
                    edge_kind=EdgeKind.DATA,
                    label=input_spec.name,
                )

docs.title: GraphAnalysis
docs.text:
Pre-computed analysis layer that extracts common information for renderers:

analysis = GraphAnalysis.from_graphspec(graph_spec)

# Lookups
node = analysis.nodes_by_id["node_123"]
children = analysis.get_children("controller_node")
is_root = analysis.is_root("node_123")

# Data flow
stuff_info = analysis.get_stuff_info(digest="abc123")
producers = analysis.get_producers(digest="abc123")
consumers = analysis.get_consumers(digest="abc123")
Attribute Purpose nodes_by_id Fast node lookup by ID containment_tree Parent → children mapping child_node_ids All nodes that have parents controller_node_ids Nodes with children root_nodes Top-level nodes stuff_registry Digest → StuffInfo stuff_producers Digest → producer node IDs, more than one for a dry-run condition's output stuff_consumers Digest → consumer node IDs shared_stuff_controllers Digest → the deepest controller containing every writer, for a stuff with several writers: its producers, and the parallel or batch controllers combining or aggregating into it. That controller's output item types the stuff in stuff_registry

docs.title: Mermaidflow
docs.text:
Converts GraphSpec to Mermaid flowchart syntax with controller subgraphs:

from pipelex.graph.mermaidflow.mermaidflow_factory import MermaidflowFactory

mermaidflow = MermaidflowFactory.make_from_graphspec(
    graph_spec,
    graph_config=graph_config,
    direction=FlowchartDirection.TOP_DOWN,
    include_subgraphs=True,
)

print(mermaidflow.mermaid_code)

Output structure:

  • Controllers rendered as subgraphs
  • Operators rendered as rectangles inside subgraphs
  • Stuff nodes (data items) rendered as stadium shapes
  • DATA edges connect producers → stuff → consumers
  • A stuff with several writers is rendered once, inside the deepest controller containing them all, never inside a parallel outcome combining into it, with an edge from each producer

In the standalone viewer (mermaidflow.html), clicking a stuff node opens its JSON content, and an image or PDF output also offers a preview rendered from the URL that JSON carries.

docs.title: ReactFlow HTML
docs.text: ReactFlow HTML is generated directly from GraphSpec — no intermediate ViewSpec layer. The HTML generator embeds GraphSpec as JSON and the client-side JavaScript handles dataflow analysis, layout, and rendering.

docs.title: Event Log Backend
docs.text:
# pipelex.toml (default values)
[runtime.tracing]
is_enabled = true
backend = "ndjson"              # "ndjson" or "dynamodb"

[runtime.tracing.ndjson]
traces_dir = ".pipelex/traces"

[runtime.tracing.dynamodb]
table_name = ""                 # Required when backend = "dynamodb"
region = ""                     # Required when backend = "dynamodb"
retention_days = 30             # Each event's `ttl` is its write time plus this many days (at least 1)

See Event-Log Transport and the Scoped Override for what each backend does with these settings.

docs.title: GraphConfig
docs.text:
# pipelex.toml (default values)
[interpreter.pipeline_execution.graph]

docs.title: IOSpec Data Capture
docs.text:
IOSpec captures input/output data for nodes:

class IOSpec(BaseModel):
    name: str  # Variable name
    concept: str | None  # Concept code
    content_type: str | None  # MIME type
    preview: str | None  # Truncated preview (max 200 chars)
    size: int | None  # Content size
    digest: str | None  # Unique identifier for data flow
    data: str | dict[str, Any] | list[str] | list[dict[str, Any]] | None  # Full serialized content
    multiplicity: bool | int | None  # True for a list, None for a single value
    extra: dict[str, Any]  # Extra markers, e.g. `optional` set on a declared-optional (`?`) output

Every site that records a stuff on a node builds its IOSpec with make_stuff_io_spec (pipelex/graph/stuff_io_spec.py): a pipe's declared inputs at its start, its main output at its end, a lifted pipe's plural companion slots, and a PipeParallel's branch outputs. concept is always the bare concept code, and multiplicity says whether the stuff is a list, in the encoding the pipe registry uses for a stuff spec: true for a variable-length list, a positive integer for a fixed count, null for a single value. A run reads it off the value it holds, so a list is true whatever its length, an empty list from a lifted plural output included, and a batch's item is single while its aggregate is a list. It never writes the item count, which would make a one-item list read as single and an empty one write 0. Because the trace events carry the IOSpec whole, both graph builders show the same marker, and a stuff reads the same on its producer's io item and on its consumers'. The Mermaid renderer labels such a stuff Record[].

Preview Truncation

Previews are automatically truncated to 200 characters. Stack traces are truncated to 2000 characters. Use --graph-full-data to capture complete content.

docs.title: Image Handling in LLM Prompts
docs.text:
This document describes how Pipelex handles images in PipeLLM prompts. The system implements a prompt template-driven inclusion model where images are sent to the LLM if and only if the prompt templates explicitly reference them.

Both prompt (user prompt) and system_prompt support image references using the same syntax.

docs.title: Design Principle
docs.text:
Images are included based on what the prompt template references, not on what the input types contain.

Scenario Images Sent? Input is Image, prompt template uses @image or $image Yes Input is Page with nested images, prompt template uses @page or $page No Input is Page with nested images, prompt template uses {{ page \| with_images }} Yes

This design prevents accidental image leakage and gives prompt template authors explicit control over what visual content reaches the LLM.

Why Prompt Template-Driven?

Sending images to LLMs costs tokens and processing time. Prompt template-driven inclusion ensures you only pay for images you actually need the LLM to see.

docs.title: Three Reference Kinds
docs.text:
The system recognizes three distinct ways images can be referenced in prompt templates:

ImageReferenceKind
├── DIRECT       → Variable is ImageContent itself
├── DIRECT_LIST  → Variable is list[ImageContent] or Image[]
└── NESTED       → Variable is struct with nested images, using | with_images filter

docs.title: DIRECT References
docs.text:
When a prompt template variable directly points to an Image type:

[pipe.describe_photo]
inputs = { photo = "Image" }
prompt = "Describe this photo: @photo"

The image is automatically included. The @photo (or $photo) reference renders as [Image 1] in the prompt text.

docs.title: DIRECT_LIST References
docs.text:
When a prompt template variable points to an Image[] (list of images):

[pipe.analyze_gallery]
inputs = { photos = "Image[]" }
prompt = "Analyze these photos: $photos"

All images in the list are included. The $photos (or @photos) reference renders as: 

[Image 1]
[Image 2]
[Image 3]

docs.title: NESTED References
docs.text:
When a struct contains images but isn't itself an image type, you must explicitly request image extraction:

[pipe.describe_document]
inputs = { doc = "Document" }
prompt = "{{ doc | with_images }}"

Without | with_images, only the text representation is sent. With it, nested images are extracted and included.

docs.title: System Prompt Support
docs.text:
Images can be referenced in both system_prompt and prompt using identical syntax:

[pipe.analyze_with_context]
inputs = { context_image = "Image", query_image = "Image" }
system_prompt = "You are analyzing images. Here is context: $context_image"
prompt = "Now analyze this image: $query_image"

docs.title: Global Numbering
docs.text:
When images appear in both prompts, they share a global sequential numbering:

  1. System prompt images are extracted first - they get lower numbers ([Image 1], [Image 2], etc.)
  2. User prompt images are extracted second - they continue the sequence ([Image 3], [Image 4], etc.)

This ensures consistent numbering across the entire prompt sent to the LLM.

docs.title: Example
docs.text:
[pipe.compare_styles]
inputs = { reference = "Image", subject = "Image" }
system_prompt = "Use this reference image for style comparison: $reference"
prompt = "Analyze the style of this image: $subject"

Results in:

  • System prompt: "Use this reference image for style comparison: [Image 1]"
  • User prompt: "Analyze the style of this image: [Image 2]"

Both images are sent to the LLM in order: [Image 1] (reference), [Image 2] (subject).

docs.title: The | with_images Filter
docs.text: The with_images filter is the key mechanism for extracting images from complex structures.

docs.title: What It Does
docs.text:
1. Walks the structure recursively
  2. Finds all ImageContent instances
  3. Registers each image with a sequential number
  4. Returns the text representation with [Image N] tokens inline

docs.title: Example Output
docs.text:
Given a Page with text and images:

PageContent(
    text_and_images=TextAndImagesContent(text=TextContent(text="Welcome to the guide"), images=[ImageContent(url="...")]),
    page_view=ImageContent(url="..."),
)

The filter produces:

text_and_images: Welcome to the guide
[Image 1]
page_view: [Image 2]

docs.title: When to Use It
docs.text: Structure Without Filter With Filter Page Text only Text + images Document Text only Text + images list[Article] Text only Text + all nested images Custom struct with images Text only Text + images

docs.title: Component Overview
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph FT["FACTORY TIME"]
        direction TB
        BP["PipeLLMBlueprint"]
        TA["TemplateImageAnalyzer"]
        IR["ImageReference[]"]

        BP -->|"template + inputs"| TA
        TA -->|"analyzes"| IR
    end

    subgraph RT["RUNTIME"]
        direction TB
        WM["Working Memory"]
        REG["ImageRegistry"]
        FLT["with_images filter"]
        LP["LLMPrompt"]

        WM -->|"values"| FLT
        FLT -->|"registers"| REG
        REG -->|"images"| LP
    end

    FT -->|"image_references"| RT

docs.title: Factory Time: Prompt Template Analysis
docs.text:
When a PipeLLM is created from a blueprint, the TemplateImageAnalyzer examines both prompt and system_prompt templates. The factory reaches it through analyze_template_file_references (pipelex.pipe_operators.shared.template_file_references), the one analysis PipeLLM, PipeImgGen and PipeJudge share, which also finds the documents a template reads and marks each reference with whether its root input is declared optional:

  1. Parse prompt template AST - Extract all variable references with their filters
  2. Resolve types - Look up each variable's type from input specifications
  3. Determine reference kind - Based on type and filters applied
  4. Pre-compute nested paths - For NESTED references, identify where images live in the structure
# Stored in PipeLLM after analysis
user_image_references = [
    ImageReference(variable_path="page", kind=ImageReferenceKind.NESTED, nested_image_paths=["text_and_images.images", "page_view"])
]
system_image_references = [ImageReference(variable_path="context_image", kind=ImageReferenceKind.DIRECT, nested_image_paths=None)]

docs.title: Runtime: Image Collection
docs.text:
When the prompt is built:

  1. Create registry - Fresh ImageRegistry for this prompt; a reference whose root input is optional and was not given is skipped here, taking no number, so the template's guard renders it out
  2. Extract system prompt images first - Direct and list references from system_prompt are processed first, getting lower numbers
  3. Extract user prompt images second - Direct and list references from prompt continue the numbering sequence
  4. Inject registry into context - Registry available to Jinja2 filters for nested image extraction
  5. Render both templates - with_images filter populates registry during rendering
  6. Collect images - Retrieve all registered images after rendering
  7. Build prompt - Both texts have tokens, images in separate list

docs.title: Data Flow
docs.text:
flowchart TB
    subgraph FT["FACTORY TIME"]
        direction TB
        PT[/"PipeLLM Blueprint"/]
        TA["TemplateImageAnalyzer"]
        IR[("ImageReference[]")]

        PT -->|"prompt + inputs"| TA
        TA -->|"analyzes"| IR
    end

    subgraph RT["RUNTIME"]
        direction TB
        WM[("Working Memory")]
        REG["ImageRegistry"]
        RENDER["with_images filter"]
        LP[/"LLMPrompt"/]

        WM -->|"values"| RENDER
        RENDER -->|"registers"| REG
        REG -->|"images"| LP
    end

    IR -->|"image_references"| RT

Factory Time: The TemplateImageAnalyzer parses both system_prompt and prompt templates, finds variables with image types or the | with_images filter, looks up their types, and pre-computes nested image paths.

Runtime: System prompt images are extracted first, then user prompt images, ensuring global sequential numbering. Values with nested images are passed through the with_images filter, which registers images to the ImageRegistry and returns text with [Image N] tokens. The final LLMPrompt contains both texts and the collected images.

docs.title: Image Registry
docs.text: The ImageRegistry manages image numbering during prompt construction.

docs.title: Key Properties
docs.text:
• 0-based indices, 1-based display - register_image returns a 0-based index; the 1-based [Image N] display number is produced at render time
  • Sequential - Images numbered in order of registration
  • Deduplicated - Same URL gets same index
class ImageRegistry:
    def register_image(self, image: Any) -> int:
        """Register an image and return its 0-based index. Same URL = same index."""
        if image.url in self._image_urls:
            # Find existing index
            for index, existing in enumerate(self._images):
                if existing.url == image.url:
                    return index
        self._images.append(image)
        self._image_urls.add(image.url)
        return len(self._images) - 1

docs.title: Deduplication Example
docs.text:
If the same image appears in multiple places:

# First registration
registry.register_image(img_a)  # Returns 0

# Second registration of same URL
registry.register_image(img_a)  # Returns 0 (not 1)

# Different image
registry.register_image(img_b)  # Returns 1

docs.title: Working with StuffArtefact
docs.text: Values from working memory arrive wrapped in StuffArtefact, a thin delegation adapter that provides template-friendly access to content fields.

docs.title: Template Access
docs.text:
StuffArtefact delegates attribute access to the underlying content:

# In template: {{ page.title }}
# StuffArtefact delegates to: page._stuff.content.title

docs.title: Filter Handling
docs.text:
The with_images filter uses the ImageRenderable protocol to handle StuffArtefact transparently:

# StuffArtefact implements ImageRenderable
if isinstance(value, ImageRenderable):
    return value.render_with_images(registry=registry, text_format=text_format)


# StuffArtefact.render_with_images() delegates to content
def render_with_images(self, *, registry, text_format) -> str:
    return self._stuff.content.render_with_images(registry=registry, text_format=text_format)

ImageRenderable Protocol

The ImageRenderable protocol uses @runtime_checkable to enable isinstance() checks without importing concrete types—avoiding circular imports between the Jinja2 layer and domain layer.

For detailed information on StuffArtefact's delegation pattern and the ImageRenderable protocol, see StuffArtefact & Image Rendering.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text: The system validates image usage at both factory time and runtime:

docs.title: Factory Time
docs.text: Condition Error \| with_images on a type with no nested images (including a direct Image) WithImagesFilterError: "Filter '| with_images' used on variable 'X' but the type has no nested images. Remove the filter or use a type with nested images."

docs.title: Runtime
docs.text:
Condition Error with_images on undefined value "Cannot use with_images filter on undefined value" with_images on non-ImageRenderable type (e.g., string) "The with_images filter received a X which does not implement the ImageRenderable protocol. This filter requires StuffArtefact, StuffContent subclasses, or lists containing such types. Did you accidentally apply another filter first that converted to string?"

The runtime check catches cases where filter chaining converts structured data to a string before with_images runs (e.g., {{ pages | tag | with_images }}).

docs.title: Direct Image
docs.text:
inputs = { photo = "Image" }
prompt = "$photo"

docs.title: Image List
docs.text:
inputs = { gallery = "Image[]" }
prompt = "$gallery"

docs.title: Multiple Image Lists
docs.text:
inputs = { before = "Image[]", after = "Image[]" }
prompt = """
Before: $before

After: $after
"""

docs.title: Nested Images
docs.text:
inputs = { report = "Report" }
prompt = "{{ report | with_images }}"

docs.title: Mixed
docs.text:
inputs = { cover = "Image", pages = "Page[]" }
prompt = """
Cover: $cover

Pages:
{{ pages | with_images }}
"""

Filter Chaining: Order Matters

The with_images filter extracts images from structured data and returns a string with [Image N] tokens. The tag filter wraps its input in tags (... or XML). Order matters when chaining these filters.

What works:

  • ✅ {{ pages | with_images }} - extracts images with tokens
  • ✅ {{ pages | tag }} - formats text output (no images)
  • ✅ {{ pages | with_images | tag }} - extracts images, then wraps result in tags
  • ✅ {{ pages | first | with_images }} - non-terminal filter before with_images is fine

What doesn't work:

  • ❌ {{ pages | tag | with_images }} - tag stringifies first, so with_images receives a string and can't extract images

Rule of thumb: with_images must receive structured data to extract images. Place it before any filter that converts to string (like tag).
