docs.title: Per-node Usage Attribution
docs.text: A run produces two artifacts that describe the same thing from different angles: pipe_output.graph_spec (the shape of the run) and pipe_output.tokens_usages (what it cost). Both are built from one trace-event stream, and every usage event in that stream already names the graph node it belongs to. This page is about the projection that keeps that link — GraphSpec.usage and NodeSpec.usage — and about the three states a usage number can be in, which is the part consumers get wrong.

docs.title: Two projections of one event stream
docs.text:
Every inference call emits a UsageReportEvent carrying node_id (from trace_context.parent_node_id) and the full internal AnyTokensUsage. That single stream is read twice:

  • UsageAggregator (pipelex/tracing/usage_aggregator.py) projects it into a flat list — one record per call, node_id dropped. That list becomes pipe_output.tokens_usages, trimmed to TokensUsageRecord at the client boundary, and feeds the console cost table and the CSV.
  • usage_attribution (pipelex/tracing/usage_attribution.py) projects it into per-node totals — node_id kept, calls folded together. Those totals become NodeSpec.usage and GraphSpec.usage, assembled by GraphSpecAssembler.

The two projections are deliberately separate — tokens_usages is a shipped, extra="forbid" client contract, and a graph is not the place to re-litigate its record shape. What they are not allowed to do is disagree on arithmetic, so both compute every dollar through the same compute_tokens_usage_cost (pipelex/cogt/usage/usage_cost.py) and define a token total the same way AggregatedCosts.total_nb_tokens does.

flowchart TB
    CALL["inference call completes"]
    EVENT["UsageReportEvent<br/>{ node_id, tokens_usage }"]

    subgraph LOG["event log — one stream, ordered by (chain, sequence)"]
        STREAM["PipeStart · PipeEndSuccess · Edge · UsageReport"]
    end

    subgraph ATTRIBUTED["attributed projection"]
        direction TB
        ASSEMBLER["GraphSpecAssembler<br/>node_id kept, calls folded"]
        GRAPH["NodeSpec.usage<br/>GraphSpec.usage"]
    end

    subgraph FLATTENED["flat projection"]
        direction TB
        AGGREGATOR["UsageAggregator<br/>node_id dropped, one record per call"]
        FLAT["PipeOutput.tokens_usages"]
        SINKS["cost table · CSV · API wire"]
    end

    CALL --> EVENT
    EVENT -- "the link exists here" --> STREAM
    STREAM --> ASSEMBLER
    STREAM --> AGGREGATOR
    ASSEMBLER --> GRAPH
    AGGREGATOR --> FLAT
    FLAT --> SINKS

docs.title: When attribution happens, and why it waits
docs.text:
GraphSpecAssembler folds usage events during pass 1, keyed by the node_id the event named — with no node lookup. Resolution against the real node set happens in pass 2. This is not an optimisation: a UsageReportEvent can legitimately be read before the PipeStartEvent of the node it names, because the two can come from different workers and the stream is ordered by (chain, sequence), the chain being the attempts of the executions that wrote the event. "Is this node real?" is only answerable once every event has been seen.

A usage event of a superseded attempt, one a later attempt of its execution or of an execution that dispatched it replaced, names a node the graph does not show, since the graph is built from current events only (see Executions and Their Attempts). Its inference was spent all the same, so the assembler counts it in the run's total, as unattributed usage.

Pass 2 then does three things: resolves each accumulated total onto its node (or into the unattributed bucket), rolls subtrees up the parent_node_id chain, and computes the run total.

docs.title: The three states of a usage number
docs.text:
This is the part that matters for anything rendering a graph. A missing number means one of three things, and they must not be conflated — $0.00 on an unrated node is a lie, and a controller that reports nothing because it was read through the wrong half looks like a bug.

State How it is encoded What a consumer may claim Not collected usage is None nothing — no measurement was taken Ran no inference usage present, inference_calls == 0 nothing (a controller may still report its subtree) Unrated cost is None with inference_calls > 0 that calls were made; no price Partial inference_calls > rated_inference_calls > 0 a price marked as a lower bound: ≥ $0.0043 Rated rated_inference_calls == inference_calls > 0 the price: $0.0043

Unrated is not an edge case: compute_tokens_usage_cost returns None whenever the model carries no rate table, and dry/mock runs hardcode an empty rate table — so every dry-run graph is unrated.

A note on token counts, for anyone rendering them. The counts are faithful to what the run reported, which is not the same as being meaningful to a reader. Two cases to handle before putting a number on screen: a dry run reports one synthetic call per would-be inference with zero tokens (or, under --mock-usage, with invented non-zero tokens — never display those, they measure nothing), and a PipeSearch reports its provider's billing unit in the token field, so a single search shows ~2,000,000 "tokens" for a correct price of $0.005. The cost is the number that survives both; mthds-ui accordingly displays cost only, and only for a real run.

docs.title: The invariants
docs.text:
NodeUsageSpec (pipelex/graph/graphspec.py) states four invariants in its docstring. They are the contract; each has a named test in tests/unit/pipelex/tracing/test_usage_attribution.py.

  1. usage is None is all-or-nothing across a graph. It means no usage was reported anywhere in the run — collection was off, or the run made zero inference calls. As soon as one usage event was seen, every node carries a spec, zeroed where nothing ran. A controller, a lifted pipe and a PipeFunc all get inference_calls=0, never usage=None. So the field never distinguishes "this node was not measured" from "that node was".
  2. cost is None ⟺ rated_inference_calls == 0. Nothing else. "Made no call" and "made only unrated calls" both land here, and inference_calls tells them apart.
  3. inference_calls > rated_inference_calls > 0 means cost is a lower bound, not a total — some of this node's calls carried no rate table. A UI that renders it as a complete figure is silently wrong about money.
  4. total_tokens is input_joined + output, the same definition as AggregatedCosts.total_nb_tokens. It is not the sum of nb_tokens_by_category: input_cached is a subset of input, not additive, so summing the dict double-counts. Never sum the dict; read total_tokens.

docs.title: The model that ran, vs the model that was asked for
docs.text:
A GraphSpec names a model in three places, and only one of them is the outcome:

Rung Where Example Authored choice pipe blueprint llm_choices.for_text $writing-factual (a preset) Requested handle execution_data.resolved_model @default-premium (still an alias) What actually ran NodeUsageSpec.by_model[].inference_model_name claude-4.6-sonnet

execution_data.resolved_model is captured from LLMSetting.model (pipe_llm.py), which is a handle: alias resolution happens later, at inference time. The name overstates what it holds — roughly a third of the nodes in a typical corpus carry an unresolved @alias there. Only by_model survives alias resolution, deck defaults, and any fallback or retry that landed somewhere other than what was requested.

by_model is a list because one node routinely uses more than one model. A PipeLLM's text pass and its object-structuring pass resolve separately (that is what resolved_model_for_object is about), and a retry can land elsewhere again. Collapsing them into "the model" would be wrong in exactly the way a single cost across mixed rated and unrated calls is wrong. An entry is one model type and name, since a handle names one model per model type: a node calling gpt-6-luna as an LLM and as a judgment model has two entries. Entries are ordered most-used first, ties broken by name and then by model type, so a consumer can take by_model[0] as the dominant model without sorting. Per-model cost follows invariant 2: None iff no call to that model was priced.

The same breakdown rolls up: subtree_by_model tells you every model a controller's whole branch used.

docs.title: Own and subtree
docs.text:
Every node carries both halves: its own inference, and its own plus every descendant's (subtree_*). A controller (PipeSequence, PipeBatch, PipeParallel) runs no inference itself, so its own numbers are always zero and only the subtree half says anything — read a controller through its own half and it reports nothing at all. Both tokens and cost roll up, so a consumer that shows either one has the branch figure available without walking the graph.

The rollup is computed once, in the assembler, for the same reason AggregatedCosts computes its totals once: several consumers read the same GraphSpec, and they must not each re-derive it and disagree.

  seq_node       calls 0 (0 rated)   subtree 3 calls (2 rated)  subtree_cost 0.0071  subtree_tokens 4210
    ├── llm_a    calls 1 (1 rated)   cost 0.0043   tokens 2130
    ├── llm_b    calls 1 (1 rated)   cost 0.0028   tokens 2080
    └── func_c   calls 0 (0 rated)   cost None     tokens 0      ← ran, made no inference

func_c has a spec present with cost=None and inference_calls=0 — invariants 1 and 2 together say "collected, ran nothing", never "unknown".

roll_up tolerates two malformed-parentage cases rather than blowing up, because a partial cross-worker event read can produce either: a parent_node_id naming an absent node makes the child a root (never a KeyError), and a cycle in the parentage chain is broken by an in-progress guard and logged (never an infinite walk). The walk is memoized and uses an explicit stack, so it is O(nodes) and independent of the interpreter's recursion limit.

docs.title: The run total and the unattributed bucket
docs.text:
GraphSpec.usage is a GraphUsageSpec with two NodeUsageSpec fields:

  • total — every usage the run reported, attributed or not. This is the graph's comparand for the cost report's own total.
  • unattributed — the part that named no live node: the UNATTRIBUTED_NODE_ID ("unknown") fallback stamped when an inference runs outside any pipe context, or a node_id whose PipeStartEvent never made it into the stream. Surfaced as its own bucket rather than dropped, so the graph's total can never silently disagree with the cost report's.

On a healthy run unattributed is zero. A non-zero one is a real signal worth looking at.

docs.title: Cross-checking against the cost report
docs.text:
The two are computed from the same events but encode "unrated" differently: CostRegistry.aggregate_costs treats an unrated usage as zero-cost, while NodeUsageSpec.cost is None. Comparing them naively manufactures a disagreement. The correct check is:

  • graph.usage.total.cost equals the cost report's total when total.rated_inference_calls == total.inference_calls;
  • when they differ, the graph total is a lower bound and the report's total is the wrong comparand — compare rated_inference_calls against the report's row count instead.

docs.title: The in-process tracer does not carry usage
docs.text:
There are two GraphSpec builders. GraphSpecAssembler produces every consumed spec. The in-process GraphTracer.teardown() output is discarded at all three of its call sites (runner.py, pipe_run.py, dry_run_in_process.py — each reads pipe_output.graph_spec, i.e. the assembler's), and GraphTracerProtocol has no method to receive usage at all.

So usage is deliberately assembler-only. That gap is asserted rather than normalized away: tests/unit/pipelex/tracing/test_assembler_equivalence.py runs a usage-bearing scenario through both builders, asserts they stay structurally equivalent, and asserts the divergence explicitly (assembler populated, tracer None). If someone later plumbs usage into the tracer, that test fails and tells them to delete the assertion — which is what a test documenting an intentional gap should do.

docs.title: PipeFunc Requirements
docs.text: A method declares the Python packages its own Python imports in a requirements.txt at the root of its method tree, under the rules of the MTHDS standard: each line is blank, a comment, or exactly one PEP 508 requirement. The author's view of the file is in Method Trees. This page is about where Pipelex checks it and how a deployment tells Pipelex what its PipeFunc sandbox holds.

docs.title: What is checked, and when
docs.text:
A method tree is checked when it lies on this host's disk, holds a requirements.txt at its root, and holds a .py file anywhere in it. Python is the proxy for "has code that could import a package" rather than "has a PipeFunc pipe", because the check reads the tree's listing and never its bundles: a load runs it before it parses any of them, and the API server, which receives a method as a tree holding its bundles and its Python together, sent in files or bundle_b64 or fetched by method_ref, writes the tree out and judges it before loading anything (see below). Python that no step names can import a package too, such as a module a step's function imports, or, in the direct mode, a module defining a concept's structure class.

The check is pipelex/libraries/method_requirements.py, and a load runs it at three places, each before any Python of the tree is imported, or scanned for structure classes on a sandbox-hosted deployment, and before any of its pipes is built. A load never imports a PipeFunc's module anyway: the step imports its function's module by its import path when it first binds it, in a validation's dry run or its first run, which comes after the load and its check, and the only Python a direct-mode load imports, the modules defining a concept's structure class, is imported after the check too.

  • LibraryManager.load_libraries checks every tree of its library directories, and the tree of each bundle file it is handed, once all of them are listed.
  • LibraryManager.load_from_blueprints checks the tree of every bundle read from this host's disk, on every load, taking as judged only a tree the run's listing holds as met (below): a blueprint an earlier load placed in its tree is judged again when that load's listing was another, and a refused one always is.
  • A dependency package, one a bundle calls by its address, is checked as soon as its tree is listed, before any of its bundles loads. The run's listing lists the package's tree once and keeps its verdict as it keeps a method's, so a package loaded again in the run, by another load or another bundle calling it, is neither listed nor judged again.

Each tree is judged once per run. The listing a run reads its method trees through, a MethodTreeListing (pipelex/libraries/method_tree_listing.py), keeps each tree a check of the run found met, by its directory and its digest, with what the verdict was judged against: the PipeFunc execution mode and the plugin factory stating its packages (PipeFuncEnvironmentSource in pipelex/libraries/package_environments.py). A later check of the same run against the same mode and factory takes the verdict as given: load_from_blueprints does not judge again a tree load_libraries just judged, and a load does not judge again a tree the API server's check of the request found met. Two loads of the run judging one tree at the same moment, in two threads of the method-load pool, judge it once, the second waiting for the first and taking its verdict (MethodTreeListing.judge_requirements_once). A check against another mode or another factory judges the tree again, a refused tree is never kept, so a check that comes after a refusal judges it again, and a load handed no listing makes one of its own, shared by its steps. The verdict does not depend on whether a refusal may name host paths, which changes only its wording, so a server's check and the load after it share it. It lasts one run, so a factory whose answer takes time keeps its own cache across runs, by the requirements' texts.

The requirements.txt judged is the one the run listed. The check reads the file against the hash its tree's listing recorded, so a file edited, replaced or removed since the listing is refused with method.package_invalid, reason tree_changed, rather than judged in place of the file the run's digest names (see Method trees).

A load never runs on the event loop. It is blocking work: it lists and hashes the method's files, asks the package-offer factory to judge its requirements, reads the methods installed on this host and may fetch a package a bundle calls by its address. So every load Pipelex reaches from asynchronous code, a run's (acquire_library_async in pipelex/pipeline/execution_seams.py), a validation's (validate_bundle) and those of the commands that run a loop, runs in a worker thread of the method-load pool through run_method_load (pipelex/libraries/method_load_threads.py), the reading and parsing of the bundles it loads included. The thread runs in a copy of its caller's context, so it reads the current library and every other context variable its caller set, and what it sets stays in its copy. When its caller is cancelled, the shutdown of asyncio.run included, a load no thread has taken yet is withdrawn and never runs, and a running one is waited for until it ends before the cancellation goes through, since a thread cannot be interrupted, so a library is torn down only when nothing still loads into it.

The method-load pool is bounded. At most METHOD_LOAD_MAX_THREADS loads, four, run at once in a process, together with the blocking work around them, such as the API server writing a request's tree to disk and judging its requirements. A load asked for while every thread is busy waits for one, its caller awaiting on the event loop without blocking it. The pool is its own rather than asyncio's default executor, so slow loads, each of which can hold its thread for seconds while a package is fetched or a sandbox resolves requirements, never take the threads every other blocking call of the process borrows, such as a DNS lookup. Loads running in parallel import the modules defining their structure classes under one lock, which their class discovery also holds, so no load takes another's module half executed.

A requirement whose marker is false in the environment is not needed there and is skipped. One is met when the environment holds a distribution of its name, compared normalized, at a version its specifier contains, pre-releases included, and when, for each extra it names, the requirements the distribution's metadata declares under that extra are met in turn. A marker that cannot be evaluated, such as one comparing as versions a value that is not one (which releases of packaging before 22 refuse), refuses its requirement rather than the load.

docs.title: The environment the check reads
docs.text:
resolve_pipe_func_package_environment in pipelex/libraries/package_environments.py picks the environment from interpreter.pipe_func.execution_mode, for one tree's requirements at a time:

Execution mode Environment What it reads direct InterpreterPackageEnvironment The distributions installed in the interpreter Pipelex runs in, through importlib.metadata, and this interpreter's own marker environment, whatever the requirements. Extras are followed through each distribution's Requires-Dist. any other mode OfferedPackageEnvironment The package set the plugin providing the mode states its sandbox offers for the tree's requirements, and nothing else: a fixed package set, or an environment the plugin builds for those requirements. A marker variable the offer does not state cannot be judged, and a requirement with extras cannot be followed, so both are refused rather than judged against this process's own values. The plugin may instead refuse the requirements with its own reason, when no environment it can build holds them, and the method is then refused with that reason.

Each tree declaring requirements is judged against the environment resolved for its own requirements, so when one check judges several trees, such as the library directories of one load, each gets the offer stated for it and never another tree's.

In the direct mode, a method's Python is imported into the process that loads it, when its steps first bind their functions, and that is the process the check judges. A distributed orchestrator, such as our Temporal plugin, never carries a method's Python to its worker: the library crate names the step's method tree by its digest, and in a sandbox mode the call's files are read through the method file store by whoever runs it, for the sandbox to import them, never this process. A worker in the direct mode therefore runs only the functions its own deployment installed, whose packages are that deployment's to install, and the API server refuses a caller's Python outright unless it is sandbox-hosted (a 501 pipelex.deployment.custom_code_requires_sandbox). So no worker needs to repeat the check.

docs.title: How a refusal names the method
docs.text:
The file is always named by its path in the method's tree, requirements.txt, on every item of a refusal. Paths on the host, the method's root and this interpreter's executable, are named only where the refusal may name them:

  • A check inside a load names them, since its refusal belongs either to the caller's own disk, as on a local run, or to the host, around a server's own library directories, where reporting_host_library_tree_faults turns it into the host's fault and withholds it from the caller. Locally, the refusal therefore names the method's folder, each requirement and why, and the uv pip install --python <this interpreter> command that installs them.
  • A dependency package is named by its address, as its bundles are, and its file by <address>/requirements.txt, never by the directory it was installed or fetched into.
  • A server checking a caller's method it holds in a directory of its own names no path on the host at all (ensure_served_method_requirements_met): the method is "the method", the interpreter is "the Python interpreter Pipelex runs in", and the install command names no interpreter path.

docs.title: A host's own library directories
docs.text: A server loads its own library directories (PIPELEXPATH, the instance defaults, installed libraries) beside a caller's bundles. A method of those directories whose requirements are not met is the deployment's fault, not the caller's: around such a load, reporting_host_library_tree_faults turns the refusal into a HostLibraryRequirementsError, carrying pipelex.config.invalid and answered with a 500 whose message, naming paths on the host, rides only the operator view's diagnostics, as it turns a tree it cannot list into a HostLibraryTreeError. Any other refusal of such a method while it loads becomes a HostLibraryLoadRefusalError, carrying pipelex.config.invalid too (see Library Configuration).

docs.title: Where the check runs on a sandbox-hosted deployment
docs.text:
On the runner first, and never in the sandbox. The runner is the process that holds the method's files, and the place a refusal reaches the caller before anything is dispatched. It writes a request's method tree into a directory of its own and judges the caller's method there first, before any library opens or any run is registered, through ensure_served_method_requirements_met, run off the event loop since it lists and hashes the method's files. The directory holds the caller's method, so the check runs inside the same translation as the load of that directory, translate_to_validate_bundle_error (pipelex/pipeline/validate_bundle_translation.py), and its refusal is the problem a local load of the method raises: a method.invalid whose errors hold one item per refused line, each under its own code and located at requirements.txt and the line. It lists the files through a MethodTreeListing (pipelex/libraries/method_tree_listing.py) it hands to the run or the validation serving the request, which loads the trees from it, so a request lists and hashes the method's files once:

  • A run (/execute, /start) with a files or bundle_b64 bundle, or by method_ref, is refused there with a 422 method.invalid, before the method's files load and before any dispatch: a requirement the sandbox does not meet is a method.dependency_missing item on its line, a line the standard refuses a method.package_invalid item on its line, and the deployment's own refusal of the requirements a method.dependency_missing item on the file alone.
  • A validation of a method tree (/validate), sent in files or fetched by method_ref, is judged there too, whether its validator runs in the runner's process or on a worker it is dispatched to, a Temporal worker for instance: ApiRunner.validate_verdict returns the same refusal as the invalid verdict, with the same items a run of the method is refused with, before the validator is reached. Inline mthds_contents carry no Python and are not checked.
  • A directory of the request that cannot be listed stays the host's fault, a 500 HostLibraryTreeError carrying pipelex.config.invalid, as the load reports it.
  • The worker running a run loads the library crate the runner built, which names each step's method tree by its digest and carries none of the tree's files, its Python and its requirements.txt included, so loading it checks nothing. A PipeFunc call's files are read on the worker, through the method file store its host installs (HubSlot.METHOD_FILE_STORE), and handed to the sandbox, which loads the same crate and checks nothing either.
  • A worker a method tree's validation is dispatched to receives the method's trees rather than a crate (BundleValidatorProtocol) and loads them, so it judges the requirements again, in its own process and through its own listing, against the package set the plugins of its own process state for the mode. Its deployment therefore registers the same offer as the runner's: a worker stating none refuses every method declaring requirements with PipeFuncPackageSetUnstatedError.

docs.title: The seam: stating the sandbox's packages
docs.text:
Pipelex cannot read a sandbox it never runs in, and it must not depend on the deployment that provides one, so the plugin providing an execution mode's executor states that mode's packages through its registrar, keyed by the same mode token. The plugin is asked for one method's requirements at a time, so a mode whose sandbox is not one fixed package set, such as one building an environment for each method, states the environment it would run that method in:

from pipelex.libraries.method_requirements import requirements_needed_in
from pipelex.plugins.pipe_func_package_offer_registry import PipeFuncPackageOffer, PipeFuncPackageOfferRequest, PipeFuncPackageRefusal


def _sandbox_package_offer(request: PipeFuncPackageOfferRequest) -> PipeFuncPackageOffer | PipeFuncPackageRefusal | None:
    base = read_my_sandbox_package_set()  # the plugin's own reading of its image's lock, cached
    if base is None:
        return None
    # Only what the sandbox needs: a requirement whose marker is false in its interpreter is neither built nor refused.
    needed = requirements_needed_in(requirements=request.requirements, marker_environment=base.marker_environment)
    environment = environment_for(needed)  # resolved over the base, cached by the requirements' texts
    if environment.unresolvable:
        return PipeFuncPackageRefusal(environment="the Example sandbox", reason=environment.explanation)
    return PipeFuncPackageOffer(
        environment=f"the Example sandbox image '{environment.image}'",
        distributions={package.name: package.version for package in environment.packages},
        marker_environment=base.marker_environment,
    )


class ExampleSandboxPlugin:
    def register(self, registrar: PluginRegistrar) -> None:
        registrar.add_pipe_func_executor(mode="example", factory=_make_executor)
        registrar.add_pipe_func_package_offer(mode="example", factory=_sandbox_package_offer)

A mode with one fixed package set ignores the requirements and answers its package set whatever they are.

  • The request, PipeFuncPackageOfferRequest (pipelex/plugins/pipe_func_package_offer_registry.py), carries the PipeFuncConfig and requirements, every requirement the method's requirements.txt declares, in the file's order, each a RequirementLine (pipelex/core/method_trees/requirements_file.py: its line number, its text as written and the parsed PEP 508 requirement). A plugin judging them against a package set of its own uses Pipelex's judgment, unmet_requirements with an OfferedPackageEnvironment, so it sets aside exactly what the check would find met.
  • The markers are the factory's to evaluate. The requirements arrive with their markers unevaluated, since Pipelex cannot evaluate a marker before it knows the environment the mode would run the method in. A requirement whose marker is false in that environment is not needed there, and the check skips it, so the factory evaluates the markers against the marker environment of the place it would offer, builds nothing for a requirement the place does not need, and never refuses for one: a refusal rests only on requirements whose markers hold there. requirements_needed_in (pipelex/libraries/method_requirements.py) picks them out as the check would, keeping a requirement whose marker reads a variable the marker environment does not state, or cannot be evaluated, which the check refuses rather than skips.
  • PipeFuncPackageOffer is closed, frozen plain data: environment, the place as a refusal names it to the method's author; distributions, each distribution's name with its exact installed version, the names compared normalized; and marker_environment, the PEP 508 marker values of the sandbox's interpreter. A variable left out of marker_environment, such as python_full_version when the image pins only its minor version, makes every requirement whose marker reads it refused. Pipelex judges every requirement against the offer, one built for them included, so an offer that does not meet them refuses the method as a fixed package set would, naming each requirement.
  • PipeFuncPackageRefusal is the answer when no environment of the mode can hold the requirements the place needs, such as a version conflicting with a package the sandbox's base pins, or a package with no wheel for the sandbox: environment, the place as the refusal names it, and reason, the plugin's own words, such as its resolver's explanation. The method is refused with MethodRequirementsNotMetError, a fault of the method's carrying method.dependency_missing, whose message, "The method needs Python packages that the Example sandbox cannot offer, as its requirements.txt declares: …", carries the reason, with one item on the file and no line, since the reason is about the requirements together. The reason reaches the method's author, a server's caller included, so it names no path on the host.
  • The factory is synchronous and never called on a thread running an event loop, and caching by the requirements is the plugin's job. The check runs inside the library load, which is synchronous, and every load Pipelex reaches from asynchronous code runs in a worker thread of the method-load pool, as the API server's check of a served method does, while a synchronous caller, such as a command loading a method before it starts a loop, calls it on its own thread, which runs none. So a factory may block for as long as its work takes, and it must not use an event loop of its caller's, since none runs on its thread and the one its caller's code runs on, if any, belongs to another thread. Pipelex enforces the rule: a factory about to be called on a thread running an event loop is not called, and the load fails with PipelexUnexpectedError, so a host that calls a load itself from asynchronous code, such as a worker's activity loading a library directly, moves it off the loop the same way, with run_method_load. An asynchronous factory would buy nothing short of making every load asynchronous, so the seam stays synchronous. Pipelex calls the factory for each tree declaring requirements the first time a check of a run judges it, never at registration, and keeps the tree's verdict for the rest of the run only when the tree meets its requirements: a load asks once per tree, however many of its steps judge the tree, and on the API server the check of a served method asks for the request, the load after it asking nothing. Pipelex keeps no answer across runs, so the next run, or the next request, asks again for the same requirements. A factory whose answer takes time, such as one resolving the requirements with uv, which takes seconds the first time, bounds the work with a timeout of its own and caches its answers by the requirements' texts, so only a process's first check of a requirement set pays for it.
  • A fault of the plugin's own is not a refusal. A resolver the plugin cannot reach, or one outlasting its timeout, says nothing about the method: the factory raises it as an error of the plugin's, which Pipelex lets through, rather than answering a PipeFuncPackageRefusal, which would blame the method's author.
  • It fails closed. A mode with no registered offer, or whose factory answers None, meets no requirement: a method declaring one is refused with PipeFuncPackageSetUnstatedError, a fault of the deployment carrying runtime.misconfigured, whose message only the operator view carries, rather than loading and failing inside the sandbox at its first import. Its message says which of the two happened: no plugin registers an offer for the mode, or the registered one could not state the packages, whose remedy is in the plugin's configuration. A method declaring none still loads.
  • It is interpreter-layer, like add_pipe_func_executor: a plugin published under pipelex.plugins.kernel that calls it is refused with PluginLayerViolationError. A second plugin stating the same mode is refused with DuplicatePipeFuncPackageOfferError, naming both.

Pipelex.setup builds the PipeFuncPackageOfferRegistry from the registrar beside the PipeFuncExecutorRegistry and puts it on the InterpreterHub (get_pipe_func_package_offer_registry).

docs.title: What our Daytona plugin supplies
docs.text: For the hosted API, the Daytona sandbox plugin states the package set of the Daytona sandbox snapshot it boots, the lock its snapshot image is built from: the snapshot's distributions and versions, and the marker environment of its base image. The runner, which checks a method before dispatching anything, must resolve the same snapshot name the worker's sandboxes boot from, since the worker is the process that creates them; a runner that cannot resolve it answers None and refuses every method declaring requirements. A method needing packages the base snapshot lacks runs in an environment the plugin builds for its requirements when a PipeFunc call provisions its box, and since the factory receives the requirements, the plugin can state that environment when the method loads, or refuse the requirements with its resolver's explanation.

docs.title: Errors
docs.text:
Error Code When MethodRequirementsFileError method.package_invalid The file holds a line the standard refuses, naming each, or is not UTF-8 text. MethodRequirementsNotMetError method.dependency_missing The environment does not meet a requirement, naming each and why, or the deployment refuses the requirements with its own reason, no environment it can build holding them. For a requirement not met, its name is the distribution that fails the requirement: the one required, or one an extra of it needs, with the reason not_found when it is missing and no_matching_version when the version held is one the requirement refuses. HostLibraryRequirementsError pipelex.config.invalid A method of a host's own library directories, loaded beside a caller's bundles, is refused for its requirements. PipeFuncPackageSetUnstatedError runtime.misconfigured A sandbox-hosted deployment states no package set for its execution mode.

The first two are LibraryLoadingErrors carrying one blueprint validation item per line, whose source is the file's path in the tree and whose line is the line's number, so a validation reports them as an invalid verdict located on the line, and a run, locally or on the API server, as the method.invalid problem carrying the same items, each under the error's code. They are deliberately not MethodTreeLoadErrors, which a server reports as its own fault around the library directories it loads.

docs.title: Per-Pipe IO Contracts
docs.text:
Every valid validate report carries a pipe_io_contracts map: for each pipe, the typed contract of what it takes in and what it produces. It sits beside the input-form descriptor on the same report, and the two are keyed identically — by the namespaced pipe_ref (domain.code) — over exactly the same set of pipes, PipeSignature placeholders included.

Reach for pipe_io_contracts when you need the schema and the declared contract; reach for input_form when you are building a form and want field kinds, defaults, and choices without reading schemas.

docs.title: Where it lives
docs.text:
• mthds.protocol.pipe_io_contracts — the wire models (PipeInputContract, PipeOutputContract, PipeIOContract, IOMultiplicity, PresenceMarker), declared by the MTHDS standard's Python client and mirroring its pipe-io-contracts page. Pipelex does not declare a second copy of them.
  • pipelex/pipeline/pipe_io_contracts.py — the one public derivation, build_pipe_io_contracts(pipes), which imports and re-exports those models. Because it constructs the standard's own closed shapes, a projection that drifted from the standard fails at derivation rather than on the wire.
  • PipelexValidationReport.pipe_io_contracts (pipelex/pipeline/validation_report.py) — where the artifact travels.
  • pipelex/pipeline/validate_in_process.py — the in-process assembly derives it inside the validation library's window, right beside build_input_form. Iterating the same loaded pipes is what makes the two key sets equal by construction.

docs.title: What an entry carries
docs.text:
Each pipe gets an inputs map and one output.

An input entry carries the concept_ref, the JSON Schema of its content (json_schema), and two facts about the slot as declared:

  • presence — the authored marker, verbatim: plain, optional (?, the caller may omit it and the pipe handles absence itself), or force (!, must be provided, and the author asserted so). plain and force are both required; the distinction is the assertion, which lint and graph surfaces read.
  • multiplicity — single, variable (Concept[], unbounded), or fixed (Concept[N]), with item_count carrying the exact N on the fixed arm and null otherwise. Concept[1] is single: no list framing.

An output entry carries concept_ref, the same multiplicity / item_count pair, and a two-valued optional — ! is rejected on outputs, so there is nothing three-valued to report. It carries no json_schema: the schema render runs per input only. A consumer that wants the output's payload shape gets it from build output --format schema, not from this contract.

docs.title: Where the concept identity sits on the schema
docs.text:
The JSON Schema on an input names its concept: title is the concept_ref, description the concept's authored description. On a single slot those sit at the top level; on variable and fixed slots the schema is an array wrap that keeps them on items, and a fixed count adds minItems/maxItems on the wrap itself. A variable list carries no bounds.

{
  "type": "array",
  "items": { "type": "object", "title": "my_domain.Gadget", "description": "…", "properties": { "…": "…" } },
  "minItems": 2,
  "maxItems": 2
}

docs.title: The one concept with no structure class: native.Anything
docs.text:
native.Anything is the only concept that declares no structure class, so its input schema cannot come from a pydantic render. (That is a different question from the three natives which declare no pinned structure — Dynamic, Anything, Composite — and therefore render as unknown in the input-form descriptor.) It publishes the identity annotations every rendered input schema carries and one constraint — {"title": "native.Anything", "description": "…", "not": {"type": ["array", "null"]}}. An Anything value is any JSON value but an array or null: a list is the multiplicity's to express, as Anything[], and null is never an input. Multiplicity wraps exactly as above: Anything[] is an array of that schema, so every item carries the same exclusion, and a fixed count adds the bounds.

The schema and the input shaper agree on what a value may be: a string, a number, a boolean or an object at an Anything slot is shaped into its natural content (text, number, yes/no, JSON object) under the native.Anything concept, and an array or null at a single slot is refused, as the schema says. The two differ in two places the schema does not state: it wraps a single bare value sent to an Anything[] input into a one-item list, and it refuses an Anything[] item keyed exactly concept and content, which reads as an envelope.

docs.title: Which surfaces carry it
docs.text: The protocol validate operation carries pipe_io_contracts on its report. The Agent CLI does not: pipelex-agent validate emits the verdict, pending_signatures, is_runnable, and its own advisory warnings array, and stops there — the typed contracts are not part of its envelope.

docs.title: Seeing it
docs.text: pipelex-dev trace-input-semantics captures the contracts as hop5_pipe_io_contracts.json beside hop5_input_form.json, so an authored fact can be checked on both projections at once — see Tracing Input Semantics. The emitted shapes are pinned by tests/integration/pipelex/pipeline/test_pipe_io_contracts.py.

  • Understanding Optionality — the markers behind presence
  • Understanding Multiplicity — the bracket notation behind multiplicity

docs.title: Pipe Routing & Execution
docs.text: Pipelex runs pipes either direct (single-process) or distributed on a host runtime. Both share the same pipe definitions, library loading, and controller logic. The key difference is where the pipe runs and how the PipeJob travels to get there. The distributed host runtime is a durable backend — Temporal-backed execution or a Mistral Workflows integration — delivered through the Pipelex platform (see Distributed Execution). Both reach pipe execution through the same framework-agnostic runtime bridge.

docs.title: Terminology
docs.text:
Term Meaning Direct execution All pipes run in the same Python process. Library, class registry, and pipe resolution are shared in-memory. Distributed execution PipeJob is serialized and sent to a remote worker — a Pipelex Temporal worker, or a Mistral Workflows activity. The worker is a separate process (potentially on a different machine).

The runtime bridge

Both distributed paths reach pipe execution through the framework-agnostic runtime bridge. The open pipelex/runtime_bridge/ keeps the boot, serialization, mode/delivery, and worker-side hydration (primitives/hydration.py) pieces; the cross-process dispatch primitives — classifying controller pipes as child workflows and leaf operators as activities (pipe_classification), flushing trace events (trace_flush), and delivering results (delivery) — were extracted out of open core, and both commercial host-runtime plugins get them from the closed side. Graph and token-usage assembly is not a bridge primitive — it lives in pipelex/pipe_run/tracing_assembly.py and runs the same way for local and distributed runs.

docs.title: Design Principle
docs.text:
Every pipe execution — regardless of mode — follows the same pattern:

  1. Setup: pipeline_run_setup() loads the library, resolves the pipe, initializes working memory, and creates a PipeJob
  2. Route: A router (PipeRouter for direct mode, or the booted orchestrator's distributed router) receives the PipeJob and dispatches it
  3. Execute: The pipe's run_pipe() method runs, potentially resolving and executing child pipes

The PipeJob is the universal unit of execution. It carries everything needed to run a single pipe.

docs.title: The PipeJob Model
docs.text:
PipeJob encapsulates all information needed to execute a pipe.

Field Type Purpose pipe PipeAbstract The resolved pipe object (concrete operator or controller) working_memory WorkingMemory \| None Runtime data store — typed Stuff objects keyed by variable name working_memory_raw dict \| None Raw JSON dict of WorkingMemory for deferred hydration (Temporal only) pipe_run_params PipeRunParams Execution config: run mode (LIVE/DRY), output multiplicity, pipe stack for cycle detection job_metadata JobMetadata Pipeline run ID, user ID, OTel tracing context, graph tracing context output_name str \| None Override for the output variable name library_crate LibraryCrate \| None Serializable library snapshot for distributed execution

PipeJob is created by pipeline_run_setup(), which handles library loading, pipe resolution, working memory initialization, and telemetry setup. For distributed dispatch, a transport-prep step outside open core moves working_memory to working_memory_raw (deferred hydration) and ensures the crate is attached.

The setup registers the run under its pipeline_run_id, opens its library and, when tracing is on, its graph tracer. A host that sets a run up and then cannot hand it over, such as a dispatch to an orchestrator that fails, calls release_run_setup() with the job, the library and the caller's current library as the setup found it, which releases all three, so the same pipeline_run_id can be submitted again.

Build PipeRunParams through its factory

PipeRunParamsFactory.make_run_params() is the single writer of the fields that carry a run-scoped invariant: run_mode, pipe_stack_limit and batch_max_concurrency. None of the three has a default — for each, a silently-defaulted value would point at the dangerous direction (real spend, an unbounded pipe stack, a fan-out that launches every branch at once), and for batch_max_concurrency the would-be default None is also the resolved value of an authored max_concurrency = "unbounded", so "never written" and "authored unbounded" would be indistinguishable. Constructing PipeRunParams by hand and omitting any of them raises a ValidationError — at the constructor and at the wire boundary alike.

docs.title: Library Loading
docs.text:
Before a pipe can execute, the library must be loaded. The library contains:

  • Pipes — all pipe definitions (operators and controllers), resolved by code via get_required_pipe()
  • Concepts — semantic type definitions that determine what data a Stuff object holds
  • Domains — namespaces that group related pipes and concepts

docs.title: Base vs Custom Libraries
docs.text:
• Base libraries are loaded from directories listed in PIPELEXPATH. They contain shared pipe/concept definitions available to all executions.
  • Custom bundles are per-request mthds_content strings. Each API call can bring its own definitions.

docs.title: Dynamic Class Generation
docs.text:
When a .mthds file declares a concept like RawText = "Raw input text...", the library loading process:

  1. ConceptFactory._handle_basic_blueprint() detects the concept declaration
  2. StructureGenerator.generate_from_structure_blueprint() dynamically creates a Python class (e.g., RawText inheriting from TextContent)
  3. The class is registered with the active ClassRegistry (accessed via hub.get_class_registry()) so it can be serialized/deserialized

These dynamically-generated classes become the content type of Stuff objects in WorkingMemory.

Why Dynamic Classes Matter

When WorkingMemory crosses to a Temporal worker, dump_for_transport() stamps content with pipelex-private __pipelex_class__ / __pipelex_module__ markers instead of Kajson's __class__ / __module__ — deliberately keeping Kajson's universal decoder out of the loop at the data-converter boundary. Pipelex's hydrator resolves those markers against the per-workflow ClassRegistry, the only place these dynamic concept classes are registered.

docs.title: Direct Execution
docs.text: In direct execution, everything runs in a single Python process. This is the default mode when no orchestrator plugin is booted.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
pipeline_run_setup()
  ├── Load library (library_manager singleton)
  ├── Generate dynamic concept classes
  ├── Register classes with Kajson
  ├── Resolve pipe via get_required_pipe(pipe_code)
  ├── Initialize WorkingMemory from inputs
  └── Return PipeJob

PipeRouter.run(pipe_job)
  ├── Notify observers (before)
  ├── _run_pipe_job(pipe_job)
  │   └── pipe_job.pipe.run_pipe(...)     ← delegates directly to the pipe
  │       ├── Concrete pipe: execute operator logic (LLM call, template, etc.)
  │       └── Controller: resolve child pipes via get_required_pipe(),
  │           then recursively call child.run_pipe()
  ├── Notify observers (after)
  └── Return PipeOutput

docs.title: Router Selection
docs.text:
The router is selected during Pipelex.setup() by resolving the hub's PIPE_ROUTER slot. A boot-orchestrator plugin (e.g. our closed Temporal plugin) claims that slot in its register() when boot_orchestrator names it; otherwise the default in-process router is used:

# A boot-orchestrator plugin swaps in its distributed router when
# boot_orchestrator == its own name; otherwise this default runs.
effective_pipe_router = self._resolve_hub_slot(
    slot=HubSlot.PIPE_ROUTER,
    default=lambda: PipeRouter(observer=multi_observer),  # Direct, in-process
)

docs.title: How PipeRouter Works
docs.text:
PipeRouter implements PipeRouterProtocol with a minimal _run_pipe_job():

async def _run_pipe_job(self, pipe_job: PipeJob) -> PipeOutput:
    return await pipe_job.pipe.run_pipe(
        job_metadata=pipe_job.job_metadata,
        working_memory=pipe_job.get_working_memory(),
        output_name=pipe_job.output_name,
        pipe_run_params=pipe_job.pipe_run_params,
        library_crate=pipe_job.library_crate,
    )

The router does not route by pipe type — it delegates to the pipe itself. Controllers handle their own orchestration internally.

docs.title: The batch-branch hook
docs.text:
PipeRouterProtocol carries one more entry point beside run:

async def run_batch_branch(self, pipe_job: PipeJob) -> PipeOutput:
    return await self.run(pipe_job)

PipeBatch calls it instead of run for each per-item fan-out dispatch. That is the only place in the pipe tree where the dispatch carries semantics its PipeJob cannot express: a branch job holds the branch pipe and the item's memory, which is byte-for-byte the shape of any other dispatch. The hook is how a router learns "this one is a fan-out branch".

The default body IS the behavior for in-process routers — a branch is just a run, so PipeRouter deliberately does not override it and nothing about direct execution changed. A distributed router may override it to give each branch its own isolation (own retry, own history partition) while every other dispatch it receives runs inline. Because the default delegates to run and not to _run_pipe_job, batch branches still pass through the observer hooks.

docs.title: Pipe Controllers
docs.text:
Controllers are pipes that orchestrate the execution of other pipes. They resolve child pipes at runtime via get_required_pipe() from the library.

Controller Behavior PipeSequence Executes sequential_sub_pipes one after another. Each step receives working memory with outputs from previous steps. PipeBatch Iterates over a ListContent input. For each item, loads branch_pipe and executes it with a deep copy of working memory. Items run concurrently via asyncio. PipeCondition Evaluates a Jinja2 expression against working memory, maps the result via outcome_map to a pipe code, and executes that pipe. PipeParallel Loads multiple child pipes and executes them concurrently, each with its own working memory copy.

All controllers follow the same pattern:

  1. Call get_required_pipe(child_pipe_code) to resolve the child pipe from the library
  2. Route through get_pipe_router().run(PipeJob(...)) — the hub auto-selects the right router. PipeBatch is the one exception: its per-item branch dispatches go through run_batch_branch instead, so a distributed router can isolate them.
  3. Aggregate results into working memory or output

docs.title: Auto-Switching Router
docs.text:
The hub (get_pipe_router()) returns the router for whichever orchestrator the process is booted under:

  • Direct execution: the in-process PipeRouter — child pipes run in the same process.
  • Distributed execution: the booted host-runtime orchestrator's router, which has claimed the hub's PIPE_ROUTER slot. That router auto-detects whether it is dispatching from the submitter (start a unit of durable work) or from inside a running one (continue within it, or spawn a nested unit).

How much of a controller tree a distributed backend spreads across separate durable units is that backend's call, not core's — core's contract is only that every dispatch reaches the router, and that batch branches are labelled as such via run_batch_branch. See the backend's own documentation for the topology it chooses.

Library Dependency

Controllers depend on the library being loaded in the current process. get_required_pipe() queries the library scoped to the current run via ContextVar, which must have been populated by loading a LibraryCrate. In distributed execution, each worker-side job loads the crate from the PipeJob into a per-run Library instance before resolving child pipes. (Temporal-specific detail: the backend disables the Temporal sandbox via --no-sandbox because library loading is a side effect incompatible with replay semantics.) See Runtime Bridge & Transport for how the crate and working memory cross the boundary.

docs.title: Distributed Execution
docs.text: In distributed execution, the PipeJob is serialized and sent to a host-runtime worker for execution. The concrete dispatch shape below is illustrated with Pipelex's Temporal backend; the boundary mechanics (LibraryCrate, deferred hydration, per-call isolation) are backend-neutral and documented in Runtime Bridge & Transport.

docs.title: Flow
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant S as Submitter (API/CLI)
    participant T as Temporal Server
    participant W as Worker

    Note over S: pipeline_run_setup()
    S->>S: Load library, generate dynamic classes
    S->>S: Resolve pipe, build LibraryCrate
    S->>S: Create PipeJob (crate attached)

    Note over S: TemporalPipeRouter.run() (submitter side)
    S->>S: transport prep (closed)<br/>(WM → working_memory_raw)
    S->>T: Submit run workflow(PipeJob)
    T->>W: Dispatch workflow

    Note over W: run workflow
    W->>W: Create per-workflow ClassRegistry
    W->>W: Load LibraryCrate (register classes)
    W->>W: Hydrate working_memory_raw → WM
    W->>W: pipe.run_pipe()

    alt Concrete pipe
        W->>W: Execute via Activity
    else Dispatch the backend chooses to isolate
        W->>T: Child workflow (crate propagates)
        T->>W: Child result
    end

    W->>W: Dehydrate PipeOutput<br/>(WM → working_memory_raw)
    W->>T: Return dehydrated PipeOutput
    T->>S: Workflow result
    S->>S: Hydrate PipeOutput<br/>(working_memory_raw → WM)

docs.title: Key components (the backend's role)
docs.text:
A host-runtime orchestrator supplies the pieces that turn this generic shape into real workflows. The contract each implements is open core; the concrete classes are backend-specific. In Pipelex's Temporal backend:

  • a router implementing PipeRouterProtocol (TemporalPipeRouter) that dispatches via Temporal instead of running in-process;
  • a worker-side job (a Temporal workflow) that receives a deserialized PipeJob, loads the crate, hydrates working memory, and calls pipe.run_pipe() — exactly like the direct router;
  • a data converter that uses Kajson to (de)serialize Pydantic models with subclass types preserved — critical because PipeJob.pipe is a PipeAbstract subclass and WorkingMemory holds Stuff objects with concept-specific content classes;
  • a worker entry point that calls Pipelex.make(boot_orchestrator="temporal") and starts the worker with its registered workflows and activities (shipped as the plugin's own worker console command).

The concrete modules live in our closed Temporal plugin and are documented with it. The open contracts they satisfy — PipeRouterProtocol, the boundary DTOs, serialization — are listed in the Orchestrator SPI.

docs.title: Content generation activities
docs.text:
Concrete pipe operators (PipeLLM, PipeCompose, PipeExtract, PipeImgGen) dispatch their actual leaf work as host-runtime activities, invoked from inside the worker-side job via the runtime's in-workflow content generator — no intermediate child workflow per content-generation call. A backend can route those activities to different task queues per activity (and, where applicable, per handle); in the Temporal backend that routing is configured under the plugin's own [worker_config.activity_queues] config (in the plugin's temporal.toml, not core config), falling back to the job's own task queue when unset. The concrete activity set and queue-routing reference live in our Temporal plugin's own docs; see also Content Generation Across Boundaries for the backend-neutral serialization mechanism.

Future Improvement: Per-Pipe Routing

Router selection is currently global and binary: either all pipes go through the distributed backend, or none do. A simple PipeCompose (microseconds of Jinja2 rendering) gets the same dispatch overhead as a PipeLLM (minutes of API call time). Per-pipe or per-type routing decisions could improve efficiency.

docs.title: Crossing the boundary: crate, hydration, isolation
docs.text:
Distributed execution introduces three mechanisms that don't exist in direct mode, because the worker is a separate process that shares none of the submitter's library, class registry, or working-memory state. They are backend-neutral; for the full walkthrough see Runtime Bridge & Transport. In short:

  • LibraryCrate propagation — the submitter attaches a serializable snapshot of all pipes and concepts to the PipeJob; every worker-side job loads it (idempotently, by fingerprint) so get_required_pipe() resolves at every level.
  • Deferred hydration — WorkingMemory crosses as a raw JSON dict (working_memory_raw) on both PipeJob inputs and PipeOutput return values, avoiding deserialization failures when a receiving process hasn't registered the bundle's dynamic concept classes. The transport-prep helpers are not part of open core; the raw field and the hydration helper are.
  • Per-call isolation — every Library the manager opens carries its own ClassRegistry (pre-seeded from the global registry), and a job's library is scoped via ContextVar, so concurrent loads with conflicting concept names (e.g., two bundles that both define Result with different fields) don't cross-contaminate — jobs, and any other load sharing the process, a validate included.

Known backend limitation: StuffArtefact in dry-run

On a host runtime whose data converter serializes working memory for internal templating activities (Temporal's act_jinja2_gen_text, dispatched by PipeCondition and PipeCompose), dry-run mode can fail: working memory then holds StuffArtefact debug objects that are not JSON-serializable. PipeSequence and PipeParallel are unaffected — they dispatch child pipes without internal templating activities. This is a backend-specific concern; see our Temporal plugin's own docs for details and fix direction.
